title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
The accurate way to measure a man’s body fat is to weigh him under water: fat floats, muscle and bone sink. It needs a tank and takes time. A tape measure costs nothing. So we would like a formula that predicts the percentage of body fat from measurements that anyone can take: neck, chest, abdomen, hip, thigh and so on.
There are 13 candidates. Do we need all of them? Stepwise regression lets the computer choose: it adds the predictor that helps most, or removes the one that helps least, and repeats until nothing improves.
It is one of the most used methods of data analysis, and one of the most criticised (Harrell, 2015; Smith, 2018). This page does both things. It shows how the method works, step by step, and then it tests it: on the same data, on shuffled data, on resampled data, and against simpler alternatives.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(leaps)     # regsubsets(): the best model of every size
library(glmnet)    # lasso and ridge, for comparison

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 0), "%")

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
1. The data
The data come from a study of 252 men by K. W. Penrose, A. G. Nelson and A. G. Fisher, published in 1985. Johnson (1996) made them available for teaching. The file has no header, so we give the names:


Code
raw <- read.table("https://jse.amstat.org/datasets/fat.dat.txt")
names(raw) <- c(
  "case", "brozek", "siri", "density", "age", "weight", "height", "adiposity", "fat_free_weight",
  "neck", "chest", "abdomen", "hip", "thigh", "knee", "ankle", "biceps", "forearm", "wrist"
)
dim(raw)


[1] 252  19


The outcome is siri, the percentage of body fat worked out from the density under water with Siri’s equation. adiposity is the body mass index and fat_free_weight is computed from the body fat itself, so neither belongs among the predictors. The circumferences are in centimetres; weight is in pounds and height in inches, which we convert.
Three rows need a decision before anything else:


Code
raw[c(39, 42, 182), c("case", "siri", "density", "age", "weight", "height", "abdomen")]


    case siri density age weight height abdomen
39    39 35.2  1.0202  46 363.15  72.25   148.1
42    42 32.9  1.0250  44 205.00  29.50   104.3
182  182  0.0  1.1089  40 118.50  68.00    69.4



Case 42 is 29.5 inches tall (75 cm) and weighs 205 pounds. That is almost certainly a typing error for 69.5, which we correct.
Case 182 has 0% fat, which no living person has: the equation gave a negative value that was set to zero. We drop him.
Case 39 weighs 363.1 pounds (164.7 kg), 100.4 pounds more than the next man. It is probably a correct value, but a formula for ordinary men should not be steered by him. We drop him too, and say so.



Code
predictors <- c("age", "weight", "height", "neck", "chest", "abdomen", "hip", "thigh",
                "knee", "ankle", "biceps", "forearm", "wrist")
men <- raw
men$height[42] <- 69.5
men$weight <- men$weight * 0.45359237     # kg
men$height <- men$height * 2.54           # cm
men <- men[-c(39, 182), c("siri", predictors)]
names(men)[1] <- "fat"
rownames(men) <- NULL
nrow(men)


[1] 250


Code
summary(men$fat)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.70   12.50   19.20   19.16   25.27   47.50 


That leaves 250 men between 22 and 81 years old, with 0.7 to 47.5 percent body fat.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
cors <- cor(men)
ord  <- order(cors["fat", ])
long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cors[ord, ord]))
names(long) <- c("a", "b", "r")

ggplot(long, aes(a, b, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sub("^-0.0$", "0.0", formatC(r, format = "f", digits = 1)))
    ),
    size = 2.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#eb6834",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2a78d6",
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "r"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Correlations, ordered by the correlation with body fat", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())









The abdomen has by far the strongest correlation with body fat, r = .82. But the measurements are also strongly correlated with each other: a heavy man is large everywhere. Weight and hip correlate at .93, weight and chest at .89. The predictors carry the same information many times over, and this is exactly the situation in which stepwise methods struggle.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
section: 3. The method step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the trade-off
Every predictor that is added lowers the sum of squared residuals, the RSS, even a column of random numbers. So a criterion must put a price on each predictor. The usual one is Akaike’s information criterion. For a linear regression with \(k\) estimated coefficients,
\[\text{AIC} = n \log\!\left(\frac{\text{RSS}}{n}\right) + 2k\]
The smaller the better: the first part rewards fit, and each coefficient costs 2. The BIC charges \(\log(n)\) per coefficient instead of 2. With \(n\) = 250 that is 5.52, so BIC keeps fewer predictors.


Step 2: one step forward
Start with no predictor. Try each of the 13 alone, and take the one with the smallest AIC:


Code
n <- nrow(men)
aic_of <- function(vars) {                     # AIC of the model with these predictors
  fit <- lm(reformulate(if (length(vars)) vars else "1", "fat"), data = men)
  n * log(sum(resid(fit)^2) / n) + 2 * length(coef(fit))
}
first <- sapply(predictors, function(v) aic_of(v))
c(none = aic_of(character(0)), head(sort(first), 4))


     none   abdomen     chest       hip    weight 
1056.2087  778.0058  894.4207  931.7096  941.1935 


The abdomen wins by a wide margin. Keep it, try each of the other 12 next to it, and continue:


Code
chosen <- character(0)
path <- data.frame(step = 0, added = "(none)", AIC = aic_of(chosen))
repeat {
  left  <- setdiff(predictors, chosen)
  tries <- sapply(left, function(v) aic_of(c(chosen, v)))
  if (!length(left) || min(tries) >= tail(path$AIC, 1)) break    # nothing improves: stop
  chosen <- c(chosen, names(which.min(tries)))
  path   <- rbind(path, data.frame(step = nrow(path), added = tail(chosen, 1), AIC = min(tries)))
}
path


  step   added       AIC
1    0  (none) 1056.2087
2    1 abdomen  778.0058
3    2  weight  742.6230
4    3   wrist  733.4977
5    4  biceps  731.6885
6    5     age  731.0730
7    6   thigh  730.7690


Forward selection stops after 6 predictors.


Step 3: backward, and both ways
Backward elimination starts from the model with all 13 and removes, one at a time, the predictor whose removal lowers the AIC most. Both directions is forward selection that checks, after each addition, whether an earlier predictor can now go.


Step 4: what AIC means as a p value
Removing one predictor is an improvement if the AIC falls, that is if the likelihood-ratio statistic of that predictor is below 2. In a large sample this statistic follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom, so
\[\text{AIC keeps a predictor when } p < P(\chi^2_1 > 2) = .157\]
and BIC, with \(n = 250\), when \(p < P(\chi^2_1 > \log n) = .019\). The old versions of stepwise regression used p values directly, with “\(F\) to enter” and “\(F\) to remove”. All of them are the same idea with a different price.


Step 5: how many models are we choosing from?
With 13 candidates there are \(2^{13}\) = 8,192 possible models. Stepwise looks at a small part of them, and reports the winner as if it had been the only one.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output


Code
full  <- lm(fat ~ ., data = men)                     # all 13
empty <- lm(fat ~ 1, data = men)                     # none
everything <- formula(full)

forward  <- step(empty, scope = everything, direction = "forward",  trace = 0)
backward <- step(full,                      direction = "backward", trace = 0)
both     <- step(empty, scope = everything, direction = "both",     trace = 0)
# k: the price per coefficient
bic <- step(full, direction = "backward", trace = 0, k = log(nrow(men)))

vars_of <- function(fit) names(coef(fit))[-1]
models <- list(
  "Forward, AIC" = forward,
  "Backward, AIC" = backward,
  "Both ways, AIC" = both,
  "Backward, BIC" = bic
)
chosen_table <- sapply(models, function(m) ifelse(predictors %in% vars_of(m), "x", ""))
rownames(chosen_table) <- predictors
print(chosen_table, quote = FALSE)


        Forward, AIC Backward, AIC Both ways, AIC Backward, BIC
age     x            x             x              x            
weight  x                          x                           
height               x                            x            
neck                 x                                         
chest                x                                         
abdomen x            x             x              x            
hip                                                            
thigh   x                          x                           
knee                                                           
ankle                                                          
biceps  x                          x                           
forearm              x                                         
wrist   x            x             x              x            


Code
in_all <- predictors[rowSums(chosen_table == "x") == length(models)]


The directions do not agree. Forward selection keeps 6 predictors and backward elimination 7, and they share only 3 (abdomen, wrist, age). Forward takes weight, backward throws it out and takes height, neck and chest instead. The data are the same, the criterion is the same. Only the route differs.
The output of the backward model looks like that of any regression:


Code
summary(backward)



Call:
lm(formula = fat ~ age + height + neck + chest + abdomen + forearm + 
    wrist, data = men)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-10.6391  -3.1341  -0.2619   3.1770   9.3904 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  6.39303    8.20342   0.779  0.43656    
age          0.06061    0.02477   2.447  0.01512 *  
height      -0.12716    0.04744  -2.680  0.00786 ** 
neck        -0.32038    0.21884  -1.464  0.14449    
chest       -0.14206    0.08779  -1.618  0.10693    
abdomen      0.87515    0.06476  13.513  < 2e-16 ***
forearm      0.35281    0.19182   1.839  0.06711 .  
wrist       -1.74340    0.48375  -3.604  0.00038 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.231 on 242 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7445,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7371 
F-statistic: 100.7 on 7 and 242 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16




Code
p_back <- summary(backward)$coefficients[-1, 4]
aics   <- c(full = extractAIC(full)[2], sapply(models, function(m) extractAIC(m)[2]))
round(aics, 1)


          full   Forward, AIC  Backward, AIC Both ways, AIC  Backward, BIC 
         736.5          730.8          729.1          730.8          730.5 


The tempting way to read it: \(R^2\) = .744, almost that of the full model (.749), with 4 predictors that have p < .05. Two details already look odd. First, the signs: a larger wrist and neck go with less fat. That part can be defended: given the abdomen, a big frame means less fat. Second, some predictors are in the model without being significant, because AIC’s threshold is p < .157.
The p values, the confidence intervals and the \(R^2\) of this output were all computed as if we had chosen these 7 predictors before seeing the data. We did not. Section 5 measures what that costs.

All subsets
regsubsets() does not take steps. It finds the best model of every size among all 8,192:


Code
subsets <- summary(regsubsets(fat ~ ., data = men, nvmax = 13))
size <- 1:13
best <- data.frame(size = size,
                   adj_R2 = subsets$adjr2,
                   AIC    = n * log(subsets$rss / n) + 2 * (size + 1),
                   BIC    = n * log(subsets$rss / n) + log(n) * (size + 1))
best$predictors <- apply(subsets$which[, -1], 1, function(w) paste(predictors[w], collapse = " "))
best[c(1:4, which.min(best$AIC)), c("size", "adj_R2", "AIC", "predictors")]


  size    adj_R2      AIC                                 predictors
1    1 0.6726703 778.0058                                    abdomen
2    2 0.7169914 742.6230                             weight abdomen
3    3 0.7282092 733.4977                       weight abdomen wrist
4    4 0.7324939 730.5068                   age height abdomen wrist
7    7 0.7374730 728.7296 age height neck chest abdomen biceps wrist




Code
curve <- rbind(data.frame(size = size, value = best$AIC - min(best$AIC), criterion = "AIC"),
               data.frame(size = size, value = best$BIC - min(best$BIC), criterion = "BIC"))

ggplot(curve, aes(size, value, colour = criterion)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(AIC = "#2a78d6", BIC = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = size) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 40)) +
  labs(title = "The best model of each size, compared with the best of all",
       subtitle = "0 = the winner; differences of 1 or 2 mean next to nothing",
       x = "number of predictors", y = "criterion minus its minimum") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
near_best <- sum(best$AIC - min(best$AIC) < 2)


The bottom of the AIC curve is flat: the best models of 6 different sizes are within 2 points of the winner. The data cannot tell them apart. Searching all subsets finds the true minimum, but the minimum of a flat curve is decided by noise.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
5. Testing the method

Test 1: an outcome with no relation to anything
We shuffle the body-fat column. Now each man has the body fat of another man, and all 13 predictors are useless by construction. A good method should come back empty-handed:


Code
set.seed(2026)
shuffled <- t(replicate(500, {
  fake     <- men
  fake$fat <- sample(fake$fat)
  m  <- step(lm(fat ~ ., data = fake), trace = 0)
  s  <- summary(m)
  p  <- s$coefficients[-1, 4]
  fs <- s$fstatistic
  c(kept        = length(p),
    significant = sum(p < .05),
    R2          = s$r.squared,
    p_model     = if (length(p)) pf(fs[[1]], fs[[2]], fs[[3]], lower.tail = FALSE) else 1)
}))
colMeans(shuffled[, 1:3])


       kept significant          R2 
 2.88200000  1.46600000  0.03390794 


Code
c(
  any_significant = mean(shuffled[, "significant"] > 0),
  model_significant = mean(shuffled[, "p_model"] < .05)
)


  any_significant model_significant 
            0.732             0.530 


In 500 shuffled data sets, backward elimination kept 2.9 predictors on average. In 73% of them at least one had p < .05, and in 53% the F test of the whole model was significant, where the promise is 5%. This is known as Freedman’s paradox (Freedman, 1983): screen many noise variables, refit with the survivors, and the final model looks convincing.


Test 2: would the same predictors be chosen again?
We cannot measure 250 new men, but we can draw 250 men from our own with replacement, many times, and repeat the whole selection on each of these bootstrap samples:


Code
set.seed(2027)
B <- 1000
kept <- t(replicate(B, {
  again <- men[sample(nrow(men), replace = TRUE), ]
  m <- step(lm(fat ~ ., data = again), trace = 0)
  predictors %in% names(coef(m))
}))
colnames(kept) <- predictors
frequency <- sort(colMeans(kept), decreasing = TRUE)
cbind(frequency)


        frequency
abdomen     1.000
wrist       0.985
age         0.838
height      0.660
neck        0.595
chest       0.537
forearm     0.481
biceps      0.466
thigh       0.460
hip         0.411
ankle       0.352
weight      0.313
knee        0.207


Code
as_text   <- apply(kept, 1, function(k) paste(predictors[k], collapse = " "))
n_models  <- length(unique(as_text))
our_model <- paste(predictors[predictors %in% vars_of(backward)], collapse = " ")
c(different_models = n_models, most_common = max(table(as_text)), ours = sum(as_text == our_model))


different_models      most_common             ours 
             457               18               10 




Code
freq_data <- data.frame(predictor = factor(names(frequency), levels = rev(names(frequency))),
                        share = frequency, chosen = names(frequency) %in% vars_of(backward))

ggplot(freq_data, aes(share, predictor, fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = "#2a78d6", `FALSE` = "grey70"),
    labels = c(`TRUE` = "in our backward model", `FALSE` = "not in it"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%"), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "How often each predictor is chosen in 1,000 bootstrap samples",
    x = "share of the samples",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Only 2 predictors, abdomen and wrist, are chosen nearly always. Most of the others are a coin toss. The 1,000 samples produced 457 different models; the most common one came up 18 times, and the model that backward elimination chose in our data only 10 times. A statement such as “the predictors of body fat are age, height, neck, chest, abdomen, forearm and wrist” is a statement about this sample.


Test 3: are the coefficients right?
A predictor with a weak effect gets in when, by luck, its effect looks strong in the sample. So among the selected, weak effects are overestimated (the “winner’s curse”). To see this we need to know the truth, so we make one: new body-fat values that follow the full model exactly, with its coefficients and its residual spread.


Code
set.seed(2028)
truth <- coef(full)
sims  <- 1000
estimates <- matrix(NA, sims, length(predictors), dimnames = list(NULL, predictors))
for (i in seq_len(sims)) {
  new     <- men
  new$fat <- fitted(full) + rnorm(nrow(men), 0, sigma(full))
  b <- coef(step(lm(fat ~ ., data = new), trace = 0))
  estimates[i, intersect(names(b), predictors)] <- b[intersect(names(b), predictors)]
}
curse <- data.frame(predictor = predictors, true = truth[predictors],
                    selected = colMeans(!is.na(estimates)),
                    mean_when_selected = colMeans(estimates, na.rm = TRUE))
curse$ratio <- curse$mean_when_selected / curse$true
curse <- curse[order(-curse$selected), ]
print(data.frame(predictor = curse$predictor, round(curse[, -1], 2)), row.names = FALSE)


 predictor  true selected mean_when_selected ratio
   abdomen  0.90     1.00               0.89  0.99
     wrist -1.85     0.99              -1.88  1.02
       age  0.07     0.82               0.08  1.10
    height -0.11     0.66              -0.15  1.37
      neck -0.39     0.61              -0.52  1.32
     chest -0.14     0.53              -0.21  1.53
   forearm  0.26     0.48               0.43  1.65
    biceps  0.19     0.48               0.35  1.86
     thigh  0.16     0.44               0.28  1.76
       hip -0.15     0.40              -0.26  1.73
     ankle  0.17     0.34               0.39  2.21
    weight -0.02     0.31              -0.13  6.17
      knee -0.04     0.21              -0.11  2.70




Code
curse_of <- function(v, col) curse[curse$predictor == v, col]


The abdomen and the wrist are nearly always selected, and their average estimate is close to the truth. The forearm has a true coefficient of 0.26; it is selected in 48% of the samples, and then its average estimate is 0.43, 1.7 times too large. (For the predictors that are strongly correlated with others, such as weight and hip, the coefficient also changes meaning when the others are left out, so the ratio mixes two things.)


Test 4: is the fit as good as it looks?
The \(R^2\) of a chosen model is too good, because the choice and the fit used the same men. Cross-validation measures honestly: hide a tenth of the men, do everything on the rest, predict the hidden ones. The word everything is important. If the predictors are chosen on all the men first and only the fit is cross-validated, the hidden men have already helped to choose, and the result is still too good.


Code
set.seed(2029)
cv_once <- function() {
  fold <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(men)))
  pred <- matrix(
    NA,
    nrow(men),
    8,
    dimnames = list(
      NULL,
      c("full", "backward", "chosen_before", "bic", "abdomen", "abdomen_weight", "lasso", "ridge")
    )
  )
  for (k in 1:10) {
    train <- men[fold != k, ]
    test <- men[fold == k, ]
    x <- as.matrix(train[, predictors])
    xt <- as.matrix(test[, predictors])
    m <- lm(fat ~ ., data = train)
    out <- list(
      m,
      step(m, trace = 0), # selection inside the fold: honest
      lm(formula(backward), data = train), # predictors chosen on all men: cheating
      step(m, trace = 0, k = log(nrow(train))),
      lm(fat ~ abdomen, data = train),
      lm(fat ~ abdomen + weight, data = train)
    )
    pred[fold == k, 1:6] <- sapply(out, predict, newdata = test)
    pred[fold == k, 7] <- predict(cv.glmnet(x, train$fat, alpha = 1), xt, s = "lambda.min")
    pred[fold == k, 8] <- predict(cv.glmnet(x, train$fat, alpha = 0), xt, s = "lambda.min")
  }
  sqrt(colMeans((pred - men$fat)^2))
}

On the men it was built from, the backward model misses by 4.16 points. On new men, with an honest cross-validation, by 4.43.
If the selection is left out of the cross-validation, the error looks like 4.30, better than it really is. This mistake is easy to make, and hard to see in a published paper.
Choosing did not help here. The full model, with all 13, has 4.37, the lasso 4.38 and ridge 4.49. Two predictors that a physician could have named beforehand, abdomen and weight, have 4.42, and the abdomen alone 4.74.
Apart from the model with the abdomen alone, the differences are small next to the error itself: a tape measure predicts body fat to within about \(\pm\) 8.6 points, whatever the model.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
6. What to do instead



Your aim
Do this




Explain: test a theory, estimate an effect
Choose the predictors from theory before you look. Fit that model, report it, whatever the p values. Dropping a confounder because p > .05 does not make it harmless


Predict, with enough data
Keep the full model, or shrink it: ridge, lasso or elastic net (see regularized regression)


Predict, many correlated predictors
Principal components or partial least squares regression


A short formula for practical use
Choose from the cost of the measurements first. If you must select by data, use backward elimination with AIC, report the bootstrap frequencies, shrink the coefficients, and validate with the selection inside the cross-validation


Explore
Use whatever you like, and call it exploration. The test is the next data set



Two predictors, abdomen and weight, do almost as well as anything. This is the usual result with correlated predictors: many models are equally good, and which of them you use is a matter of convenience. What you cannot do is to say that the predictors that were left out do not matter.
Is the choice of predictors in blocks, planned before, stepwise regression? No. That is hierarchical regression: the order comes from the theory, and the p values mean what they say.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

The p values of a selected model are not p values. They ignore the search. There are corrections for some procedures (post-selection inference; Taylor & Tibshirani, 2015), but the ordinary output of summary() is not one of them.
“Not selected” does not mean “no effect”. Weight was not selected by backward elimination, although it correlates at .61 with body fat: its information was already in the other measurements.
The starting point matters. Backward elimination from the full model is usually preferred to forward selection, because it judges every predictor next to all the others (Heinze et al., 2018). It needs a full model that can be fitted: at the very least more rows than predictors, better 10 to 20 rows per candidate. Here there are 19.2.
Count the candidates, not the survivors. A model with 3 predictors chosen among 50 has the overfitting of a much larger model.
Whole factors. A factor with four levels is three columns that belong together: step() keeps or drops them together. Interactions should not stay without their main effects; step() respects that too.
Missing values. Adding a predictor with missing values changes the rows that are used, and the AICs are then not comparable. Decide on the rows first (or impute, see missing data).
The odd rows matter. We dropped two men and corrected one. With unstable selection a single unusual row can change the chosen set, so check influence before you select.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
If you use selection, the report (APA 7th edition) must let the reader judge it: all the candidates, the algorithm and its criterion, the stability, and an honest estimate of the error. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
s_back <- summary(backward)$coefficients
ci_back <- confint(backward)
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Intercept", vars_of(backward)),
  b  = f2(s_back[, 1]),
  SE = f2(s_back[, 2]),
  CI = paste0("[", f2(ci_back[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci_back[, 2]), "]"),
  freq = c("—", pct(frequency[vars_of(backward)])),
  full = f2(coef(full)[c("(Intercept)", vars_of(backward))]))


Method (data analysis):

We developed a formula for percentage of body fat, measured by underwater weighing, in 250 men (Johnson, 1996), after correcting one height that was a typing error and excluding one man with an impossible value of 0% and one man of 164.7 kg. The candidates were age, weight, height and 10 circumferences (13 in all; 19.2 men per candidate). We used backward elimination with the AIC, starting from the model with all the candidates. Stability was assessed with 1,000 bootstrap samples, and prediction error with 10-fold cross-validation, repeated 20 times, in which the selection was repeated in every fold. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

Backward elimination kept 7 of the 13 candidates (Table 1), R² = .74 (full model: R² = .75). Only abdomen and wrist were selected in more than 90% of the bootstrap samples; the 1,000 samples gave 457 different models, and the model in Table 1 was chosen in 10 of them. The cross-validated prediction error was 4.43 percentage points (4.16 in the data used for the development), compared with 4.37 for the full model and 4.42 for a model with abdomen and weight only. Because of the selection, the confidence intervals in Table 1 are too narrow, and the table should not be read as a list of the determinants of body fat.

Points to remember:

List all the candidates, not only those that survived.

Do not call the selected predictors “the significant predictors”, nor the others “not significant”.

title: Stepwise Regression: Which Body Measurements Predict Body Fat?
text:
9. Summary



What it is
The computer adds or removes predictors one at a time, by AIC, BIC or p value


How (R)
step(lm(y ~ ., d)) backward with AIC; k = log(n) for BIC; scope and direction for forward; leaps::regsubsets() for all subsets


What it costs
p values too small, intervals too narrow, weak effects too large, \(R^2\) too high


What it found in noise
A significant model in 53% of the shuffled data sets


How stable it was
457 different models in 1,000 bootstrap samples


Check it with
Bootstrap inclusion frequencies, and cross-validation that repeats the selection


Better
Predictors chosen beforehand, the full model, or shrinkage (ridge, lasso)


Not the same as
Hierarchical regression, where the analyst decides the order

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
text:
Look at a map of unemployment in Europe, and the colours come in patches. Regions with many unemployed lie next to each other, and so do those with few. A region of southern Spain looks like the region beside it, whatever its schools and its income.
This matters for two reasons. Statistically, regions are not independent observations: neighbours repeat each other’s information, and the standard errors of ordinary regression are too small. Substantively, the patches may be a result in themselves. Perhaps unemployment spreads: people commute across the border, firms sell to the region next door, and a closed factory hurts both sides.
Spatial regression puts the neighbours into the model. This page fits the two classic models, shows how to read them (their coefficients are not the effects), and asks at the end what the patches really are.


Code
library(jsonlite)     # Eurostat answers in JSON
library(sf)           # maps
library(spdep)        # neighbours, Moran's I, Lagrange multiplier tests
library(spatialreg)   # spatial regression models
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
text:
1. The data
Eurostat publishes statistics for the NUTS-2 regions of Europe, and the maps that belong to them. Both are free and need no login. We use 2019, the last year before the pandemic.


Code
eurostat <- function(code, query) {
  j <- fromJSON(paste0(
    "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/",
    code,
    "?format=JSON&lang=EN&geoLevel=nuts2&time=2019&",
    query
  ))
  place <- unlist(j$dimension$geo$category$index)
  value <- unlist(j$value)
  data.frame(
    NUTS_ID = names(place),
    value = unname(value[match(as.character(place), names(value))])
  )
}
unemp <- eurostat("lfst_r_lfu3rt", "sex=T&age=Y15-74") # unemployment rate (%)
# adults with tertiary education (%)
degree <- eurostat("edat_lfse_04", "sex=T&age=Y25-64&isced11=ED5-8")
# GDP per head, purchasing power standards
gdp <- eurostat("nama_10r_2gdp", "unit=PPS_EU27_2020_HAB")
map <- st_read(
  "https://gisco-services.ec.europa.eu/distribution/v2/nuts/geojson/NUTS_RG_20M_2016_4326_LEVL_2.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
)

map$unemp  <- unemp$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, unemp$NUTS_ID)]
map$degree <- degree$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, degree$NUTS_ID)]
map$gdp    <- gdp$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, gdp$NUTS_ID)]
map <- st_transform(
  subset(map, !is.na(unemp) & !is.na(degree) & !is.na(gdp) & CNTR_CODE != "TR"),
  3035
) # a projection in metres
xy  <- st_coordinates(suppressWarnings(st_centroid(map)))
# without the islands far away (Canaries, Azores, overseas)
europe <- map[xy[, 1] > 2.5e6 & xy[, 2] > 1.3e6, ]
xy  <- st_coordinates(suppressWarnings(st_centroid(europe)))
d   <- st_drop_geometry(europe)
d$log_u <- log(d$unemp); d$log_gdp <- log(d$gdp / 30000); d$deg10 <- (d$degree - 33) / 10
c(regions = nrow(d), countries = length(unique(d$CNTR_CODE)))


  regions countries 
      234        31 


Code
round(
  sapply(d[, c("unemp", "degree", "gdp")], function(v) {
    c(min = min(v), median = median(v), max = max(v))
  }),
  1
)


       unemp degree   gdp
min      1.3   11.7  8500
median   5.1   30.1 28100
max     27.0   56.1 78700


There are 234 regions of 31 countries. The unemployment rate goes from 1.3% to 27.0%. Because it is skewed, we use its logarithm. deg10 is the share of adults with a degree, in steps of 10 points from 33%, and log_gdp the log of the income per head, relative to 30,000.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
text:
2. Look at the map


Code
ggplot(europe) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = unemp), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "B",
    direction = -1,
    trans = "log",
    breaks = c(2, 4, 8, 16),
    name = "%"
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(2.5e6, 6e6), ylim = c(1.4e6, 5.3e6)) +
  labs(title = "Unemployment in the regions of Europe, 2019") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())










Who is whose neighbour?
A spatial model needs a definition of neighbours, the weights matrix \(W\). Regions that share a border is one choice, but islands have none. We take the five nearest regions (by the distance of their centres), and give each the weight 1/5. The rows of \(W\) sum to 1, so \(Wy\) is the mean of the neighbours of each region, the spatial lag of \(y\).


Code
W <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 5)), style = "W")
d$lag_u <- lag.listw(W, d$log_u)                        # the mean of the five neighbours
moran <- moran.test(d$log_u, W)
moran$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]


[1] 0.7208608




Code
ggplot(d, aes(log_u, lag_u)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834") +
  labs(
    title = "Each region and the mean of its five neighbours",
    x = "log unemployment of the region",
    y = "mean of its neighbours"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Moran’s I is a correlation between a region and its neighbours: the slope of the line in this chart. It is 0.72, where 0 would be no pattern. Unemployment is strongly clustered.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 3. What it does to least squares
text:
3. What it does to least squares


Code
ols <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d)
round(coef(summary(ols)), 3)


            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    1.648      0.040  40.714        0
deg10          0.193      0.052   3.744        0
log_gdp       -0.920      0.125  -7.378        0


Code
mr <- lm.morantest(ols, W)
c(Moran_I_of_the_residuals = mr$estimate[[1]], p = mr$p.value[[1]])


Moran_I_of_the_residuals                        p 
            6.727311e-01             2.783120e-72 


OLS finds that richer regions have less unemployment (-0.92: 10% more income, 8.4% less unemployment) and, oddly, that regions with more graduates have more of it, once income is held constant. Both are “highly significant”. But the residuals have a Moran’s I of 0.67: the model has explained almost nothing of the map. The 234 regions are not 234 independent pieces of information, and neither result can be trusted.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 4. The two classic models, with formulas
text:
4. The two classic models, with formulas

The spatial lag model (SAR)
\[y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon\]
The unemployment of the neighbours is a cause of the region’s own. It is a story of contagion, and a circle: my neighbour’s unemployment depends on mine, too. Solved for \(y\):
\[y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + \varepsilon)\]
A change in one region travels to its neighbours, to their neighbours, and back.


The spatial error model (SEM)
\[y = X\beta + u, \qquad u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon\]
Here the neighbours do not act on each other. They share unmeasured things, such as history, industry, and laws, which are in the error. OLS is unbiased, and only its standard errors are wrong. It is the spatial cousin of GLS with autocorrelated errors.


Why not just put \(Wy\) into lm()?
Because of the circle. \(Wy\) is correlated with the error. Maximum likelihood takes it into account with one extra term, the log of the determinant of \(I - \rho W\):
\[\log L = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \log|I - \rho W| - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert y - \rho Wy - X\beta \rVert^2\]
For a given \(\rho\), \(\beta\) is an ordinary regression of \(y - \rho Wy\) on \(X\). So we need to search over \(\rho\) only:


Code
y <- d$log_u; X <- model.matrix(ols); n <- nrow(X)
Wm <- listw2mat(W); Wy <- drop(Wm %*% y); ev <- eigen(Wm, only.values = TRUE)$values
profile_ll <- function(rho) {
  e <- lm.fit(X, y - rho * Wy)$residuals
  -n / 2 * (log(2 * pi * mean(e^2)) + 1) + sum(Re(log(as.complex(1 - rho * ev))))
}
rho_hat <- optimize(profile_ll, c(-0.9, 0.99), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
sar <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W)
naive <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + lag_u, data = d)
rbind(
  by_hand = c(rho = rho_hat, lm.fit(X, y - rho_hat * Wy)$coefficients),
  lagsarlm = c(sar$rho, sar$coefficients),
  `wrong: lm with the lag` = coef(naive)[c(4, 1:3)]
)


                             rho (Intercept)      deg10    log_gdp
by_hand                0.7641734   0.3782375 0.05019551 -0.3730810
lagsarlm               0.7641573   0.3782643 0.05019852 -0.3730925
wrong: lm with the lag 0.8874702   0.1733785 0.02712854 -0.2847873

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 5. Fitting the models and reading the output
text:
5. Fitting the models and reading the output


Code
sem  <- errorsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W)
# with the neighbours' X as well
sdm <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W, Durbin = TRUE)
tab <- rbind(
  OLS = c(coef(summary(ols))[2, 1:2], coef(summary(ols))[3, 1:2], NA, AIC(ols)),
  `spatial lag` = c(summary(sar)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sar)$Coef[3, 1:2], sar$rho, AIC(sar)),
  `spatial error` = c(summary(sem)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sem)$Coef[3, 1:2], sem$lambda, AIC(sem)),
  `spatial Durbin` = c(summary(sdm)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sdm)$Coef[3, 1:2], sdm$rho, AIC(sdm))
)
colnames(tab) <- c("deg10", "SE", "log_gdp", "SE", "rho or lambda", "AIC")
round(tab, 3)


               deg10    SE log_gdp    SE rho or lambda     AIC
OLS            0.193 0.052  -0.920 0.125            NA 431.684
spatial lag    0.050 0.033  -0.373 0.086         0.764 241.133
spatial error  0.083 0.049  -0.534 0.128         0.793 242.401
spatial Durbin 0.060 0.051  -0.470 0.132         0.779 242.637


Code
resid_I <- c(
  OLS = mr$estimate[[1]],
  lag = moran.test(residuals(sar), W)$estimate[[1]],
  error = moran.test(residuals(sem), W)$estimate[[1]]
)
round(resid_I, 3)


   OLS    lag  error 
 0.673 -0.018 -0.050 



From OLS to the lag model the AIC falls by 190.6 points, with one more parameter. The residuals have no spatial pattern left (Moran’s I -0.02 and -0.05).
\(\rho\) = 0.76 and \(\lambda\) = 0.79: very strong dependence.
The strange result about the graduates is gone (for now: see section 7). The coefficient is 0.05 instead of 0.19, with a z of 1.5.
That of income is smaller: -0.37 (lag) and -0.53 (error). But the coefficients of the lag model are not effects, as section 6 shows.


Lag or error? The Lagrange multiplier tests


Code
rs <- lm.RStests(ols, W, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"))
rs_tab <- t(sapply(rs, function(t) c(statistic = unname(t$statistic), p = unname(t$p.value))))
round(rs_tab, 4)


         statistic      p
RSerr     296.9890 0.0000
RSlag     284.3996 0.0000
adjRSerr   18.1518 0.0000
adjRSlag    5.5623 0.0184


Both simple tests are huge, because each also reacts to the other kind of dependence. The adjusted (robust) versions correct for this (Anselin et al., 1996). Here both are significant, the error version more clearly (18.2 against 5.6). The AICs of the two models are 241.1 and 242.4. The data do not decide between the two stories, and this is the usual outcome.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 6. Effects in the lag model: direct and indirect
text:
6. Effects in the lag model: direct and indirect
In the lag model a change of \(x\) in one region changes the unemployment of all regions, through \((I - \rho W)^{-1} = I + \rho W + \rho^2W^2 + \dots\). LeSage and Pace (2009) split the effect of \(x\) into

the direct effect: on the region itself, with the echo that comes back through the neighbours;
the indirect effect (spillover): on all the others together.



Code
S <- solve(diag(n) - sar$rho * Wm)                              # (I - rho W)^-1
by_hand <- sapply(c("deg10", "log_gdp"), function(v) {
  M <- S * sar$coefficients[[v]]
  c(direct = mean(diag(M)), total = mean(rowSums(M)))
})
by_hand <- rbind(by_hand, indirect = by_hand["total", ] - by_hand["direct", ])
round(by_hand, 3)


         deg10 log_gdp
direct   0.060  -0.447
total    0.213  -1.582

by_package <- sapply(imp$res[c("direct", "indirect", "total")], as.numeric)
rownames(by_package) <- c("deg10", "log_gdp")
round(by_package, 3)


        direct indirect  total
deg10    0.060    0.153  0.213
log_gdp -0.447   -1.135 -1.582


Code
imp_ci <- t(sapply(
  c(direct = "direct_sum", indirect = "indirect_sum", total = "total_sum"),
  function(k) imp[[k]]$quantiles[2, c("2.5%", "97.5%")]

round(imp_ci, 2)


          2.5% 97.5%
direct   -0.63 -0.27
indirect -1.90 -0.70
total    -2.44 -1.02


The coefficient of log income is -0.37. The direct effect is -0.45, and the total -1.58, 95% CI [-2.44, -1.02]: if all the regions became 10% richer, unemployment would be 14.0% lower. Most of this, says the model, is spillover. But the split is a consequence of the formula: in a lag model the ratio of the indirect to the direct effect is the same for every predictor, whatever the data. It is a strong claim, and it rests on \(\rho\) being contagion.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
text:
7. What are the patches? Countries
Look again at the map. The edges of the patches are often national borders. Unemployment depends on the labour laws, the wages and the economy of the country. So give every country its own level:


Code
ols_c <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d)
mc    <- lm.morantest(ols_c, W)
sar_c <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d, listw = W)
sem_c <- errorsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d, listw = W)
comp <- rbind(
  `OLS` = c(coef(ols)[2:3], mr$estimate[[1]], AIC(ols)),
  `spatial lag` = c(sar$coefficients[2:3], resid_I[["lag"]], AIC(sar)),
  `OLS + countries` = c(coef(ols_c)[2:3], mc$estimate[[1]], AIC(ols_c)),
  `spatial lag + countries` = c(
    sar_c$coefficients[2:3],
    moran.test(residuals(sar_c), W)$estimate[[1]],
    AIC(sar_c)
  )
)
colnames(comp) <- c("deg10", "log_gdp", "Moran's I of the residuals", "AIC")
round(comp, 2)


                        deg10 log_gdp Moran's I of the residuals    AIC
OLS                      0.19   -0.92                       0.67 431.68
spatial lag              0.05   -0.37                      -0.02 241.13
OLS + countries          0.12   -0.84                       0.08 129.71
spatial lag + countries  0.10   -0.75                      -0.02 120.84


Code
c(rho_without_countries = sar$rho, rho_with_countries = sar_c$rho)


rho_without_countries.rho    rho_with_countries.rho 
                0.7641573                 0.2410725 


With country effects, plain OLS leaves a Moran’s I of 0.08, instead of 0.67. The \(\rho\) of the lag model falls from 0.76 to 0.24, and the AIC by another 111.4 points for the simple model with countries. Most of the “contagion” was the country. Within countries, unemployment falls with income (-0.84), and what is left of the neighbours is small. And the positive coefficient of the graduates is back (0.12, t = 2.4): the spatial models had hidden it. Within a country, regions with more graduates than their income suggests have a little more unemployment. The big cities may be part of it, but these data cannot say.


Code
pairs <- data.frame(i = rep(seq_len(n), each = 5), j = unlist(W$neighbours))
pairs$same <- d$CNTR_CODE[pairs$i] == d$CNTR_CODE[pairs$j]
gap <- tapply(abs(d$log_u[pairs$i] - d$log_u[pairs$j]), pairs$same, mean)
gap


    FALSE      TRUE 
0.5555752 0.2816538 


Code
set.seed(142)
random_gap <- mean(abs(d$log_u - sample(d$log_u)))
random_gap


[1] 0.7494134


Neighbours in the same country differ by 0.28 on the log scale, neighbours across a border by 0.56, and two random regions by 0.75. The border explains a good part of the pattern, but not all of it: neighbours across a border are still more alike than strangers (compare Overman & Puga, 2002).
This is the general problem of spatial regression: a spatial lag absorbs whatever is missing and has a shape on the map. Gibbons and Overman (2012) gave their critique of the field the title “Mostly pointless spatial econometrics?” for this reason. A spatial model is a good way to get honest standard errors and to see that something is missing. It is a weak way to prove that things spread.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 8. Does the definition of neighbours matter?
text:
8. Does the definition of neighbours matter?


Code
make_W <- list(
  `4 nearest` = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 4))),
  `5 nearest` = W,
  `8 nearest` = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 8))),
  `within 300 km` = nb2listw(dnearneigh(xy, 0, 300000), zero.policy = TRUE)
)
sens <- t(sapply(make_W, function(w) {
  m <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = w, zero.policy = TRUE)
  c(rho = m$rho, m$coefficients[2:3], AIC = AIC(m))
}))
round(sens, 3)


              rho.rho deg10 log_gdp     AIC
4 nearest       0.741 0.051  -0.361 247.229
5 nearest       0.764 0.050  -0.373 241.133
8 nearest       0.817 0.049  -0.351 239.145
within 300 km   0.706 0.105  -0.467 287.683


The definition changes the numbers (most of all with every region within 300 km) and not the story. Report more than one.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

Start with the map and Moran’s I of the residuals. If there is no pattern left, no spatial model is needed.
First add what is missing (countries, cities, coasts), then model what remains.
Lag for interaction, error for nuisance. Choose by theory. The tests rarely decide.
Never read the coefficients of a lag or Durbin model as effects. Use impacts.
\(W\) is chosen, not estimated. Say how, and try others.
Areas are arbitrary. Results can change with other borders or a finer division (the modifiable areal unit problem), and nothing follows for persons (the ecological fallacy, see beta regression).
Points instead of areas (sensors, houses): geostatistics, kriging (a Gaussian process on the map) or a smooth of the coordinates, mgcv::gam(y ~ x + s(lon, lat)).
Robust alternative: OLS with standard errors that allow for spatial correlation (Conley), if only the standard errors are the problem.

title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the units, the weights matrix, Moran’s I before and after, the models and how they were chosen, impacts instead of coefficients for lag models, and the sensitivity to the weights. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("OLS", "Spatial lag", "Spatial error", "OLS with country effects"),
  deg = paste0(
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 1], coef(ols_c)[[2]])),
    " (",
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 2], coef(summary(ols_c))[2, 2])),
    ")"
  ),
  gdp = paste0(
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 3], coef(ols_c)[[3]])),
    " (",
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 4], coef(summary(ols_c))[3, 2])),
    ")"
  ),
  rho = c("—", f2(c(sar$rho, sem$lambda)), "—"),
  I = f2(c(mr$estimate[[1]], resid_I[["lag"]], resid_I[["error"]], mc$estimate[[1]])),
  AIC = f1(c(AIC(ols), AIC(sar), AIC(sem), AIC(ols_c)))
)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the log unemployment rate (15–74 years, 2019) of 234 NUTS-2 regions of 31 European countries (Eurostat, 2024) with the share of adults with tertiary education and the log of GDP per head as predictors. Neighbours were the five nearest regions, with row-standardised weights. Spatial dependence was assessed with Moran’s I, and Lagrange multiplier tests (Anselin et al., 1996) compared a spatial lag and a spatial error model, estimated by maximum likelihood. For the lag model we report direct and total impacts (LeSage & Pace, 2009). Models with country effects and with other definitions of neighbours served as checks. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages spdep and spatialreg (Bivand & Piras, 2015).

Results:

Unemployment was strongly clustered, Moran’s I = 0.72, as were the residuals of the OLS model, I = 0.67, p < .001. Both spatial models fitted better (Table 1; ρ = 0.76, λ = 0.79), and the robust Lagrange multiplier tests did not clearly favour one of them (error: 18.2, lag: 5.6). In the lag model the total impact of log GDP was -1.58, 95% CI [-2.44, -1.02] (direct -0.45). With country effects, OLS left little spatial correlation in the residuals, I = 0.08, had a lower AIC than the spatial models, and gave a coefficient of -0.84 for log GDP: much of the spatial dependence is differences between countries.

Say which story you assume, interaction or shared causes, and why.

When
Observations have places, and neighbours resemble each other beyond the predictors

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
text:
An employer hires customer-service advisers. Every applicant takes a reasoning test, and only those above a cut score are hired. A year later each new adviser’s supervisor rates their job performance. The employer wants to know: how well does the test predict performance? That number, the correlation between test scores and performance, is the test’s validity coefficient.
The obvious answer is to correlate the test scores of the hires with their ratings. That correlation is almost always too low, for two reasons:

Range restriction. Performance ratings exist only for the people who were hired, and they all scored above the cut. Among them the test scores vary much less than among all applicants, and a correlation computed on a narrow range of scores is smaller. But the test is used to choose among applicants, so the validity that matters is the one among applicants.
An unreliable criterion. Supervisors disagree. Part of each rating is the supervisor’s personal view, not the adviser’s performance, and that noise lowers the correlation with anything.

So we need to be clear about which validity we mean:










Validity
Test
Performance
People
Used for




Observed
observed scores
one supervisor’s ratings
the hires
what the data give


Operational
observed scores
true performance
all applicants
decisions about using the test


Construct-level
true ability
true performance
all applicants
theory: how strongly the ability itself matters



The operational validity is the one for practical decisions: the test is used as it is, with its measurement error, on applicants, to predict their real performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998). As in other pages of this site, we simulate the applicant pool, so we know every true value and can check each correction against it.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(mvtnorm)    # pmvnorm(): areas of the bivariate normal distribution (section 6)

title: Selection Test Validity: Range Restriction, Reliability, Utility
