    data = subset(near, margin < 0),
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = subset(near, margin >= 0),
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Democratic share in the next election against the margin now",
    subtitle = "Blue: means of bins 2.5 points wide. Orange: a smooth curve on each side",
    x = "margin of the Democratic candidate (points)",
    y = "next share (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
naive <- t.test(vote ~ won, s)
c(
  mean_lost = naive$estimate[[1]],
  mean_won = naive$estimate[[2]],
  difference = diff(naive$estimate)[[1]]
)


 mean_lost   mean_won difference 
  40.92053   62.62170   21.70118 


Seats that the Democrats won have 21.7 points more in the next election than seats they lost. That number mixes the effect of holding the seat with the colour of the state. The curves rise on both sides, as they must. What we want is the jump at zero.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: what is estimated
Write \(Y(1)\) for the next share if the party wins now, \(Y(0)\) if it loses, and \(X\) for the margin. If both average curves are continuous at the cutoff, then
\[\tau = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = 0] = \lim_{x \downarrow 0} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow 0} E[Y \mid X = x]\]
Nothing is assumed about the rest of the line. The effect is for elections at the cutoff.


Step 2: a window
The simplest answer: take the elections with a margin below 1 point (or 2, or 5) and compare the two groups with a t test.


Code
windows <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10), function(k) {
    z <- subset(s, abs(margin) < k)
    t <- t.test(vote ~ won, z)
    data.frame(
      window = k,
      lost = sum(z$won == 0),
      won = sum(z$won),
      difference = diff(t$estimate)[[1]],
      low = -t$conf.int[2],
      high = -t$conf.int[1]
    )
  })
)
print(round(windows, 2), row.names = FALSE)


 window lost won difference  low  high
    0.5    9  14      10.37 3.39 17.35
    1.0   18  25      10.46 5.79 15.13
    2.0   49  47      10.17 6.36 13.98
    3.0   76  65       9.21 6.07 12.36
    5.0  128 117       7.79 5.49 10.08
   10.0  245 206       9.62 7.87 11.37


The narrower the window, the more alike the two groups, and the fewer the elections. In the wide windows the slope of the curves gets into the comparison: winners by 8 points are in other states than losers by 8 points.


Step 3: a line on each side
Better than a narrow window: allow for the slope. Fit a straight line on each side, only with the elections within a bandwidth \(h\), and give more weight to those near the cutoff (triangular kernel):
\[\min \sum_i w_i \left(y_i - \alpha - \tau D_i - \beta x_i - \gamma D_i x_i\right)^2, \qquad w_i = \max(0,\ 1 - |x_i|/h)\]
\(D\) is 1 for a win, and \(\tau\) is the jump. The package chooses \(h\); we take its value (Step 4) and do the rest by hand:


Code
fit_rd <- rdrobust(s$vote, s$margin)
h <- fit_rd$bws["h", "left"]
local <- function(h, p, d = s) {
  # weighted least squares on each side, p: degree; returns the jump and its robust (HC0) SE
  side <- function(keep) {
    X <- outer(d$margin[keep], 0:p, "^")
    w <- 1 - abs(d$margin[keep]) / h
    A <- solve(crossprod(X, w * X))
    b <- A %*% crossprod(X, w * d$vote[keep])
    e <- drop(d$vote[keep] - X %*% b)
    V <- A %*% crossprod(X * (w * e)) %*% A
    c(b[1], V[1, 1])
  }
  l <- side(d$margin < 0 & d$margin > -h)
  r <- side(d$margin >= 0 & d$margin < h)
  c(jump = r[1] - l[1], SE = sqrt(l[2] + r[2]))
}
z <- subset(s, abs(margin) < h); z$w <- 1 - abs(z$margin) / h
wls <- lm(vote ~ won * margin, z, weights = w)
rbind(
  by_hand = local(h, 1),
  lm_with_weights = c(coef(wls)[["won"]], sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(wls, type = "HC0")["won", "won"])),
  rdrobust_hc0 = with(
    rdrobust(s$vote, s$margin, h = h, vce = "hc0"),
    c(coef["Conventional", 1], se["Conventional", 1])
  )
)


                    jump       SE
by_hand         7.414131 1.455029
lm_with_weights 7.414131 1.455029
rdrobust_hc0    7.414131 1.455029


Three times the same: a jump of 7.4 points. The line through the points on the left ends at 45.2%, the one on the right starts at 52.6%.


Step 4: how wide?
A wide bandwidth uses many elections (little noise), but the curve may bend, and the straight line misses the edge (bias). A narrow one is the reverse. The error is roughly
\[\text{MSE}(h) \approx h^4 B^2 + \frac{V}{n h},\]
with \(B\) from the curvature at the cutoff and \(V\) from the scatter there. The best \(h\) is proportional to \((V/(B^2 n))^{1/5}\). rdrobust() estimates \(B\) and \(V\) from the data and finds h = 17.8 points, which keeps 683 elections.


Code
hs  <- seq(4, 60, by = 1); bw <- t(sapply(hs, function(v) c(local(v, 1), local(v, 2))))
bwd <- rbind(
  data.frame(h = hs, est = bw[, 1], se = bw[, 2], fit = "straight lines"),
  data.frame(h = hs, est = bw[, 3], se = bw[, 4], fit = "quadratic curves")
)
bwd$fit <- factor(bwd$fit, levels = c("straight lines", "quadratic curves"))
ggplot(subset(bwd, h >= 6), aes(h, est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = h, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~fit) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated jump for every bandwidth",
    subtitle = "Dashed: the bandwidth chosen by rdrobust",
    x = "bandwidth (points of margin)",
    y = "jump in the next share"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









With straight lines the estimate lies between 6.1 and 8.0 for all bandwidths from 10 to 60. The interval never includes 0.


Step 5: the interval that knows about the bias
The best bandwidth for the estimate leaves a bias: at the minimum of the formula above it is exactly half a standard error. So the usual interval (estimate ± 1.96 SE) is centred at the wrong place, and contains the truth in 92% instead of 95% of the samples. Calonico et al. (2014) subtract an estimate of the bias, and add the noise of that estimate to the standard error: the robust bias-corrected interval. It sounds complicated and has a simple core: if the bias is estimated with the same bandwidth, it is exactly the local quadratic fit.


Code
rb <- rdrobust(s$vote, s$margin, h = h, b = h, vce = "hc0")
rbind(
  local_quadratic_by_hand = local(h, 2),
  rdrobust_robust_same_bandwidth = c(rb$coef["Robust", 1], rb$se["Robust", 1])
)


                                   jump       SE
local_quadratic_by_hand        8.321204 2.057432
rdrobust_robust_same_bandwidth 8.321204 2.057432


By default rdrobust() uses a larger bandwidth for the bias (28.0 points), which is less noisy.

Code
ci <- fit_rd$ci["Robust", ]



Estimate: 7.4 percentage points. This is the local linear estimate, and it is what one reports as the effect.
Interval: the robust one, [4.1, 10.9]. It is not centred at the estimate. That is on purpose.
Standard errors are by default of the nearest-neighbour type (they compare each election with its neighbours instead of the line), so they differ slightly from ours.

A party that just wins a seat gets about 7.4 points more in the next election than a party that just loses it.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
text:
5. Can we believe it?
The assumption (continuity) cannot be tested directly. Four checks come close.

Could someone steer the margin?
If candidates could just push themselves over the line, there would be too few narrow losses and too many narrow wins (McCrary, 2008). Count:


Code
counts <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10), function(k) {
    l <- sum(s$margin < 0 & s$margin > -k)
    r <- sum(s$margin >= 0 & s$margin < k)
    data.frame(within = k, lost = l, won = r, p = binom.test(r, l + r)$p.value)
  })
)
print(transform(counts, p = round(p, 3)), row.names = FALSE)


 within lost won     p
    0.5    9  14 0.405
    1.0   18  25 0.360
    2.0   49  47 0.919
    3.0   76  65 0.400
    5.0  128 117 0.523
   10.0  245 206 0.073


Code
dens <- suppressWarnings(rddensity(s$margin))
c(T = dens$test$t_jk, p = dens$test$p_jk)


         T          p 
-0.7599917  0.4472596 


Code
ggplot(subset(s, abs(margin) < 30), aes(margin, fill = margin >= 0)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(-30, 30, by = 2), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Number of elections by margin",
    subtitle = "A jump at zero would be suspicious",
    x = "margin (points)",
    y = "elections"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









No sign of steering: for example 18 narrow losses and 25 narrow wins within 1 point (p = .360), and the density test of Cattaneo et al. (2020) has p = .447. (Simple counts are for narrow windows only. Within 10 points there are 245 losses and 206 wins, and the slope of the distribution begins to matter; the density test allows for it.)


Do things jump that cannot be affected?
What was fixed before the election must not jump at the cutoff. We have the state’s population, the terms of the candidate, the year, and, best of all, the result of the previous election for the same seat (made from the file itself):


Code
o <- order(senate$state, senate$class, senate$year); sorted <- senate[o, ]
key <- paste(sorted$state, sorted$class)
lag1 <- function(v) ave(v, key, FUN = function(x) c(NA, head(x, -1)))
sorted$previous_margin <- ifelse(sorted$year - lag1(sorted$year) == 6, lag1(sorted$margin), NA)
sorted$log_population <- log(sorted$population)
placebo <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("previous_margin", "termshouse", "termssenate", "log_population", "year"), function(v) {
    m <- rdrobust(sorted[[v]], sorted$margin)
    data.frame(
      variable = v,
      jump = m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      low = m$ci["Robust", 1],
      high = m$ci["Robust", 2],
      p = m$pv["Robust", 1],
      bandwidth = m$bws["h", "left"],
      n = sum(m$N_h)
    )
  })
)
print(data.frame(placebo[1], round(placebo[2:6], 3), n = placebo$n), row.names = FALSE)


        variable   jump    low   high     p bandwidth   n
 previous_margin  0.714 -7.047 10.906 0.674    17.825 577
      termshouse -0.173 -1.269  0.689 0.561    15.657 539
     termssenate -0.192 -1.555  1.368 0.900    16.443 558
  log_population -0.112 -0.517  0.290 0.581    18.472 747
            year  2.771 -6.594 13.560 0.498    16.891 693


None of the five jumps is significant. The margin of the previous election jumps by 0.7 points, with an interval from -7.0 to 10.9: not zero for certain, but no pattern either.


Placebo cutoffs and the donut
At other values of the margin nobody wins or loses anything, so there should be no jump. And the result should not depend on the few elections right at the edge:


Code
cuts <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(-20, -15, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20), function(k) {
    zz <- if (k < 0) {
      subset(s, margin < 0)
    } else if (k > 0) {
      subset(s, margin >= 0)
    } else {
      s
    }
    m <- rdrobust(zz$vote, zz$margin, c = k)
    data.frame(
      cutoff = k,
      jump = m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      low = m$ci["Robust", 1],
      high = m$ci["Robust", 2],
      p = m$pv["Robust", 1],
      n = sum(m$N_h)
    )
  })
)
print(round(cuts, 3), row.names = FALSE)

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
section: 6. What not to do: a global polynomial
text:
6. What not to do: a global polynomial
Before local regression became common, people fitted a high polynomial in the running variable to all data and read off the jump:


Code
global <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:6, function(p) {
    m <- lm(vote ~ won * poly(margin, p, raw = TRUE), s)
    data.frame(
      degree = p,
      jump = coef(m)[["won"]],
      SE = sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = "HC1")["won", "won"])
    )
  })
)
print(round(global, 2), row.names = FALSE)


 degree jump   SE
      1 6.04 0.89
      2 4.93 1.13
      3 7.32 1.40
      4 9.41 1.66
      5 7.96 1.97
      6 6.63 2.29


The answer goes from 4.9 to 9.4 with the degree, and each has a small standard error that knows nothing of the choice. A polynomial lets elections that were won by 80 points have a say about the edge (Gelman & Imbens, 2019). Local lines do not.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
section: 7. Are the intervals right? A simulation
text:
7. Are the intervals right? A simulation
We make a population that looks like ours: the curve is a polynomial of degree 4 on each side (so the true jump is known), the margins come from the data, the noise is normal. Draw 500 samples and let rdrobust() do everything, bandwidth included.


Code
sim_rd <- function(degree, reps = 500) {
  ml <- lm(vote ~ poly(margin, degree, raw = TRUE), s, subset = won == 0)
  mr <- lm(vote ~ poly(margin, degree, raw = TRUE), s, subset = won == 1)
  mu <- ifelse(s$won == 1, predict(mr, s), predict(ml, s))
  truth <- coef(mr)[[1]] - coef(ml)[[1]]
  sigma <- sd(s$vote - mu)
  r <- replicate(reps, {
    i <- sample(nrow(s), replace = TRUE)
    m <- rdrobust(mu[i] + rnorm(nrow(s), 0, sigma), s$margin[i], masspoints = "off")
    c(
      m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      m$ci["Conventional", 1] < truth & truth < m$ci["Conventional", 2],
      m$ci["Robust", 1] < truth & truth < m$ci["Robust", 2],
      m$bws["h", "left"]
    )
  })
  data.frame(
    degree = degree,
    true_jump = truth,
    mean_estimate = mean(r[1, ]),
    mean_bandwidth = mean(r[4, ]),
    coverage_usual = mean(r[2, ]),
    coverage_robust = mean(r[3, ])
  )
}
set.seed(221); sims <- do.call(rbind, lapply(3:5, sim_rd))
print(round(sims, 3), row.names = FALSE)


 degree true_jump mean_estimate mean_bandwidth coverage_usual coverage_robust
      3     7.319         7.052         19.631          0.952           0.960
      4     9.407         8.735         16.498          0.910           0.950
      5     7.958         7.950         17.866          0.948           0.948


The usual interval contains the truth in 91.0% to 95.2% of the samples, depending on how much the curve bends at the edge. The robust interval has 94.8% to 96.0%. Where the true curve bends strongly at the edge, the local linear estimate is too low on average (degree 4: 8.7 instead of 9.4), and the robust interval is what saves us.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
text:
8. What the number means

It is the effect at the cutoff, for elections that were nearly tied. A safe seat may be different.
It is the advantage of the party that holds the seat, not of the person: the candidate in the next election may be a new one.
What about winning again? The same design with the outcome “the Democrat gets more than half of the votes next time”:



Code
s$wins_next <- as.numeric(s$vote > 50)
win <- rdrobust(s$wins_next, s$margin); clustered <- rdrobust(s$vote, s$margin, cluster = s$state)
c(
  jump_in_the_probability_to_win = win$coef["Conventional", 1],
  low = win$ci["Robust", 1],
  high = win$ci["Robust", 2]
)


jump_in_the_probability_to_win                            low                           high 
                     0.3301591                      0.1847127                      0.4604589 


Code
cbind(
  value = c(
    effect_on_the_share_clustered_by_state = clustered$coef["Conventional", 1],
    low = clustered$ci["Robust", 1],
    high = clustered$ci["Robust", 2]
  )
)


                                           value
effect_on_the_share_clustered_by_state  7.394838
low                                     3.984970
high                                   11.024943


A narrow win raises the probability of a majority next time by 33.0 percentage points, 95% CI [18.5, 46.0]. (With more than two candidates more than half is stricter than winning.) With standard errors clustered by state, the interval for the share is [4.0, 11.0]: no important change.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

Draw the plot first. If you cannot see the jump, be careful with the number.
Know the rule. Is the threshold applied strictly? Do other things change at the same threshold (another law at age 18)? Then the jump is the effect of all of them.
Fuzzy RD: when crossing the threshold only raises the probability of treatment, divide the jump in the outcome by the jump in the treatment. That is instrumental variables at the cutoff: rdrobust(y, x, fuzzy = treatment).
Discrete running variables (age in years, whole test points): there is no “just above”; the methods need care.
Control variables are not needed. They can shorten the interval (covs =), and must be fixed before the treatment.
Report the bandwidth, its selection, the kernel, the number of observations on each side within it, and the robust interval. Show other bandwidths.
Power is low: only the observations near the edge count. Here 683 of 1,297.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the rule and the running variable, the cutoff, the estimator (degree, kernel, bandwidth and how it was chosen), the numbers of observations on each side within the bandwidth, the estimate with a robust interval, and the checks. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
line <- function(label, m, scale = 1) {
  data.frame(
    Outcome = label,
    n = paste(m$N_h, collapse = " / "),
    h = f1(m$bws["h", "left"]),
    jump = f2(scale * m$coef["Conventional", 1]),
    ci = paste0("[", f2(scale * m$ci["Robust", 1]), ", ", f2(scale * m$ci["Robust", 2]), "]"),
    p = sub("= ", "", pval(m$pv["Robust", 1]))
  )
}
pm <- function(v) rdrobust(sorted[[v]], sorted$margin)
apa_table <- rbind(
  line("Share in the next election (%)", fit_rd),
  line("Majority in the next election (percentage points)", win, 100),
  line("Margin of the previous election (placebo)", pm("previous_margin")),
  line("Earlier terms in the House (placebo)", pm("termshouse")),
  line("Earlier terms in the Senate (placebo)", pm("termssenate")),
  line("Log population (placebo)", pm("log_population"))
)


Method (data analysis):

The effect of holding a US Senate seat on the party’s share in the next election was estimated with a sharp regression discontinuity design (Lee, 2008), using 1,297 elections between 1914 and 2004 (Cattaneo et al., 2015). The running variable was the Democratic margin of victory, with a cutoff of zero. We fitted local linear regressions with a triangular kernel on each side of the cutoff, with the bandwidth that minimises the mean squared error, and report robust bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (Calonico et al., 2014; R package rdrobust). The assumption that parties could not steer the margin was examined with the density test of Cattaneo et al. (2020), and the continuity assumption with predetermined outcomes, false cutoffs, and the removal of the elections nearest the cutoff. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

A narrow win raised the party’s share in the next election by 7.4 percentage points, robust 95% CI [4.1, 10.9], p < .001 (bandwidth 17.8 points; 360 elections below and 323 above the cutoff; Table 1), and the probability of a majority by 33.0 percentage points, 95% CI [18.5, 46.0]. There was no evidence of a discontinuity in the density of the margin (T = -0.76, p = .447) or in the predetermined variables (p ≥ .498). Of eight false cutoffs, 1 showed a jump with p < .05. Estimates for bandwidths between 10 and 60 points ranged from 6.1 to 8.0.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Does Winning by a Hair Help You Win Again?
text:
11. Summary



When
A treatment is given by a threshold in a running variable that nobody controls exactly


The effect
The jump of the regression function at the cutoff


Estimator
Weighted lines on each side, within a bandwidth: lm(y ~ D * x, weights = triangle)


Bandwidth
Minimises the mean squared error (rdrobust)


Interval
Robust bias-corrected (with the same bandwidth for the bias: the local quadratic fit)


How (R)
rdrobust(y, x, c = 0), rddensity(x), rdplot(y, x)


Checks
Density, placebo outcomes, false cutoffs, donut, other bandwidths


Not
Global polynomials


Related pages
Instrumental variables, LOESS, simple regression

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
A detached house costs more than a terraced house, and a home in London costs more than one elsewhere. Everybody knows that. The question for this page is: by how much, and is it the same amount for cheap homes and for expensive ones?
An ordinary regression (OLS) answers with one number per predictor: the difference in the mean price. But house prices are strongly skewed: most homes sell for a modest sum and a few sell for millions. A predictor can move the cheap end of the market by a little, the middle by more, and the expensive end by far more. The mean blends all of that into one figure that describes nobody in particular.
Quantile regression (Koenker & Bassett, 1978) fits a separate line for any quantile of the outcome: the 10th percentile (the cheapest tenth of homes), the median, the 90th percentile, and so on. The model is a family of regressions, one for each quantile \(\tau\) (the Greek letter tau):








Quantile \(\tau\)
What the line describes
In this example




0.1
the lower tail
the price below which 10% of comparable homes sell


0.5
the median
the middle price


0.9
the upper tail
the price below which 90% of comparable homes sell



Where a predictor’s coefficient is the same at every \(\tau\), it only shifts the distribution. Where it changes with \(\tau\), the predictor changes the shape of the distribution: its spread, its skew.


Code
library(quantreg)   # rq(): quantile regression
library(ggplot2)

# the site's colours, in order
blue <- "#2a78d6"; orange <- "#eb6834"; green <- "#1baf7a"; yellow <- "#eda100"; pink <- "#e87ba4"

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
k    <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "£", f0(abs(x)), "k")   # a price in thousands of pounds, for the text

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
1. The data
HM Land Registry, the government register of property ownership in England and Wales, publishes the Price Paid Data: one row for every residential sale registered since 1995, free, with no login, under the Open Government Licence v3.0. The yearly files are large (about 170 MB each), so this page uses the small monthly update file, the sales registered with the Land Registry in the latest month.


Code
url  <- "https://price-paid-data.publicdata.landregistry.gov.uk/pp-monthly-update-new-version.csv"
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download_time <- system.time(download.file(url, file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE))[["elapsed"]]
file_mb <- file.size(file) / 1e6


The download is 17.1 MB and took 0.2 seconds. The file has no header row. The columns are documented on the Land Registry’s about the Price Paid Data page, and we read only the ones we need:







Column
Meaning (from the documentation)




2
Price: the sale price stated on the transfer deed, in pounds


3
Date of transfer: when the sale was completed, as stated on the deed


5
Property type: D detached, S semi-detached, T terraced (including end-of-terrace), F flat or maisonette, O other. Bungalows are not separate


6
Old/new: Y a newly built property, N an established one


14
County


15
PPD category: A a standard sale of a single residential property; B additional transactions, such as repossessions, buy-to-lets identified by a mortgage and transfers to non-private individuals


16
Record status (monthly file only): A added, C changed, D deleted





Code
columns <- rep("NULL", 16)                      # "NULL" skips a column
columns[c(2, 3, 5, 6, 14, 15, 16)] <- "character"
raw <- read.csv(file, header = FALSE, colClasses = columns)
names(raw) <- c("price", "date", "type", "new", "county", "category", "status")
nrow(raw)


[1] 98103


Code
table(raw$status)



    A     C     D 
93495  3056  1552 


The file holds 98,103 rows. We keep what the question needs:


Code
raw$date <- as.Date(substr(raw$date, 1, 10))
homes <- subset(raw, status == "A" &                          # added records, not changes or deletions
                  category == "A" &                           # standard sales of a single home
                  type %in% c("T", "F", "S", "D") &           # the four named types of home
                  date > max(date) - 365)                     # sales completed in the last 12 months

homes$k      <- as.numeric(homes$price) / 1000                # price in £ thousand
homes$type   <- factor(homes$type, levels = c("T", "F", "S", "D"),
                       labels = c("Terraced", "Flat", "Semi-detached", "Detached"))
homes$new    <- factor(homes$new, levels = c("N", "Y"), labels = c("Established", "New build"))
homes$london <- factor(ifelse(homes$county == "GREATER LONDON", "London", "Elsewhere"),
                       levels = c("Elsewhere", "London"))
n <- nrow(homes)


That leaves 73,902 sales completed between 01 October 2025 and 30 September 2026 (61% of them in the last two months, because sales are registered some weeks after completion). The three predictors:

type: the type of home, with terraced as the reference, because it is the most common type;
new: newly built or established;
london: in Greater London, or elsewhere in England and Wales.
the outcome k is the price in thousands of pounds, so a coefficient of 50 means £50,000.



Code
table(homes$type, homes$london)


               
                Elsewhere London
  Terraced          17611   2258
  Flat               7637   3926
  Semi-detached     21311   1283
  Detached          19492    384


What these data cannot say. The Price Paid Data has no floor area, number of bedrooms, condition or street-level location. A detached house in the data is bigger than a terraced one, and the coefficient on type includes that. Nor does one monthly file cover all sales in England and Wales in a year: it holds the ones registered in one month, which is a large and mixed set, but not a random sample of the year. This page is a worked example of a method, not a house price index.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
mean_k   <- mean(homes$k)
median_k <- median(homes$k)

ggplot(homes, aes(k)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, boundary = 0, fill = "grey80", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median_k, colour = "Median", linetype = "Median"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_k, colour = "Mean", linetype = "Mean"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Median = blue, Mean = orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Median = "solid", Mean = "dashed")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1500)) +
  labs(title = "Sale prices of homes, England and Wales",
       subtitle = "The chart stops at £1.5 million",
       x = "price (£ thousand)", y = "sales", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
qs <- quantile(homes$k, c(.1, .5, .9, .99))
over <- mean(homes$k > 1500)


Prices pile up on the left and trail off to the right. The median is £300k, the mean £376k: a few very expensive sales pull the mean up. The cheapest tenth of homes sold for up to £145k, and the dearest tenth for £653k or more. The chart cuts off 1.1% of the sales, those above £1.5 million; the dearest sale in the data is £25,400k.
The skew matters because the London gap is not one number. The same quantiles in the two areas:


Code
taus <- seq(.05, .95, by = .05)
by_area <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(homes$london), function(a)
  data.frame(area = a, tau = taus, price = quantile(homes$k[homes$london == a], taus, names = FALSE))))
by_area$area <- factor(by_area$area, levels = c("Elsewhere", "London"))

ggplot(by_area, aes(tau, price, colour = area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Elsewhere = blue, London = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  labs(title = "Sale price quantiles, London and elsewhere",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "price (£ thousand)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
q_area <- tapply(homes$k, homes$london, quantile, probs = c(.1, .5, .9))


At the 10th percentile, a London home sells for £295k against £140k elsewhere, a difference of £155k. At the median the difference is £246k, and at the 90th percentile £670k. The London premium grows steadily from the bottom of the market to the top. An OLS coefficient would report one number, somewhere in the middle of those, and say nothing about this.
These are the raw differences. Quantile regression does the same thing while holding the type of home, and whether it is new, fixed.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: one line per quantile
For a quantile \(\tau\) between 0 and 1, the model says that the \(\tau\)-th quantile of the price, given the predictors \(x_i\), is a linear function of them:
\[Q_\tau(y_i \mid x_i) = \beta_0(\tau) + \beta_1(\tau)\,x_{i1} + \dots + \beta_p(\tau)\,x_{ip}\]
The coefficients carry \((\tau)\) because each quantile has its own. The conditional quantile \(Q_\tau(y_i \mid x_i)\) is the price below which a fraction \(\tau\) of the homes with these characteristics sell. OLS models the conditional mean, \(E(y_i \mid x_i)\), in the same way, with one set of coefficients.


Step 2: the check (pinball) loss
OLS finds the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals. Quantile regression minimises a different sum, with the check loss (also called the pinball loss because of its shape). For a residual \(u = y - \hat y\):
\[\rho_\tau(u) = u\,\bigl(\tau - I(u < 0)\bigr) = \begin{cases} \tau\,u & \text{if } u \ge 0 \text{ (the price is above the line)}\\ (\tau - 1)\,u = (1-\tau)\,|u| & \text{if } u < 0 \text{ (the price is below the line)}\end{cases}\]
where \(I(u < 0)\) is 1 when the residual is negative and 0 otherwise. The coefficients are
\[\hat\beta(\tau) = \arg\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho_\tau\bigl(y_i - x_i^\top \beta\bigr)\]
The loss is a pair of straight lines: a point above the fitted line costs \(\tau\) per unit of distance, a point below it costs \(1-\tau\). Three cases:

\(\tau = 0.5\): both sides cost 0.5, so the loss is half the absolute residual, \(\tfrac12|u|\). This is median regression, or least absolute deviations (LAD): the line that minimises the sum of the absolute residuals.
\(\tau = 0.9\): a point above the line costs 0.9, a point below costs only 0.1. The line is pushed up until 90% of the points are below it.
\(\tau = 0.1\): the reverse: the line is pushed down until 10% of the points are below it.



Step 3: why minimising it gives the quantile
Start with no predictors, only a single number \(c\) as the fit. The expected loss is
\[E\,\rho_\tau(y - c) = (\tau - 1)\int_{-\infty}^{c} (y - c)\,dF(y) + \tau \int_{c}^{\infty} (y - c)\,dF(y)\]
where \(F\) is the distribution function of \(y\). Differentiating with respect to \(c\) gives
\[\frac{d}{dc}\,E\,\rho_\tau(y - c) = (1 - \tau)\,F(c) - \tau\,\bigl(1 - F(c)\bigr) = F(c) - \tau\]
which is zero when \(F(c) = \tau\): the value \(c\) below which a fraction \(\tau\) of the data lies, which is the \(\tau\)-th quantile. In the same way, squared loss gives the mean, and absolute loss gives the median. A small numeric check with 11 real sales, drawn at random from the data:


Code
rho <- function(u, tau) u * (tau - (u < 0))     # the check loss

set.seed(2026)
few    <- sort(sample(homes$k, 11))
cand   <- seq(0, max(few) * 1.05, length.out = 1500)
tau_set <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)

loss <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(tau = t, c = cand, loss = sapply(cand, function(cc) mean(rho(few - cc, t))))))
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(tau = t, c = loss$c[loss$tau == t][which.min(loss$loss[loss$tau == t])],
             loss = min(loss$loss[loss$tau == t]))))
best$quantile <- sapply(tau_set, function(t) quantile(few, t, type = 1, names = FALSE))
best


  tau        c      loss quantile
1 0.1 206.4977  9.904112    206.5
2 0.5 240.0150 38.089319    240.0
3 0.9 390.2652 23.584683    390.0




Code
loss$panel <- factor(paste("τ =", loss$tau), levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))
best$panel <- factor(paste("τ =", best$tau), levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tau_set, function(t)
  data.frame(panel = paste("τ =", t), x = few)))
pts$panel <- factor(pts$panel, levels = paste("τ =", tau_set))

ggplot(loss, aes(c, loss)) +
  geom_line(colour = blue, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = best, colour = orange, size = 3) +
  geom_rug(data = pts, aes(x = x, y = NULL), colour = "grey35", sides = "b") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Average check loss for a single fitted value c",
       subtitle = "Orange: the lowest point. Grey ticks: the 11 sale prices.",
       x = "c, the fitted price (£ thousand)", y = "average check loss") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.08))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines"))









The loss curve is made of straight pieces that bend at the data points, and its lowest point (orange) sits on a data value: £206k for \(\tau\) = 0.1, £240k for the median and £390k for \(\tau\) = 0.9. Those are the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the 11 prices (£206k, £240k and £390k). The same check on all 73,902 sales, by trying every candidate price on a fine grid:


Code
grid <- seq(0, 1500, by = 0.5)
by_search <- sapply(tau_set, function(t) grid[which.min(sapply(grid, function(cc) mean(rho(homes$k - cc, t))))])
rbind(`minimising the loss` = by_search,
      `quantile()` = quantile(homes$k, tau_set, type = 1, names = FALSE))


                    [,1] [,2] [,3]
minimising the loss  145  300  653
quantile()           145  300  653




Step 4: how the line is found
The check loss has a corner at zero, so there is no formula like the normal equations of OLS. rq() solves the problem as a linear programme (the Barrodale and Roberts simplex algorithm, method = "br", the default), which is fast for samples up to a few thousand rows; for very large data method = "fn" (an interior point method) is quicker. When the minimum is a flat stretch rather than a single point, as happens when many prices are the same round number, R warns “Solution may be nonunique”. The warning is harmless here: any value on the flat stretch fits equally well.


Step 5: what the coefficients mean
\(\beta_j(\tau)\) is the change in the \(\tau\)-th conditional quantile of the price when \(x_j\) goes up by one unit, with the other predictors fixed. With a categorical predictor, it is the difference between the \(\tau\)-th quantiles of the two groups, adjusting for the other predictors. Section 7 spells out what this does and does not mean.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output
The model is k ~ type + new + london. rq() takes a formula, the data and the quantile or quantiles in tau:


Code
f <- k ~ type + new + london

fit_ols <- lm(f, data = homes)
fit10   <- rq(f, tau = 0.1, data = homes)
fit50   <- rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)
fit90   <- rq(f, tau = 0.9, data = homes)
summary(fit50, se = "nid")



Call: rq(formula = f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)

tau: [1] 0.5

Coefficients:
                  Value     Std. Error t value   Pr(>|t|) 
(Intercept)       229.50000   1.21415  189.02077   0.00000
typeFlat          -59.50000   1.91511  -31.06868   0.00000
typeSemi-detached  40.49900   1.58774   25.50729   0.00000
typeDetached      190.50000   1.95280   97.55209   0.00000
newNew build       29.20400   2.23098   13.09024   0.00000
londonLondon      310.50000   3.80080   81.69333   0.00000


The output looks like lm(): Value is the coefficient, then its standard error, t and p. The intercept is the median price of the reference home: an established terraced house elsewhere in England and Wales (the £230k, which is also the median of that group). The other lines are the differences from it:


Code
coefs <- cbind(`τ = 0.1` = coef(fit10), `τ = 0.5` = coef(fit50), `τ = 0.9` = coef(fit90), OLS = coef(fit_ols))
round(coefs, 1)


                  τ = 0.1 τ = 0.5 τ = 0.9    OLS
(Intercept)           120   229.5   415.0  260.9
typeFlat              -42   -59.5   -89.6 -101.7
typeSemi-detached      40    40.5    65.0   45.1
typeDetached          130   190.5   410.0  247.1
newNew build           50    29.2    -1.8    8.5
londonLondon          205   310.5   799.6  475.9


Code
b10 <- coef(fit10); b50 <- coef(fit50); b90 <- coef(fit90); bo <- coef(fit_ols)






\(\tau\) = 0.1
Median
\(\tau\) = 0.9
OLS (mean)




Detached (against terraced)
£130k
£190k
£410k
£247k


Flat (against terraced)
-£42k
-£60k
-£90k
-£102k


London (against elsewhere)
£205k
£310k
£800k
£476k


New build (against established)
£50k
£29k
-£2k
£8k




London. The London difference is £205k in the cheap end of the market, £310k at the median and £800k in the expensive end: about 3.9 times bigger at the top than at the bottom. OLS reports £476k, a number that is not the London difference for any group of homes: it is above the median difference because the mean follows the long right tail.
Detached. A detached house costs £130k more than a terraced one at \(\tau\) = 0.1, £190k more at the median and £410k more at \(\tau\) = 0.9.
New build. This is where the mean misleads the most. The new-build difference is £50k in the cheap end, £29k at the median, and -£2k at \(\tau\) = 0.9: new homes sell for more than established ones at the bottom of the market, and for a little less at the top. OLS says £8k, which hides the sign change. The data cannot say why: they have no information on size or exact location, which may differ between new and established homes.
Flat. Flats are cheaper than terraced houses, by £42k at \(\tau\) = 0.1 and £90k at \(\tau\) = 0.9.

All the models here have categorical predictors only. The fitted lines are then the quantiles of price within each combination of type, new and London, tied together by the model’s additive form (no interactions). With a continuous predictor, such as floor area, each \(\tau\) would give a slope instead of a gap: the reading is the same.

Three ways to calculate the standard errors
summary.rq() offers several methods for the standard errors, set with se =:








se =
The idea
When it fits




"iid"
Assumes the errors have the same distribution for every observation: one common density at the quantile
Only if the spread of the outcome is the same for all values of the predictors. Not here


"nid"
A sandwich estimator (Hendricks & Koenker, 1992) that allows the density at the quantile to differ from one observation to the next. The default for samples above 1,000
The usual choice with heteroscedastic data


"ker"
A sandwich estimator that estimates the density with a kernel (Powell, 1991)
An alternative to "nid"


"boot"
Bootstrap: resample the rows with replacement (the default bsmethod = "xy" resamples (x, y) pairs), refit, and take the standard deviation of the estimates
Needs no density at all, but slow: each bootstrap sample is a new fit



The standard error of a quantile depends on how thinly the data are spread around that quantile, since a coefficient is more uncertain where observations are sparse. The sandwich methods estimate this density, and "iid" takes it to be the same everywhere, which is wrong when the spread of price differs between London and elsewhere. A comparison on a random subsample of 5,000 sales (a bootstrap of the full 73,902 sales would be much slower), at \(\tau\) = 0.9:


Code
set.seed(2026)
sub   <- homes[sample(n, 5000), ]
fit_s <- rq(f, tau = 0.9, data = sub)
se_methods <- sapply(c("iid", "nid", "ker", "boot"), function(m) {
  s <- if (m == "boot") summary(fit_s, se = m, R = 200) else summary(fit_s, se = m)
  s$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
})
round(se_methods, 1)


                   iid  nid  ker boot
(Intercept)       15.5  8.8  9.5  9.5
typeFlat          25.9 19.0 15.5 18.3
typeSemi-detached 21.1 16.8 17.2 16.3
typeDetached      22.3 21.6 21.6 24.6
newNew build      34.0 36.3 23.0 33.9
londonLondon      27.3 77.5 70.0 80.9


For the London coefficient the standard error is 27.3 with "iid" and 77.5 with "nid", 70.0 with "ker" and 80.9 with the bootstrap. "iid" is 2.8 times too small: London prices are much more spread out than prices elsewhere, which the "iid" method does not allow. The three methods that allow unequal spread are in the same range for London, but they do not agree exactly: for the new-build coefficient the standard errors run from 23.0 to 36.3. The bootstrap makes the fewest assumptions. A quick rule: use "nid" for large samples (it is the default) and "boot" for the final results of a smaller study, with a larger R (1,000 or more).
The rest of the page uses "nid" on the full data.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 5. The classic chart: coefficients across the quantiles
text:
5. The classic chart: coefficients across the quantiles
Three quantiles tell the story in a table. The whole story is a chart: fit the model at 19 quantiles from \(\tau\) = 0.05 to 0.95, and draw each coefficient against \(\tau\), with its 95% confidence band. The OLS estimate, with its interval, is a single horizontal line: if the quantile coefficients stay near the OLS line, the mean tells the story; if they drift away from it, it does not.


Code
fits_path <- rq(f, tau = taus, data = homes)
sums_path <- summary(fits_path, se = "nid")

names_short <- c(typeFlat = "Flat (vs terraced)", `typeSemi-detached` = "Semi-detached (vs terraced)",
                 typeDetached = "Detached (vs terraced)", `newNew build` = "New build (vs established)",
                 londonLondon = "London (vs elsewhere)")
terms <- names(names_short)

path <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(taus), function(i) {
  cm <- sums_path[[i]]$coefficients[terms, , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(tau = taus[i], term = terms, est = cm[, "Value"],
             lo = cm[, "Value"] - qnorm(.975) * cm[, "Std. Error"],
             hi = cm[, "Value"] + qnorm(.975) * cm[, "Std. Error"])
}))
path$term <- factor(names_short[path$term], levels = names_short)

ols_ci  <- confint(fit_ols)
ols_ref <- data.frame(term = factor(names_short, levels = names_short),
                      est = coef(fit_ols)[terms], lo = ols_ci[terms, 1], hi = ols_ci[terms, 2])

ggplot(path, aes(tau)) +
  geom_rect(data = ols_ref, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "OLS (mean)"),
            alpha = 0.18, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(data = ols_ref, aes(yintercept = est, colour = "OLS (mean)"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "Quantile regression"), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = est, colour = "Quantile regression"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = est, colour = "Quantile regression"), size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) +
  labs(title = "How each coefficient changes along the price distribution",
       subtitle = "Bands: 95% confidence intervals (standard errors by nid)",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "difference in price (£ thousand)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









(The base R version is plot(summary(rq(f, tau = taus, data = homes))), which draws the same panels, with the OLS line in red.) Reading the panels:


Code
p <- function(term, t) path$est[path$term == names_short[[term]] & abs(path$tau - t) < 1e-9]
inside <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(path)), path$term, function(i) {
  o <- ols_ref[ols_ref$term == path$term[i[1]], ]
  mean(path$est[i] >= o$lo & path$est[i] <= o$hi)
})



London and Detached: the coefficient climbs steadily with \(\tau\), from £170k and £121k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 to £1,105k and £545k at \(\tau\) = 0.95. The OLS line cuts across the middle and describes none of the ends.
New build: the coefficient falls from £55k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 to -£10k at \(\tau\) = 0.95, and first drops below zero at \(\tau\) = .90. OLS is a small positive number, £8k, for all.
Flat: the gap against terraced homes widens from £32k to £90k. The OLS gap, £102k, is bigger than the quantile gap at 19 of the 19 quantiles: here the mean gap is larger than the gap at the quantiles, because the few very dear sales pull the mean.
Semi-detached: changes least. It is £40k at \(\tau\) = 0.05 and £40k at the median, and rises only in the top tail, to £95k at \(\tau\) = 0.95. For most of the market, OLS (£45k) is not misleading for this predictor.

The confidence bands widen at the extremes: there are fewer observations near the 5th and 95th percentiles to pin the line down. Remember that the bands are for each \(\tau\) separately; they are not a simultaneous band for the whole curve.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 6. Do the slopes differ across quantiles?
text:
6. Do the slopes differ across quantiles?
The chart suggests that they do. anova() on rq fits at several quantiles tests it (Koenker & Bassett, 1982): the null hypothesis is that the coefficients of the predictors are the same at every \(\tau\) in the set, which is the pure location-shift model in which the predictors move the whole distribution up or down by the same amount and leave its shape alone.


Code
test_joint <- anova(fit10, fit50, fit90)
test_joint


Quantile Regression Analysis of Deviance Table

Model: k ~ type + new + london
Joint Test of Equality of Slopes: tau in {  0.1 0.5 0.9  }

  Df Resid Df F value    Pr(>F)    
1 10   221696   419.3 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
test_terms <- anova(fit10, fit50, fit90, joint = FALSE)
test_terms


Quantile Regression Analysis of Deviance Table

Model: k ~ type + new + london
Tests of Equality of Distinct Slopes: tau in {  0.1 0.5 0.9  }

                  Df Resid Df  F value    Pr(>F)    
typeFlat           2   221704   77.187 < 2.2e-16 ***
typeSemi-detached  2   221704   25.654 7.239e-12 ***
typeDetached       2   221704 1160.060 < 2.2e-16 ***
newNew build       2   221704   41.665 < 2.2e-16 ***
londonLondon       2   221704  658.493 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The first test is a joint test of all five predictors at the three quantiles (10 restrictions: each predictor’s coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.1 and at 0.9 equal to the median’s): F(10, 221,696) = 419.3, p < .001. The slopes are not the same at the three quantiles. The second test takes one predictor at a time: all five are significant, with the largest statistics for Detached (vs terraced) (1,160.1) and London (vs elsewhere) (658.5), and the smallest for Semi-detached (vs terraced) (25.7).
Two cautions. With 73,902 sales, even a small difference is “significant”, so the size of the differences (the chart) matters more than the p value. And the test compares only the quantiles you give it: a set of \(\tau\) values such as 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 can miss differences elsewhere.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
7. Interpretation: a conditional quantile effect
A coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.9 is easy to misread. It is not “the effect of being in London on the people at the top of the market”. Two ideas separate:

A conditional quantile is a quantile of price among homes that share the same values of the predictors. \(\beta_{\text{London}}(0.9)\) is the gap between the 90th percentile of London homes and the 90th percentile of the other homes of the same type and age. A 90th-percentile London flat is not the same home as a 90th-percentile detached house elsewhere: “the top” is defined within each group of comparable homes.
An unconditional quantile is a quantile of the whole market: the dearest 10% of all sales in the country, whatever their type or location. A coefficient at \(\tau\) = 0.9 does not say what would happen to the dearest 10% of the whole market if the predictor changed. That is a different question, with a different method (Firpo et al., 2009).

In plain words: the median regression tells you how the typical London home compares with the typical home elsewhere, and the 90th percentile regression tells you how an expensive London home compares with an expensive home elsewhere. Nothing is said about individual homes: a person who buys at the 90th percentile of a cheap area does not move to the 90th percentile of London by moving there.
The numbers are also differences between groups, not changes in a home: the Price Paid Data holds one sale per home, so the coefficients describe how the groups differ, not what would happen to a given house if it were in London.
A chart of the model’s predictions for six typical homes, all established, makes the point concrete: the middle 80% of the predicted prices (from \(\tau\) = 0.1 to 0.9) with the median and, for contrast, the OLS mean.


Code
cases <- expand.grid(type = c("Terraced", "Flat", "Detached"), london = c("Elsewhere", "London"),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cases$new    <- "Established"
cases$type   <- factor(cases$type, levels = levels(homes$type))
cases$new    <- factor(cases$new, levels = levels(homes$new))
cases$london <- factor(cases$london, levels = levels(homes$london))
cases$label  <- paste0(cases$type, ", ", ifelse(cases$london == "London", "London", "elsewhere"))
cases <- cases[order(cases$london, match(cases$type, c("Flat", "Terraced", "Detached"))), ]

pred <- data.frame(label = cases$label,
                   q10 = predict(fit10, cases), q50 = predict(fit50, cases), q90 = predict(fit90, cases),
                   mean = predict(fit_ols, cases))
pred$label <- factor(pred$label, levels = rev(pred$label))
round(pred[, -1], 0)


  q10 q50  q90 mean
2  78 170  325  159
1 120 230  415  261
3 250 420  825  508
5 283 480 1125  635
4 325 540 1215  737
6 455 730 1625  984


Code
ggplot(pred, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q10, xmax = q90), colour = "grey55", linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = q50, colour = "Median"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean, colour = "Mean (OLS)"), size = 3.2, shape = 18) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Median = blue, `Mean (OLS)` = orange)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted prices of six typical homes",
       subtitle = "Grey bar: the 10th to the 90th percentile of the quantile regression",
       x = "price (£ thousand)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The grey bars say what OLS cannot: the range of prices to expect. A detached home in London has a predicted median of £730k, and the middle 80% of its predicted prices runs from £455k to £1,625k; a flat elsewhere is far tighter, from £78k to £325k. The OLS mean for the detached home in London, £984k, is above the median: the mean is pulled up by the right tail.
How well do the fitted lines do their job? By definition, a fraction \(\tau\) of the sales should lie below the line at \(\tau\). The check:


Code
below <- sapply(list(fit10, fit50, fit90), function(m) mean(homes$k < fitted(m)))
setNames(round(below, 3), c("τ = 0.1", "τ = 0.5", "τ = 0.9"))


τ = 0.1 τ = 0.5 τ = 0.9 
  0.097   0.499   0.899 


The shares below the lines are 9.7%, 49.9% and 89.9%, close to 10%, 50% and 90% (not exactly so because many prices are round numbers, such as £250,000, and tie with the fitted values).

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
8. Practical points

Quantile crossing
The quantile of 0.9 must never be below the quantile of 0.8, but separate fits do not know that. With a continuous predictor, the fitted lines can cross, usually at extreme values of the predictor, and then give an impossible prediction: a 90th percentile lower than the 80th. Crossing signals that the linear model is wrong for that part of the data, or that the extrapolation goes too far.


Code
fit_ends <- rq(f, tau = c(0.01, 0.99), data = homes)
all_taus <- c(0.01, taus, 0.99)
B <- cbind(coef(fit_ends)[, 1], coef(fits_path), coef(fit_ends)[, 2])
all_cells <- expand.grid(type = levels(homes$type), new = levels(homes$new), london = levels(homes$london))
pred_all  <- model.matrix(~ type + new + london, all_cells) %*% B      # one row per kind of home, one column per tau
crossings <- sum(apply(pred_all, 1, function(x) any(diff(x) < 0)))


I checked all 16 combinations of type, new and London at 21 quantiles from 0.01 to 0.99: 0 of them have crossing quantiles. Crossing here is unlikely, because the predictors are categorical and every combination has many sales. If it does happen, the usual remedies are to fit a simpler model, to restrict predictions to the range of the data, or to rearrange: sort the predicted quantiles of each case into increasing order, which can only improve the estimates (Chernozhukov et al., 2010). In R, sort() on the row of predictions does it.


A log outcome, and back-transformation
Prices are often analysed on the log scale: then the coefficients are percentages and the skew is much smaller. For quantiles the log scale has a special property. Quantiles commute with monotone transformations; means do not:
\[Q_\tau\bigl(\log y\bigr) = \log Q_\tau(y) \qquad\text{but}\qquad E\bigl(\log y\bigr) \ne \log E(y)\]
The median of the logs is the log of the median. The mean of the logs is the log of the geometric mean, which is smaller than the mean. So a quantile regression of \(\log y\) can be back-transformed with exp() and gives a quantile of the price itself, whereas back-transforming an OLS of \(\log y\) gives the geometric mean (or, with a “smearing” correction, an estimate of the mean that depends on the distribution of the errors).


Code
c(`log of the median` = log(median(homes$k)), `median of the logs` = median(log(homes$k)),
  `log of the mean` = log(mean(homes$k)), `mean of the logs` = mean(log(homes$k)))


 log of the median median of the logs    log of the mean   mean of the logs 
          5.703782           5.703782           5.930437           5.720243 


Code
f_log   <- log(k) ~ type + new + london
log_fit <- rq(f_log, tau = taus, data = homes)
log_ols <- lm(f_log, data = homes)

# the median regression on the log scale, back-transformed, against the median regression on the price
log50   <- rq(f_log, tau = 0.5, data = homes)
back    <- exp(predict(log50, cases))
rbind(`median regression of price` = pred$q50[match(cases$label, pred$label)],
      `median regression of log price, exp()` = back) |> round(0) |> `colnames<-`(cases$label)


                                      Flat, elsewhere Terraced, elsewhere Detached, elsewhere Flat, London Terraced, London Detached, London
median regression of price                        170                 230                 420          480              540              730
median regression of log price, exp()             179                 227                 415          437              555             1014


The two models estimate the same quantile, but one is additive in pounds and the other additive in logs, so they only agree where an additive model is a good description: for a terraced home elsewhere they give £230k and £179k, but for a detached home in London £730k and £1,014k. Back-transforming a quantile is exact for one variable; it is no reason to expect two different models to agree. exp(coef) on the log scale is a ratio: a London home has a median price 2.44 times that elsewhere, that is 144% more. The question changes with the scale: on the pound scale the London premium grows from the bottom to the top of the market; as a percentage it does not, as the chart shows:


Code
lb <- coef(log_fit)[terms, , drop = FALSE]
log_path <- data.frame(tau = rep(taus, each = length(terms)),
                       term = factor(rep(names_short, times = length(taus)), levels = names_short),
                       pc = 100 * (exp(as.vector(lb)) - 1))
log_ols_pc <- data.frame(term = factor(names_short, levels = names_short),
                         pc = 100 * (exp(coef(log_ols)[terms]) - 1))

ggplot(log_path, aes(tau, pc)) +
  geom_hline(data = log_ols_pc, aes(yintercept = pc, colour = "OLS (geometric mean)"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "Quantile regression"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "Quantile regression"), size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Quantile regression` = blue, `OLS (geometric mean)` = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) +
  labs(title = "The same model on the log scale, as percentage differences",
       x = expression("quantile " * tau), y = "difference in price (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
lp <- function(term, t) 100 * (exp(coef(log_fit)[term, which.min(abs(taus - t))]) - 1)
test_log <- anova(rq(f_log, tau = 0.1, data = homes), log50, rq(f_log, tau = 0.9, data = homes))


On the percentage scale the London premium is 185% at \(\tau\) = 0.1, 144% at the median and 193% at \(\tau\) = 0.9. It is lowest near the middle (144%) and rises towards both ends, so across the middle 80% of the market it varies much less than the £205k to £800k in pounds. Prices in London are higher by a multiple rather than by a fixed sum, and part of the “growing” effect in pounds is just proportions on a skewed outcome. The shape of the curve depends on the scale: a steady rise in pounds becomes a U in percentages. A test of equal slopes on the log scale is still significant (F(10, 221,696) = 106.3, p < .001) but the differences are smaller. A report should say which scale it uses: the pound scale answers “how many pounds more?”, the log scale “how many times more?”.


Median regression resists outliers in y
OLS minimises squared residuals, so a single huge price pulls the line towards it. The median regression minimises absolute residuals: an extreme price costs a little more than a moderate one, but not squared. Only the ordering of the prices around the line matters, not how far away they are, which is why the median regression is a robust method, in the same spirit as robust regression (which also handles outliers in the predictors, which median regression does not). To see it, simulate a data-entry error: 100 random sales are entered with two extra zeros (£250,000 becomes £25,000,000).


Code
set.seed(2026)
dirty <- homes
bad   <- sample(n, 100)
dirty$k[bad] <- dirty$k[bad] * 100

effect <- rbind(
  OLS_clean    = coef(lm(f, homes)),
  OLS_dirty    = coef(lm(f, dirty)),
  median_clean = coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = homes)),
  median_dirty = coef(suppressWarnings(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = dirty))))
round(effect[, c("typeDetached", "londonLondon")], 1)


             typeDetached londonLondon
OLS_clean           247.1        475.9
OLS_dirty           289.7        543.4
median_clean        190.5        310.5
median_dirty        190.2        310.2


With 100 wrong prices out of 73,902 (0.14%), the OLS coefficient for London goes from £476k to £543k, and the one for detached homes from £247k to £290k. The median regression moves from £310k to £310k for London and from £190k to £190k for detached homes. A fully robust method would also resist bad predictors, and quantile regression does not, but for outliers in the outcome it is hard to beat. The same data contain real outliers too (the dearest sale is £25,400k): median regression is not disturbed by them.


Other points

Sample size. The extreme quantiles (\(\tau\) = 0.01 or 0.99) need many observations, since the line is fitted to a few points in the tail. As a rule of thumb, you want at least 10 or so observations in the tail for each parameter.
Dependence. Sales in the same street or town are alike, and the standard errors assume independent rows. With clustered data use a cluster bootstrap (boot.rq()) or see the multilevel page.
Weights and heteroscedasticity. Quantile regression does not need constant variance: unequal spread is the thing it describes. If the aim is a better mean line instead, see weighted least squares and generalised least squares.
Trees instead of lines. The random forest page shows quantile regression forests: the same idea with a flexible, non-linear model in place of a straight one.
Not causal. A London coefficient is a difference between groups of homes that differ in many other ways.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) states the data, the quantiles, the standard error method, the coefficients at the quantiles that matter, the comparison with OLS and the test of equal slopes.


Code
ci_of <- function(model, tau) {
  s <- summary(model, se = "nid")$coefficients
  cbind(est = s[, "Value"], lo = s[, "Value"] - qnorm(.975) * s[, "Std. Error"],
        hi = s[, "Value"] + qnorm(.975) * s[, "Std. Error"])
}
c10 <- ci_of(fit10); c50 <- ci_of(fit50); c90 <- ci_of(fit90)
co  <- cbind(est = coef(fit_ols), confint(fit_ols))
cell <- function(m, term) paste0(f0(m[term, 1]), " [", f0(m[term, 2]), ", ", f0(m[term, 3]), "]")

apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Flat (vs terraced)", "Semi-detached (vs terraced)", "Detached (vs terraced)",
                "New build (vs established)", "London (vs elsewhere)"),
  `τ = .10` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c10, t)),
  `τ = .50` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c50, t)),
  `τ = .90` = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(c90, t)),
  OLS       = sapply(terms, function(t) cell(co, t)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed 73,902 sales of homes in England and Wales completed between October 2025 and September 2026, from the HM Land Registry Price Paid Data (standard sales of detached, semi-detached, terraced and flat properties; Open Government Licence v3.0). The outcome was the sale price in thousands of pounds. The predictors were the type of home (reference: terraced), whether it was newly built and whether it was in Greater London. Price was strongly right-skewed (median = £300k, mean = £376k), so we estimated linear quantile regressions at τ = .10, .50 and .90, and on a grid from .05 to .95, with the quantreg package (Version 6.1; Koenker, 2005), and compared them with ordinary least squares. Standard errors for the quantile regressions were of the nid (sandwich) type (Hendricks & Koenker, 1992). Equality of the coefficients across τ = .10, .50 and .90 was tested with the Wald-type test of Koenker and Bassett (1982). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

The effects of the predictors differed across the price distribution (Table 1). The London difference was £205k at the 10th percentile, 95% CI [200, 210], £310k at the median, 95% CI [303, 318], and £800k at the 90th percentile, 95% CI [762, 837]; the OLS estimate for the mean was £476k, 95% CI [468, 484]. Detached homes cost £130k, £190k and £410k more than terraced homes at the three quantiles. New builds were £50k dearer than established homes at the 10th percentile, but at the 90th the difference was -£2k, 95% CI [-22, 18]. The coefficients were not equal across the three quantiles, F(10, 221,696) = 419.3, p < .001. On the log scale the percentage London premium varied less (185% at τ = .10, 144% at τ = .50 and 193% at τ = .90), though the slopes still differed, F(10, 221,696) = 106.3, p < .001.

Points to remember:

Say which quantiles you fitted, and why those.
Say that coefficients are conditional quantile differences, and name the units.
Say which standard error method you used (nid, boot, …) and the number of bootstrap samples.
Report the test of equal slopes, but base the conclusion on the size of the differences.
Say whether the outcome is on the original or the log scale.
Show the coefficients against τ: a table of three quantiles cannot show the shape.

title: Quantile Regression: Who Pays More for a Home, the Cheap End or the Expensive End?
text:
10. Summary



When
The effect of a predictor may differ between the low and high ends of the outcome: skewed outcomes (prices, wages, incomes), or interest in the tails (risk, growth charts)


The model
\(Q_\tau(y \mid x) = x^\top \beta(\tau)\): one linear regression for each quantile \(\tau\)


The loss
Check loss \(\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - I(u < 0))\). Median: \(\tau = 0.5\), least absolute deviations


How (R)
quantreg::rq(y ~ x, tau = c(.1, .5, .9), data = d); summary(fit, se = "nid") or se = "boot"


Standard errors
"nid" for large samples; "boot" when in doubt; not "iid" with unequal spread


Equal slopes?
anova(fit10, fit50, fit90) (joint test), joint = FALSE (one predictor at a time)


Reading it
A difference in a conditional quantile, not an effect on the people at the top


Advantages
No normality or constant variance needed; robust to outliers in \(y\); quantiles commute with log and other monotone transformations


Dangers
Crossing quantiles; extreme \(\tau\) with small samples; dependent data; not robust to outliers in \(x\)


Alternatives
Robust regression, WLS and GLS for the mean; quantile forests for non-linear quantiles; unconditional quantile regression (RIF) for effects on the whole market

title: Principal Components Regression: What Does the Yield Curve Say About Next Year’s Economy?
text:
The United States borrows money for three months, for a year, for five, for ten. Each of these loans has its own interest rate, and together they form the yield curve. People who watch the economy look at its shape. When the long rates are much higher than the short ones, the economy usually grows. When the short rates climb above the long ones, the curve is inverted, and a recession often follows (Estrella & Hardouvelis, 1991).
So: can the eight interest rates of today predict how much the economy will grow in the next year?
A regression with eight predictors is easy to run and hopeless to read. The eight rates rise and fall together; two neighbours correlate above .99. Least squares cannot tell them apart, and its coefficients explode.
Principal components regression (PCR) goes around the problem in two steps. First it replaces the eight rates by a few new variables that summarise them and do not correlate with each other. Then it uses these in an ordinary regression. This example is a kind one, because the new variables have a meaning that anybody can see. It also shows the weak point of the method, in its purest form.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(pls)        # pcr(): principal components regression, with cross-validation
library(sandwich)   # NeweyWest(): standard errors for overlapping time series
library(lmtest)     # coeftest(), coefci()
library(glmnet)     # ridge regression, for comparison

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Principal Components Regression: What Does the Yield Curve Say About Next Year’s Economy?
text:
1. The data
FRED, the database of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, gives every series as a CSV file, free and with no login. We take the monthly interest rates for eight maturities, average them over each quarter, and the real gross domestic product (GDP) of the quarter (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, n.d.; U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, n.d.).


Code
fred <- function(id) {
  d <- read.csv(paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id), na.strings = ".")
  names(d) <- c("date", "value")
  quarter <- paste0(substr(d$date, 1, 4), "Q", (as.integer(substr(d$date, 6, 7)) + 2) %/% 3)
  tapply(d$value, quarter, mean) # the mean of the months of the quarter
}
maturities <- c(`3 months` = "TB3MS", `6 months` = "TB6MS", `1 year` = "GS1", `2 years` = "GS2",
                `3 years` = "GS3", `5 years` = "GS5", `7 years` = "GS7", `10 years` = "GS10")
rates <- lapply(maturities, fred)
gdp   <- fred("GDPC1")

quarters <- names(rates[["2 years"]]) # the shortest series: it starts in 1976
quarters <- quarters[quarters >= "1976Q3" & quarters <= "2018Q4"]
X <- sapply(rates, function(r) r[quarters])                            # 8 columns: percent per year
at <- match(quarters, names(gdp))
y <- as.numeric(100 * (gdp[at + 4] / gdp[at] - 1)) # growth in the NEXT four quarters, in %
n  <- nrow(X)
c(quarters = n, rates = ncol(X))


quarters    rates 
     170        8 


Code
summary(y)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 -3.979   1.798   2.882   2.781   4.111   8.578 


A row is a quarter. The predictors are the rates of that quarter; the outcome is the growth of real GDP over the following four quarters, so it is a forecast. The sample ends with the rates of 2018Q4, whose outcome is the growth until the end of 2019: the pandemic of 2020 was not in any yield curve. There are 170 quarters. Mean growth was 2.8% a year, with a standard deviation of 2.0.

title: Principal Components Regression: What Does the Yield Curve Say About Next Year’s Economy?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
time  <- as.numeric(substr(quarters, 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(quarters, 6, 6)) - 1) / 4
long <- data.frame(
  time = rep(time, 8),
  rate = as.vector(X),
  maturity = factor(rep(colnames(X), each = n), levels = colnames(X))
)
pa <- ggplot(long, aes(time, rate, colour = maturity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.9, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Eight interest rates", x = NULL, y = "% per year") + theme_bw()
pb <- ggplot(data.frame(time, y), aes(time, y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth of the economy in the following year",
    x = "quarter in which the rates were observed",
    y = "%"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)









Code
R <- cor(X)
range(R[lower.tri(R)])


[1] 0.9444643 0.9988344


The eight lines move as one. The correlations are between 0.94 and 0.999. What distinguishes the quarters, apart from the level, is how far the lines are spread.

text:
3. Why least squares fails

ols <- lm(y ~ X)
ols_table <- coef(summary(ols))[-1, ]
rownames(ols_table) <- colnames(X)
round(ols_table, 2)


         Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
3 months    -0.24       1.22   -0.20     0.84
6 months     0.06       2.39    0.02     0.98
1 year      -4.57       1.93   -2.37     0.02
2 years      8.23       3.55    2.32     0.02
3 years     -1.86       3.98   -0.47     0.64
5 years     -5.56       3.37   -1.65     0.10
7 years      5.39       3.28    1.64     0.10

Code
vif <- diag(solve(R))                      # variance inflation factors
round(vif)


3 months 6 months   1 year  2 years  3 years  5 years  7 years 10 years 
    1084     4158     3106    10243    12176     7932     6946     1791 


Code
c(R2 = summary(ols)$r.squared)


       R2 
0.2990087 


Read the column of estimates. The 2-year rate: 8.2. The 5-year rate: -5.6. So the economy should grow by 8.2 points more when the 2-year rate is one point higher and everything else stays the same. But everything else never stays the same. When the 2-year rate rises, the 1-year and the 3-year rates rise with it.
The variance inflation factor says how many times the variance of a coefficient is larger than it would be with uncorrelated predictors. A usual warning level is 10. Here it goes up to 12,176. The fit is not the problem: the predictions of least squares are still meaningful as long as the rates move together. But the coefficients are noise, and they change wildly if a few quarters are left out:


Code
half <- time < 1998
round(
  cbind(
    first_half = coef(lm(y ~ X, subset = half))[-1],
    second_half = coef(lm(y ~ X, subset = !half))[-1]
  ),
  1
)


          first_half second_half
X3 months       -1.0         6.3
X6 months        1.3       -14.3
X1 year         -6.7         9.7
X2 years        12.5        -5.3
