All at the same values of the other predictors:

Respect matters most: each step up the scale, for example from “agree” to “strongly agree”, multiplies the odds of a higher satisfaction answer by 2.07.
Autonomy (1.48 per step) and job security (1.47) also go with more satisfaction.
Stress goes the other way: each step more often stressful cuts the odds of a higher answer by 31% (odds ratio 0.69).
The self-employed have 1.57 times the odds of employees of a higher answer, and the odds rise by 16% with every 10 years of age.
Working from home: the confidence intervals include 1. Once autonomy, respect, security and stress are held constant, there is no clear difference between those who work from home and those who never do.

Working from home alone does go with more satisfaction, as section 2 showed:


Code
home_alone <- polr(satisfaction ~ home, data = d)
round(exp(coef(home_alone)), 2)


homeSome days    homeMainly 
         1.38          1.25 


On its own, working from home some days has an odds ratio of 1.38; with the other predictors, 1.17. The jobs that can be done from home also give more freedom and security, and these, not the place of work, carry the difference.


The same numbers by hand
Steps 2 and 3 for a typical worker: the median answer to each question, the median age, never works from home, an employee.


Code
sapply(d[c("autonomy", "respect", "security", "stress", "age10")], median)   # the medians


autonomy  respect security   stress    age10 
     3.0      3.0      4.0      3.0      4.1 


Code
x    <- c(autonomy = 3, respect = 3, security = 4, stress = 3,
          "homeSome days" = 0, homeMainly = 0, self_employedYes = 0, age10 = 4.1)
eta  <- sum(b * x[names(b)])                      # the place on the hidden scale
cum  <- plogis(theta - eta)                       # step 3: P(Y <= j), j = 1, 2, 3
prob <- setNames(diff(c(0, cum, 1)), satisfaction)  # P(Y = j)
round(prob, 3)


    Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied  Moderately satisfied        Very satisfied 
                0.023                 0.088                 0.507                 0.381 


Code
# new people for predict(), with the factor levels of the model
people <- function(...) {
  x <- data.frame(...)
  for (v in intersect(names(x), c("home", "self_employed"))) x[[v]] <- factor(x[[v]], levels = levels(d[[v]]))
  x
}
typical <- people(autonomy = 3, respect = 3, security = 4, stress = 3, home = "Never",
                  self_employed = "No", age10 = 4.1)
round(predict(fit, newdata = typical, type = "probs"), 3)   # the same, from R


    Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied  Moderately satisfied        Very satisfied 
                0.023                 0.088                 0.507                 0.381 


The typical worker is moderately satisfied with probability 51% and very satisfied with probability 38%.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model
text:
5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model

The hidden scale
Step 5 of section 3, with the fitted numbers: the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker if they disagree, and if they strongly agree, that they are treated with respect. Everything else stays the same.


Code
two <- people(autonomy = 3, respect = c(2, 4), security = 4, stress = 3, home = "Never",
              self_employed = "No", age10 = 4.1)
person <- c("Disagrees that they are treated with respect", "Strongly agrees that they are treated with respect")
centre <- eta + b[["respect"]] * (c(2, 4) - 3)        # eta of each: the typical worker has respect = 3
probs2 <- predict(fit, newdata = two, type = "probs")

grid   <- seq(-2.5, 11, by = 0.01)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(k)
  data.frame(person = person[k], y = grid, density = dlogis(grid, centre[k]),
             answer = cut(grid, c(-Inf, theta, Inf), labels = satisfaction))))
curves$person <- factor(curves$person, levels = person)

# the probability of each answer, printed above its part of the scale
middle <- c(theta[1] - 0.9, (theta[1] + theta[2]) / 2, (theta[2] + theta[3]) / 2, theta[3] + 1.6)
labels <- data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 4), levels = person),
                     y = rep(middle, 2), share = as.vector(t(probs2)))

ggplot(curves, aes(y, density)) +
  geom_area(aes(fill = answer, group = answer), position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey20") +
  # the thresholds stop below their names, the centre at the top of the curve
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(x = theta), aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = 0.31),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(person = factor(person, levels = person), x = centre),
               aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = dlogis(0)), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(y, 0.29, label = pct(share)), size = 3.2, colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 3), levels = person), y = rep(theta, 2),
                              label = rep(paste0("theta[", 1:3, "]"), 2)),
            aes(y, 0.33, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ person, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.345), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Where the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker falls",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines: the thresholds. Solid line: the centre of the distribution, eta.\nThe percentages are the areas: the probability of each answer.",
       x = "hidden satisfaction (Y*)", y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))









Strongly agreeing instead of disagreeing moves the centre of the distribution by \(2\beta\) = 1.45 to the right. The thresholds stay where they are, so more of the area falls above \(\theta_3\): the probability of “very satisfied” goes from 23% to 56%.


Predicted probabilities, one predictor at a time
The typical worker again, changing one predictor at a time:


Code
vary <- function(v, values) {
  x <- typical[rep(1, length(values)), ]
  x[[v]] <- values
  pr <- predict(fit, newdata = x, type = "probs")
  labels <- paste0(questions[[v]], ": ", answers[[v]][values])
  data.frame(question = factor(questions[[v]], levels = questions),
             answer = factor(rep(labels, 4), levels = rev(labels)),
             satisfaction = factor(rep(satisfaction, each = length(values)), levels = satisfaction),
             share = as.vector(pr))
}
predicted <- rbind(vary("respect", 1:4), vary("autonomy", 1:4), vary("stress", 1:5))
predicted$question <- droplevels(predicted$question)
stacked(predicted, "predicted probability of each answer, for the typical worker")









Code
p_resp   <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 4), ], respect = 1:4), type = "probs")
p_stress <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 5), ], stress = 1:5), type = "probs")



From “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” that they are treated with respect, the probability that the typical worker is very satisfied rises from 13% to 56%, and the probability of being dissatisfied (very or a little) falls from 35% to 6%.
From work that is never stressful to work that is always stressful, “very satisfied” falls from 57% to 22%.
The odds ratio is the same at every step, the change in probability is not. Each step up the respect scale multiplies the odds by 2.07, but moves the probability of “very satisfied” by 10, 15, 18 percentage points: the effect on a probability depends on where a person starts.

Unlike the observed shares of section 2, these predictions follow the pattern of the model: every step up the respect scale helps, including the step from “strongly disagree” to “disagree”, which the few people who strongly disagree did not show.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 6. Testing the predictors and the model
text:
6. Testing the predictors and the model
The likelihood-ratio test compares the deviances of two nested models. First the whole model against a model with thresholds only, then each predictor: drop it and see how much worse the model gets.


Code
null <- polr(satisfaction ~ 1, data = d)
model_test <- anova(null, fit)
model_test


Likelihood ratio tests of ordinal regression models

Response: satisfaction
                                                                  Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df LR stat. Pr(Chi)
1                                                                     1      2164   4632.148                              
2 autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10      2156   4065.195 1 vs 2     8 566.9527       0


Code
tests <- drop1(fit, test = "Chisq")
tests


Single term deletions

Model:
satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + 
    self_employed + age10
              Df    AIC     LRT  Pr(>Chi)    
<none>           4087.2                      
autonomy       1 4128.6  43.387 4.491e-11 ***
respect        1 4188.0 102.836 < 2.2e-16 ***
security       1 4127.8  42.591 6.748e-11 ***
stress         1 4148.2  62.972 2.096e-15 ***
home           2 4086.9   3.657  0.160641    
self_employed  1 4095.6  10.395  0.001264 ** 
age10          1 4108.2  23.048 1.580e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
mcfadden <- 1 - deviance(fit) / deviance(null)   # McFadden's pseudo-R squared
mcfadden


[1] 0.1223952



Every predictor except working from home is significant. The \(\chi^2\) values rank them: respect (102.84), stress (62.97), autonomy (43.39) and job security (42.59), then age and self-employment. Working from home: \(\chi^2\)(2) = 3.66, p = .161.
McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = 0.12: one minus the deviance of the model divided by the deviance of the model with thresholds only. It runs much lower than the \(R^2\) of a linear regression; use it to compare models fitted to the same data.

Is the order worth using? The same predictors in a multinomial model, which ignores the order:


Code
multi <- nnet::multinom(formula(fit), data = d, trace = FALSE)
data.frame(model      = c("ordinal (polr)", "multinomial (multinom)"),
           parameters = c(length(b) + length(theta), length(coef(multi))),
           AIC        = round(c(AIC(fit), AIC(multi)), 1))


                   model parameters    AIC
1         ordinal (polr)         11 4087.2
2 multinomial (multinom)         27 4115.9


The ordinal model fits better by AIC, with 11 parameters instead of 27: the multinomial model spends 16 more parameters and gains less than they cost.
How often does the model pick the right answer, if it picks the most likely one for each person?


Code
guess <- predict(fit, type = "class")
table(observed = d$satisfaction, predicted = guess)


                       predicted
observed                Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied Moderately satisfied Very satisfied
  Very dissatisfied                     6                    12                   48              9
  A little dissatisfied                 4                    10                  165             34
  Moderately satisfied                  1                    16                  574            323
  Very satisfied                        1                     8                  289            667


Code
accuracy  <- mean(as.character(guess) == as.character(d$satisfaction))
base_rate <- max(overall)   # always guessing the most common answer
c(model = accuracy, most_common_answer = base_rate)


             model most_common_answer 
         0.5800646          0.4453161 


58% right, against 45% for always guessing the most common answer. The model almost never predicts the two dissatisfied answers: they are rare, so for almost nobody are they the most likely answer. As in the multinomial example, the predicted probabilities carry the information, not the single best guess.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
7. The proportional odds assumption
The model gives each predictor one slope for all three splits. Does it need three? A visual check first: fit a separate logistic regression at each split and compare the slopes.


Code
splits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) {
  dj <- transform(d, higher = as.integer(satisfaction) > j)   # TRUE above split j
  m  <- glm(update(formula(fit), higher ~ .), family = binomial, data = dj)
  data.frame(split = j, term = names(coef(m))[-1], b = coef(m)[-1], se = sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[-1])
}))
short <- c(autonomy = "Autonomy", respect = "Respect", security = "Job security", stress = "Stress",
           "homeSome days" = "Home: some days", homeMainly = "Home: mainly",
           self_employedYes = "Self-employed", age10 = "Age (10 years)")
splits$term <- factor(short[splits$term], levels = short)
common      <- data.frame(term = factor(short, levels = short), b = b[names(short)])

ggplot(splits, aes(split, b)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_hline(data = common, aes(yintercept = b), colour = "#1c5cab", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = b - 1.96 * se, ymax = b + 1.96 * se), width = 0.15, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "grey15") +
  facet_wrap(~ term, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, limits = c(0.6, 3.4)) +
  labs(title = "The slope of each predictor at each split",
       subtitle = "Points: the slope from a separate logistic regression, with its 95% CI.\nDashed line: the one slope of the ordinal model.\nSplits: 1 very dissatisfied | the rest, 2 dissatisfied | satisfied, 3 very satisfied | the rest",
       x = "split", y = "slope (log odds of a higher answer)") +
  theme_bw()









Code
security_splits <- splits$b[splits$term == short[["security"]]]


If the proportional odds assumption holds, the three points of each panel scatter around the dashed line, within their error bars. Most do. The clearest exception is job security: its slope grows from 0.07 at the first split to 0.45 at the third. Good job security seems to separate the very satisfied from the moderately satisfied more than it protects against being very dissatisfied. The confidence intervals are wide at the first split, though: only 75 people are very dissatisfied.
The formal test: fit the same model with clm() from the package ordinal, which can relax the assumption one predictor at a time. nominal_test() does that for each predictor and compares the two models with a likelihood-ratio test:


Code
# the same model as polr(), with the same estimates
clm_fit <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10, data = d)
nominal <- nominal_test(clm_fit)
nominal


Tests of nominal effects

formula: satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10
              Df  logLik    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>           -2032.6 4087.2                
autonomy       2 -2032.5 4091.0 0.1898   0.9095
respect        2 -2031.5 4088.9 2.2979   0.3170
security       2 -2030.8 4087.6 3.5963   0.1656
stress         2 -2032.3 4090.7 0.4917   0.7821
home           4 -2031.4 4092.9 2.3305   0.6752
self_employed  2 -2032.5 4090.9 0.2827   0.8682
age10          2 -2032.2 4090.4 0.7607   0.6836


No predictor needs its own slopes: the smallest p is .166, for job security. The differences that the chart shows could be chance. The Brant test (Brant, 1990), in the package brant, is a common alternative that answers the same question.

If the assumption fails: a partial proportional odds model
If a predictor did fail the test, it could get one slope per split while the others keep one slope: a partial proportional odds model (Peterson & Harrell, 1990). In clm(), the predictors in nominal get their own slopes:


Code
partial <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10,
               nominal = ~ security, data = d)
coef(partial)[grep("security", names(coef(partial)))]


   Very dissatisfied|A little dissatisfied.security A little dissatisfied|Moderately satisfied.security        Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied.security 
                                         -0.1968220                                          -0.3232832                                          -0.4471662 


Code
anova(clm_fit, partial)


Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
 
        formula:                                                                             nominal:  link: threshold:
clm_fit satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10 ~1        logit flexible  
partial satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10            ~security logit flexible  

        no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)
clm_fit     11 4087.2 -2032.6                      
partial     13 4087.6 -2030.8  3.5963  2     0.1656


clm() writes these slopes as shifts of the thresholds, so the effect of security on a higher answer is the number shown with its sign changed: 0.20, 0.32, 0.45 at the three splits. The likelihood-ratio test is the same as the security row of nominal_test(), and the AIC is a little worse: two more parameters that do not pay for themselves. We keep the simple model. If several predictors failed, the alternatives are a model with every slope free (nominal = ~ ., the generalized ordered logit) or the multinomial model.


Four more things to keep in mind


Code
# answers given as categories instead of numbers: one coefficient per answer
fit_steps <- update(fit, . ~ . - autonomy - respect - security - stress +
                      factor(autonomy) + factor(respect) + factor(security) + factor(stress))
steps_test <- anova(fit, fit_steps)
stress_steps <- coef(fit_steps)[paste0("factor(stress)", 2:5)]   # hardly ever ... always, against never

# the people who answered on the web against those interviewed in person or by phone
very_by_mode <- prop.table(table(d$web, d$satisfaction), 1)[, "Very satisfied"]
fit_mode <- update(fit, . ~ . + web)
round(cbind(without_mode = coef(fit), with_mode = coef(fit_mode)[names(coef(fit))]), 2)


                 without_mode with_mode
autonomy                 0.39      0.39
respect                  0.73      0.73
security                 0.38      0.37
stress                  -0.38     -0.37
homeSome days            0.16      0.17
homeMainly              -0.08     -0.06
self_employedYes         0.45      0.44
age10                    0.15      0.15



Equal steps. The four scored questions count each step up the scale the same. Treating the answers as categories instead, with a coefficient for each answer, fits somewhat better, \(\chi^2\)(9) = 21.73, p = .010: the steps are not all equal. For stress, for example, the coefficients of “hardly ever”, “sometimes”, “often” and “always” against “never” are -0.64, -0.83, -1.41, -1.59, not evenly spaced. The scored model is easier to read and tells the same story.
Web or interview. In 2022 most people answered the GSS on the web. 41% of them said “very satisfied”, against 49% of those interviewed in person or by phone, as people often give more positive answers when an interviewer is listening. Adding the mode to the model leaves the other coefficients almost unchanged (above).
The sample, not the population. These are unweighted estimates for the people in the survey. To describe all US workers, use the GSS weights (wtssps) and the design of the survey, for example with svyolr() in the package survey (Lumley, 2010).
Association, not cause. People who like their work may also see their workplace in a better light, and judge it more respectful and more secure. One survey at one point in time cannot tell which comes first.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its order, the predictors and how they were scored, the model test, the check of the proportional odds assumption and the odds ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:


Code
n_model <- nrow(d)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci_text <- function(t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(ci[t, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[t, 2]), "]")


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2,167 employed respondents to the 2022 General Social Survey (Davern et al., 2024) who answered the job satisfaction question and the Quality of Working Life questions used here. Job satisfaction (very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied) was analysed with an ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds model). The predictors were autonomy, respect at work and job security (each scored 1–4) and work stress (scored 1–5), with higher scores meaning more; how often the respondent worked from home (never, some days, mainly); self-employment; and age. The proportional odds assumption was checked with likelihood-ratio tests of nominal effects. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002) and ordinal (Christensen, 2026) packages.

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over a thresholds-only model, χ²(8) = 566.95, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .12, and no predictor departed from the proportional odds assumption (smallest p = .166). Holding the other predictors constant, respondents who felt more respected at work were more satisfied with their job, OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.80, 2.39], as were those with more autonomy, OR = 1.48, 95% CI [1.32, 1.67], and better job security, OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.31, 1.64]. More frequent stress went with lower satisfaction, OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.62, 0.75]. Self-employed and older respondents were more satisfied (Table 1). How often respondents worked from home was not related to job satisfaction once the other predictors were held constant, χ²(2) = 3.66, p = .161.

Points to remember:

Say which way the outcome runs, and whether an odds ratio above 1 means a higher or a lower answer: programs differ.
Report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
Report the check of the proportional odds assumption, and what you did if it failed.
Predicted probabilities for typical people are easier to understand than odds ratios; show them where they help.
Cite R and the packages; citation("MASS") and citation("ordinal") give the references.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
text:
9. Summary







When
The outcome is a category with three or more values in a natural order


Why not linear regression
It assumes equal steps between the answers and predicts values nobody can give


Why not multinomial logistic regression
It ignores the order and needs a set of coefficients for every answer


How (R)
MASS::polr(y ~ x, data, Hess = TRUE), with y an ordered factor; or ordinal::clm()


Output
Thresholds (one per split) and one slope per predictor; exp() of a slope is a cumulative odds ratio


Easiest to read
Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")


Tests
Likelihood-ratio tests with anova() and drop1(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)


Assumptions
Independent observations; proportional odds (the same slopes at every split)


If proportional odds fails
A partial proportional odds model, clm(..., nominal = ~ x); or a multinomial model

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
A straight line is the wrong shape for most things. Splines bend it, one predictor at a time. A neural network goes further: it adds up many little bent lines, each of which looks at all predictors at once, and it finds out by itself where to bend and which predictors to combine.
That sounds like magic and is ordinary regression: there are parameters (called weights), there is a sum of squared errors, and a computer makes the sum small. The site’s page about handwritten digits uses networks to sort things into classes. Here the network predicts a number: the electrical power of a plant from the weather.
This page writes a network by hand, derivatives included, and finds the same solution as the package. Then it asks the question that matters more than the method: what is a fair test? The answer changes the ranking of the methods.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(nnet)        # nnet(): networks with one hidden layer (comes with R)
library(mgcv)        # bam(): a GAM, to compare with
# also used, with package::function: readxl (read_excel), ranger (ranger), FNN (knn.reg)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

        9568           41

plant <- unique(raw)
summary(plant)


  temperature        vacuum         pressure         humidity          power      
 Min.   : 1.81   Min.   :25.36   Min.   : 992.9   Min.   : 25.56   Min.   :420.3

The data come from a combined cycle power plant (Tüfekci, 2014; Tüfekci & Kaya, 2014), in which gas turbines and a steam turbine work together. Each row is the average of one hour at full load, between 2006 and 2011. The outcome is the net electrical power (MW). The predictors are the temperature of the air (°C), the pressure of the air (mbar), the relative humidity (%), and the exhaust vacuum of the steam turbine (cm Hg). 41 rows are exact copies of others; we drop them, so that no row can be in the training data and in the test at once. 9,527 are left.
Two details of this file will matter later. The file has been shuffled, and there is no date. And the vacuum takes only 634 different values, although it is given with two decimals.

2. Look at the data

Warm air is thin, and a gas turbine gets less of it: temperature alone has a correlation of -0.95 with power. The relationship is nearly straight, with a bend. So a straight line will already do well, and a network can only win by details.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: standardise
Every variable gets mean 0 and SD 1 (with the mean and SD of the training data). Weights of different predictors then have comparable sizes, and the search starts in a sensible region.


Code
standardise <- function(train, d) as.data.frame(scale(d, colMeans(train), apply(train, 2, sd)))
z <- standardise(plant, plant)
X <- as.matrix(z[, c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity")]); y <- z$power




Step 2: one neuron
A neuron takes a weighted sum of the predictors and sends it through an S-shaped function, the logistic function \(\sigma(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})\), the one from logistic regression:
\[h = \sigma(a_0 + a_1 x_1 + \dots + a_K x_K)\]
It is flat on the left, flat on the right and rises in between. The weights decide where the rise is, how steep, and in which direction.


Step 3: the network
The hidden layer has \(J\) neurons. The output is a linear regression on them:
\[\hat y = b_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{J} b_j\, \sigma\!\Big(a_{0j} + \sum_{k=1}^K a_{kj} x_k\Big)\]
That makes \(J(K + 1) + J + 1\) weights: with 4 predictors and 10 neurons, 61. Already a few S-curves add up to all kinds of shapes:


Code
x1 <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)
parts <- data.frame(
  x = rep(x1, 3),
  h = c(1.6 * plogis(-4 + 6 * x1), -2.2 * plogis(1 + 3 * x1), 1.5 * plogis(5 + 4 * x1)),
  neuron = rep(paste("neuron", 1:3), each = 200)
)
ggplot(parts, aes(x, h)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = neuron), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x1, h = tapply(parts$h, rep(1:200, 3), sum)), linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three neurons (dashed) and their sum (black)", x = "x", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()









With enough neurons such a sum can come as close as you like to any continuous function (Hornik et al., 1989). That is a statement about what is possible. It does not say how many neurons or how much data you need, nor that the search will find it.


Step 4: the loss
As in least squares, with a penalty for large weights, called weight decay (\(\lambda\)). It is the penalty of ridge regression:
\[E(w) = \sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + \lambda \sum w^2\]


Step 5: the derivatives (backpropagation)
To go downhill one needs the slope of \(E\) in the direction of every weight. The chain rule gives it, from the output backwards (Rumelhart et al., 1986). With \(r_i = -2(y_i - \hat y_i)\) and the output of neuron \(j\) for row \(i\), \(h_{ij}\):
\[\frac{\partial E}{\partial b_j} = \sum_i r_i\, h_{ij} + 2\lambda b_j, \qquad
\frac{\partial E}{\partial a_{kj}} = \sum_i \underbrace{r_i\, b_j\, h_{ij}(1 - h_{ij})}_{\text{the error of neuron } j}\, x_{ik} + 2\lambda a_{kj}\]


Code
forward <- function(w, X, J) {
  # weights in the order that nnet uses
  K <- ncol(X)
  A <- matrix(w[1:(J * (K + 1))], K + 1)
  b <- w[-(1:(J * (K + 1)))]
  h <- plogis(cbind(1, X) %*% A)
  list(h = h, b = b, yhat = drop(cbind(1, h) %*% b))
}
loss <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) sum((y - forward(w, X, J)$yhat)^2) + decay * sum(w^2)
gradient <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) {
  f <- forward(w, X, J); r <- -2 * (y - f$yhat)
  neuron_error <- (r %o% f$b[-1]) * f$h * (1 - f$h)
  c(crossprod(cbind(1, X), neuron_error), crossprod(cbind(1, f$h), r)) + 2 * decay * w
}
set.seed(202)
w0 <- runif(2 * 5 + 3, -0.7, 0.7) # 2 neurons, 13 weights, a random start
numeric_slope <- sapply(seq_along(w0), function(i) {
  d <- replace(numeric(13), i, 1e-5)
  (loss(w0 + d, X, y, 2, 0.1) - loss(w0 - d, X, y, 2, 0.1)) / 2e-5
})
max(abs(numeric_slope / gradient(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1) - 1))                    # relative difference


[1] 3.351439e-10


The formula and the numerical slopes agree. (Always do this check when you write derivatives yourself.)


Step 6: go downhill
R’s optimiser optim() does the walking. nnet() gets the same start, so that we can compare:


Code
by_hand <- optim(
  w0,
  loss,
  gradient,
  X = X,
  y = y,
  J = 2,
  decay = 0.1,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 1000, abstol = 1e-4, reltol = 1e-8)
)
package <- nnet(X, y, size = 2, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, Wts = w0, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
cbind(
  value = c(
    loss_at_the_start = loss(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1),
    loss_by_hand = by_hand$value,
    loss_nnet = package$value,
    largest_difference_in_the_weights = max(abs(by_hand$par - package$wts))
  )
)


                                         value
loss_at_the_start                 1.928871e+04
loss_by_hand                      5.797301e+02
loss_nnet                         5.797300e+02
largest_difference_in_the_weights 1.312188e-04


The two arrive at the same place.


Two classic mistakes


Code
set.seed(203)
forgot_scaling <- nnet(power ~ ., plant, size = 10, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
forgot_linout  <- nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
c(
  SD_of_power = sd(plant$power),
  RMSE_without_scaling = rmse(predict(forgot_scaling, plant), plant$power),
  RMSE_without_linout = sd(plant$power) * rmse(predict(forgot_linout, z), z$power)
)


         SD_of_power RMSE_without_scaling  RMSE_without_linout 
            17.03908             17.03819             17.03819 


Code
rbind(
  predictions_without_linout = range(predict(forgot_linout, z)),
  outcome_standardised = range(z$power)
)


                                [,1]     [,2]
predictions_without_linout  0.000000 0.000000
outcome_standardised       -1.999868 2.431122


Without standardising, the weighted sums are in the thousands, every neuron is stuck on its flat part, and the network predicts the mean (RMSE 17.0 MW, the SD of power). Without linout = TRUE the output itself goes through the S-function and cannot leave the interval from 0 to 1; here every prediction is 0. No error message in either case.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
4. Different starts, different answers
A network has many minima. First on forty rows, with temperature as the only predictor, so that we can see the curves:


Code
set.seed(204)
forty <- z[sample(nrow(z), 40), ]
grid <- data.frame(temperature = seq(-2.6, 2.9, length.out = 300))
curves <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0, 0.1), function(dc) {
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:4, function(s) {
        set.seed(s)
        m <- nnet(
          power ~ temperature,
          forty,
          size = 15,
          decay = dc,
          linout = TRUE,
          trace = FALSE,
          maxit = 2000
        )
        data.frame(
          temperature = grid$temperature,
          power = drop(predict(m, grid)),
          start = s,
          train_rmse = rmse(predict(m, forty), forty$power),
          setting = ifelse(dc == 0, "no decay", "decay 0.1")
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
back <- function(v, name) v * sd(plant[[name]]) + mean(plant[[name]])
ggplot(
  curves,
  aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power"), group = start, colour = factor(start))
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    data = forty,
    aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power")),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~setting) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(415, 505)) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "15 neurons on 40 hours, four random starts each",
    x = "temperature (°C)",
    y = "power (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
aggregate(train_rmse ~ setting, curves, function(v) round(range(v) * sd(plant$power), 2))


    setting train_rmse.1 train_rmse.2
1 decay 0.1         3.95         3.95
2  no decay         1.58         2.46


With 46 weights and 40 points the network without decay runs through the gaps as it likes: four starts, four curves, and the differences are largest where there are few data. A little decay makes the four curves the same. Now with all rows and all predictors:


Code
fits <- lapply(1:6, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 600)
})
loss_values <- sapply(fits, function(m) m$value)
preds <- sapply(fits, function(m) back(drop(predict(m, z)), "power"))
round(loss_values, 1)


[1] 542.3 544.7 545.7 544.7 542.4 545.8


Code
cbind(
  value = c(
    largest_difference_in_a_weight = max(apply(sapply(fits, function(m) m$wts), 1, function(v) {
      diff(range(v))
    })),
    typical_SD_between_the_predictions = mean(apply(preds, 1, sd)),
    RMSE_of_the_first = rmse(preds[, 1], plant$power)
  )
)


                                       value
largest_difference_in_a_weight     5.9772949
typical_SD_between_the_predictions 0.4560367
RMSE_of_the_first                  4.0272418


Six starts end at different places (loss between 542.3 and 545.8), with quite different weights. But the predictions differ by only 0.46 MW on average. So single weights mean nothing, and nobody should interpret them. The predictions are what one can use. Averaging the predictions of several networks (an ensemble) makes them more stable; section 6 shows by how much.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
5. What is a fair test?
How many neurons? The usual recipe is cross-validation with random folds. But look at the data again. 99.5% of the rows share their value of the vacuum, to two decimals, with other rows: 634 values in 9,527 hours. The most likely explanation is that the vacuum was recorded less often than the rest, and that rows with the same value come from the same period. The file does not say, and its order is destroyed. But if so, then random folds put hours of the same period in the training data and in the test. A method that remembers its neighbours would be rewarded for remembering.
So we use two kinds of folds: random rows, and whole groups of rows with the same vacuum, so that the test has conditions that the model has never seen.


Code
set.seed(205)
group   <- as.integer(factor(plant$vacuum)); n_group <- max(group)
folds3 <- list(
  random = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
net_predict <- function(train, test, size, decay, starts = 1, maxit = 400) {
  a <- standardise(train, train)
  b <- standardise(train, test)
  p <- sapply(starts, function(s) {
    set.seed(s)
    drop(predict(
      nnet(
        power ~ .,
        a,
        size = size,
        decay = decay,
        linout = TRUE,
        trace = FALSE,
        maxit = maxit,
        MaxNWts = 5000
      ),
      b
    ))
  })
  mean(train$power) + sd(train$power) * p
}
grid <- expand.grid(size = c(2, 5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.01, 0.1, 1))
cv <- do.call(
  cbind,
  lapply(folds3, function(f) {
    sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
      e <- numeric(nrow(plant))
      for (k in 1:3) {
        e[f == k] <- net_predict(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ], grid$size[i], grid$decay[i])[,
          1
        ] -
          plant$power[f == k]
      }
      sqrt(mean(e^2))
    })
  })
)
print(round(cbind(grid, cv), 3), row.names = FALSE)


 size decay random new conditions
    2  0.01  4.203          4.251
    5  0.01  4.167          4.277
   10  0.01  4.048          4.306
   20  0.01  3.970          4.368
    2  0.10  4.202          4.251
    5  0.10  4.169          4.272
   10  0.10  4.066          4.300
   20  0.10  4.015          4.322
    2  1.00  4.213          4.271
    5  1.00  4.202          4.286
   10  1.00  4.198          4.280
   20  1.00  4.184          4.276




Code
cv_long <- data.frame(
  size = rep(grid$size, 2),
  decay = factor(rep(grid$decay, 2)),
  rmse = as.vector(cv),
  folds = rep(colnames(cv), each = nrow(grid))
)
ggplot(cv_long, aes(size, rmse, colour = decay)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 5, 10, 20)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of the network against its size, for two kinds of folds",
    x = "neurons",
    y = "RMSE (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
best_r <- grid[which.min(cv[, "random"]), ]; best_g <- grid[which.min(cv[, "new conditions"]), ]
rbind(
  random = cbind(best_r, rmse = min(cv[, "random"])),
  `new conditions` = cbind(best_g, rmse = min(cv[, "new conditions"]))
)


               size decay     rmse
random           20  0.01 3.969926
new conditions    2  0.10 4.250756


With random folds the larger networks keep getting better, and the best has 20 neurons and a decay of 0.01. With new conditions they get worse, unless a strong decay holds them back, and the best has 2 neurons. All settings lie between 4.25 and 4.37 MW. What the larger networks gained with random folds was mostly memory of the vacuum values in the data.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
6. The network against others
Both kinds of folds again, with new folds, for seven methods: a straight line, a GAM, the 5 nearest neighbours, a random forest, the small network that the second kind of folds chose (2 neurons, decay 0.1), the large one that random folds chose (20 neurons, decay 0.01), and the average of three such large networks.


Code
set.seed(206)
folds5 <- list(
  `random folds` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
methods <- function(train, test) {
  zt <- standardise(train, train)
  zn <- standardise(train, test)
  large <- net_predict(train, test, best_r$size, best_r$decay, starts = 1:3)
  cbind(
    `straight line` = predict(lm(power ~ ., train), test),
    GAM = as.numeric(predict(
      bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = train),
      test
    )),
    `nearest neighbours` = FNN::knn.reg(zt[, 1:4], zn[, 1:4], train$power, k = 5)$pred,
    `random forest` = predict(
      ranger::ranger(power ~ ., train, num.trees = 300, seed = 1),
      test
    )$predictions,
    `small network` = net_predict(train, test, best_g$size, best_g$decay)[, 1],
    `large network` = large[, 1],
    `3 large networks, averaged` = rowMeans(large)
  )
}
results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(folds5), function(kind) {
    f <- folds5[[kind]]
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:5, function(k) {
        p <- methods(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ])
        data.frame(
          folds = kind,
          fold = k,
          method = colnames(p),
          rmse = apply(p, 2, rmse, plant$power[f == k]),
          mse = apply(p, 2, function(v) sum((v - plant$power[f == k])^2))
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
total <- aggregate(mse ~ method + folds, results, sum); total$rmse <- sqrt(total$mse / nrow(plant))
wide <- reshape(
  total[, c("method", "folds", "rmse")],
  idvar = "method",
  timevar = "folds",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(wide) <- c("method", "new", "random")
wide <- wide[order(wide$new), ]
print(
  data.frame(
    method = wide$method,
    random_folds = round(wide$random, 2),
    new_conditions = round(wide$new, 2)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)


                     method random_folds new_conditions
 3 large networks, averaged         3.90           4.21
              small network         4.20           4.23
                        GAM         4.17           4.24
              large network         3.96           4.33
              random forest         3.22           4.43
              straight line         4.56           4.58
         nearest neighbours         3.79           4.80




Code
results$method <- factor(results$method, levels = rev(wide$method[order(wide$random)]))
ggplot(results, aes(rmse, method)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = transform(total, method = factor(method, levels = levels(results$method))),
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of seven methods, two kinds of folds",
    subtitle = "Orange: all rows. Blue: single folds",
    x = "RMSE (MW)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")









Code
w  <- function(m, v) wide[[v]][wide$method == m]
by_fold <- function(m) subset(results, folds == "new conditions" & method == m)$rmse
cbind(
  value = c(
    folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest = sum(
      by_fold("small network") < by_fold("random forest")
    ),
    folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network = sum(
      by_fold("3 large networks, averaged") < by_fold("large network")
    )
  )
)


                                                   value
folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest      4
folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network     4



With random folds the random forest wins by far: 3.22 MW, against 3.90 for the averaged large networks, 4.17 for the GAM and 4.56 for the straight line. (In the paper that introduced the data, bagged trees came first among many methods, with an RMSE of 3.79 MW and folds of shuffled rows; Tüfekci, 2014.)
With new conditions the order is another one. The averaged large networks (4.21), the small network (4.23) and the GAM (4.24) are practically tied; the forest has 4.43, the straight line 4.58. The small network beats the forest in 4 of the 5 folds. The nearest neighbours, which were well ahead of the straight line before, are the last with 4.80.
The stiff methods (straight line, GAM, small network) have nearly the same error in both tests, for example 4.17 and 4.24 for the GAM. They cannot remember single periods. The flexible ones lose a lot: the forest goes from 3.22 to 4.43, the large network from 3.96 to 4.33.
Averaging three large networks changed the error from 4.33 to 4.21 (new conditions) and from 3.96 to 3.90 (random folds): it helped, at three times the cost.

Which of the two tests is right? It depends on the use. To fill a missing hour in the past, random folds. To forecast the power of next week, the second, and even that may be too kind, since vacuum values close to the left-out ones are still in the training data. Choose the folds so that the test is like the use.
The gain from all that flexibility is modest here. From the straight line to the best method with new conditions, the RMSE falls from 4.58 to 4.21 MW.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
7. What has the network learned?
The partial dependence of a predictor: set it to a value in every row, predict, and average. For three large networks, the small one and the GAM:


Code
set.seed(207); bg <- plant[sample(nrow(plant), 400), ]; zbg <- standardise(plant, bg)
one_net <- function(size, decay, s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = size, decay = decay, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
}
nets <- c(
  lapply(1:3, function(s) one_net(best_r$size, best_r$decay, s)),
  list(one_net(best_g$size, best_g$decay, 1))
)
gam_all <- bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = plant)
pd <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity"), function(v) {
    q <- seq(quantile(plant[[v]], 0.01), quantile(plant[[v]], 0.99), length.out = 25)
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(q, function(x0) {
        b2 <- bg
        b2[[v]] <- x0
        zb <- standardise(plant, b2)
        data.frame(
          predictor = v,
          x = x0,
          model = c(paste("large", 1:3), "small", "GAM"),
          power = c(
            sapply(nets, function(m) mean(back(drop(predict(m, zb)), "power"))),
            mean(predict(gam_all, b2))
          )
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
pd$kind <- factor(
  ifelse(
    grepl("large", pd$model),
    "three large networks",
    ifelse(pd$model == "small", "small network", "GAM")
  ),
  levels = c("three large networks", "small network", "GAM")
)
ggplot(pd, aes(x, power, group = model, colour = kind, linewidth = kind)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(0.5, 1, 1), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence of power on each predictor", x = NULL, y = "power (MW)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
span <- function(v, m) { p <- subset(pd, predictor == v & model == m); diff(range(p$power)) }
spans <- sapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "humidity", "pressure"), function(v) {
  sapply(c("small", "GAM", "large 1"), function(m) span(v, m))
})
round(spans, 1)


        temperature vacuum humidity pressure
small          50.9   11.3      6.3      4.4
GAM            48.3   10.3      6.7      2.9
large 1        42.5   15.0      7.2      2.5


In the small network, temperature moves the power by 50.9 MW over its range (from the 1st to the 99th percentile), the vacuum by 11.3, humidity by 6.3 and air pressure by 4.4. The GAM draws nearly the same curves. The three large networks agree with them in the middle and fan out at the ends, where rows are few and where partial dependence asks for combinations that hardly occur (a cold hour with a high vacuum). When a network and a GAM show the same picture, the GAM is the better story: it can be written down, and it comes with intervals.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Standardise the predictors and the outcome, with the means and SDs of the training data. In R’s nnet() add linout = TRUE for a number.
Try several starts, set the seed, and average the predictions.
Use decay (or stop early). With enough of it the exact number of neurons matters little.
Choose with folds that look like the use: groups, sites, times, persons.
Small tables: for a few thousand rows and a handful of predictors, trees (random forest, boosting), GAMs and Gaussian processes are usually as good and less work. Networks pay off with images, sound, text and very many rows.
Deeper networks have several hidden layers and other functions (ReLU instead of \(\sigma\)), and are trained on small batches with packages such as torch or keras3. The principles on this page are the same.
Outside the data S-curves become flat, so the network predicts a constant. It never says that it does not know. (Gaussian processes do, with the limits shown there.)
No intervals and no tests come with it. Use the bootstrap, ensembles or conformal prediction for intervals.
Weights are not effects. Report partial dependence instead, and remember that predictors that belong together (temperature and vacuum, r = 0.84) make partial dependence an average over combinations that never occur.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the data and any dropped rows, the standardisation, the architecture and the number of weights, the loss, decay, optimiser and number of starts, how the settings were chosen, how the test was made, and the comparison with simple models. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(Method = wide$method, random = f2(wide$random), new = f2(wide$new))
n_weights <- function(size) size * 6 + 1


Method (data analysis):

The net hourly electrical power of a combined cycle power plant (N = 9,527 hours at full load, after removing 41 exact duplicates; Tüfekci, 2014) was predicted from air temperature, air pressure, relative humidity and exhaust vacuum. Neural networks with one hidden layer (logistic units, linear output) were fitted to standardised variables by minimising the sum of squared errors with a weight-decay penalty, with the quasi-Newton optimiser of the R package nnet (Venables & Ripley, 2002). Because the vacuum takes only 634 different values and hours with the same value probably come from the same period, cross-validation was done in two ways: with random folds and with folds of whole vacuum values. The number of hidden units (2–20) and the decay (0.01–1) were chosen by 3-fold cross-validation, which gave 20 units (121 weights) and a decay of 0.01 with random folds, and 2 units (13 weights) and a decay of 0.1 with folds of whole vacuum values. Both networks, the average of three large ones from different random starts, linear regression, a generalized additive model, 5-nearest neighbours, and a random forest were then compared with 5-fold cross-validation on new folds. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

With random folds, the random forest had the lowest root mean squared error (RMSE = 3.22 MW; Table 1). With folds of whole vacuum values, its error was 4.43 MW, and the average of three large networks (4.21 MW), the small network (4.23 MW) and the generalized additive model (4.24 MW) were more accurate, with practically the same error; linear regression had an error of 4.58 MW. A single large network went from 3.96 to 4.33 MW. In the small network, the partial dependence of power on temperature spanned 50.9 MW, on the vacuum 11.3 MW.

Points to remember:

Report the size, the decay, the number of starts and the seeds.
Report a simple model next to the network.
Say how the folds were made, and why.
Do not interpret single weights.

title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
text:
10. Summary



When
Many rows, many predictors, unknown shapes and interactions, prediction is the goal


The model
\(\hat y = b_0 + \sum_j b_j\,\sigma(a_{0j} + \sum_k a_{kj}x_k)\)


Loss
Squared errors plus \(\lambda\sum w^2\)


Derivatives
Chain rule, backwards: backpropagation


Settings
Number of neurons, decay; several starts; average


How (R)
nnet::nnet(y ~ ., size = , decay = , linout = TRUE, maxit = ) on standardised data


Check
Cross-validation with folds that look like the use; a simple model as comparison


Danger
Not scaled, no linout, one start, random folds for grouped data


Related pages
Splines and GAMs, Gaussian processes, nearest neighbours, handwritten digits

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
In 2025 the US federal government lost staff in several ways at once. In January, most federal employees were offered a deferred resignation: stop working, stay on the payroll until 30 September 2025, then resign. Agencies offered early retirement, carried out reductions in force (layoffs) and dismissed staff. And people kept quitting and retiring, as they do every year.
So everyone who left federal service in 2025 left in one of six ways. This page asks: among the people who left, what made one way of leaving more likely than another? Did the young quit and the old retire? Who took the deferred resignation? Who was laid off?
The outcome is a category with six values and no natural order: quitting is not “more” or “less” than being laid off. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:



Outcome
Regression
Example




Two categories
logistic
hired or not


Ordered categories
ordinal logistic
a performance rating from 1 to 5


Unordered categories
multinomial logistic
how someone left: quit, retired, laid off…



A multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the reference and fits a logistic regression of each of the other categories against it, all at the same time. The data are real: the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) publishes a record for every federal employee who leaves.


Code
library(nnet)         # multinom(): multinomial logistic regression (comes with R)
library(nanoparquet)  # read_parquet(): reads the Parquet files that OPM publishes
library(ggplot2)

# one colour per way of leaving, the same in every chart
exits   <- c("Quit", "Retired", "Early retirement", "Deferred resignation", "Laid off", "Terminated")
colours <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300"), exits)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "white", "white", "#0b0b0b", "white", "white"), exits)  # labels on the bars

# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rr   <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
                           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))                   # relative risk ratios

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
1. The data
OPM’s Federal Workforce Data has a file for every month with one row per separation: a civilian employee leaving federal service. Each row says how the person left, their age group, years of service, agency, occupation, type of appointment and more. The files are free, need no login, and come through an API as Parquet files of one to four MB.
A monthly file holds the separations processed in that month, and some of them took effect months earlier: separations of September 2025 were still arriving in 2026. So we download every file from October 2023 to the latest one, and sort the separations by the date they took effect.


Code
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads

# the list of monthly files, with the current version of each
files <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations?current=true")
files <- files[as.integer(files$year) * 100 + as.integer(files$month) >= 202310, ]
latest <- max(as.Date(paste(files$year, files$month, "01", sep = "-")))

# the columns we need, out of the 69 in each file
columns <- c("personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm", "separation_category", "drp_indicator",
             "age_bracket", "length_of_service_years", "supervisory_status",
             "appointment_type", "stem_occupation")

# one month: download the file and read the columns; try again if OPM asks us to slow down
read_month <- function(year, month, version) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations/%s/%s/%s/download", year, month, version)
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    ok <- tryCatch(download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (ok) break
    Sys.sleep(10 * attempt)
  }
  if (!ok) stop("Could not download ", url)
  as.data.frame(read_parquet(path, col_select = columns))
}

raw <- do.call(rbind, Map(read_month, files$year, files$month, files$version))
nrow(raw)


[1] 808769


That is 36 monthly files, up to September 2026. The US federal fiscal year runs from October to September: fiscal year 2025 (FY2025) is October 2024 to September 2025. We keep FY2024, a year before the changes, and FY2025:


Code
ym <- as.integer(raw$personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm)   # e.g. 202509 = September 2025
raw$month       <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", ym %/% 100, ym %% 100))
raw$fiscal_year <- ym %/% 100 + (ym %% 100 >= 10)              # October 2024 to September 2025 = 2025

d <- subset(raw, fiscal_year %in% 2024:2025)
table(d$separation_category, d$fiscal_year)

On paper, most people who took the deferred resignation quit or retired. But they took a different route from people who quit or retired in the ordinary way, so we give them a category of their own. The six ways of leaving:








Way of leaving
OPM category
What it means




Quit
QUIT
Resigned


Retired
RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY, RETIREMENT - OTHER
Retired on a pension


Early retirement
RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT
Took the agency’s offer of an early pension: age 50 with 20 years of service, or any age with 25 years


Deferred resignation
any of the above with drp_indicator = Y
Accepted the 2025 offer; most left on 30 September 2025


Laid off
REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)
The position was abolished


Terminated
TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)
A temporary appointment ended, or the agency ended the employment, for example during the probationary period



We leave out transfers to another agency (those people are still federal employees) and “other separation”, which includes deaths.


Code
exit <- c("QUIT"                             = "Quit",
          "RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY"           = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - OTHER"               = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT"           = "Early retirement",
          "REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)"         = "Laid off",
          "TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)" = "Terminated")[d$separation_category]
exit[!is.na(exit) & d$drp_indicator %in% "Y"] <- "Deferred resignation"
d$exit <- factor(exit, levels = exits)
d <- subset(d, !is.na(exit))     # drops the transfers and the other separations


The predictors are five characteristics of each person. Years of service are cut where the rules change: the first year is usually a probationary period, early retirement needs 20 or 25 years, and a full pension needs, for example, 30 years from age 55 to 57 or 20 years at age 60.


Code
age <- ifelse(d$age_bracket %in% c("LESS THAN 20", "20-24"), "Under 25",
       ifelse(d$age_bracket == "65 OR MORE", "65+", d$age_bracket))
d$age <- factor(age, levels = c("Under 25", "25-29", "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49",
                                "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65+"))

years <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d$length_of_service_years))
years[years > 60] <- NA          # a few impossible values (up to 1,800 years of service)
d$service <- cut(years, c(-Inf, 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                 labels = c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"))

# supervisors and managers; team leaders count as non-supervisors
supervisors  <- c("SUPERVISOR OR MANAGER", "SUPERVISOR (CSRA)", "MANAGEMENT OFFICIAL (CSRA)")
d$supervisor <- factor(ifelse(d$supervisory_status == "INVALID", NA,
                              ifelse(d$supervisory_status %in% supervisors, "Yes", "No")),
                       levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# a permanent or a temporary (nonpermanent) appointment
d$permanent <- factor(ifelse(d$appointment_type == "INVALID", NA,
                             ifelse(grepl("NONPERMANENT", d$appointment_type), "No", "Yes")),
                      levels = c("Yes", "No"))

# STEM, health or other occupations; "UNSPECIFIED" becomes NA
d$occupation <- factor(c("ALL OTHER OCCUPATIONS" = "Other", "STEM OCCUPATIONS" = "STEM",
                         "HEALTH OCCUPATIONS" = "Health")[d$stem_occupation],
                       levels = c("Other", "STEM", "Health"))

vars <- c("exit", "age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation")
d    <- d[complete.cases(d[vars]), ]
fy25 <- subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025)
table(d$fiscal_year)

172225 329911

Code
share      <- function(group) prop.table(table(fy25[[group]], fy25$exit), 1)
by_age     <- share("age")
by_service <- share("service")
by_job     <- share("occupation")
middle     <- c("30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59", "60-64")



Quitting is the usual way out up to age 45; from 50 on, people retire.
Early retirement happens at 50 to 59 and with 20 to 29 years of service: the eligibility rules.
The deferred resignation is the odd one: between 32% and 38% of the people in every age group from 30 to 64 took it, and a similar share at every length of service from one year up. Ordinary quitting and retiring each belong to one end of a career; the deferred resignation drew from all of it.
Layoffs hit the middle of careers: 8.7% of the people aged 45 to 49 who left, 7.6% of those with 10 to 19 years of service.
Terminations belong to the young and the new: 36% of the people under 25 and 35% of those with less than a year of service.
Occupations differ too: only 4.5% of the people in health occupations took the deferred resignation, against 45% in STEM and 34% in other occupations. Agencies could exclude positions from the offer.

Age and years of service go together, so these charts cannot tell whether age or service drives an exit. The model can: it estimates each effect holding the others constant.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a reference category
Choose one way of leaving as the yardstick. We use Quit, an ordinary resignation: every other way of leaving is compared with quitting. Any category could be the reference; the predicted probabilities are the same, only the comparisons in the output change. In R the reference is the first level of the factor (levels(fy25$exit)[1] is Quit), and relevel() changes it.


Step 2: one equation for every other category
For person \(i\) and each way of leaving \(k\) other than quitting:
\[\eta_{ik} = \ln\frac{P(\text{exit}_i = k)}{P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit})} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_{pk}x_{pi}\]
That is five equations, each with its own intercept and its own slopes. The left side is the log of the relative risk: how much more likely leaving by \(k\) is than quitting. Each equation looks like a logistic regression; the difference is that the five are estimated together, so that every person’s six probabilities add up to 1.


Step 3: from the equations to probabilities
\[P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit}) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}} \qquad P(\text{exit}_i = k) = \frac{e^{\eta_{ik}}}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}}\]
The sums run over the five categories other than Quit. Each probability is between 0 and 1, and the six add up to 1. This is the softmax function, the same formula that neural networks use to classify.


Step 4: what a coefficient means
\(e^{\beta}\) is the relative risk ratio (RRR): the number by which the ratio \(P(k)/P(\text{Quit})\) is multiplied when the predictor moves from its reference level to this level, with the other predictors held constant. An RRR of 2 means twice as likely to leave by \(k\) rather than by quitting. Some books and programs call it an odds ratio; either way it compares two categories with each other, not one category with all the others.


Step 5: how R finds the β’s
By maximum likelihood: R looks for the \(\beta\)’s that make the exits that people actually took as probable as possible,
\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(\text{exit}_i = \text{the exit that person } i \text{ took})\]
multinom() maximises it. It fits the model as a neural network without a hidden layer, which is why it lives in the package nnet.


Step 6: count the parameters
A predictor with \(c\) categories gets \(c - 1\) coefficients: age has 10 groups (9 coefficients), service 7 (6), supervisor and appointment 2 each (1 each) and occupation 3 (2). That is 19 slopes plus an intercept, 20 per equation, and 5 equations make 100 parameters. Multinomial models grow fast: every category needs enough people for a whole set of coefficients of its own.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
text:
4. Fitting the model
Every predictor is a category, so the 329,911 people fall into a limited number of combinations of age group, service, supervisor, appointment, occupation and exit. Fitting the model to the count of people in each combination gives the same estimates as fitting the people one by one: 300 people with the same values add the same term to the log-likelihood 300 times, which is what weights = Freq does. It takes a second instead of minutes.


Code
g <- as.data.frame(table(fy25[vars]))   # one row per combination; Freq = the number of people
g <- subset(g, Freq > 0)
nrow(g)


[1] 2416


Code
fit <- multinom(exit ~ age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation,
                data = g, weights = Freq, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)

s    <- summary(fit)
b    <- coef(fit)                      # one row per way of leaving, one column per term
se   <- s$standard.errors
z    <- b / se
p    <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))             # summary() prints no p values: compute them
rrr  <- exp(b)                         # relative risk ratios
low  <- exp(b - qnorm(0.975) * se)     # their 95% confidence intervals
high <- exp(b + qnorm(0.975) * se)

Meaning
Here

One row per way of leaving, compared with Quit; one column per predictor level. Each number is \(b\): the change in the log relative risk

The standard error of each \(b\); smaller is more precise
0.03

\(-2 \ln L\): how badly the model fits; smaller is better. Used for the tests in section 6
638,895


AIC
The deviance plus 2 for every parameter, for comparing models fitted to the same data
639,095




There are no p values. Compute them as above: \(z = b / SE\), and \(p\) from the normal distribution. For supervisorYes in the row Laid off, z = 13.43, p < .001.
The intercepts are the log relative risks of the reference person: under 25, less than a year of service, not a supervisor, on a permanent appointment, in an occupation that is neither STEM nor health.

They are common with categorical predictors and say little on their own; the predicted probabilities of section 5 are easier to read.
Every coefficient compares with Quit. supervisorYes in the row Laid off says nothing about being laid off rather than retiring. For that comparison, subtract the two rows, b(Laid off) − b(Retired), or change the reference with relevel() and fit again.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
section: 5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model
text:
5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model
A relative risk ratio compares two exits; a predicted probability says how likely each exit is for a given kind of person. Six typical people, along a career:


Code
career <- people(age        = c("25-29", "25-29", "35-39", "45-49", "55-59", "60-64"),
                 service    = c("1-4",   "1-4",   "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"),
                 supervisor = "No",
                 permanent  = c("Yes",   "No",    "Yes",   "Yes",   "Yes",   "Yes"),
                 occupation = "Other")
label <- c("25-29, 1-4 years", "25-29, 1-4 years, temporary", "35-39, 10-19 years",
           "45-49, 20-24 years", "55-59, 25-29 years", "60-64, 30+ years")
probs <- predict(fit, newdata = career, type = "probs")

m <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(label, ncol(probs)), levels = label),
                exit  = factor(rep(colnames(probs), each = nrow(probs)), levels = exits),
                share = as.vector(probs))
stacked(m, "age, years of service", "predicted probability of each way of leaving, FY2025")









Code
rownames(probs) <- label



Early in a career (25 to 29, one to four years) people quit or took the deferred resignation: 49% and 46%.
The same person on a temporary appointment was most likely terminated (52%): the appointment ran out.
In mid-career the risk of being laid off was at its highest: 11% at 35 to 39 with 10 to 19 years of service, 9% at 45 to 49 with 20 to 24 years.
With 25 to 29 years of service at 55 to 59, early retirement became a real option (24%), next to an ordinary retirement (35%) and the deferred resignation (37%).
At 60 to 64 with 30 years or more, people mostly retired (66%).

These are probabilities for a person who left. They do not say how likely such a person was to leave at all: the data hold only the people who left.

section: 6. Testing the predictors and the model
text:
6. Testing the predictors and the model
The likelihood-ratio test compares the deviances of two nested models. First the whole model against a model with no predictors, then each predictor: fit the model without it and see how much worse it gets.


Code
null <- multinom(exit ~ 1, data = g, weights = Freq, trace = FALSE)
model_test <- anova(null, fit)
model_test


                                                Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df LR stat. Pr(Chi)
1                                                   1     12075   990841.8           NA       NA      NA
2 age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation     11980   638894.9 1 vs 2    95 351946.9       0


Code
tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation"), function(v) {
  a <- anova(update(fit, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", v))), fit)
  data.frame(predictor = v, chi_square = round(a$"LR stat."[2], 1), df = a$"   Df"[2],
             p = format.pval(a$"Pr(Chi)"[2], eps = 0.001))
}))
tests


   predictor chi_square df       p
1        age    55481.1 45 < 0.001
2    service    55065.8 30 < 0.001
3 supervisor      664.2  5 < 0.001
4  permanent    68523.4  5 < 0.001
5 occupation    15478.5 10 < 0.001


Code
mcfadden <- 1 - deviance(fit) / deviance(null)   # McFadden's pseudo-R squared
mcfadden


[1] 0.3551999


Code
ranked <- unname(c(age = "age", service = "years of service", supervisor = "supervisor status",
                   permanent = "appointment type", occupation = "occupation")[tests$predictor[order(-tests$chi_square)]])



Every predictor is significant: with 329,911 people even a tiny effect is. The \(\chi^2\) values show which predictors matter most: appointment type, age and years of service; supervisor status matters least. The degrees of freedom are the coefficients a predictor adds to all five equations: 9 age groups × 5 = 45.
McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = 0.36: one minus the deviance of the model divided by the deviance of the model with no predictors. It is not a share of explained variance and it runs much lower than the \(R^2\) of a linear regression; use it to compare models fitted to the same data.

How often does the model name the right exit, if it picks the most likely one for each person?


Code
predicted <- factor(colnames(fitted(fit))[max.col(fitted(fit), ties.method = "first")], levels = exits)
accuracy  <- weighted.mean(predicted == g$exit, g$Freq)
base_rate <- max(prop.table(table(fy25$exit)))   # always guessing the most common exit
c(model = accuracy, most_common_exit = base_rate)


           model most_common_exit 
       0.5502969        0.3332353

round(100 * prop.table(xtabs(Freq ~ exit + predicted, data = cbind(g, predicted)), 1))

exit                   Quit Retired Early retirement Deferred resignation Laid off Terminated
  Quit                   57       1                0                   24        0         18
  Retired                 1      79                0                   19        0          1
  Early retirement        0      21                1                   77        0          1
  Deferred resignation   29      28                0                   39        0          5
  Laid off               35       4                0                   54        0          7
  Terminated             14       1                0                    5        0         81


The model names the right exit for 55% of the people, against 33% for always guessing the most common one. But it almost never predicts an early retirement or a layoff, even though it knows who is most at risk of them: these exits are rare, so for almost nobody are they the most likely one. Accuracy is a poor guide when some categories are rare, as Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome shows; the predicted probabilities carry the information.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
section: 7. An assumption to check: independence of irrelevant alternatives
text:
7. An assumption to check: independence of irrelevant alternatives
The model assumes that the ratio of two probabilities, for example \(P(\text{Retired}) / P(\text{Quit})\), does not depend on what other ways of leaving there are: the independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA). The textbook example: a city adds a blue bus identical to its red bus. IIA predicts that the blue bus takes passengers from cars and from the red bus in proportion; in reality it takes them almost only from the red bus.
The deferred resignation was a new way of leaving in 2025. Under IIA it drew people from the other exits in proportion. A simple check: fit the model again without it, that is without the category and without the people who took it, and compare the coefficients that remain. If IIA holds, they hardly change.

g2   <- droplevels(subset(g, exit != "Deferred resignation"))
fit2 <- update(fit, data = g2)

show <- c("age55-59", "age60-64", "service25-29", "service30+", "supervisorYes", "permanentNo")
iia  <- expand.grid(term = show, exit = rownames(coef(fit2)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
iia$all_six   <- exp(coef(fit)[cbind(iia$exit, iia$term)])
iia$without   <- exp(coef(fit2)[cbind(iia$exit, iia$term)])
knitr::kable(data.frame(exit = iia$exit, term = iia$term, rr(iia$all_six), rr(iia$without)),

The coefficients of retirement and early retirement move a lot: for 25 to 29 years of service, the RRR of retiring rather than quitting goes from 671 to 1,980. Those of layoffs and terminations move much less (a typical change of 12% and 11%, against 110% for retirement). So IIA is doubtful for the exits that are close to the deferred resignation. Models that relax it, the nested logit (similar exits share a “nest”) and the mixed logit, are in the package mlogit (Croissant, 2020). The formal version of this check, the Hausman–McFadden test (mlogit::hmftest()), would flag even trivial differences with this many people; the size of the changes tells more.
Three more things to keep in mind:

People in the same agency are not independent. Layoffs and early-retirement offers were decided agency by agency, so the standard errors above are too small. Agency as a predictor, or a multilevel multinomial model, would take this into account.
Only people who left. The model compares ways of leaving among the people who left; it says nothing about the people who stayed. Whether supervisors were more likely to leave at all needs the employment files too, which OPM also publishes.
The data keep changing. OPM calls the newest data preliminary, and late reports keep arriving: run this page again in a few months and the counts will be a little higher.

title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its reference category, the predictors, the model test and the relative risk ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:


Code
n_model <- sum(g$Freq)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci      <- function(k, t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(low[k, t]), ", ", f2(high[k, t]), "]")
# the cells of Table 1 whose p is .001 or more, for the note under it
big_p   <- which(p[, names(terms)] >= .001, arr.ind = TRUE)
p_note  <- if (nrow(big_p) == 0) "All *p* < .001." else
  paste0("All *p* < .001 except ", paste0(terms[colnames(p[, names(terms)])[big_p[, "col"]]], ", ",
         tolower(rownames(p)[big_p[, "row"]]), ": *p* ", sapply(p[, names(terms)][big_p], pval),
         collapse = "; "), ".")


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 329,911 separations from the US federal civil service that took effect in fiscal year 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), as recorded in the Federal Workforce Data of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (2026), excluding transfers between agencies, other separations and records with missing predictors. The way of leaving (quit, retirement, early retirement, deferred resignation, reduction in force, termination) was analysed with a multinomial logistic regression, with quitting as the reference category and age group, years of service, supervisory status, appointment type (permanent or temporary) and occupation group (STEM, health, other) as predictors. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the nnet package (Venables & Ripley, 2002).

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over an intercept-only model, χ²(95) = 351,947, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .36. Holding the other predictors constant, supervisors were more likely than non-supervisors to be laid off rather than to quit, RRR = 1.49, 95% CI [1.40, 1.57], employees on temporary appointments were more likely to be terminated rather than to quit, RRR = 22.39, 95% CI [21.62, 23.20], and employees in health occupations were less likely to take the deferred resignation rather than to quit, RRR = 0.08, 95% CI [0.08, 0.09] (Table 1). Compared with employees with less than a year of service, those with 25 to 29 years were more likely to take the deferred resignation rather than to quit, RRR = 33.93, 95% CI [30.72, 37.48].
