Points to remember:

Name the reference category: every coefficient compares with it.
Report relative risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
With hundreds of thousands of people every p is tiny: report the size of the effects, and predicted probabilities where they help.
Say which categories you merged or left out, and why.
Cite R and the packages; citation("nnet") gives the reference.

text:
9. Summary



When
The outcome is a category with three or more values and no order


Why not separate logistic regressions
Their probabilities do not add up to 1, and there is no single test of a predictor


Why not ordinal logistic regression
The categories have no order


How (R)
nnet::multinom(y ~ x, data); with counts per combination of values, weights = n


Output
One equation per category against the reference; exp() of a coefficient is a relative risk ratio


Easiest to read
Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")


Tests
Likelihood-ratio tests with anova(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)


Assumptions
Independent observations; independence of irrelevant alternatives; enough people in every category for its own set of coefficients


If IIA fails
A nested or mixed logit, with mlogit

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
A female lawyer loses a promotion to a less qualified male colleague. In one version of the story she protests the decision; in the other she accepts it. Do people like her more or less when she protests?
Garcia, Schmitt, Branscombe and Ellemers (2010) asked 129 women to read one of the versions, chosen at random, and to rate how much they liked the lawyer. Two other questions make the data interesting:

When does protesting pay off? The answer may depend on who is judging: on how common the reader believes sex discrimination to be. That is a question of moderation.
Why does protesting change how much she is liked? Perhaps because readers judge protest to be an appropriate response, and like people who respond appropriately. That is a question of mediation.










Moderation
Mediation




Question
When, or for whom, does X affect Y?
How, or why, does X affect Y?


The third variable
A moderator W changes the size or direction of the effect of X
A mediator M carries the effect: X changes M, and M changes Y


In a model
An interaction X × W
Two regressions and the product of two paths, \(a \times b\)


Here
Does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?
Does protest raise liking by making her response seem more appropriate?





Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(boot)       # bootstrap confidence intervals
library(lavaan)     # the mediation model as a path model




Code
# a path diagram: boxes, arrows between them, and labels on the arrows
draw_paths <- function(boxes, arrows, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_label(data = boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, fill = "white",
               label.padding = unit(0.45, "lines"), lineheight = 0.9) +
    geom_text(data = arrows, aes(lx, ly, label = label), size = 3.8, colour = "#E74C3C", fontface = "bold") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.5, 6)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle)
}
moderation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Perceived sexism\n(W)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.7, 5), y = c(1.5, 4.5), xend = c(7.3, 5), yend = c(1.5, 1.6),
                      label = c("", ""), lx = 0, ly = 0),
  title = "Moderation", subtitle = "W changes the effect of X on Y")
mediation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Appropriateness\n(M)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.1, 6.4, 2.7), y = c(2.2, 4.6, 1.5), xend = c(3.7, 7.9, 7.3), yend = c(4.6, 2.2, 1.5),
                      label = c("a", "b", "c′"), lx = c(2.4, 7.6, 5), ly = c(3.6, 3.6, 1.0)),
  title = "Mediation", subtitle = "X affects Y through M (a × b), and directly (c′)")
moderation + mediation









Both use real data: the Garcia data set of the psych package (data("GSBE", package = "psych")), the same data Hayes (2022) uses in his book on these methods.

    geom_label(data = boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, fill = "white",
               label.padding = unit(0.45, "lines"), lineheight = 0.9) +
    geom_text(data = arrows, aes(lx, ly, label = label), size = 3.8, colour = "#E74C3C", fontface = "bold") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.5, 6)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle)
}
moderation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Perceived sexism\n(W)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.7, 5), y = c(1.5, 4.5), xend = c(7.3, 5), yend = c(1.5, 1.6),
                      label = c("", ""), lx = 0, ly = 0),
  title = "Moderation", subtitle = "W changes the effect of X on Y")
mediation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Appropriateness\n(M)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.1, 6.4, 2.7), y = c(2.2, 4.6, 1.5), xend = c(3.7, 7.9, 7.3), yend = c(4.6, 2.2, 1.5),
                      label = c("a", "b", "c′"), lx = c(2.4, 7.6, 5), ly = c(3.6, 3.6, 1.0)),
  title = "Mediation", subtitle = "X affects Y through M (a × b), and directly (c′)")
moderation + mediation









Both use real data: the Garcia data set of the psych package (data("GSBE", package = "psych")), the same data Hayes (2022) uses in his book on these methods.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
1. The data


Code
data("GSBE", package = "psych")       # loads the data frame Garcia
d <- data.frame(protest  = Garcia$prot2,      # 0 = she did not protest, 1 = she protested
                sexism   = Garcia$sexism,     # how pervasive the reader believes sex discrimination is (1-7)
                respappr = Garcia$respappr,   # how appropriate the reader found her response (1-7)
                liking   = Garcia$liking)     # how much the reader liked her (1-7)
table(protest = d$protest)


protest
 0  1 
41 88 


Code
round(aggregate(cbind(sexism, respappr, liking) ~ protest, data = d, FUN = mean), 2)


  protest sexism respappr liking
1       0   5.07     3.88   5.31
2       1   5.14     5.32   5.79


Code
round(sapply(d, sd), 2)


 protest   sexism respappr   liking 
    0.47     0.78     1.35     1.05 










Variable
Role
Meaning




protest
X
0 = the lawyer accepted the decision (41 readers), 1 = she protested (88 readers; the original study had two kinds of protest, combined here)


sexism
W, the moderator
The reader’s belief that sex discrimination is pervasive in society, 1 to 7


respappr

How appropriate the reader found the lawyer’s response, 1 to 7


liking

On average the lawyer who protested was liked a little more (5.79 against 5.31) and her response was judged much more appropriate (5.32 against 3.88). Because the version of the story was assigned at random, the two groups do not differ in perceived sexism.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 2. Moderation: does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?
text:
2. Moderation: does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?

The model
Moderation is an interaction: we add the product of X and W to the regression.
\[\text{liking} = b_0 + b_1\,\text{protest} + b_2\,\text{sexism} + b_3\,(\text{protest} \times \text{sexism}) + e\]
Rearranging shows what \(b_3\) does. The effect of protest is no longer one number; it is a line that depends on sexism:
\[\text{effect of protest} = \theta(\text{sexism}) = b_1 + b_3 \times \text{sexism}\]
If \(b_3 = 0\), protest has the same effect for every reader. If \(b_3 > 0\), protest helps more the more pervasive the reader believes discrimination to be.


Mean-centre the moderator first
In the equation above, \(b_1\) is the effect of protest when sexism is 0. But sexism runs from 1 to 7, so “sexism = 0” is a reader who does not exist. Subtracting the mean first (mean-centring) makes 0 mean “a reader of average sexism”:


Code
d$sexism_c <- d$sexism - mean(d$sexism)   # 0 = average perceived sexism
fit_raw <- lm(liking ~ protest * sexism,   data = d)
fit_mod <- lm(liking ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)   # protest * sexism_c = protest + sexism_c + protest:sexism_c
round(rbind(uncentred = coef(fit_raw), centred = coef(fit_mod)), 3)


          (Intercept) protest sexism protest:sexism
uncentred       7.706  -3.773 -0.472          0.834
centred         5.289   0.493 -0.472          0.834



The interaction (0.834) is the same in both models, with the same test, and so are the fit and every prediction.
The protest coefficient changes meaning. Uncentred, -3.77 is the effect of protest for an impossible reader with sexism 0. Centred, 0.49 is the effect for a reader of average sexism.

You may read that centring is needed to “avoid multicollinearity” between X and X × W. It lowers that correlation, but it changes nothing in the test of the interaction (Echambadi & Hess, 2007). Centre for interpretation.


Code
summary(fit_mod)



Call:
lm(formula = liking ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.9894 -0.6381  0.0478  0.7404  2.3650 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        5.2885     0.1547  34.184  < 2e-16 ***
protest            0.4926     0.1872   2.631  0.00958 ** 
sexism_c          -0.4725     0.2038  -2.318  0.02205 *  
protest:sexism_c   0.8336     0.2436   3.422  0.00084 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9888 on 125 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1335,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1127 
F-statistic: 6.419 on 3 and 125 DF,  p-value: 0.0004439




How to read the output







Row
Meaning here




(Intercept)
Predicted liking when protest = 0 and sexism is average: 5.29


protest
The effect of protest for a reader of average sexism: 0.49 points more liking


sexism_c
The effect of sexism when she did not protest (protest = 0): readers who see more discrimination like the non-protesting lawyer less


protest:sexism_c
How much the effect of protest grows for each point of sexism: 0.83. This is the moderation test



With an interaction in the model, the “main effects” are conditional effects: each is the effect of one variable when the other is 0. That is why centring matters.


Moderation as a ΔR² step
The interaction can also be tested as one more step of a hierarchical regression: first the two predictors, then their product.


Code
fit_main <- lm(liking ~ protest + sexism_c, data = d)
anova(fit_main, fit_mod)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: liking ~ protest + sexism_c
Model 2: liking ~ protest * sexism_c
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    126 133.66                                  
2    125 122.21  1    11.451 11.713 0.0008396 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
c(R2_main_effects = summary(fit_main)$r.squared, R2_with_interaction = summary(fit_mod)$r.squared,
  delta_R2 = summary(fit_mod)$r.squared - summary(fit_main)$r.squared,
  t_squared = unname(coef(summary(fit_mod))["protest:sexism_c", "t value"]^2))


    R2_main_effects R2_with_interaction            delta_R2           t_squared 
         0.05229818          0.13349060          0.08119242         11.71256985 


The interaction adds 8.1% of explained variance. The F-change is the square of the interaction’s t: for one added term the two tests are the same test.


Simple slopes: the effect of protest at chosen levels of sexism
The conditional effect of protest at a value \(w\) of (centred) sexism is \(\theta(w) = b_1 + b_3 w\). Its standard error comes from the variances and the covariance of the two coefficients, all in vcov(fit_mod):
\[SE[\theta(w)] = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(b_1) + w^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3) + 2w \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)}\]
A common choice is to probe at one SD below the mean, the mean, and one SD above (Aiken & West, 1991):


Code
b <- coef(fit_mod); V <- vcov(fit_mod)
w <- c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(d$sexism)                                 # centred values: -1 SD, mean, +1 SD
theta <- b["protest"] + b["protest:sexism_c"] * w
se    <- sqrt(V["protest", "protest"] + w^2 * V["protest:sexism_c", "protest:sexism_c"] +
              2 * w * V["protest", "protest:sexism_c"])
df_res <- df.residual(fit_mod)
slopes <- data.frame(level = c("-1 SD", "mean", "+1 SD"), sexism = w + mean(d$sexism),
                     effect = theta, se = se, t = theta / se, p = 2 * pt(-abs(theta / se), df_res),
                     lower = theta - qt(.975, df_res) * se, upper = theta + qt(.975, df_res) * se)
slopes[, -1] <- round(slopes[, -1], 3)
slopes


  level sexism effect    se      t     p  lower upper
1 -1 SD  4.333 -0.161 0.263 -0.611 0.542 -0.681 0.360
2  mean  5.117  0.493 0.187  2.631 0.010  0.122 0.863
3 +1 SD  5.901  1.146 0.272  4.216 0.000  0.608 1.684



For readers who see little discrimination (sexism 4.33), protest makes no difference (-0.16, p = 0.54).
For readers who see a lot (sexism 5.90), the lawyer who protests is liked 1.15 points more.

A check: centring sexism at a chosen value turns the protest coefficient into the simple slope at that value, with the same standard error.


Code
fit_high <- lm(liking ~ protest * I(sexism - (mean(sexism) + sd(sexism))), data = d)
coef(summary(fit_high))["protest", ]


    Estimate   Std. Error      t value     Pr(>|t|) 
1.145923e+00 2.718268e-01 4.215637e+00 4.736022e-05 




Johnson–Neyman: where exactly is the effect significant?
The ±1 SD points are arbitrary. The Johnson–Neyman technique finds the values of the moderator where the effect of protest is just significant: where \(|\theta(w) / SE[\theta(w)]|\) equals the critical t. Squaring both sides gives a quadratic equation in \(w\):
\[\left[b_3^2 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3)\right] w^2 + 2\left[b_1 b_3 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)\right] w + \left[b_1^2 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_1)\right] = 0\]


Code
tc <- qt(.975, df_res)
A <- b[4]^2 - tc^2 * V[4, 4]
B <- 2 * (b[2] * b[4] - tc^2 * V[2, 4])
C <- b[2]^2 - tc^2 * V[2, 2]
jn <- sort((-B + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(B^2 - 4 * A * C)) / (2 * A)) + mean(d$sexism)   # back to the 1-7 scale
c(jn_lower = jn[1], jn_upper = jn[2])


jn_lower jn_upper 
3.508712 4.975297 


Code
c(share_below_lower = mean(d$sexism < jn[1]), share_above_upper = mean(d$sexism > jn[2]))


share_below_lower share_above_upper 
       0.01550388        0.55813953 


Protest has a significant positive effect for readers with sexism above 4.98 (56% of the sample), and a significant negative effect below 3.51, a region with only 2 readers, too few to say much about. In between, the effect is not significantly different from 0.


Code
grid_w <- seq(min(d$sexism), max(d$sexism), length.out = 200)
wc <- grid_w - mean(d$sexism)
th <- b[2] + b[4] * wc
se_w <- sqrt(V[2, 2] + wc^2 * V[4, 4] + 2 * wc * V[2, 4])
jn_df <- data.frame(sexism = grid_w, effect = th, lower = th - tc * se_w, upper = th + tc * se_w,
                    significant = th - tc * se_w > 0 | th + tc * se_w < 0)
ggplot(jn_df, aes(sexism, effect)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = jn, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#E74C3C") +
  annotate("text", x = jn, y = max(jn_df$upper), label = sprintf("%.2f", jn), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5,
           colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_rug(data = data.frame(sexism = d$sexism + (rank(d$sexism, ties.method = "first") %% 5 - 2) * 0.02),
           aes(x = sexism), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.3) +   # spread a little: many readers share a score
  labs(title = "The effect of protest on liking, at each level of perceived sexism",
       x = "perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (W)",
       y = "effect of protest (95% CI)")









Where the blue band does not include 0, the effect is significant. The dashed lines are the Johnson–Neyman points, and the ticks at the bottom show the readers’ actual sexism scores (one tick per reader, spread a little where readers share a score): most lie to the right of 4.98.


The interaction plot


Code
pred <- expand.grid(protest = c(0, 1), sexism = grid_w)
pred$sexism_c <- pred$sexism - mean(d$sexism)
pr <- predict(fit_mod, newdata = pred, interval = "confidence")
pred <- cbind(pred, pr)
pred$condition <- factor(pred$protest, labels = c("did not protest", "protested"))
d$condition <- factor(d$protest, labels = c("did not protest", "protested"))
ggplot(pred, aes(sexism, fit, colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_point(data = d, aes(y = liking), alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#E74C3C"), aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  labs(title = "Protest pays off with readers who see discrimination as pervasive",
       x = "perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (W)", y = "liking of the lawyer",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The lines cross. Among readers who believe discrimination is rare, the lawyer who stays quiet is liked about as much, or slightly more. Among readers who believe it is everywhere, the protester is liked much more, and the quiet lawyer much less.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 3. Mediation: why does protest change liking?
text:
3. Mediation: why does protest change liking?

The paths
Three regressions describe a simple mediation model:
\[\text{total effect:}\qquad Y = i_1 + c\,X + e_1\]
\[\text{a path:}\qquad M = i_2 + a\,X + e_2\]
\[\text{b and c′ paths:}\qquad Y = i_3 + c'\,X + b\,M + e_3\]

\(a\): how much protest changes the perceived appropriateness of her response.
\(b\): how much appropriateness changes liking, among readers who read the same version.
\(c'\): the direct effect, the effect of protest on liking that does not go through appropriateness.
\(a \times b\): the indirect effect, the part of the effect that does go through it.
\(c\): the total effect. In linear regression it splits exactly: \(c = c' + ab\).



Code
fit_c <- lm(liking ~ protest, data = d)                # total effect c
fit_a <- lm(respappr ~ protest, data = d)              # a path
fit_b <- lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = d)     # b and c' paths
a  <- unname(coef(fit_a)["protest"])
bp <- unname(coef(fit_b)["respappr"])
cp <- unname(coef(fit_b)["protest"])
cc <- unname(coef(fit_c)["protest"])
round(c(a = a, b = bp, direct_c_prime = cp, indirect_ab = a * bp, total_c = cc, c_prime_plus_ab = cp + a * bp), 3)


              a               b  direct_c_prime     indirect_ab         total_c c_prime_plus_ab 
          1.440           0.402          -0.101           0.579           0.479           0.479 


Protest raised perceived appropriateness by 1.44 points (a), and each point of appropriateness went with 0.40 points more liking (b). The indirect effect is \(1.44 \times 0.40 = 0.58\). The direct effect is practically 0 (-0.10), so the whole total effect of 0.48 runs through appropriateness.


Why not Baron and Kenny’s steps, or the Sobel test?
For decades mediation was tested with the causal steps of Baron and Kenny (1986): (1) X must affect Y (\(c\) significant), (2) X must affect M (\(a\)), (3) M must affect Y controlling for X (\(b\)), and (4) \(c'\) must be smaller than \(c\) (“full” mediation if \(c'\) is not significant). Today this approach is not recommended (Hayes, 2022; Zhao et al., 2010):

It never tests the indirect effect \(ab\) itself, only its pieces, one at a time.
Step 1 is not needed. An indirect effect can exist without a significant total effect, for example when the direct effect has the opposite sign and cancels it out.
“Full” versus “partial” mediation depends on sample size: with enough data, any \(c'\) becomes significant.

The Sobel test does test \(ab\), dividing it by an approximate standard error, \(\sqrt{b^2 \operatorname{Var}(a) + a^2 \operatorname{Var}(b)}\), and comparing it with the normal distribution. But the product of two estimates is not normally distributed: its sampling distribution is skewed, so symmetric normal intervals are wrong and the test has low power (MacKinnon et al., 2004).


Code
se_sobel <- sqrt(bp^2 * vcov(fit_a)["protest", "protest"] + a^2 * vcov(fit_b)["respappr", "respappr"])
c(z = a * bp / se_sobel, lower = a * bp - 1.96 * se_sobel, upper = a * bp + 1.96 * se_sobel)


        z     lower     upper 
4.3206484 0.3165276 0.8421410 




The bootstrap: the recommended test of the indirect effect
The bootstrap makes no assumption about the shape of the sampling distribution of \(ab\). Draw a new sample of 129 readers with replacement from the data, fit the two regressions, compute \(ab\), and repeat thousands of times. The middle 95% of the \(ab\) values is the percentile bootstrap confidence interval (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). If it does not contain 0, the indirect effect is significant.


Code
indirect <- function(data, i) {
  x <- data[i, ]                                     # one bootstrap sample
  a_i <- coef(lm(respappr ~ protest, data = x))["protest"]
  b_i <- coef(lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = x))["respappr"]
  c(ab = unname(a_i * b_i), ab_partially_std = unname(a_i * b_i / sd(x$liking)))
}
set.seed(2026)
boot_ab <- boot(d, indirect, R = 5000)
ci_ab <- quantile(boot_ab$t[, 1], c(.025, .975))
ci_ab


     2.5%     97.5% 
0.3198499 0.9059003 




Code
bd <- data.frame(ab = boot_ab$t[, 1])
xs <- seq(min(bd$ab), max(bd$ab), length.out = 300)
ggplot(bd, aes(ab)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(ab = xs, density = dnorm(xs, a * bp, se_sobel)), aes(y = density),
            colour = "#f39c12", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_ab, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "5,000 bootstrap indirect effects (blue) and the normal curve\nthe Sobel test assumes (orange)",
       x = "indirect effect a × b", y = "density")









The bootstrap distribution is skewed to the right: its interval [0.32, 0.91] reaches further above the estimate (0.58) than below it. The Sobel interval is symmetric by construction. Here both exclude 0, because the effect is large; in smaller samples, or with smaller effects, they can disagree, and the bootstrap is the one to trust.


The same model in lavaan
lavaan fits the two regressions at once as a path model. Labels (a*, b*, cp*) name the paths, and := defines new quantities from them:


Code
model <- '
  respappr ~ a * protest                # a path
  liking   ~ cp * protest + b * respappr  # direct effect and b path
  indirect := a * b
  total    := cp + a * b
'
set.seed(2026)
fit_sem <- sem(model, data = d, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 1000)
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit_sem, boot.ci.type = "perc")
pe[pe$op %in% c("~", ":="), c("label", "lhs", "op", "rhs", "est", "se", "pvalue", "ci.lower", "ci.upper")]


     label      lhs op      rhs    est    se pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1        a respappr  ~  protest  1.440 0.247   0.00    0.952    1.939
2       cp   liking  ~  protest -0.101 0.203   0.62   -0.497    0.297
3        b   liking  ~ respappr  0.402 0.080   0.00    0.246    0.554
7 indirect indirect :=      a*b  0.579 0.153   0.00    0.311    0.896
8    total    total :=   cp+a*b  0.479 0.221   0.03    0.066    0.906



est are the same estimates as from lm().
se are bootstrap standard errors, and ci.lower, ci.upper percentile bootstrap intervals (boot.ci.type = "perc").
We used 1,000 bootstrap samples to keep this page fast; lavaan refits the whole model each time, which is slow. For a report, use 5,000 or more, as with boot() above. With more samples, the interval limits change only in the second decimal.



How big is the indirect effect?
\(ab\) is in the units of the outcome: protest raises liking by 0.58 points of a 1 to 7 scale through appropriateness. Two standardised versions make it comparable across studies (Hayes, 2022):

Partially standardised: \(ab / SD_Y\), the indirect effect in standard deviations of Y. Use it when X is a two-group variable, as here: the groups differ by 0.55 SD of liking through this path.
Completely standardised: \(ab \times SD_X / SD_Y\), for a continuous X: the change in Y, in SDs, for one SD more of X.



Code
ci_ps <- quantile(boot_ab$t[, 2], c(.025, .975))
round(c(partially_standardised = a * bp / sd(d$liking), lower = unname(ci_ps[1]), upper = unname(ci_ps[2])), 3)


partially_standardised                  lower                  upper 
                 0.552                  0.331                  0.826 


Avoid the “proportion mediated” (\(ab / c\)): it is unstable in all but very large samples, and meaningless when \(c\) is small or the paths have opposite signs.


What mediation needs to be causal
A mediation analysis tells a causal story, X → M → Y, and the numbers alone cannot prove it.

X was randomised. Readers were assigned to the versions of the story at random, so the effects of protest, \(a\) and \(c\), are causal.
M was not. Appropriateness was measured, not manipulated. The \(b\) path (and therefore \(c'\) and \(ab\)) is causal only if nothing else affects both appropriateness and liking. A reader’s general sympathy for the lawyer, for example, could raise both, and would make \(b\) too large. This no unmeasured confounding assumption cannot be tested with these data (Imai et al., 2010).
Temporal order. M must come after X and before Y. Here M and Y were measured at the same moment, so “liking makes her response seem appropriate” is also possible.
Cross-sectional data (all variables measured at once, nothing randomised) make mediation estimates especially doubtful when the process unfolds over time (Maxwell & Cole, 2007).

Report mediation as consistent with a mechanism, not as proof of it, unless the design supports the causal claims.


Code
s_a <- coef(summary(fit_a)); s_b <- coef(summary(fit_b))
stars <- function(p) if (p < .001) "***" else if (p < .01) "**" else if (p < .05) "*" else ""
draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Appropriateness\n(M)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.1, 6.4, 2.7), y = c(2.2, 4.6, 1.5), xend = c(3.7, 7.9, 7.3), yend = c(4.6, 2.2, 1.5),
                      label = c(sprintf("a = %.2f%s", a, stars(s_a["protest", 4])),
                                sprintf("b = %.2f%s", bp, stars(s_b["respappr", 4])),
                                sprintf("c′ = %.2f%s", cp, stars(s_b["protest", 4]))),
                      lx = c(1.7, 8.3, 5), ly = c(3.6, 3.6, 1.0)),
  title = sprintf("Indirect effect ab = %.2f, 95%% bootstrap CI [%.2f, %.2f]; total effect c = %.2f",
                  a * bp, ci_ab[1], ci_ab[2], cc))

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 4. Moderated mediation: does the indirect effect depend on sexism?
text:
4. Moderated mediation: does the indirect effect depend on sexism?
The two questions can be combined. Section 2 showed that perceived sexism moderates the effect of protest on liking. Perhaps it does so through the mediator: readers who see discrimination everywhere find protest more appropriate. Then the \(a\) path depends on sexism, and so does the indirect effect:
\[M = i_2 + a_1 X + a_2 W + a_3\,XW + e_2, \qquad Y = i_3 + c' X + b M + e_3\]
\[\text{conditional indirect effect} = (a_1 + a_3 W) \times b, \qquad \text{index of moderated mediation} = a_3 \times b\]
The index of moderated mediation (Hayes, 2015) is how much the indirect effect changes per point of W. If its bootstrap interval excludes 0, the indirect effect depends on the moderator. (This is model 7 of Hayes’s PROCESS macro.)


Code
fit_a_mod <- lm(respappr ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)
coef(summary(fit_a_mod))


                   Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)       3.8598115  0.1790674 21.555078 6.302118e-44
protest           1.4580301  0.2167041  6.728208 5.523771e-10
sexism_c         -0.5290051  0.2358875 -2.242617 2.668359e-02
protest:sexism_c  0.8099844  0.2819135  2.873167 4.776441e-03


Code
w_vals <- c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(d$sexism)
cond_indirect <- function(data, i) {
  x <- data[i, ]
  x$sexism_c <- x$sexism - mean(d$sexism)            # centre at the mean of the original sample
  a_i <- coef(lm(respappr ~ protest * sexism_c, data = x))
  b_i <- coef(lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = x))["respappr"]
  c(index = unname(a_i["protest:sexism_c"] * b_i),
    setNames((a_i["protest"] + a_i["protest:sexism_c"] * w_vals) * b_i, c("at_minus_1_SD", "at_mean", "at_plus_1_SD")))
}
set.seed(2026)
boot_mm <- boot(d, cond_indirect, R = 5000)
mm <- data.frame(estimate = boot_mm$t0, t(apply(boot_mm$t, 2, quantile, c(.025, .975))))
names(mm)[2:3] <- c("lower", "upper")
round(mm, 3)


              estimate lower upper
index            0.326 0.034 0.666
at_minus_1_SD    0.331 0.079 0.612
at_mean          0.587 0.329 0.905
at_plus_1_SD     0.842 0.420 1.357



Protest made the response seem more appropriate especially to readers who see discrimination as pervasive (the protest:sexism_c row of the \(a\) model).
The index of moderated mediation is 0.33, 95% CI [0.03, 0.67]: the interval excludes 0, so the indirect effect depends on sexism.
The indirect effect is 0.33 for readers one SD below the mean in sexism and 0.84 for readers one SD above.

In words: protesting is judged more appropriate, and therefore the protester is liked more, mainly by readers who already believe that discrimination is common.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 5. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
5. Reporting the results in APA style


Code
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
sm   <- coef(summary(fit_mod)); ci_mod <- confint(fit_mod)
dR2  <- summary(fit_mod)$r.squared - summary(fit_main)$r.squared
F_change <- anova(fit_main, fit_mod)$F[2]


Method (data analysis):

Moderation was tested by regressing liking on protest condition (0 = no protest, 1 = protest), perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (mean-centred), and their product, and probed with simple slopes at ±1 SD and the Johnson–Neyman technique. The indirect effect of protest on liking through perceived response appropriateness was estimated with ordinary least squares regression and tested with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals based on 5,000 resamples. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the boot and lavaan packages.

Results:

The effect of protest on liking depended on perceived sexism, b = 0.83, SE = 0.24, t(125) = 3.42, p < .001, 95% CI [0.35, 1.32], ΔR² = .08, F(1, 125) = 11.71. At low perceived sexism (−1 SD), protest did not affect liking, b = -0.16, p = .542; at high perceived sexism (+1 SD), the lawyer who protested was liked more, b = 1.15, p < .001. The Johnson–Neyman technique showed a significant positive effect of protest for perceived sexism above 4.98 (56% of participants). Protest increased perceived response appropriateness, a = 1.44, p < .001, which in turn predicted liking, b = 0.40, p < .001. The indirect effect was significant, ab = 0.58, 95% CI [0.32, 0.91], partially standardised ab = 0.55, whereas the direct effect was not, c′ = -0.10, p = .616. The indirect effect was moderated by perceived sexism, index of moderated mediation = 0.33, 95% CI [0.03, 0.67].

Points to remember:

For moderation, say how the moderator was centred, report the interaction with its ΔR², and probe it: simple slopes at stated values, or the Johnson–Neyman region.
For mediation, report the \(a\), \(b\), direct and indirect effects, and test the indirect effect with a bootstrap confidence interval, giving the number of resamples. Do not rely on the causal steps or the Sobel test.
State the causal assumptions, and which of the paths the design supports.
Cite R and the packages; citation(), citation("boot") and citation("lavaan") in R give the exact references.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
6. Summary







Moderation
When does X affect Y? lm(y ~ x * w); the interaction \(b_3\) is the test


Centring
Subtract the mean of W so that \(b_1\) is the effect of X at average W; it does not change the interaction test


ΔR²
The interaction as one more step: anova(main_effects, with_interaction); F-change = \(t^2\)


Probing
Simple slopes \(b_1 + b_3 w\) with \(SE = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(b_1) + w^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3) + 2w \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)}\); the Johnson–Neyman points where the effect is just significant


Mediation
How does X affect Y? \(a\) from lm(m ~ x), \(b\) and \(c'\) from lm(y ~ x + m); indirect effect \(ab\); \(c = c' + ab\)


Testing \(ab\)
Percentile bootstrap CI (boot(), or lavaan with se = "bootstrap"), not causal steps or Sobel


Effect size
Partially standardised \(ab / SD_Y\) for a two-group X; completely standardised \(ab \cdot SD_X / SD_Y\) for a continuous X


Moderated mediation
A moderated path makes the indirect effect conditional; test with the index of moderated mediation


Causality
Needs randomisation or strong assumptions: no unmeasured confounding of M and Y, and M measured between X and Y

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
One of the best-known charts in the world shows the temperature of the planet, year by year, as grey points, and a smooth line through them. NASA’s version of the chart says in its legend: Lowess smoothing. The line has no formula. Nobody claims that the temperature follows a parabola or an exponential. The line simply goes where the points go, without their jumps from year to year.
This page explains how the line is made, makes it, and then checks it against the numbers that NASA publishes. The method is called LOESS (or LOWESS: locally weighted scatterplot smoothing; Cleveland, 1979). It is the default of geom_smooth() in ggplot2, so many people use it every day without knowing what it does.
The idea fits in one sentence: to find the height of the curve at a year, fit a straight line to the years around it, giving the nearer years more weight, and read its value there. Then do the same for every other year.


Code
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
f4   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4, big.mark = ",")

library(ggplot2)

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
1. The data
NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies publishes the chart and the numbers behind it. The file has three columns: the year, the temperature, and NASA’s own smooth line.


Code
address <- paste0("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/graphs_v4/graph_data/",
                  "Global_Mean_Estimates_based_on_Land_and_Ocean_Data/graph.csv")
lines <- readLines(address)
start <- grep("^Year", lines)                        # the lines above the header are a title
earth <- read.csv(text = lines[start:length(lines)])
names(earth) <- c("year", "temp", "nasa")
earth <- earth[complete.cases(earth), ]
n <- nrow(earth)
n


[1] 146


Code
tail(earth, 3)


    year temp nasa
144 2023 1.17 1.12
145 2024 1.28 1.17
146 2025 1.19 1.23


There are 146 years, 1880 to 2025. temp is an anomaly: the difference, in °C, from the average of 1951–1980. An anomaly of 1.19 means 1.19 °C warmer than that average. nasa is the published line, rounded to two decimals. We shall try to reproduce it.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
ggplot(earth, aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(aes(y = nasa), colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1880, 2020, 20)) +
  labs(title = "Global temperature, and NASA's smooth line",
       subtitle = "Difference from the average of 1951–1980", x = NULL, y = "°C") +
  theme_bw()









No simple formula fits this. The record is flat or falling until about 1910, rises to the 1940s, pauses for three decades, and then rises steeply. A straight line would be wrong everywhere, and a polynomial of a high degree would swing at the ends (see polynomial regression).

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
section: 3. The method step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The method step by step, with formulas
We find the height of the curve at one year, \(x_0 = 1945\).

Step 1: choose the neighbours
Take the \(q\) nearest years. The fraction \(f = q/n\) is the span. We use \(q = 10\), so \(f\) = 10/146.


Code
q  <- 10
x0 <- 1945
distance <- abs(earth$year - x0)
h  <- sort(distance)[q]               # the distance of the 10th nearest year
h


[1] 5




Step 2: weight them by distance
The nearest years count most, and the weight falls smoothly to zero at the distance \(h\) of the \(q\)-th neighbour. The tricube function does this:
\[w(x) = \left(1 - \left|\frac{x - x_0}{h}\right|^3\right)^3 \quad\text{for } |x - x_0| < h, \qquad 0 \text{ otherwise}\]


Code
tricube <- function(u) ifelse(abs(u) < 1, (1 - abs(u)^3)^3, 0)
earth$w <- tricube(distance / h)
subset(earth, w > 0, select = c(year, temp, w))


   year  temp         w
62 1941  0.18 0.1162143
63 1942  0.06 0.4818903
64 1943  0.09 0.8200259
65 1944  0.20 0.9761915
66 1945  0.09 1.0000000
67 1946 -0.07 0.9761915
68 1947 -0.03 0.8200259
69 1948 -0.11 0.4818903
70 1949 -0.11 0.1162143


The year 1945 has weight 1, its neighbours less, and the years at distance 5 or more have weight 0.


Step 3: fit a straight line with these weights
This is an ordinary weighted least squares line, in the neighbourhood only:
\[\min_{a, b}\; \sum_i w_i \,\big[y_i - a - b\,(x_i - x_0)\big]^2\]
Because \(x\) is centred at \(x_0\), the intercept \(a\) is the height of the curve at \(x_0\). The slope \(b\) is the local slope: how fast the temperature was changing. Keep only \(a\), and throw the line away.


Code
local <- lm(temp ~ I(year - x0), data = earth, weights = w)
coef(local)


 (Intercept) I(year - x0) 
  0.04321339  -0.04022633 




Code
near <- subset(earth, abs(year - x0) <= 15)
near$line <- coef(local)[[1]] + coef(local)[[2]] * (near$year - x0)

ggplot(near, aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = w, colour = w > 0)) +
  geom_line(
    data = subset(near, abs(year - x0) < h),
    aes(y = line),
    colour = "#2a78d6",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  annotate("point", x = x0, y = coef(local)[[1]], size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "#eb6834") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey25", `FALSE` = "grey80"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size(range = c(1.5, 6), name = "weight") +
  labs(
    title = "One local line, for 1945",
    subtitle = "The size of a point is its weight. The orange point is the height of the curve in 1945",
    x = NULL,
    y = "°C"
  ) +
  theme_bw()











Step 4: repeat for every year, and join the points


Code
smooth_by_hand <- function(x, y, q, robust = rep(1, length(y))) {
  sapply(x, function(x0) {
    d <- abs(x - x0)
    w <- tricube(d / sort(d)[q]) * robust
    sum(w * y) / sum(w) -> centre                     # fallback, if all the weight is on one point
    fit <- lm.wfit(cbind(1, x - x0), y, w)
    if (is.na(fit$coefficients[2])) centre else fit$coefficients[[1]]
  })
}
pass0 <- smooth_by_hand(earth$year, earth$temp, q)
check <- lowess(earth$year, earth$temp, f = q / n, iter = 0)$y    # the function that comes with R
max(abs(pass0 - check))


[1] 1.367795e-13


Our own function agrees with R’s lowess(), to the last digit.


Step 5: make it robust
A single strange year can pull the local lines. So LOWESS looks at the residuals \(e_i\) of the first pass, and gives a robustness weight to each point: close to 1 if its residual is ordinary, 0 if it is more than six times the median absolute residual \(s\).
\[r_i = \left(1 - \left(\frac{e_i}{6 s}\right)^2\right)^2 \quad\text{if } |e_i| < 6s, \qquad 0 \text{ otherwise}\]
Then it repeats step 4 with the weights \(w_i \cdot r_i\). This is the bisquare function of robust regression. Three rounds are the default of lowess().


Code
fitted <- pass0
for (round in 1:3) {
  e <- earth$temp - fitted
  s <- median(abs(e))
  r <- ifelse(abs(e) < 6 * s, (1 - (e / (6 * s))^2)^2, 0)
  fitted <- smooth_by_hand(earth$year, earth$temp, q, robust = r)
}
check3 <- lowess(earth$year, earth$temp, f = q / n, iter = 3)$y
max(abs(fitted - check3))


[1] 1.71681e-09


Code
round(range(r), 2)          # the smallest and the largest robustness weight


[1] 0.61 1.00

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
4. Reproducing NASA’s line
NASA calls the column Lowess(5). If the 5 means five years on each side, the neighbourhood is 10 years. With the three robustness rounds of the default:


Code
ours <- lowess(earth$year, earth$temp, f = 10 / n, iter = 3)$y
difference <- ours - earth$nasa
c(
  largest_difference = max(abs(difference)),
  same_at_two_decimals = mean(round(ours, 2) == earth$nasa)
)


  largest_difference same_at_two_decimals 
         0.004970085          1.000000000 


The largest difference in 146 years is 0.00497 °C, smaller than the rounding of the published numbers (0.005). We have made NASA’s line. Other settings do not:


Code
settings <- expand.grid(q = c(6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15), iter = c(0, 3))
settings$largest_difference <- mapply(
  function(q, iter) {
    max(abs(lowess(earth$year, earth$temp, f = q / n, iter = iter)$y - earth$nasa))
  },
  settings$q,
  settings$iter
)
reshape(settings, idvar = "q", timevar = "iter", direction = "wide")


   q largest_difference.0 largest_difference.3
1  6           0.07826353          0.066661487
2  8           0.04370872          0.030170050
3  9           0.04370872          0.030092652
4 10           0.01869774          0.004970085
5 11           0.01846298          0.010487081
6 12           0.02924354          0.019873181
7 15           0.05517324          0.044990614


Only \(q = 10\) with the robustness rounds is inside the rounding error. The line is completely determined by two choices: how many neighbours, and how many rounds.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
section: 5. The span: how smooth should it be?
text:
5. The span: how smooth should it be?
The span is the one choice that matters. Small: the line follows every jump (low bias, high variance). Large: it irons out real changes (low variance, high bias). R has two functions with different defaults, which is a common source of confusion:









lowess()
loess()




Interface
lowess(x, y, f, iter)
formula: loess(y ~ x, data, span, degree, family)


Local model
straight line
parabola by default (degree = 2)


Default span
2/3
0.75


Robust
yes, 3 rounds by default
only with family = "symmetric"


Predictions, standard errors
no
yes, predict(fit, newdata, se = TRUE)


geom_smooth(method = "loess")

this one, with its defaults





Code
spans <- c(
  `0.07 (10 years)` = 10 / n,
  `0.21 (30 years)` = 30 / n,
  `0.41 (60 years)` = 60 / n,
  `0.75 (default)` = 0.75
)
span_lines <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(spans), function(s) {
    data.frame(
      year = earth$year,
      temp = predict(loess(temp ~ year, data = earth, span = spans[[s]], degree = 1)),
      span = s
    )
  })
)
span_lines$span <- factor(span_lines$span, levels = names(spans))

ggplot(earth, aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = span_lines, colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ span) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2000, 50)) +
  labs(title = "The same data, four spans (local straight lines)", x = NULL, y = "°C") +
  theme_bw()










How many parameters does a curve without parameters have?
Each fitted value is a weighted sum of the observations, \(\hat y = L y\), with a matrix \(L\) that depends on the years and the span, not on the temperatures. In linear regression the trace of such a matrix is the number of coefficients. So the trace of \(L\) is the equivalent number of parameters:


Code
hat_matrix <- function(x, q, degree = 1) {
  t(sapply(x, function(x0) {
    d <- abs(x - x0); w <- tricube(d / (sort(d)[min(q, length(x))]))
    X <- outer(x - x0, 0:degree, "^")
    solve(crossprod(X, w * X), t(w * X))[1, ]          # the row that gives the fitted value at x0
  }))
}
L <- hat_matrix(earth$year, 30)
c(trace = sum(diag(L)), largest_difference_from_loess =
    max(abs(L %*% earth$temp - predict(loess(temp ~ year, earth, span = 30 / n, degree = 1,
                                             control = loess.control(surface = "direct"))))))


                        trace largest_difference_from_loess 
                 9.193349e+00                  8.881784e-16 


A span of 30 years is worth about 9.2 parameters. (We asked loess() to compute every value directly. By default it computes some and interpolates between them, which is faster and almost the same.)


Choosing the span by numbers
With \(\text{tr}(L)\) we can write the criteria that compare fit and complexity: GCV (generalised cross-validation) and AICc (Hurvich et al., 1998). Leave-one-out cross-validation needs no refitting: the error of predicting year \(i\) without year \(i\) is \(e_i / (1 - L_{ii})\).
\[\text{GCV} = \frac{n \sum e_i^2}{(n - \text{tr} L)^2}, \qquad \text{AICc} = \log\frac{\sum e_i^2}{n} + 1 + \frac{2(\text{tr} L + 1)}{n - \text{tr} L - 2}\]
Both assume that the years are independent. They are not: warm years come in runs, for example because of El Niño. To a criterion that expects independence, a run of warm years looks like a piece of the curve. So we also try a cross-validation that leaves out blocks of 11 years and predicts only the middle year of the block:


Code
block_error <- function(q, half) {
  mean(sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    keep <- abs(earth$year - earth$year[i]) > half
    d <- abs(earth$year[keep] - earth$year[i]); w <- tricube(d / sort(d)[q])
    fit <- lm.wfit(cbind(1, earth$year[keep] - earth$year[i]), earth$temp[keep], w)
    (earth$temp[i] - fit$coefficients[[1]])^2
  }))
}
qs <- c(6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100)
criteria <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(qs, function(q) {
    L <- hat_matrix(earth$year, q)
    e <- earth$temp - L %*% earth$temp
    tr <- sum(diag(L))
    rss <- sum(e^2)
    data.frame(
      q,
      parameters = tr,
      GCV = n * rss / (n - tr)^2,
      AICc = log(rss / n) + 1 + 2 * (tr + 1) / (n - tr - 2),
      LOO = sqrt(mean((e / (1 - diag(L)))^2)),
      block = sqrt(block_error(q, 5))
    )
  })
)

The block criterion, which cannot use the neighbouring year to guess a warm spell, chooses 40, and is nearly flat between 15 and 50. There is no single right answer, because there is no single question. NASA’s 10 years show the variation from decade to decade. Thirty years are the usual definition of climate, and show the long-term change. Say which one you want, and why.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
section: 6. What the line cannot tell by itself: uncertainty
text:
6. What the line cannot tell by itself: uncertainty
loess() gives standard errors, as in a regression with \(\text{tr}(L)\) parameters:


Code
fit30  <- loess(temp ~ year, data = earth, span = 30 / n, degree = 1)
pred   <- predict(fit30, se = TRUE)
band   <- data.frame(year = earth$year, fit = pred$fit,
                     low  = pred$fit - qt(0.975, pred$df) * pred$se.fit,
                     high = pred$fit + qt(0.975, pred$df) * pred$se.fit)
fit30


Call:
loess(formula = temp ~ year, data = earth, span = 30/n, degree = 1)

Number of Observations: 146 
Equivalent Number of Parameters: 7.97 
Residual Standard Error: 0.09902 


Code
c(trace_of_L = sum(diag(L)), trace_of_LLt = sum(L^2))


  trace_of_L trace_of_LLt 
    9.193349     7.786526 


Code
lag1 <- acf(resid(fit30), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
lag1


[1] 0.3194288


(The Equivalent Number of Parameters that loess prints, 8.0, is a relative of ours: the trace of \(LL^\top\) instead of the trace of \(L\).)


Code
ggplot(earth, aes(year, temp)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = band,
    aes(x = year, ymin = low, ymax = high),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2a78d6",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(data = band, aes(y = fit), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1880, 2020, 20)) +
  labs(title = "Local lines over 30 years, with a 95% band for the curve", x = NULL, y = "°C") +
  theme_bw()









Read the band with two warnings.

It is a band for the smoothed curve, not for the truth. Where the true curve bends, the local line cuts the corner, and the band does not contain this bias.
It assumes independent years. The residuals correlate with the next year’s at 0.32, so the true band is wider, by about \(\sqrt{(1 + r)/(1 - r)}\) = 1.39 times if the correlation fades year by year (see generalized least squares).


The slope: how fast is it warming?
Each local line has a slope, which we threw away. It is the answer to a good question:


Code
local_slope <- function(x0, q) {
  d   <- abs(earth$year - x0)
  fit <- lm.wfit(cbind(1, earth$year - x0), earth$temp, tricube(d / sort(d)[q]))
  10 * fit$coefficients[[2]]                                # °C per decade
}
warming <- data.frame(year = earth$year, rate = sapply(earth$year, local_slope, q = 30))
rate_of <- function(y) warming$rate[warming$year == y]
warming[warming$year %in% c(1900, 1930, 1960, 1990, 2010, max(earth$year)), ]


    year        rate
21  1900 -0.09514022
51  1930  0.13175320
81  1960  0.01825696
111 1990  0.14301530
131 2010  0.22513966
146 2025  0.30142158




Code
ggplot(warming, aes(year, rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1880, 2020, 20)) +
  labs(title = "The local slope: warming per decade", subtitle = "Local lines over 30 years",
       x = NULL, y = "°C per decade") +
  theme_bw()









Around 1960 the temperature was hardly changing (0.02 °C per decade). Around 1990 it rose by 0.14, around 2010 by 0.23 °C per decade. The value for 2025, 0.30, uses only years on one side, and the next section shows why it deserves little trust.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
section: 7. Why the end of the line keeps changing
text:
7. Why the end of the line keeps changing
In the middle, a local line rests on years on both sides. At the last year there is only the past, so one or two warm years pull the end up. When the next years arrive, the end is recomputed. To see how much, we pretend to live in an earlier year, smooth the data known then, and compare the last value with what the line says about the same year today:


Code
today <- ours                                        # NASA's recipe, all years
last_years <- 2000:(max(earth$year) - 5)             # 5 later years are enough for the final value
revision <- t(sapply(last_years, function(end) {
  known <- subset(earth, year <= end)
  then  <- tail(lowess(known$year, known$temp, f = 10 / nrow(known), iter = 3)$y, 1)
  c(end = end, then = then, today = today[earth$year == end])
}))
revision <- as.data.frame(revision)
revision$change <- revision$today - revision$then
middle_change <- mean(abs(revision$change))
c(mean_absolute_revision = middle_change, largest = max(abs(revision$change)))


mean_absolute_revision                largest 
             0.0376888              0.0774982 


Code
revision[which.max(abs(revision$change)), ]


    end      then     today    change
14 2013 0.6592726 0.7367708 0.0774982




Code
ggplot(revision, aes(end)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = end, y = then, yend = today), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(y = then, colour = "as the last value, at the time"), size = 2.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = today, colour = "today, with the years after it"), size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The smooth value of a year: when it was the last, and today", x = NULL, y = "°C") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The last value was revised by 0.04 °C on average, and by up to 0.08 °C (for 2013). At the recent rate, that is up to 3.4 years of warming. The end of any smooth line is provisional. News about the “latest trend” is usually news about the least certain point of the curve.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
8. What robustness is for
The robustness rounds protect the line from single bad values. We put a typing error into the data, 1950 with a value of 2 °C, and smooth with and without the rounds:


Code
bad <- earth
bad$temp[bad$year == 1950] <- 2
shown <- data.frame(
  year = rep(earth$year, 3),
  value = c(
    lowess(earth$year, earth$temp, f = 10 / n, iter = 3)$y,
    lowess(bad$year, bad$temp, f = 10 / n, iter = 0)$y,
    lowess(bad$year, bad$temp, f = 10 / n, iter = 3)$y
  ),
  line = rep(c("correct data", "with the error, not robust", "with the error, robust"), each = n)
)
at_1950 <- tapply(shown$value[shown$year == 1950], shown$line[shown$year == 1950], mean)
round(at_1950, 3)


              correct data with the error, not robust     with the error, robust 
                    -0.075                      0.301                     -0.055 




Code
ggplot(
  subset(shown, year >= 1930 & year <= 1970),
  aes(year, value, colour = line, linetype = line)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "dashed"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "One wrong value (2 °C in 1950), with and without robustness rounds",
    x = NULL,
    y = "°C"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Without the rounds the curve has a bump of 0.38 °C. With them, it differs by 0.02 °C. But robustness is not always what you want: if the strange value is real, such as the year of a volcanic eruption, the robust line hides it.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

It is a picture, not a model. There are no coefficients to report and no formula to hand on. To predict, you need the data.
No extrapolation. predict() of a loess fit returns NA outside the data, and it is right to do so.
Degree 1 or 2? Local lines are safer at the ends. Local parabolas follow peaks and valleys better, and need a larger span for the same smoothness.
The default span of 0.75 is not a recommendation. With geom_smooth() you may be looking at a curve that is far too smooth, or too rough. Change span and look again.
Large data. loess() gets slow beyond a few thousand rows; geom_smooth() switches to a GAM at 1,000.
Several predictors. loess() takes up to four (Cleveland & Devlin, 1988), and the neighbourhoods become empty quickly. Splines and GAMs, which add one smooth curve per predictor, are the usual next step.
The peak of a smooth curve is lower than the true peak, and its valleys are shallower. Do not read extreme values off it.
Smoothing before an analysis creates correlated points. Never regress on smoothed values, and never compute correlations between two smoothed series.

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
The report (APA 7th edition) must contain everything that is needed to make the same line: the function, the span, the degree and the robustness rounds, and how the span was chosen. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
show_years <- c(1900, 1920, 1940, 1960, 1980, 2000, max(earth$year))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Year = show_years,
  Anomaly = f2(earth$temp[match(show_years, earth$year)]),
  L10 = f2(ours[match(show_years, earth$year)]),
  L30 = f2(pred$fit[match(show_years, earth$year)]),
  CI = paste0(
    "[",
    f2(band$low[match(show_years, earth$year)]),
    ", ",
    f2(band$high[match(show_years, earth$year)]),
    "]"
  ),
  rate = f2(warming$rate[match(show_years, earth$year)])
)


Method (data analysis):

We smoothed the annual global mean temperature anomalies of GISTEMP v4 (1880–2025, N = 146 years; GISTEMP Team, 2026; Lenssen et al., 2019) with local linear regression and tricube weights (Cleveland, 1979). Two neighbourhoods were used: 10 years with three robustness iterations, which reproduces the line published by NASA, and 30 years without robustness iterations (equivalent number of parameters = 9.2), for the long-term change. The slope of the local line is reported as the rate of warming. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

With a neighbourhood of 10 years, our line differed from the published one by less than 0.005 °C in every year, which is the rounding of the published values. With a neighbourhood of 30 years, the smoothed anomaly was -0.03 °C in 1960 and 0.70 °C in 2010 (Table 1). The rate of warming was 0.02 °C per decade around 1960, 0.14 around 1990 and 0.23 around 2010. Values at the end of the record are provisional: since 2000, the last value of the 10-year line was later revised by 0.04 °C on average.

Points to remember:

title: LOESS: The Smooth Line in NASA’s Temperature Chart
text:
11. Summary



When
You want to see the shape of a relation without assuming a formula


The idea
At each point, a weighted straight line (or parabola) through the nearest neighbours


Weights
Tricube in the distance; bisquare in the residuals for robustness


How (R)
lowess(x, y, f, iter); loess(y ~ x, span, degree, family) with standard errors


The choice
The span: small follows the data, large smooths them


Complexity
The trace of the matrix \(L\) in \(\hat y = L y\): the equivalent number of parameters


Choosing the span
The question first; AICc, GCV or cross-validation in blocks if neighbours are correlated


Weak points
The ends, correlated errors, extrapolation, many predictors


Related pages
Polynomial regression, weighted least squares, robust regression, isotonic regression

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
Before a football match a bookmaker offers odds. Odds of 2.00 for the home team mean: bet one euro, and get two back if it wins. So the bookmaker believes that the home team wins about half of the time. Every odd contains a probability.
Are these probabilities right? If we take all the matches in which the bookmaker said 60%, did the home team win 60% of them? And those with 20%, or 80%? We want the curve that turns the bookmaker’s probability into the true one.
We do not know the shape of that curve. It may bend anywhere. But we know one thing: it does not go down. A match with a higher implied probability cannot be a match with a smaller chance, or the bookmaker would not be in business.
Isotonic regression finds the best-fitting curve under this one condition. It needs no formula, no degree of a polynomial, no smoothing parameter. This page uses it for its most common modern job, checking and repairing probabilities, which is called calibration.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(isotone)   # gpava(): isotonic regression with weights and other loss functions

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
f4   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
1. The data
The site Football-Data (2026) publishes results and odds as one CSV file per league and season, free and with no login. We take ten seasons of the first division of six countries, and the odds of one bookmaker (Bet365).


Code
leagues <- c(
  England = "E0",
  Germany = "D1",
  Spain = "SP1",
  Italy = "I1",
  France = "F1",
  Greece = "G1"
)
# 2015-16 to 2024-25
seasons <- c("1516", "1617", "1718", "1819", "1920", "2021", "2122", "2223", "2324", "2425")

one_file <- function(country, season) {
  url <- paste0("https://www.football-data.co.uk/mmz4281/", season, "/", leagues[[country]], ".csv")
  d <- read.csv(url, fileEncoding = "latin1")
  data.frame(
    country,
    season,
    result = d$FTR,
    odds_home = as.numeric(d$B365H),
    odds_draw = as.numeric(d$B365D),
    odds_away = as.numeric(d$B365A)
  )
}
matches <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(leagues), function(country)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seasons, function(s) one_file(country, s)))))
matches <- matches[complete.cases(matches) & matches$result %in% c("H", "D", "A"), ]
nrow(matches)


[1] 20366


Code
table(matches$country)



England  France Germany  Greece   Italy   Spain 
   3800    3548    3060    2361    3797    3800 


result is H for a home win, D for a draw and A for an away win. The odds were collected before the match, on the Friday for the matches of a weekend and on the Tuesday for those of midweek.

From odds to probabilities
Odds of \(o\) are fair if the probability is \(1/o\). But the three values of \(1/o\) (home, draw, away) add up to more than 1, and the excess is the bookmaker’s margin. The simplest correction divides by the sum:
\[p_{\text{home}} = \frac{1/o_{\text{home}}}{1/o_{\text{home}} + 1/o_{\text{draw}} + 1/o_{\text{away}}}\]


Code
total <- 1 / matches$odds_home + 1 / matches$odds_draw + 1 / matches$odds_away
matches$p <- (1 / matches$odds_home) / total          # the implied probability of a home win
matches$y <- as.integer(matches$result == "H")        # what happened
c(mean_margin = mean(total) - 1, mean_p = mean(matches$p), share_home_wins = mean(matches$y))


    mean_margin          mean_p share_home_wins 
     0.05309741      0.44278506      0.44034175 


The margin is 5.3% on average. The mean implied probability of a home win is 44.3%, and the home team did win 44.0% of the matches. So the probabilities are nearly right on average. That says nothing about 20% or 80%.

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
2. Look at the data
The usual way to check is to make bins: all the matches with 0 to 10%, with 10 to 20% and so on, and compare the mean probability with the share of home wins in each bin.


Code
binned <- function(width) {
  bin <- cut(matches$p, seq(0, 1, by = width))
  d <- data.frame(
    p = tapply(matches$p, bin, mean),
    y = tapply(matches$y, bin, mean),
    n = as.vector(table(bin))
  )
  d[d$n > 0, ]
}
bins <- rbind(cbind(binned(0.10), width = "10 bins"), cbind(binned(0.02), width = "50 bins"))

ggplot(bins, aes(p, y)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ width) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4, name = "matches") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Implied probability against what happened",
       x = "bookmaker's probability of a home win", y = "share of home wins") +
  theme_bw()









With few bins we may hide a bend, and with many bins the picture wobbles, and even goes down in places, which cannot be true. The number of bins is an arbitrary choice, and different choices can lead to different conclusions (Dimitriadis et al., 2021). Isotonic regression lets the data choose the bins.

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: least squares with one condition
Sort the matches by their probability, \(p_1 \le p_2 \le \dots \le p_n\). We look for fitted values \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n\) that minimise the sum of squares,
\[\sum_i (y_i - \mu_i)^2 \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad \mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \dots \le \mu_n\]
There are as many \(\mu\)’s as matches, and no formula that connects them. Only the order is imposed.


Step 2: the algorithm, pool adjacent violators
If the data are already in order, then \(\mu_i = y_i\) and we are done. If two neighbours are in the wrong order (the second is smaller than the first), they are violators. The best we can do for them is to make them equal, at their mean. Then look again: the new mean may violate the order with its own neighbours. Keep pooling until no violators are left. This is the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm, PAVA (Ayer et al., 1955):


Code
pava <- function(y, w = rep(1, length(y)), trace = FALSE) {
  value <- numeric(0)
  weight <- numeric(0)
  size <- integer(0) # the blocks built so far
  for (i in seq_along(y)) {
    value <- c(value, y[i])
    weight <- c(weight, w[i])
    size <- c(size, 1L)
    # as long as the last block is below the one before it, pool the two into their weighted mean
    while (length(value) > 1 && value[length(value) - 1] >= value[length(value)]) {
      k <- length(value)
      value[k - 1] <- (weight[k - 1] * value[k - 1] + weight[k] * value[k]) /
        (weight[k - 1] + weight[k])
      weight[k - 1] <- weight[k - 1] + weight[k]
      size[k - 1] <- size[k - 1] + size[k]
      value <- value[-k]
      weight <- weight[-k]
      size <- size[-k]
    }
    if (trace) cat("after value", i, ":", format(rep(round(value, 2), size)), "\n")
  }
  rep(value, size)
}

toy <- c(1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 7)
fit_toy <- pava(toy, trace = TRUE)


after value 1 : 1 
after value 2 : 1 3 
after value 3 : 1.0 2.5 2.5 
after value 4 : 1.0 2.5 2.5 4.0 
after value 5 : 1.0 2.5 2.5 3.5 3.5 
after value 6 : 1.00 2.50 2.50 3.33 3.33 3.33 
after value 7 : 1.00 2.50 2.50 3.33 3.33 3.33 7.00 


Follow it: the 3 and the 2 are in the wrong order, so both become 2.5. Then 4, 3 and 3 become 3.33. The result never goes down, and no other non-decreasing series is closer to the data.


Step 3: what the result looks like
The fit is a step function: flat blocks with jumps between them. Each block is the mean of the \(y\)’s in it, so blocks are bins, whose number and borders were chosen by the data. There is also an explicit formula, the max-min formula:
\[\hat\mu_i = \max_{s \le i}\; \min_{t \ge i}\; \text{mean}(y_s, \dots, y_t)\]
In words: the largest, over all starting points to the left, of the smallest mean that a block ending to the right can have.


Code
max_min <- sapply(seq_along(toy), function(i)
  max(sapply(1:i, function(s) min(sapply(i:length(toy), function(t) mean(toy[s:t]))))))
rbind(pava = fit_toy, max_min = max_min)


        [,1] [,2] [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6] [,7]
pava       1  2.5  2.5 3.333333 3.333333 3.333333    7
max_min    1  2.5  2.5 3.333333 3.333333 3.333333    7




Step 4: yes or no outcomes
Here \(y\) is 0 or 1, and the fitted values are probabilities. Least squares looks like the wrong criterion for that. But for isotonic regression it does not matter: the same fit also maximises the binomial likelihood, and it is the best for every other reasonable score (Barlow et al., 1972; Dimitriadis et al., 2021).


Step 5: ties and weights
Several matches with exactly the same \(p\) must get the same fitted value. We can replace them by one row with their mean, and the number of matches as its weight. PAVA with weights then takes weighted means, as in the code above.


Step 6: what is estimated, and how well
There is nothing to tune. The price is a slower convergence: the error of a smooth parametric curve shrinks with \(n^{-1/2}\), the error of an isotonic fit with \(n^{-1/3}\). Ten times the data halve the error. It is a method for large samples.

4. Fitting the model and reading the output
R has isoreg() in base:


Code
ord <- order(matches$p)
p   <- matches$p[ord]
y   <- matches$y[ord]
iso <- isoreg(p, y)
fitted_iso <- iso$yf
n_blocks   <- length(unique(round(fitted_iso, 12)))
n_blocks


[1] 50


The 20,366 matches became 50 blocks. The same from our own function, and from isotone::gpava(), both on the table of tied probabilities with weights:

different <- unique(p)                                      # p is sorted already
which_one <- match(p, different)
ties <- data.frame(
  p = different,
  y = as.vector(tapply(y, which_one, mean)),
  n = tabulate(which_one)

package <- gpava(z = ties$p, y = ties$y, weights = ties$n)$x
c(different_probabilities = nrow(ties),

blocks <- data.frame(value = round(fitted_iso, 12), p = p)
blocks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(blocks, blocks$value), function(b)
  data.frame(from = min(b$p), to = max(b$p), matches = nrow(b), home_wins = b$value[1])))

Each row is a block: from which probability to which, how many matches, and the share of home wins in it, which is the fitted value for all of them. The five largest are shown. Blocks are wide where the data could not show a rise, and narrow where the rise was clear.


Code
step <- data.frame(p = p, fit = fitted_iso)
ggplot(step, aes(p, fit)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_step(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_rug(
    data = step[seq(1, nrow(step), by = 10), ],
    aes(x = p),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.1
  ) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Isotonic regression of the result on the implied probability",
    subtitle = "Dashed: perfect calibration. The ticks show where the matches are (one in ten)",
    x = "bookmaker's probability of a home win",
    y = "fitted probability of a home win"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
at <- function(q) approx(p, fitted_iso, xout = q, method = "constant", rule = 2, ties = "ordered")$y
at(c(0.15, 0.35, 0.65, 0.85))


[1] 0.1227496 0.3386139 0.6712329 0.8690096


The curve is close to the diagonal, so the bookmaker is good. But it is not on it. Where the bookmaker says 15%, the home team won 12.3%; at 35%, 33.9%; at 65%, 67.1%; at 85%, 86.9%. The steps wobble (at 60% it won 58.2%), but on the whole the curve is steeper than the diagonal: home teams with low chances win less often than their odds say, and those with high chances more often. This is the well-known favourite–longshot bias of betting markets (Snowberg & Wolfers, 2010). Part of it may come from our way of removing the margin: we shrank the three probabilities in the same proportion, and bookmakers may put more of the margin on the outsiders.

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
5. Is it more than chance?
The fit has no standard errors. And a step function that follows the noise will never lie exactly on the diagonal, even if the probabilities are perfect. So we ask: what would the fit look like if the bookmaker were right? We can simulate that. Keep the probabilities, throw a new result for every match with exactly these probabilities, and fit again:


Code
set.seed(7)
reps <- 500
grid <- seq(0.06, 0.90, by = 0.01)
curve_at <- function(yy) {
  approx(p, isoreg(p, yy)$yf, xout = grid, method = "constant", rule = 2, ties = "ordered")$y
}
under_null <- replicate(reps, curve_at(rbinom(length(p), 1, p))) # if the bookmaker were right
band <- data.frame(p = grid, lower = apply(under_null, 1, quantile, 0.05),
                   upper = apply(under_null, 1, quantile, 0.95), fit = curve_at(y))
outside <- mean(band$fit < band$lower | band$fit > band$upper)
below   <- grid[band$fit < band$lower]          # the probabilities where the fit is under the band
above   <- grid[band$fit > band$upper]          # and over it
c(share_outside = outside, points_below = length(below), of_them_under_50 = sum(below < 0.5),
  points_above = length(above), of_them_over_50 = sum(above > 0.5))


   share_outside     points_below of_them_under_50     points_above  of_them_over_50 
       0.2705882       11.0000000       10.0000000       12.0000000       11.0000000 




Code
ggplot(band, aes(p)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower - p, ymax = upper - p), fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_step(aes(y = fit - p), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(100 * v, " points")) +
  labs(title = "Fitted minus implied probability",
       subtitle = "Grey: where 90% of the fits would be if every probability were right",
       x = "bookmaker's probability of a home win", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()









The chart shows the difference from the diagonal, which makes it easier to see. The fit leaves the 90% band at 27% of the probabilities on the grid, where chance would give about 10%. And it does so with a pattern: of the 11 points under the band, 10 are for probabilities under 50%, and of the 12 points over it, 11 are for probabilities over 50%. The bias is real.

One number: the Brier score and its three parts
The Brier score is the mean squared difference between the probability and the result, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum (p_i - y_i)^2\). Smaller is better. Isotonic regression splits it into three parts that have a meaning (Dimitriadis et al., 2021):
\[\underbrace{\text{Brier}(p)}_{\text{the score}} = \underbrace{\text{Brier}(p) - \text{Brier}(\hat\mu)}_{\text{miscalibration}} - \underbrace{\big[\text{Brier}(\bar y) - \text{Brier}(\hat\mu)\big]}_{\text{discrimination}} + \underbrace{\text{Brier}(\bar y)}_{\text{uncertainty}}\]

Uncertainty is the score of the constant \(\bar y\), the share of home wins: how hard the matches are to predict without knowing anything.
Discrimination is how much better a perfectly recalibrated version of the probabilities would be: how well they sort the matches.
Miscalibration is what we lose because the numbers are not right.



Code
decompose <- function(p, y) {
  o <- order(p)
  p <- p[o]
  y <- y[o]
  mu <- isoreg(p, y)$yf
  brier <- mean((p - y)^2)
  best <- mean((mu - y)^2)
  constant <- mean((mean(y) - y)^2)
  c(
    brier = brier,
    miscalibration = brier - best,
    discrimination = constant - best,
    uncertainty = constant
  )
}
all_matches <- decompose(p, y)
round(all_matches, 4)


         brier miscalibration discrimination    uncertainty 
        0.2067         0.0010         0.0408         0.2464 


Code
set.seed(8)
null_mcb <- replicate(500, { yy <- rbinom(length(p), 1, p); decompose(p, yy)[["miscalibration"]] })
p_mcb <- mean(c(null_mcb, all_matches[["miscalibration"]]) >= all_matches[["miscalibration"]])
c(observed = all_matches[["miscalibration"]], mean_if_right = mean(null_mcb), p = p_mcb)


     observed mean_if_right             p 
 0.0009833516  0.0007232705  0.0039920160 


The miscalibration is 0.0010. It is never zero, because the isotonic curve always fits a little better than the probabilities. If the bookmaker were right, it would be 0.0007 on average by chance alone. Only 1 of the 500 simulated values reached the observed one, p = .004. Compared with the discrimination of 0.0408 it is tiny: what limits the bookmaker is how unpredictable football is, not the calibration.


Country by country


Code
set.seed(9)
by_country <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(leagues), function(country) {
  d   <- matches[matches$country == country, ]
  dec <- decompose(d$p, d$y)
  nul <- replicate(500, decompose(d$p, rbinom(nrow(d), 1, d$p))[["miscalibration"]])
  data.frame(country, matches = nrow(d), t(dec), expected = mean(nul),
             p = mean(c(nul, dec[["miscalibration"]]) >= dec[["miscalibration"]]))
}))
print(cbind(by_country[, 1:2], round(by_country[, -(1:2)], 4)), row.names = FALSE)

  d <- matches[matches$country == country, ]
  d <- d[order(d$p), ]

greek <- by_country[by_country$country == "Greece", ]
others <- by_country[by_country$country != "Greece", ]
gr <- matches[matches$country == "Greece", ]
gr_at <- function(q) {
  approx(
    sort(gr$p),
    isoreg(gr$p, gr$y)$yf,
