One league is different. In Greece the miscalibration is 0.0055, 1.8 times what chance would give, where the other five have between 0.0025 and 0.0029. (Spain and Italy are a little above chance as well, p = .024 and .036.) When the odds said 80% for a Greek home team, it won 92.4% of the matches; when they said 45%, 37.4%. The same league has the largest discrimination (0.059): a few teams are far stronger than the rest, and the odds followed this, but not far enough. Two explanations fit: fewer people bet on this league, so the odds are less sharp, and the margin there may be spread differently. The data cannot tell which.

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
6. Repairing the probabilities
The fitted curve is also a recalibration: feed it a bookmaker’s probability and take the fitted value instead. To see if this helps, we must not judge it on the matches it was built from. Build it on eight seasons, and judge it on the last two:


Code
train <- subset(matches, season %in% seasons[1:8])
test  <- subset(matches, season %in% seasons[9:10])

isotonic_fit <- function(d) {
  # returns a function: probability in, recalibrated probability out
  o <- order(d$p)
  mu <- isoreg(d$p, d$y)$yf
  # straight lines between the points
  function(q) approx(d$p[o], mu, xout = q, rule = 2, ties = mean)$y
}
logit <- function(q) log(q / (1 - q))
logistic_fit <- function(d) {
  # logistic regression of the result on the logit of the probability
  m <- glm(y ~ logit(p), family = binomial, data = d)
  function(q) unname(predict(m, data.frame(p = q), type = "response"))
}
brier <- function(q, y) mean((q - y)^2)
judge <- function(tr, te) c(matches = nrow(te),
                            bookmaker = brier(te$p, te$y),
                            isotonic  = brier(isotonic_fit(tr)(te$p), te$y),
                            logistic  = brier(logistic_fit(tr)(te$p), te$y))
repair <- rbind(
  `all six countries` = judge(train, test),
  `Greece only` = judge(subset(train, country == "Greece"), subset(test, country == "Greece"))
)
round(repair, 4)


                  matches bookmaker isotonic logistic
all six countries    3977    0.2015   0.2012   0.2011
Greece only           473    0.1952   0.1947   0.1951


Code
# is the gain more than luck? the change of the squared error, match by match, with its standard
# error
gain <- function(tr, te, method) {
  change <- (method(tr)(te$p) - te$y)^2 - (te$p - te$y)^2
  c(change = mean(change), SE = sd(change) / sqrt(length(change)))
}
gains <- rbind(
  all_isotonic = gain(train, test, isotonic_fit),
  all_logistic = gain(train, test, logistic_fit),
  greece_isotonic = gain(
    subset(train, country == "Greece"),
    subset(test, country == "Greece"),
    isotonic_fit
  ),
  greece_logistic = gain(
    subset(train, country == "Greece"),
    subset(test, country == "Greece"),
    logistic_fit
  )
)
round(gains, 5)


                  change      SE
all_isotonic    -0.00029 0.00031
all_logistic    -0.00036 0.00012
greece_isotonic -0.00048 0.00271
greece_logistic -0.00010 0.00148


Code
logit_coefs <- coef(glm(y ~ logit(p), family = binomial, data = train))
logit_coefs


(Intercept)    logit(p) 
 0.01710627  1.06528000 


Logistic recalibration (also known as Platt scaling) assumes a shape: a straight line between the logit of the bookmaker’s probability and the logit of the true one, with two parameters. Its slope is 1.07, above 1: the probabilities should be spread further apart.

For all the matches, the Brier score on the two later seasons goes from 0.2015 to 0.2012 with isotonic regression and 0.2011 with the logistic curve.
For Greece alone, from 0.1952 to 0.1947 and 0.1951.

The gains are tiny, as the decomposition promised: there was little miscalibration to remove. For all the matches, isotonic regression gained 0.00029 with a standard error of 0.00031, and the logistic curve 0.00036 with a standard error of 0.00012. The gains are alike in size, but that of the logistic curve is steadier: it moves every probability a little, while the isotonic curve moves them in jumps. In Greece the 473 matches of the last two seasons are too few to say anything. In general, isotonic regression needs thousands of cases, because with few it follows the noise; it wins when the true shape is not what the parametric curve assumes (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005).

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

The condition must come from knowledge, not from the data. Isotonic regression always returns a non-decreasing curve, also when the truth goes up and down. It cannot discover that the order is wrong. Use it only when the order is certain.
The ends are the weak point. The first and the last block are means of few cases, and they are pulled outwards: in a binary outcome they can be exactly 0 or 1. Do not trust the extremes, and do not take the logarithm of such a probability.
Steps are not real. The true curve is probably smooth. For predictions, straight lines between the block centres are better than jumps; for a smooth curve that does not go down, there are monotone splines (package scam).
In-sample fit is optimistic. The miscalibration measured with isotonic regression is positive even for perfect probabilities, so compare it with its value under simulation, as in section 5.
A decreasing relation: fit \(-y\) and change the sign. A single peak: increasing up to each candidate and decreasing after it (unimodal regression).
Other losses. gpava(..., solver = weighted.median) gives an isotonic median (compare quantile regression), and fractiles are available too.
Other predictors. Isotonic regression has one ordered predictor. For several, generalized additive models can force some of their curves to be monotone.
The matches are not all independent: the same teams play many times. The simulation treats them as independent given the probabilities.
Not a way to win. The bias is small next to the bookmaker’s margin. A bet of one euro on every home team would have lost money in every range of the odds:



Code
matches$return <- matches$odds_home * matches$y - 1
ranges <- cut(matches$p, c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1))
round(tapply(matches$return, ranges, mean), 3)      # euros won per euro


  (0,0.2] (0.2,0.4] (0.4,0.6] (0.6,0.8]   (0.8,1] 
   -0.103    -0.099    -0.057    -0.022    -0.019

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the condition and why it is justified, how ties were treated, the number of blocks, how the uncertainty was assessed, and the fitted values at some points. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Country        = by_country$country,
  n              = num(by_country$matches),
  Brier          = nz(by_country$brier, 3),
  Miscalibration = nz(by_country$miscalibration, 4),
  Expected       = nz(by_country$expected, 4),
  p              = sapply(by_country$p, function(v) sub("^= ", "", pval(v))),
  Discrimination = nz(by_country$discrimination, 3),
  Uncertainty    = nz(by_country$uncertainty, 3))


Method (data analysis):

We compared the odds of one bookmaker with the results of 20,366 first-division football matches in six countries, seasons 2015–16 to 2024–25. The odds were converted to probabilities by dividing their reciprocals by their sum. We estimated the probability of a home win as a non-decreasing function of the implied probability with isotonic regression (pool-adjacent-violators algorithm; de Leeuw et al., 2009), which is justified because a higher implied probability should not go with a lower chance of winning. Tied probabilities were pooled. Calibration was assessed with the CORP decomposition of the Brier score (Dimitriadis et al., 2021); its miscalibration component was compared with its distribution in 500 data sets simulated from the implied probabilities. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

The isotonic fit had 50 blocks. Implied probabilities of 15%, 35%, 65% and 85% corresponded to fitted probabilities of 12.3%, 33.9%, 67.1% and 86.9%, so that home teams with low probabilities were overrated and those with high probabilities underrated. The Brier score was .207, with a miscalibration of .0010 (.0007 expected under perfect calibration, p = .004), a discrimination of .041 and an uncertainty of .246. Miscalibration was largest in Greece (Table 1). On the seasons 2023–24 and 2024–25, which were not used for the fit, isotonic recalibration changed the Brier score from .2015 to .2012.

Points to remember:

Say why the relation must be monotone.
Give the number of observations and of blocks, and fitted values at meaningful points.
Show the curve with a band, and say what the band means (here: if the probabilities were right).
If you use the curve to correct probabilities, judge it on new data, against a simple parametric correction.

title: Isotonic Regression: Are the Bookmakers’ Probabilities Right?
text:
9. Summary



When
The relation can only go up (or only down), and its shape is unknown


The model
Minimise \(\sum w_i (y_i - \mu_i)^2\) subject to \(\mu_1 \le \dots \le \mu_n\)


The algorithm
Pool adjacent violators: replace neighbours in the wrong order by their mean, until none are left


How (R)
isoreg(x, y); with weights or medians, isotone::gpava(z, y, weights, solver)


The result
A step function; every step is the mean of a block chosen by the data


Binary outcome
The same fit maximises the likelihood


Uses
Calibration of probabilities, dose and response, growth, ordered categories


Uncertainty
Simulation under calibration, or the bootstrap


Weak points
The ends, small samples, and an order that is not true


Related pages

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
People with more schooling earn more. Is it the school that makes the difference? Or would the same persons have earned more anyway, because they are able, hard-working, or from families that help? Nobody can measure all of that. So adding control variables, the remedy of ordinary regression, does not finish the job.
An instrumental variable (an instrument) takes another way. Find something that

pushes people towards more schooling,
has nothing to do with their ability or family,
and touches their wages in no other way than through schooling.

Then compare the wages of those who were pushed and those who were not. Whatever difference there is, must have come through schooling.
David Card (1993) proposed the distance to a college. A boy who grew up near a four-year college could live at home while studying. For some boys that decided the matter. This page repeats his analysis, with every step by hand, and then asks how far one can trust it. The second part is the more important one: the conditions above cannot be proved from the data.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(ivreg)       # ivreg(): two-stage least squares with diagnostics
# also used, with package::function: sandwich (robust standard errors)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# APA: no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
}
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

dim(card)

1 6.306275  548    7  29    16     1     0    1      1      0      0

Code
controls <- paste(
  "exper + expersq + black + south + smsa + smsa66",
  "+ reg662 + reg663 + reg664 + reg665 + reg666 + reg667 + reg668 + reg669"
)


3,010 men of the US National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men, 24 to 34 years old when their wages were asked in 1976. The file comes from the R package wooldridge. The variables:

lwage: the logarithm of the hourly wage (in cents). A coefficient of 0.10 means about 10% more.
educ: years of schooling.
nearc4: 1 if there was an accredited four-year college in the local labour market, judged by the county where he lived in 1966 (as a boy or very young man), otherwise 0. nearc2 is the same for two-year colleges.
The controls of Card: years of potential work experience (exper, which is age − schooling − 6, and its square), black, living in the south, living in a metropolitan area in 1976 (smsa) and in 1966 (smsa66), and the region in 1966 (eight indicator variables, reg662 to reg669).

The men who grew up near a college (2,053 of them) have 0.83 years more schooling and wages that are 0.156 higher in logs. But they are also different in other ways: fewer are black, fewer live in the south, and most come from cities. A college does not stand just anywhere. title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: why least squares is wrong
The true equation has a variable \(u\) that we cannot see, which is also related to schooling \(s\):
\[\log w = \beta\, s + u, \qquad \text{Cov}(s, u) \ne 0\]
Least squares attributes to \(s\) everything that comes along with it, \(\hat\beta_{OLS} \to \beta + \text{Cov}(s, u)/\text{Var}(s)\). The sample size does not help.


Code
nodes <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 2, 4, 3),
  y = c(0, 0, 0, 1.3),
  label = c(
    "college nearby\n(instrument)",
    "schooling",
    "wage",
    "ability, family, ...\n(not observed)"
  )
)
arrows <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.5, 2.4, 2.8, 3.2),
  y = c(0, 0, 1.05, 1.05),
  xend = c(1.55, 3.65, 2.15, 3.85),
  yend = c(0, 0, 0.15, 0.15)
)
never <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.3, 0.1),
  y = c(-0.15, 0.2),
  xend = c(3.8, 2.3),
  yend = c(-0.15, 1.2),
  curv = 1
)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = arrows,
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "#2a78d6"
  ) +
  geom_curve(
    data = never[1, ],
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = 0.25,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = never[2, ],
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4.2, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2,
    y = -0.78,
    label = "no direct way (exclusion)",
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.75,
    y = 0.95,
    label = "no connection\n(independence)",
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  xlim(-0.6, 4.6) +
  ylim(-0.95, 1.6) +
  labs(title = "What an instrument needs: the blue arrows, and not the dashed lines") +
  theme_void()











Step 2: the conditions

Relevance: the instrument changes schooling. This can be checked.
Independence: the instrument has nothing to do with \(u\) (after the controls).
Exclusion: the instrument changes wages only through schooling.
Monotonicity (for the interpretation, section 6): the instrument pushes nobody in the opposite direction.



Step 3: the Wald estimator
With one instrument that is 0 or 1 and no controls, the estimator is the ratio of two differences:
\[\hat\beta_{IV} = \frac{\bar y_{\text{near}} - \bar y_{\text{far}}}{\bar s_{\text{near}} - \bar s_{\text{far}}}\]
The numerator is the effect of the instrument on the outcome (the reduced form), the denominator its effect on schooling (the first stage).


Code
c(
  reduced_form = diff(by_near$lwage),
  first_stage = diff(by_near$educ),
  Wald = diff(by_near$lwage) / diff(by_near$educ)
)


reduced_form  first_stage         Wald 
   0.1559075    0.8290190    0.1880626 


Without controls we know that condition 2 fails, so 0.188 is not our answer.


Step 4: two-stage least squares
With controls \(X\) (and perhaps several instruments \(Z\)) the same idea is done with two regressions, two-stage least squares (2SLS):

First stage: regress schooling on the instrument and the controls, and keep the fitted values \(\hat s\). They contain only the part of schooling that the instrument and the controls can explain.
Second stage: regress the log wage on \(\hat s\) and the controls.

\[\hat\beta = (W^\top P_Z W)^{-1} W^\top P_Z\, y, \qquad P_Z = Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top\]
(\(W\): schooling and the controls; \(Z\): instrument and controls.)


Code
fml <- function(lhs, rhs) as.formula(paste(lhs, "~", rhs))
ols          <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls)), card)
first_stage  <- lm(fml("educ", paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
reduced_form <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
card$educ_hat <- fitted(first_stage)
second_stage <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ_hat +", controls)), card)

W <- model.matrix(ols); Z <- model.matrix(first_stage); y <- card$lwage
PW   <- Z %*% solve(crossprod(Z), crossprod(Z, W))                        # P_Z W
beta <- drop(solve(crossprod(PW, W), crossprod(PW, y)))
cbind(
  value = c(
    OLS = coef(ols)[["educ"]],
    reduced_form_over_first_stage = coef(reduced_form)[["nearc4"]] / coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]],
    second_stage = coef(second_stage)[["educ_hat"]],
    matrix_formula = beta[["educ"]]
  )
)


                                   value
OLS                           0.07469326
reduced_form_over_first_stage 0.13150384
second_stage                  0.13150384
matrix_formula                0.13150384


The three ways give the same 0.132. Least squares gave 0.075.


Step 5: the standard error
The second regression gives the right coefficient and a wrong standard error: its residuals are measured from \(\hat s\) instead of \(s\). The right ones use the real schooling:
\[e = y - W\hat\beta, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{e^\top e}{n - p}\,(W^\top P_Z W)^{-1}\]


Code
e  <- drop(y - W %*% beta); s2 <- sum(e^2) / (nrow(W) - ncol(W))
se <- sqrt(diag(s2 * solve(crossprod(PW))))
iv <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc4 +", controls)), data = card)
rbind(
  by_hand = c(estimate = beta[["educ"]], SE = se[["educ"]]),
  ivreg = coef(summary(iv))["educ", 1:2],
  second_stage_lm = coef(summary(second_stage))["educ_hat", 1:2]
)


                 estimate         SE
by_hand         0.1315038 0.05496367
ivreg           0.1315038 0.05496367
second_stage_lm 0.1315038 0.05651035


Code
robust_se <- sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1")["educ", "educ"]); c(robust_SE = robust_se)


 robust_SE 
0.05414362 


Here the wrong standard error happens to be close to the right one. It can be far off, in both directions. In ivreg(), the part after | lists the instruments and all controls again.

text:
4. Reading the output


Code
ci_iv <- confint(iv)["educ", ]; s_iv <- summary(iv)
round(
  rbind(
    OLS = c(coef(summary(ols))["educ", ], confint(ols)["educ", ]),
    IV = c(coef(s_iv)["educ", ], ci_iv)
  ),
  4
)


    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  2.5 % 97.5 %
OLS   0.0747     0.0035 21.3510   0.0000 0.0678 0.0816
IV    0.1315     0.0550  2.3926   0.0168 0.0237 0.2393


Code
s_iv$diagnostics


                 df1  df2 statistic      p-value
Weak instruments   1 2994 13.255785 0.0002763401
Wu-Hausman         1 2993  1.167645 0.2799726211
Sargan             0   NA        NA           NA



The IV estimate says that a year of schooling raises the wage by 0.132 (about 14%), 95% CI [0.024, 0.239]. Least squares says 0.075 (7.8%).
The interval of IV is 15.7 times as wide. That is the price. IV uses only the little variation of schooling that comes from the instrument. With the partial correlation \(r\) between instrument and schooling, the SE grows by about \(1/|r|\); here \(r\) = 0.066.
The IV estimate is higher than that of least squares. If able men stay longer in school, we expected the opposite. Section 6 comes back to this.

The numbers are those of Card’s own Table 3: 0.320 (0.088) for the first stage, 0.042 (0.018) for the reduced form and 0.132 (0.055) for the IV estimate. The three tests of the output, by hand:


Code
fs_without <- update(first_stage, . ~ . - nearc4)
# weak instruments: the F of the instrument in the first stage
F_first <- anova(fs_without, first_stage)[2, "F"]
card$v_hat <- residuals(first_stage)
# Wu-Hausman: the first-stage residual as an extra predictor
wu <- coef(summary(update(ols, . ~ . + v_hat)))["v_hat", ]
# two instruments
iv2 <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc2 + nearc4 +", controls)), data = card)
# Sargan: n R^2 of the IV residuals on all instruments
aux <- lm(fml("residuals(iv2)", paste("nearc2 + nearc4 +", controls)), card)
c(
  F_first_stage = F_first,
  F_Wu_Hausman = wu[["t value"]]^2,
  Sargan_two_instruments = nrow(card) * summary(aux)$r.squared
)


         F_first_stage           F_Wu_Hausman Sargan_two_instruments 
             13.255785               1.167645               1.248153 


Code
summary(iv2)$diagnostics; coef(summary(iv2))["educ", 1:2]


                 df1  df2 statistic      p-value
Weak instruments   2 2993  7.893096 0.0003811364
Wu-Hausman         1 2993  2.925645 0.0872860158
Sargan             1   NA  1.248153 0.2639054547


  Estimate Std. Error 
0.15705937 0.05257824 


Code
sargan <- summary(iv2)$diagnostics["Sargan", ]
weak2 <- summary(iv2)$diagnostics["Weak instruments", ]



Weak instruments: the F of the instrument in the first stage, here 13.3. More about it in section 5.
Wu–Hausman: is the IV estimate different from least squares? Put the first-stage residual into the wage equation; if it matters, schooling is endogenous. Here F = 1.17, p = .280: the data cannot tell the two apart. That does not prove that least squares is right; the IV estimate is just imprecise.
Sargan: with more instruments than needed one can check whether they tell the same story. With the two-year college as second instrument the estimate is 0.157 and the test has p = .264: no contradiction. But two instruments of the same kind can be wrong in the same way, and then the test does not notice. (The F for both together is 7.9: the second one adds almost nothing.)

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
5. Weak instruments
If the instrument hardly moves schooling, the estimator divides by a number near zero. The estimates jump around, and the usual interval (estimate ± 1.96 SE) can be wrong. A simulation where we know the truth (β = 0.08). pi is the effect of the instrument on schooling, rho the endogeneity: the correlation between what we do not see in schooling and what we do not see in wages.


Code
set.seed(211)
one <- function(pi, rho, n = 1000) {
  z <- rep(0:1, length.out = n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  s <- 12 + pi * z + 2 * (rho * u + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n))
  y <- 0.08 * s + 0.4 * u
  zc <- z - mean(z)
  fs <- sum(zc * s) / sum(zc^2)
  rf <- sum(zc * y) / sum(zc^2)
  b <- rf / fs
  e <- (y - mean(y)) - b * (s - mean(s))
  se <- sqrt(sum(e^2) / (n - 2) / sum(zc^2)) / abs(fs)
  F <- fs^2 * sum(zc^2) / (sum(((s - mean(s)) - fs * zc)^2) / (n - 2))
  d <- (y - mean(y)) - 0.08 * (s - mean(s))
  g <- sum(zc * d) / sum(zc^2)
  ar <- g / sqrt(sum((d - g * zc)^2) / (n - 2) / sum(zc^2)) # Anderson-Rubin at the truth
  c(
    iv = b,
    ols = cov(s, y) / var(s),
    F = F,
    covered = abs(b - 0.08) < 1.96 * se,
    ar_covered = abs(ar) < 1.96
  )
}
settings <- expand.grid(pi = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1), rho = c(0.6, 0.95))
sim <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(settings)), function(i) {
    r <- t(replicate(2000, one(settings$pi[i], settings$rho[i])))
    data.frame(
      settings[i, ],
      mean_F = mean(r[, "F"]),
      OLS = mean(r[, "ols"]),
      IV_median = median(r[, "iv"]),
      IV_low = quantile(r[, "iv"], 0.05),
      IV_high = quantile(r[, "iv"], 0.95),
      coverage = mean(r[, "covered"]),
      coverage_AR = mean(r[, "ar_covered"])
    )
  })
)
print(round(sim, 3), row.names = FALSE)


   pi  rho mean_F   OLS IV_median IV_low IV_high coverage coverage_AR
 0.10 0.60  1.760 0.200     0.147 -0.820   0.911    0.954       0.946
 0.25 0.60  4.963 0.200     0.084 -0.323   0.232    0.942       0.944
 0.50 0.60 16.762 0.198     0.082 -0.040   0.150    0.948       0.954
 1.00 0.60 63.829 0.193     0.081  0.031   0.118    0.954       0.951
 0.10 0.95  1.649 0.270     0.163 -0.616   0.994    0.791       0.954
 0.25 0.95  4.984 0.269     0.083 -0.465   0.183    0.890       0.954
 0.50 0.95 16.229 0.267     0.078 -0.061   0.138    0.938       0.948
 1.00 0.95 63.174 0.259     0.079  0.027   0.114    0.955       0.954


Code
si <- function(p, r) sim[sim$pi == p & sim$rho == r, ]
c(endogeneity_in_the_data_of_Card = cor(residuals(iv), residuals(first_stage)))


endogeneity_in_the_data_of_Card 
                     -0.2851473 



Least squares gives about 0.20 with an endogeneity of 0.6 and 0.27 with 0.95, instead of 0.08, whatever the instrument.
With a strong instrument (mean F = 63.8) the IV estimates lie around 0.08.
With the weakest one (mean F = 1.8) the median of the IV estimates is 0.15 or 0.16: it has moved towards least squares. And 90% of the estimates lie between -0.82 and 0.91 (endogeneity 0.6).
The usual interval contains the truth in 94% to 95% of the samples with an endogeneity of 0.6, even with weak instruments. It is right there, and very wide. With 0.95 its coverage falls to 79% for the weakest instrument.

This is why the advice in the literature looks contradictory. An old rule asks for F > 10 (Staiger & Stock, 1997). Lee et al. (2022) show that a t test with the usual 1.96 needs an F above 104.7 to have an error of at most 5% in the worst case. Angrist and Kolesár (2024) show that with one instrument the usual interval is nearly right unless the endogeneity is extreme. Card’s instrument has an F of 13.3, and the estimated endogeneity is -0.29. It is best to use an interval that does not depend on all this:

The Anderson–Rubin interval
A test that works with any strength (Anderson & Rubin, 1949): if the true effect were \(\beta_0\), then \(y - \beta_0 s\) would contain nothing of schooling, and the instrument should not predict it. Test that for many \(\beta_0\) and keep those that are not rejected. In the simulation it has the right coverage in all settings (from 94.3% to 95.4%).


Code
ar_p <- function(b0) {
  r <- lm(fml(paste0("I(lwage - ", b0, " * educ)"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
  coef(summary(r))["nearc4", 4]
}
grid  <- seq(-0.05, 0.4, by = 0.005); p_grid <- sapply(grid, ar_p)
edge  <- function(a, b) uniroot(function(v) ar_p(v) - 0.05, c(a, b))$root
ci_ar <- c(edge(-0.05, beta[["educ"]]), edge(beta[["educ"]], 0.5))
rbind(Wald = ci_iv, Anderson_Rubin = ci_ar)


                    2.5 %    97.5 %
Wald           0.02373345 0.2392742
Anderson_Rubin 0.02480370 0.2848301


Code
ggplot(data.frame(grid, p_grid), aes(grid, p_grid)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(ols)[["educ"]], colour = "#eb6834") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = coef(ols)[["educ"]] - 0.005,
    y = 0.95,
    label = "least squares",
    hjust = 1,
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Anderson-Rubin: p-value of every possible effect",
    subtitle = "Values above the dashed line (.05) form the 95% interval",
    x = "effect of a year of schooling on the log wage",
    y = "p"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









The interval goes from 0.025 to 0.285. It is longer than the usual one on the upper side, and it contains the result of least squares.

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
6. Whose effect is it?
Card’s result (IV higher than OLS) is typical for this literature. One explanation is that the effect is not the same for everybody. Boys who would go to college anyway, and boys who would never go, are not moved by the instrument. IV is about the others, the compliers. Imbens and Angrist (1994) called it the local average treatment effect (LATE). If those who are held back by cost gain more from school than the average, the IV estimate is higher, and it is right, for them.
Where on the ladder did the instrument push? Schooling is the sum of steps, \(s = \sum_k I(s \ge k)\), so the first stage can be split into steps:


Code
steps <- data.frame(k = 8:18); steps$effect <- steps$se <- NA
for (i in seq_along(steps$k)) {
  co <- coef(summary(lm(
    fml(paste0("I(educ >= ", steps$k[i], ")"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)),
    card
  )))["nearc4", ]
  steps$effect[i] <- co[1]
  steps$se[i] <- co[2]
}
ggplot(steps, aes(k, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = effect - 1.96 * se, ymax = effect + 1.96 * se), colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 8:18) +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of a college nearby on reaching at least k years",
    x = "years of schooling, k",
    y = "change in the share of men"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
all_steps <- sum(sapply((min(card$educ) + 1):max(card$educ), function(k) {
  coef(lm(fml(paste0("I(educ >= ", k, ")"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card))[["nearc4"]]
}))
c(sum_over_all_steps = all_steps, first_stage = coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]])


sum_over_all_steps        first_stage 
         0.3198989          0.3198989 


Code
top <- steps[which.max(steps$effect), ]


The sum of the steps is the first stage, 0.32 years. The largest step is at 13 years (6.4 percentage points more men reach it). So the estimate is about boys who were near the decision for or against some college, and not about the value of the tenth year of school.
Other explanations are less flattering: measurement error in schooling pulls least squares down, the instrument may be invalid, and studies with a “significant” IV result are more easily published.

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
7. Can we believe the conditions?

Does the instrument predict what it should not?
Independence cannot be tested, since \(u\) is not observed. But we can check some things that the instrument should not be related to, after the controls (with age instead of experience, because experience contains schooling):


Code
controls_age <- sub("exper + expersq", "age + I(age^2)", controls, fixed = TRUE)
check_vars <- c(
  fatheduc = "father's schooling",
  motheduc = "mother's schooling",
  momdad14 = "lived with both parents at 14",
  libcrd14 = "library card at home at 14",
  IQ = "IQ (from school records)",
  KWW = "knowledge of the world of work"
)
balance <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(check_vars), function(v) {
    m <- lm(fml(v, paste("nearc4 +", controls_age)), card)
    co <- coef(summary(m))["nearc4", ]
    data.frame(
      variable = check_vars[[v]],
      raw_difference = mean(card[[v]][card$nearc4 == 1], na.rm = TRUE) -
        mean(card[[v]][card$nearc4 == 0], na.rm = TRUE),
      with_controls = co[1],
      SE = co[2],
      p = co[4],
      n = nobs(m)
    )
  })
)
print(data.frame(balance[1], round(balance[2:5], 3), n = balance$n), row.names = FALSE)


                       variable raw_difference with_controls    SE     p    n
             father's schooling          1.135         0.280 0.177 0.113 2320
             mother's schooling          0.594        -0.016 0.144 0.913 2657
  lived with both parents at 14          0.001        -0.022 0.018 0.210 3010
     library card at home at 14          0.183         0.044 0.019 0.022 2997
       IQ (from school records)          2.596         0.904 0.752 0.229 2061
 knowledge of the world of work          2.974         0.756 0.315 0.016 2963


The controls remove most of the raw differences. What is left is small, but not nothing: 2 of the 6 have p < .05 (library card at home at 14 and knowledge of the world of work). (The last one was measured in 1966, when the men were 14 to 24 years old and a part of them had already left school, so it may partly be an effect of schooling.) Boys near a college seem to come from homes with a few more books.


Card’s own test
Card argued like this. A college nearby should matter most to boys from poor families, for whom the cost decides. So the product of “college nearby” and “parents without high school” can be the instrument, and then “college nearby” itself may go into the wage equation. If it has a direct effect on wages, it will show there. In his Table 5 the IV estimate is 0.093 (0.065) and the direct effect 0.015 (0.029). His classes of parental education are not in our file, but we can build something like them. As he did in this table, we treat experience as endogenous, with age as its instrument (the last part of this section says why):


Code
card$fa <- ifelse(is.na(card$fatheduc), mean(card$fatheduc, na.rm = TRUE), card$fatheduc)
card$mo <- ifelse(is.na(card$motheduc), mean(card$motheduc, na.rm = TRUE), card$motheduc)
card$fa_missing <- as.numeric(is.na(card$fatheduc))
card$mo_missing <- as.numeric(is.na(card$motheduc))
family <- "fa * mo + fa_missing + mo_missing + momdad14 + sinmom14 + step14"
low_defs <- list(
  `no parent known to have 12 years` = with(
    card,
    (is.na(fatheduc) | fatheduc < 12) & (is.na(motheduc) | motheduc < 12)
  ),
  `both known, both below 12 years` = with(
    card,
    !is.na(fatheduc) & !is.na(motheduc) & fatheduc < 12 & motheduc < 12
  )
)
card_test <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(low_defs), function(k) {
    card$low <- as.numeric(low_defs[[k]])
    rest <- sub("exper + expersq", "low", controls, fixed = TRUE)
    first <- lm(fml("educ", paste("nearc4 * low + age + I(age^2) +", rest, "+", family)), card)
    m <- ivreg(
      fml(
        "lwage",
        paste(
          "educ + nearc4 + exper + expersq +",
          rest,
          "+",
          family,
          "| nearc4:low + nearc4 + age + I(age^2) +",
          rest,
          "+",
          family
        )
      ),
      data = card
    )
    data.frame(
      parents = k,
      n_low = sum(card$low),
      college_effect_others = coef(first)[["nearc4"]],
      extra_for_low = coef(first)[["nearc4:low"]],
      SE_extra = coef(summary(first))["nearc4:low", 2],
      IV = coef(m)[["educ"]],
      SE_IV = coef(summary(m))["educ", 2],
      direct_effect = coef(m)[["nearc4"]],
      SE_direct = coef(summary(m))["nearc4", 2]
    )
  })
)
tab <- t(round(card_test[-(1:2)], 3))
colnames(tab) <- card_test$parents
tab


                      no parent known to have 12 years both known, both below 12 years
college_effect_others                            0.187                           0.385
extra_for_low                                    0.339                          -0.107
SE_extra                                         0.180                           0.199
IV                                               0.133                           0.119
SE_IV                                            0.093                           0.391
direct_effect                                   -0.001                           0.004
SE_direct                                        0.038                           0.140


With the first definition (1,431 men with less educated parents) the picture is the one of Card: the college matters more for the sons of less educated parents (0.19 years for the others, 0.34 more for them), the IV estimate is 0.133 (SE 0.093), and the direct effect is -0.001 (SE 0.038). With the second definition (815 men) the extra effect has the wrong sign, and nothing can be estimated (SE of the IV estimate 0.39). The test says what Card wrote himself: “although imprecise”, there is no evidence against the instrument. That is not the same as evidence for it.


How large a violation would change the answer?
Suppose that growing up near a college raises wages directly by \(\gamma\) (better labour market, better schools). Then the right estimate would be
\[\hat\beta(\gamma) = \frac{\text{reduced form} - \gamma}{\text{first stage}}\]
(Conley et al., 2012, develop this idea.)


Code
rf <- coef(reduced_form)[["nearc4"]]; fs <- coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]]
gamma <- seq(0, 0.06, length.out = 100)
g_ols <- rf - coef(ols)[["educ"]] * fs
ggplot(data.frame(gamma, b = (rf - gamma) / fs), aes(gamma, b)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = coef(ols)[["educ"]], colour = "#eb6834") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.058,
    y = coef(ols)[["educ"]] + 0.008,
    label = "least squares",
    hjust = 1,
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "IV estimate, if the instrument also had a direct effect on wages",
    x = "direct effect of a college nearby on the log wage",
    y = "effect of a year of schooling"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
cbind(
  value = c(
    reduced_form = rf,
    first_stage = fs,
    gamma_for_the_OLS_result = g_ols,
    gamma_for_zero = rf
  )
)


                              value
reduced_form             0.04206794
first_stage              0.31989894
gamma_for_the_OLS_result 0.01817364
gamma_for_zero           0.04206794


A direct effect of only 1.8% on wages would bring the estimate down to the one of least squares, and one of 4.2% to zero. Because IV divides by a small first stage, small violations become large errors. And nobody can rule out a direct effect of 2%.


A control that is not innocent
exper is age − schooling − 6. It contains schooling, the very variable that we consider endogenous. Two remedies: use age instead of experience, or treat experience as endogenous too and use age as its instrument. Card did the second in his panel B of Table 3 and found 0.122 (0.046):


Code
iv_age <- ivreg(
  fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls_age, "| nearc4 +", controls_age)),
  data = card
)
iv_exper <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc4 +", controls_age)), data = card)
ols_age  <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls_age)), card)
alt <- rbind(
  `OLS, experience` = coef(summary(ols))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, experience as in Card` = coef(summary(iv))["educ", 1:2],
  `OLS, age` = coef(summary(ols_age))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, age` = coef(summary(iv_age))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, experience instrumented by age` = coef(summary(iv_exper))["educ", 1:2]
)
F_age <- summary(iv_age)$diagnostics["Weak instruments", "statistic"]
round(alt, 3); c(first_stage_F_with_age = F_age)


                                   Estimate Std. Error
OLS, experience                       0.075      0.003
IV, experience as in Card             0.132      0.055
OLS, age                              0.034      0.003
IV, age                               0.083      0.046
IV, experience instrumented by age    0.122      0.046


first_stage_F_with_age 
              11.89729 


The last row gives his number. With age, the first stage is weaker (F = 11.9), and the IV estimate is 0.083 (SE = 0.046). At a given age, a man with one more year of school has one year less experience, so the two versions do not measure the same thing: with experience held constant the coefficient is larger by the value of that year of work. The choice must be made by the question, and reported.

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

The instrument is an argument, not a statistic. Write down why it should be independent, and why there is no other way to the outcome.
Always show the first stage, the reduced form and the OLS result next to the IV result. The reduced form is an ordinary regression: if you cannot see the effect there, it is probably not there (Angrist & Krueger, 2001).
Weak instruments: report the (robust) first-stage F and an Anderson–Rubin interval. Many weak instruments are worse than one good one: 2SLS then moves towards OLS. (LIML is better.)
Do not put fitted values from a logistic first stage into a second regression. 2SLS wants linear first stages, also for a 0/1 treatment.
All controls belong in both stages.
Standard errors: use ivreg(), not the second lm(); robust or clustered by the unit to which the instrument belongs (here the county, which is not in the file).
LATE: the estimate is for those whom the instrument moved.
Measurement error in the predictor is another reason to use IV: a second, independent measurement is an instrument for the first. (With known error variances, see Deming regression.)
Relatives: regression with selection uses the same kind of exclusion; panel data removes what is constant over time without any instrument.

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the instrument and the argument for it, the controls, the first stage with its F, the reduced form, OLS and IV with standard errors, a weak-instrument-robust interval, and the group to which the estimate refers. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
row <- function(m, term) { co <- coef(summary(m))[term, ]; c(f3(co[1]), f3(co[2])) }
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Regression = c(
    "First stage (years of schooling on college nearby)",
    "Reduced form (log wage on college nearby)", "Log wage on schooling, OLS",
    "Log wage on schooling, 2SLS", "Log wage on schooling, 2SLS, two instruments"
  ),
  rbind(
    row(first_stage, "nearc4"),
    row(reduced_form, "nearc4"),
    row(ols, "educ"),
    row(iv, "educ"),
    row(iv2, "educ")
  )
)
names(apa_table) <- c("Regression", "b", "SE")
apa_table$CI <- c(apply(
  rbind(
    confint(first_stage)["nearc4", ],
    confint(reduced_form)["nearc4", ],
    confint(ols)["educ", ],
    ci_iv,
    confint(iv2)["educ", ]
  ),
  1,
  function(v) paste0("[", f3(v[1]), ", ", f3(v[2]), "]")
))


Method (data analysis):

The return to schooling was estimated for 3,010 men of the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men (log hourly wage in 1976; Card, 1993). Because unobserved ability and family background may influence both schooling and wages, schooling was instrumented with the presence of a four-year college in the local labour market of residence in 1966, which lowered the cost of college for boys who could live at home. All models contained experience, experience squared, and indicators for black, residence in the south, metropolitan residence in 1966 and 1976, and region in 1966. Two-stage least squares was used (R package ivreg); the strength of the instrument was judged with the first-stage F, and a 95% Anderson–Rubin interval (Anderson & Rubin, 1949) was computed because it is valid with weak instruments. Endogeneity was tested with the Wu–Hausman test, and the robustness of the result to a direct effect of the instrument was examined (Conley et al., 2012). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

After adjustment for the controls, men who grew up near a college had 0.32 more years of schooling (SE = 0.09, F(1, 2,994) = 13.3, p < .001) and 4.3% higher wages (log wage: b = 0.042, SE = 0.018, p = .020; Table 1). The two-stage least squares estimate of the effect of one year of schooling on the log wage was b = 0.132 (SE = 0.055, p = .017), 95% Anderson–Rubin CI [0.025, 0.285], compared with 0.075 (SE = 0.003) with ordinary least squares. The Wu–Hausman test did not distinguish the two, F(1, 2,993) = 1.17, p = .280. A direct effect of the instrument of 1.8% on wages would suffice to reduce the estimate to that of least squares.

Note. All models contain the controls named in the text. The confidence intervals are the usual ones; the Anderson–Rubin interval for the fourth row is [0.025, 0.285]. Two instruments: four-year and two-year college nearby (Sargan test p = .264).
Points to remember:

Argue for the instrument before showing numbers.
Report the first stage, the reduced form, OLS and IV together.
Give the first-stage F and an interval that is valid for weak instruments.
Say for whom the estimate holds, and how large a violation would change it.

title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
text:
10. Summary



When
A predictor is related to something unseen that also affects the outcome, and there is a source of variation that is not


Conditions
Relevance (testable), independence, exclusion (not testable), monotonicity


One 0/1 instrument
Difference in the outcome, divided by the difference in the predictor


In general
Two-stage least squares, \(\hat\beta = (W^\top P_Z W)^{-1}W^\top P_Z y\)


How (R)
ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls); also fixest::feols()


Check
First-stage F, Wu–Hausman, Sargan (with extra instruments), balance, sensitivity


Interval
Anderson–Rubin when the instrument is not very strong


Meaning
The effect for those whom the instrument moved (LATE)


Related pages
Simple regression, selection models, panel data

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
text:
In the 1970s the United States made an experiment that has not been repeated: the RAND Health Insurance Experiment. Thousands of families were assigned at random to different health insurance. For some, care was free. Others had to pay 25%, 50% or 95% of every bill, up to a yearly limit. Does it matter for how much care people use (Manning et al., 1987)?
The outcome is the medical spending of a person in a year, and it has two awkward features:

many people spend nothing at all;
among those who spend, most spend little and a few spend enormous amounts.

No ordinary distribution looks like that. But there is a natural way to think about it. A person first decides whether to see a doctor at all. Once there, the person and the doctor decide how much is done. The price may act on the first step, on the second, or on both. Two-part models (also called hurdle models; Cragg, 1971) model the two steps separately and then put them together.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(pscl)       # hurdle(): hurdle models for counts
library(MASS)       # glm.nb(): negative binomial regression (comes with R)
library(survival)   # survreg(): the Tobit model, for comparison (comes with R)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

text:
1. The data


Code
rand_all <- read.csv(
  "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/sampleSelection/RandHIE.csv"
)
rand <- subset(rand_all, year == 2 & !is.na(educdec)) # the second year, one row per person
rand <- with(
  rand,
  data.frame(
    spending = meddol, # medical spending in the year, US dollars
    visits = mdvis, # visits to a physician
    plan = factor(
      coins,
      levels = c(0, 25, 50, 95, 100),
      labels = c("free", "25%", "50%", "95%", "deductible")
    ),
    age = xage,
    female,
    child,
    income = income / 1000,
    disease = disea,
    fair_poor = as.integer(hlthf + hlthp > 0),
    education = educdec
  )
)
rand$any <- as.integer(rand$spending > 0)
nrow(rand)


[1] 5574


Code
table(rand$plan)



      free        25%        50%        95% deductible 
      3069       1108        373        753        271 


We use the second year of the experiment, 5,574 people. plan is the share of the bill that the family paid. The last group, “deductible”, paid 95% of outpatient care up to a limit per person, and nothing for hospital care. disease is the number of chronic diseases, fair_poor is 1 for people who described their health as fair or poor, income is in thousands of dollars.
Because the plans were assigned at random, the groups are comparable, and the differences between the plans are effects. The families were randomised, not the persons, and the file has no family number. So the standard errors of this page are a little too small.

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
pa <- ggplot(rand, aes(pmin(spending, 800))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, boundary = 0, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Spending (800 = 800 or more)", x = "US dollars per year", y = "people") + theme_bw()
pb <- ggplot(subset(rand, any == 1), aes(log(spending))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.3, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Log of the spending above zero", x = "log(dollars)", y = NULL) + theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb)

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: split the mean
Every mean of a variable with zeros can be written as a product:
\[E(y \mid x) = \underbrace{P(y > 0 \mid x)}_{\text{part 1: whether}} \times \underbrace{E(y \mid y > 0, x)}_{\text{part 2: how much}}\]
It is not an assumption. It is arithmetic. The assumptions come with the models for the two factors.


Step 2: part 1, a model for yes or no
A logistic regression, on everybody:
\[\log \frac{p_i}{1 - p_i} = x_i^\top \alpha\]


Step 3: part 2, a model for positive amounts
On those with some spending only. There are two usual choices:

Log-normal: \(\log y_i = x_i^\top\beta + \varepsilon_i\), by OLS on the logarithm.
Gamma with a log link: \(E(y_i \mid y_i > 0) = \exp(x_i^\top\beta)\), with a variance proportional to the square of the mean.

In both, \(e^{\beta}\) is a ratio: how many times more the users spend.


Step 4: from logs back to dollars, the smearing estimator
The mean of \(y\) is not the exponential of the mean of \(\log y\). If \(\log y\) has the mean \(x^\top\beta\), then \(E(y) = e^{x^\top\beta} \times E(e^{\varepsilon})\), and the second factor is larger than 1. If the errors were normal it would be \(e^{\sigma^2/2}\). Duan (1983) showed that the normal distribution is not needed. Use the average of the exponentiated residuals, the smearing factor:
\[\hat S = \frac{1}{n_+} \sum_{i:\, y_i > 0} e^{\hat\varepsilon_i}, \qquad \hat E(y \mid y > 0, x) = \hat S\, e^{x^\top\hat\beta}\]
The gamma model does not need this, because it models the mean in dollars directly.


Step 5: the two parts are estimated separately
The likelihood of a two-part model is a product of two pieces with no parameters in common, so each part can be fitted by itself. There is no correlation to estimate, unlike in the Heckman model. The reason is that the zeros here are real zeros. Nobody asks what the non-users “would have spent”.


Step 6: effects
A predictor can appear in both parts. Its effect on the mean has two sources (with \(\mu\) the mean of the second part):
\[\underbrace{p_1\mu_1 - p_0\mu_0}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(p_1 - p_0)\,\mu_0}_{\text{more users}} + \underbrace{p_1\,(\mu_1 - \mu_0)}_{\text{more per user}}\]

Read the two parts side by side:


Code
or <- exp(coef(part1)); ratio_g <- exp(coef(part2_gamma)); ratio_l <- exp(coef(part2_log))
p1 <- coef(summary(part1))[, 4]
p2 <- coef(summary(part2_gamma))[, 4]
p2l <- coef(summary(part2_log))[, 4]



The plan and whether. Compared with free care, the odds of using any care are 0.43 times as high with the 95% plan (p < .001). The price keeps people away from the first visit.
The plan and how much. Among the users, those on the 95% plan spend 0.73 times as much as those with free care by the gamma model (p = .042) and 0.79 times by the log-normal one (p < .001).
Illness acts on both. Each chronic disease multiplies the odds of any use by 1.06 and the amount by 1.03.
Women use care more often (odds ratio 1.45), but do not clearly spend more once they do (ratio 1.05, p = .605, gamma). The log-normal model disagrees: ratio 1.23, p < .001. The two compare different things. The log model compares the typical (geometric mean) amounts, the gamma model the means, which the largest bills dominate. For costs, the mean is usually what counts.

A predictor can matter in one part and not in the other, and even with opposite signs. One-part models cannot show that.

The smearing factor
The exponential of the mean log is 3.2 times too small. With a normal distribution of the errors it would have to be multiplied by 2.7: the errors of the logs are not quite normal, and the residuals decide. One more trap: if the spread of the errors differs between the plans, one smearing factor for all is wrong.

5. Putting the parts together

Predictions

standardised <- t(sapply(levels(rand$plan), function(pl) {
  d <- rand; d$plan <- factor(pl, levels = levels(rand$plan))
  p <- predict(part1, d, type = "response"); m <- predict(part2_gamma, d, type = "response")
  c(p = mean(p), amount = sum(p * m) / sum(p), mean = mean(p * m))
}))

deductible 0.69 257.37 177.98        186.05


Each row answers: if all the 5,574 people had this plan, what share would use care, how much would the users spend, and how much is that per person? (The amount per user is averaged over the users that each plan would have.)


The effect, with a bootstrap interval
There is no formula for the standard error of a product of two predictions averaged over people. The bootstrap resamples people and repeats everything:


Code
effect_of <- function(d) {
  m1 <- glm(formula(part1), family = binomial, data = d)
  m2 <- glm(
    formula(part2_gamma),
    family = Gamma("log"),
    data = subset(d, any == 1),
    control = list(maxit = 100)
  )
  s <- sapply(c("free", "25%", "95%"), function(pl) {
    z <- d
    z$plan <- factor(pl, levels = levels(rand$plan))
    p <- predict(m1, z, type = "response")
    m <- predict(m2, z, type = "response")
    c(p = mean(p), amount = sum(p * m) / sum(p), mean = mean(p * m))
  })
  total <- s["mean", "95%"] - s["mean", "free"]
  whether <- (s["p", "95%"] - s["p", "free"]) * s["amount", "free"]
  c(
    total = total,
    whether = whether,
    how_much = total - whether,
    ratio = s["mean", "95%"] / s["mean", "free"],
    d_p = s["p", "95%"] - s["p", "free"],
    d_amount = s["amount", "95%"] - s["amount", "free"]
  )
}
set.seed(51)
point <- effect_of(rand)
boot  <- replicate(500, effect_of(rand[sample(nrow(rand), replace = TRUE), ]))
ci    <- apply(boot, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
round(rbind(estimate = point, ci), 2)

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
text:
6. Against one-part models
What if we model the spending in one piece?


Code
f_rhs  <- ~ plan + age + I(age^2) + female + child + income + disease + fair_poor + education
ols    <- lm(update(f_rhs, spending ~ .), data = rand)
# log link, zeros allowed
quasi <- glm(update(f_rhs, spending ~ .), family = quasipoisson, data = rand)
tobit <- survreg(
  update(f_rhs, Surv(log(spending + 1), spending > 0, type = "left") ~ .),
  data = rand,
  dist = "gaussian"
)

tobit_mean <- function(d) {
  # E(y) by the Tobit model for log(y + 1): by simulation
  mu <- predict(tobit, d)
  set.seed(1)
  z <- rnorm(400)
  mean(sapply(z, function(e) mean(pmax(exp(mu + tobit$scale * e) - 1, 0))))
}
plan_mean <- function(pl, kind) {
  d <- rand
  d$plan <- factor(pl, levels = levels(rand$plan))
  switch(
    kind,
    OLS = mean(predict(ols, d)),
    `one-part, log link` = mean(predict(quasi, d, type = "response")),
    Tobit = tobit_mean(d),
    `two-part` = mean(predict_mean(d))
  )
}
kinds <- c("OLS", "one-part, log link", "Tobit", "two-part")
models <- sapply(kinds, function(k) sapply(c("free", "25%", "95%"), plan_mean, kind = k))
round(cbind(models, observed = by_plan[c("free", "25%", "95%"), "mean_all"]), 0)


     OLS one-part, log link Tobit two-part observed
free 182                181   531      183      182
25%  158                159   435      170      159
95%  114                109   184      112      103


Code
negative <- mean(predict(ols) < 0)
c(OLS_negative_predictions = negative)


OLS_negative_predictions 
               0.0367779 



OLS gets the averages right, and predicts negative spending for 3.7% of the people. Its coefficients are dollars, the same for everybody.
The one-part model with a log link (quasi-Poisson) also gets the averages right, zeros and all. If only \(E(y \mid x)\) is of interest, it is a simple and good choice. It says nothing about the two decisions.
Tobit (on the log scale) predicts 531 dollars for free care, against 182 observed. It assumes that the same line decides whether and how much, and that the zeros are the hidden part of a normal distribution. Neither is true here.

rand$tenth <- cut(
  rand$predicted,
  quantile(rand$predicted, 0:10 / 10),
  include.lowest = TRUE,
  labels = 1:10
)

cal_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(tenth = cal$tenth, dollars = cal$predicted, what = "predicted by the two-part model"),
  data.frame(tenth = cal$tenth, dollars = cal$spending, what = "observed")
)
ggplot(cal_long, aes(tenth, dollars, colour = what, group = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(observed = "grey30", `predicted by the two-part model` = "#2a78d6"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean spending in tenths of the predicted spending",
    x = "tenth of the people, by predicted spending",
    y = "dollars"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The two-part model sorts people well, from 38 dollars observed in the lowest tenth to 491 in the highest, with the noise that a few large bills bring.

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
section: 7. The same idea for counts: hurdle models
text:
7. The same idea for counts: hurdle models
For counts such as the number of visits, the second part is a zero-truncated count distribution: a Poisson or negative binomial without its zero. The hurdle is the step from 0 to 1 (Mullahy, 1986). pscl::hurdle() fits both parts at once:


Code
hurdle_nb <- hurdle(
  visits ~ plan + age + I(age^2) + female + child + income + disease + fair_poor + education,
  data = rand,
  dist = "negbin",
  zero.dist = "binomial"
)
nb <- glm.nb(
  visits ~ plan + age + I(age^2) + female + child + income + disease + fair_poor + education,
  data = rand
)
pois <- glm(formula(nb), family = poisson, data = rand)
hs <- summary(hurdle_nb)$coefficients
round(
  cbind(
    zero_part = hs$zero[c("plan95%", "female", "disease"), c(1, 2, 4)],
    count_part = hs$count[c("plan95%", "female", "disease"), c(1, 2, 4)]
  ),
  3
)

female     0.357      0.061        0    0.119      0.048    0.014
disease    0.049      0.006        0    0.027      0.004    0.000

counts_aic <- AIC(pois, nb, hurdle_nb)
counts_aic


          df      AIC
pois      13 34130.98
nb        14 23552.37
hurdle_nb 27 23378.89


Code
zeros <- c(observed = sum(rand$visits == 0), poisson = sum(dpois(0, fitted(pois))),
           negative_binomial = sum(dnbinom(0, mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta)),
           hurdle = sum(predict(hurdle_nb, type = "prob")[, 1]))
round(zeros)


         observed           poisson negative_binomial            hurdle 
             1832               553              1873              1832 


The hurdle model reproduces the number of zeros exactly, because it has a separate part for them. Poisson regression expects 553 people without a visit, and there are 1,832. The negative binomial, which allows more variation, expects 1,873. By the AIC the hurdle model is 173 points better than the negative binomial.
A zero-inflated model is the close relative: there, zeros come from two sources, people who never go and people who could have gone but did not. A hurdle model has only one kind of zero. Here one can argue either way, and the two often fit equally well.

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Whose question? If you need only the mean, a one-part model with a log link is enough. Use two parts when the two decisions are of interest, or when the predictors act differently on them.
The second part compares selected groups. The users on the 95% plan are fewer, and probably sicker, than the users with free care. So the ratio of the second part is not an effect of the price on given people, even in a randomised experiment. The effects that the randomisation supports are those on the share of users and on the mean of everybody.
Report the combination, with an interval. Two tables of coefficients leave the reader to multiply. (Belotti et al., 2015, review the model and its marginal effects.)
Two-part, Tobit or Heckman? Real zeros: two-part. Zeros that hide a value (below a detection limit): Tobit. An outcome that exists but is seen only for a selected group: Heckman.
The tail. One bill of 39,182 dollars is 4.1% of all the spending. Gamma models are less sensitive to it than OLS, but not immune. See how the results change without the top few values.
Never use log(y + 1) to get rid of the zeros. The result depends on the 1: with cents instead of dollars it would be another answer.
Choose between the gamma and the log-normal by their residuals and their calibration. Use separate smearing factors if the spread differs between groups.

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the share of zeros, the model of each part, the estimates of both, and the combined effect with its interval. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
show <- c(
  "plan25%", "plan50%", "plan95%", "plandeductible", "female", "disease", "fair_poor", "income"
)
ci1 <- exp(confint.default(part1)); ci2 <- exp(confint.default(part2_gamma))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Plan: 25%", "Plan: 50%", "Plan: 95%", "Plan: deductible", "Female", "Chronic diseases (each)",
    "Fair or poor health", "Income ($1,000)"
  ),
  or = f2(or[show]),
  orci = paste0("[", f2(ci1[show, 1]), ", ", f2(ci1[show, 2]), "]"),
  rr = f2(ratio_g[show]),
  rrci = paste0("[", f2(ci2[show, 1]), ", ", f2(ci2[show, 2]), "]")
)


Method (data analysis):

Medical spending in the second year of the RAND Health Insurance Experiment (N = 5,574) was zero for 23% of the participants and strongly skewed for the others. We used a two-part model: a logistic regression for any spending, and a gamma regression with a log link for the amount among those with some spending (n = 4,281). Both parts contained the insurance plan (reference: free care) and age, its square, sex, child status, family income, education, the number of chronic diseases and self-rated health. The effect of the plan on mean spending combines both parts, standardised over the sample; confidence intervals are from 500 bootstrap samples of persons. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

Participants who had to pay 95% of their bills were less likely than those with free care to have any spending, OR = 0.43, 95% CI [0.36, 0.51], p < .001. Among those with some spending, the amount was 0.73 times that of users with free care, 95% CI [0.54, 0.99], p = .042 (Table 1). Together, mean spending differed by -70 dollars per person and year, 95% CI [-97, -42]: -35 dollars because fewer people used care, and -35 because of less spending per user.

Points to remember:

Give the share of zeros, and say why they are real zeros.
Report both parts, with the same predictors, and the combined effect with an interval.
Do not call the ratio of the second part an effect.
Say how you came back from logs, if you used them.

title: Hurdle and Two-Part Models: Does Free Health Care Make People Use More of It?
text:
10. Summary



When
Many real zeros, and a positive, skewed amount (or count) for the others


The identity
\(E(y) = P(y > 0) \times E(y \mid y > 0)\)


Part 1
Logistic (or probit) regression on everybody


Part 2
Gamma regression with a log link, or OLS on logs with smearing, on the positive cases


How (R)
glm(y > 0 ~ x, binomial) and glm(y ~ x, Gamma("log"), subset = y > 0); for counts pscl::hurdle()


Combine
Multiply the predictions; bootstrap the effects


Advantage
Shows whether and how much separately


Careful
The users are a selected group


Related pages
Tobit, Heckman, generalized linear models

title: Heckman Selection Model: What Would the Women Who Did Not Work Have Earned?
text:
How much more does a woman earn for each year of education? In 1975 a study asked 753 married American women. But only 428 of them worked for pay. For the other 325 there is no wage. Not because the question was left out: there was none to report.
A regression of the wage on education, for the women who worked, describes the women who worked. But the question is usually about all women: what would education be worth to a woman who is at home now? If those who work are a special group, if for example they are the ones who were offered a good wage, then the sample is selected by the very thing we want to explain, and the regression may be wrong.
James Heckman (1979) proposed a model for this situation, with two equations: one that decides who is in the sample, and one for the outcome. It brought him a Nobel Prize, and it is one of the most used, and most misused, models of social science. This page shows what it does, and what it can and cannot repair.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(sampleSelection)   # selection(): two-step and maximum likelihood

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Heckman Selection Model: What Would the Women Who Did Not Work Have Earned?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: two equations
The outcome equation, for every woman, whether she works or not. It is the wage that she is or would be offered:
\[y_i^* = x_i^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i\]
The selection equation. She works if the advantage of working, \(d_i^*\), is positive:
\[d_i^* = z_i^\top \gamma + u_i, \qquad \text{we see } y_i = y_i^* \text{ only if } d_i^* > 0\]


Step 2: the errors may be correlated
\[\begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_i \\ u_i \end{pmatrix} \sim N\!\left(0, \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2 & \rho\sigma \\ \rho\sigma & 1 \end{pmatrix}\right)\]
\(u_i\) is whatever makes her more likely to work than \(z_i\) says: ambition, health, a well-connected aunt. \(\varepsilon_i\) is whatever makes her wage higher than \(x_i\) says: ambition, health, a well-connected aunt. If the two are related (\(\rho \ne 0\)), then those who work have, on average, errors \(\varepsilon\) that are not zero. This is the whole problem. If \(\rho = 0\), selection may depend on everything in \(z\), and OLS on the workers is still fine.


Step 3: the bias of OLS is a missing predictor
For the women who work, the expected error is
\[E(\varepsilon_i \mid u_i > -z_i^\top\gamma) = \rho\sigma\,\lambda_i, \qquad \lambda_i = \frac{\phi(z_i^\top\gamma)}{\Phi(z_i^\top\gamma)}\]
\(\lambda_i\) is the inverse Mills ratio. It is large for women who work although the model says they hardly would (they must have a large \(u\)), and near 0 for those who would work anyway. So
\[E(y_i \mid \text{works}) = x_i^\top\beta + (\rho\sigma)\,\lambda_i\]
OLS leaves out \(\lambda_i\). In Heckman’s words, selection bias is a specification error: an omitted variable.


Step 4: the two-step estimator

Fit a probit regression of working on \(z\), for all the women. Compute \(\hat\lambda_i\).
Fit OLS of the wage on \(x\) and \(\hat\lambda\), for the women who work.

The coefficient of \(\hat\lambda\) estimates \(\rho\sigma\). Its t test is a test of whether there is selection at all. The ordinary standard errors of step 2 are wrong, because \(\hat\lambda\) is estimated and the errors have unequal variances.


Step 5: maximum likelihood
Both equations at once. A woman who does not work contributes \(P(d^* \le 0)\). A woman who works contributes the density of her wage, times the probability of working given that wage:
\[\log L = \sum_{d_i = 0} \log \Phi(-z_i^\top\gamma) + \sum_{d_i = 1} \left[ \log \frac{1}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{e_i}{\sigma}\right) + \log \Phi\!\left(\frac{z_i^\top\gamma + \rho\, e_i/\sigma}{\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}}\right) \right]\]
with \(e_i = y_i - x_i^\top\beta\).
It is more precise than the two steps if the bivariate normal model is right.


Step 6: exclusion restrictions
If \(x\) and \(z\) contain the same variables, the only thing that tells \(\lambda_i\) from the predictors in \(x\) is its curvature, and over most of its range it is nearly a straight line. The model is then identified by the assumption of normality alone, which is not much. To identify it properly there must be at least one variable in \(z\) that is not in \(x\): something that makes a woman work, but does not change the wage that she would be offered. Here: the income of the rest of the family, her age, and her children. Whether employers really did not care about a woman’s children in 1975 is a question that the model cannot answer.

Code
Z <- model.matrix(probit); X <- model.matrix(~ educ + exper + I(exper^2), data = women)
y <- ifelse(works, women$logwage, 0)
minus_loglik <- function(par) {
  g <- par[1:ncol(Z)]
  b <- par[ncol(Z) + 1:ncol(X)]
  s <- exp(par[length(par) - 1])
  r <- tanh(par[length(par)])
  a <- drop(Z %*% g)
  e <- (y - drop(X %*% b)) / s
  -sum(ifelse(
    works,
    dnorm(e, log = TRUE) - log(s) + pnorm((a + r * e) / sqrt(1 - r^2), log.p = TRUE),
    pnorm(-a, log.p = TRUE)
  ))
}
hand <- optim(
  c(coef(probit), coef(ols), log(sigma(ols)), 0),
  minus_loglik,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(
    maxit = 2000,
    reltol = 1e-12,
    parscale = c(0.5, 0.01, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.05, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.1, 0.1)
  )
)

  two_step = coef(two_step)[9:12], SE_2 = sqrt(diag(vcov(two_step)))[9:12],

If \(\rho = 0\), the likelihood of the model is that of the probit times that of the OLS regression. So the likelihood-ratio test of selection compares the two: \(\chi^2\)(1) = 0.03, p = .858. We find no sign of selection bias. The return to a year of education is 0.107 with OLS, 0.109 with the two steps and 0.108 with maximum likelihood.
That the correction changes nothing is a common result, and a legitimate one. It does not mean that the workers are like the others: they differ in education, experience and children. It means that what is left, after these, seems not to be related to the wage. Or that our restrictions cannot show it.

title: Heckman Selection Model: What Would the Women Who Did Not Work Have Earned?
section: 6. Everything depends on the exclusion restrictions
text:
6. Everything depends on the exclusion restrictions
What if we had no excluded variables, and the probit contained only what is in the wage equation?


Code
probit0 <- glm(lfp ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2), family = binomial("probit"), data = women)
zg0 <- predict(probit0, type = "link"); women$mills0 <- dnorm(zg0) / pnorm(zg0)
r2_with <- summary(lm(mills ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2), data = women, subset = works))$r.squared
r2_without <- summary(lm(
  mills0 ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2),
  data = women,
  subset = works
))$r.squared
c(R2_of_mills_on_x_with_exclusions = r2_with, without = r2_without)


R2_of_mills_on_x_with_exclusions                          without 
                       0.5392472                        0.9861982 


Code
no_excl <- selection(
  lfp ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2),
  logwage ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2),
  data = women,
  method = "2step"
)
mills_est <- c(with = coef(two_step)[["invMillsRatio"]], without = coef(no_excl)[["invMillsRatio"]])
mills_se <- c(
  with = sqrt(vcov(two_step)["invMillsRatio", "invMillsRatio"]),
  without = sqrt(vcov(no_excl)["invMillsRatio", "invMillsRatio"])
)
# education in the wage equation
educ_est <- c(with = coef(two_step)[[10]], without = coef(no_excl)[[6]])
educ_se   <- c(with = sqrt(vcov(two_step)[10, 10]), without = sqrt(vcov(no_excl)[6, 6]))
rbind(education = educ_est, SE_education = educ_se, mills = mills_est, SE_mills = mills_se)


                   with     without
education    0.10906552  0.09347007
SE_education 0.01552295  0.05141541
mills        0.03226186 -0.27018113
SE_mills     0.13362464  0.94919661


Without exclusions, 98.6% of the variation of \(\hat\lambda\) is already in the predictors of the wage (with them, 54%). The inverse Mills ratio is nearly a copy of \(x\). Its coefficient is estimated as -0.27 with a standard error of 0.95, and the standard error of the education coefficient grows from 0.016 to 0.051. The correction is then worse than the disease.

A known truth
A simulation with the real predictors shows both sides. The true return to education is 0.10. We set the correlation \(\rho\) of the errors to 0, 0.5 and 0.8, and estimate with OLS, with the two steps, and with the two steps without exclusion restrictions (the data are generated with them):


Code
set.seed(41)
beta  <- c(-0.5, 0.10, 0.04, -0.0008); s0 <- 0.66; gamma0 <- coef(probit)
reps  <- 500
heck  <- function(yy, d, Zm) {                                         # two-step, by hand, fast
  p  <- suppressWarnings(glm.fit(Zm, d, family = binomial("probit")))
  a  <- drop(Zm %*% p$coefficients); m <- dnorm(a) / pnorm(a)
  unname(lm.fit(cbind(X[d == 1, ], m[d == 1]), yy[d == 1])$coefficients[2])
}
one <- function(rho) {
  u <- rnorm(nrow(X))
  e <- s0 * (rho * u + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(nrow(X)))
  d <- as.integer(drop(Z %*% gamma0) + u > 0)
  yy <- drop(X %*% beta) + e
  c(
    OLS = unname(lm.fit(X[d == 1, ], yy[d == 1])$coefficients[2]),
    two_step = heck(yy, d, Z),
    no_exclusions = heck(yy, d, X)
  )
}
sims <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0, 0.5, 0.8), function(rho) {
    r <- t(replicate(reps, one(rho)))
    data.frame(
      rho,
      method = colnames(r),
      mean = colMeans(r),
      SD = apply(r, 2, sd),
      RMSE = sqrt(colMeans((r - 0.10)^2)),
      row.names = NULL
    )
  })
)
print(
  transform(sims, mean = round(mean, 4), SD = round(SD, 4), RMSE = round(RMSE, 4)),
  row.names = FALSE
)
