text:
1. The data


Code
raw <- read.csv("https://gml.noaa.gov/webdata/ccgg/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.csv", comment.char = "#")
co2 <- data.frame(year = raw$decimal.date, t = raw$decimal.date - 2000, ppm = raw$average)
past   <- subset(co2, year < 2007)            # what the model may see
future <- subset(co2, year >= 2007)           # the test: nearly twenty years
c(past = nrow(past), future = nrow(future))


  past future 
   586    238 


The monthly means of CO₂ in parts per million (ppm), from NOAA (Lan & Keeling, 2026), as on the polynomial page: 586 months until the end of 2006 for learning, and 238 months since then for the test. t is the number of years since 2000.

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
section: 2. The method step by step, with formulas
text:
2. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a kernel is an opinion about functions
The squared exponential (or radial) kernel says that the values at two times \(t\) and \(t'\) are similar if the times are close:
\[k(t, t') = s^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(t - t')^2}{2\ell^2}\right)\]
\(s\) is how far the function strays from its mean, \(\ell\) (the length scale) how far one must go until it has forgotten where it was. A Gaussian process with this kernel is a distribution over functions: the values at any set of times have a multivariate normal distribution, whose covariances are the kernel. So we can draw functions from it:


Code
k_rbf <- function(a, b, s, l) s^2 * exp(-outer(a, b, "-")^2 / (2 * l^2))
draw  <- function(K, n) t(chol(K + 1e-8 * diag(nrow(K)))) %*% matrix(rnorm(nrow(K) * n), ncol = n)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 150); set.seed(171)
draws <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.5, 2), function(l) {
    f <- draw(k_rbf(x, x, 1, l), 5)
    data.frame(
      x = rep(x, 5),
      f = as.vector(f),
      id = rep(1:5, each = length(x)),
      l = paste("length scale", l)
    )
  })
)
ggplot(draws, aes(x, f, group = id, colour = factor(id))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~l) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Functions drawn from a Gaussian process, before seeing any data",
    x = "t",
    y = "f(t)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()











Step 2: condition on the data
We observe \(y_i = f(t_i) + \varepsilon_i\) with noise of variance \(\sigma^2\). Data and unknown values are jointly normal, so the rule for conditional normal distributions gives everything. With \(K\) the kernel matrix of the data, \(k_*\) the vector of kernels between the data and a new time \(t_*\):
\[\hat f(t_*) = k_*^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad \text{Var}\,f(t_*) = k(t_*, t_*) - k_*^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} k_*\]
The mean is a weighted sum of the data. The variance starts from the prior variance and is reduced by what the data say. It does not depend on \(y\) at all, only on where the data are.


Code
gp_fit <- function(t, y, kern, sigma) {
  L <- chol(kern(t, t) + sigma^2 * diag(length(t)))
  list(
    t = t,
    L = L,
    a = backsolve(L, backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)),
    kern = kern,
    sigma = sigma
  )
}
gp_predict <- function(m, new) {
  Ks <- m$kern(new, m$t)
  V <- backsolve(m$L, t(Ks), transpose = TRUE)
  list(mean = drop(Ks %*% m$a), sd = sqrt(pmax(diag(m$kern(new, new)) - colSums(V^2), 0)))
}

set.seed(172); t5 <- c(1, 2.2, 3, 6, 6.8); y5 <- sin(t5) + rnorm(5, 0, 0.1)
toy  <- gp_fit(t5, y5, function(a, b) k_rbf(a, b, 1, 1), 0.1)
pr   <- gp_predict(toy, x)
Kxx <- k_rbf(x, x, 1, 1)
post <- Kxx - k_rbf(x, t5, 1, 1) %*% solve(k_rbf(t5, t5, 1, 1) + 0.01 * diag(5), k_rbf(t5, x, 1, 1))
some <- pr$mean + draw(post + 1e-6 * diag(150), 5)
ggplot(
  data.frame(x, m = pr$mean, lo = pr$mean - 1.96 * pr$sd, hi = pr$mean + 1.96 * pr$sd),
  aes(x, m)
) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = data.frame(x = rep(x, 5), f = as.vector(some), id = rep(1:5, each = 150)),
    aes(x, f, group = id),
    colour = "grey60",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(t5, y5), aes(t5, y5), size = 2.6) +
  labs(
    title = "The same process after five observations",
    subtitle = "Blue: mean and 95% band. Grey: five functions that are still possible",
    x = "t",
    y = "f(t)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
check <- gausspr(
  matrix(t5),
  y5,
  kernel = "rbfdot",
  kpar = list(sigma = 1 / 2),
  var = 0.01,
  scaled = FALSE,
  fit = FALSE
) # kernlab's sigma is 1/(2 l^2)
max(abs(predict(check, matrix(x)) - pr$mean))


[1] 9.103829e-15


Between the points and beyond the last one, the functions disagree and the band opens. Far away the mean returns to the prior mean (0) and the band to the prior SD. kernlab gives the same curve.


Step 3: learn the kernel from the data
Where do \(s\), \(\ell\) and \(\sigma\) come from? From the marginal likelihood, the probability of the data with all possible functions averaged:
\[\log p(y) = -\tfrac12\, y^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y - \tfrac12 \log|K + \sigma^2 I| - \tfrac n2 \log 2\pi\]
The first term rewards fit, the second punishes a kernel that could explain anything. No cross-validation is needed for this trade-off.


Step 4: kernels can be added
The sum of two independent processes is a process whose kernel is the sum of the kernels. So we build a model from parts, each with its meaning (Roberts et al., 2013, show this for time series).

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
3. A kernel for CO₂
Rasmussen and Williams (2006) used this very record as an example. We use a simplified version of their kernel, with four parts:








Part
Kernel
Meaning




trend
\(s_1^2 \exp(-r^2 / 2\ell_1^2)\)
a smooth change over decades


season
\(s_2^2 \exp(-r^2/2\ell_2^2 - 2\sin^2(\pi r)/p^2)\)
repeats every year; its shape may change slowly


swings
\(s_3^2 \exp(-r/\ell_3)\)
irregular, some months to years, such as El Niño


noise
\(\sigma^2\) on the diagonal
single months



(\(r = |t - t'|\) in years.)


Code
part <- function(a, b, th, which) {
  r <- abs(outer(a, b, "-"))
  switch(which, trend = th[["s1"]]^2 * exp(-r^2 / (2 * th[["l1"]]^2)),
         season = th[["s2"]]^2 * exp(-r^2 / (2 * th[["l2"]]^2) - 2 * sin(pi * r)^2 / th[["p"]]^2),
         swings = th[["s3"]]^2 * exp(-r / th[["l3"]]))
}
kernel <- function(a, b, th, parts) Reduce(`+`, lapply(parts, function(w) part(a, b, th, w)))

parts_A <- c("trend", "season", "swings")          # version A
parts_B <- c("season", "swings")                   # version B, with a mean function
H <- function(t) cbind(1, t, t^2)                  # the columns of that mean function

# marginal likelihood; H: columns of a mean function with unknown coefficients (estimated by
# generalized least squares)
neg_ml <- function(log_th, t, y, parts, H = NULL) {
  th <- as.list(exp(log_th)); K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2
  L <- try(chol(K), silent = TRUE); if (inherits(L, "try-error")) return(1e6)
  z <- backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(H)) { A <- backsolve(L, H, transpose = TRUE); z <- qr.resid(qr(A), z) }
  sum(log(diag(L))) + sum(z^2) / 2 + length(y) / 2 * log(2 * pi)
}



Version A: no mean, everything in the kernel
The common default: subtract the overall mean and let the kernel do the rest.


Code
start_A <- log(c(s1 = 60, l1 = 60, s2 = 3, l2 = 100, p = 1.3, s3 = 0.8, l3 = 2, sigma = 0.2))
opt_A <- optim(
  start_A,
  neg_ml,
  t = past$t,
  y = past$ppm - mean(past$ppm),
  parts = parts_A,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 80)
)
th_A  <- as.list(exp(opt_A$par))
round(unlist(th_A), 2)


    s1     l1     s2     l2      p     s3     l3  sigma 
 85.35  77.44   2.98 164.89   1.55   0.89   4.14   0.17 


The length scale of the trend is 77.4 years, the season keeps its shape for a long time (\(\ell_2\) = 164.9 years), the swings have an SD of 0.89 ppm and the noise of single months is 0.17 ppm.


Version B: a quadratic mean, and the kernel for the rest
We know something that the kernel does not: the rise has been speeding up for a century. Give the process a mean function \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 t^2\) with unknown coefficients, and the kernels of the season and of the swings for the deviations from it:


Code
start_B <- log(c(s2 = 3, l2 = 100, p = 1.3, s3 = 0.8, l3 = 2, sigma = 0.2))
opt_B <- optim(
  start_B,
  neg_ml,
  t = past$t,
  y = past$ppm,
  parts = parts_B,
  H = H(past$t),
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 80)
)
th_B  <- as.list(exp(opt_B$par))
round(unlist(th_B), 2)


    s2     l2      p     s3     l3  sigma 
  2.43 155.61   1.43   0.80   3.32   0.17 


The prediction now has one more source of uncertainty, the coefficients of the mean. This is universal kriging, and it is generalized least squares for the \(\beta\)’s plus the GP for the residuals:


Code
gp <- function(t, y, th, parts, H = NULL, new, H_new = NULL) {
  K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts)
  diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2
  L <- chol(K)
  z <- backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)
  Ks <- kernel(new, t, th, parts)
  V <- backsolve(L, t(Ks), transpose = TRUE)
  v <- rowSums(sapply(parts, function(w) diag(part(new, new, th, w)))) - colSums(V^2)
  if (is.null(H)) {
    return(list(mean = drop(crossprod(V, z)), sd = sqrt(pmax(v, 0) + th$sigma^2)))
  }
  A <- backsolve(L, H, transpose = TRUE)
  XtX <- solve(crossprod(A))
  beta <- XtX %*% crossprod(A, z)
  R <- H_new - crossprod(V, A) # what the mean adds that the data cannot fix
  list(
    mean = drop(H_new %*% beta + crossprod(V, z - A %*% beta)),
    sd = sqrt(pmax(v, 0) + rowSums((R %*% XtX) * R) + th$sigma^2),
    beta = drop(beta),
    beta_se = sqrt(diag(XtX))
  )
}

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
4. Inside the data
How well do the two versions predict single months of the past? Leave each month out and predict it from all the others. For a GP that needs no refitting. With \(Q = K_y^{-1} - K_y^{-1}H(H^\top K_y^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K_y^{-1}\), where \(K_y = K + \sigma^2 I\) and \(H\) holds the columns of the mean function (without a mean function \(Q = K_y^{-1}\)):
\[y_i - \hat y_{-i} = \frac{[Qy]_i}{Q_{ii}}, \qquad \text{Var}_{-i} = \frac{1}{Q_{ii}}\]


Code
loo <- function(t, y, th, parts, H = NULL) {
  K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2; Q <- solve(K)
  if (!is.null(H)) { KH <- Q %*% H; Q <- Q - KH %*% solve(crossprod(H, KH), t(KH)) }
  data.frame(err = drop(Q %*% y) / diag(Q), sd = 1 / sqrt(diag(Q)))
}
loo_A <- loo(past$t, past$ppm - mean(past$ppm), th_A, parts_A)
loo_B <- loo(past$t, past$ppm, th_B, parts_B, H(past$t))
inside <- sapply(list(A = loo_A, B = loo_B), function(l) {
  c(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(l$err^2)),
    coverage_95 = mean(abs(l$err) < 1.96 * l$sd),
    coverage_50 = mean(abs(l$err) < 0.674 * l$sd)
  )
})
round(inside, 3)


                A     B
RMSE        0.237 0.237
coverage_95 0.949 0.949
coverage_50 0.532 0.531


Code
c(log_marginal_likelihood_A = -opt_A$value, log_marginal_likelihood_B = -opt_B$value)


log_marginal_likelihood_A log_marginal_likelihood_B 
                -128.5221                 -117.2624 


Single months are predicted to within 0.24 ppm by version A and 0.24 ppm by version B, and the 95% intervals contain 95% and 95% of them. Inside the data the two versions are the same, and their error bars can be believed. Only the marginal likelihood sees a difference (-117.3 for B against -128.5 for A).

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
5. The test: twenty years later


Code
pA <- gp(past$t, past$ppm - mean(past$ppm), th_A, parts_A, new = future$t)
pA$mean <- pA$mean + mean(past$ppm)
pB <- gp(past$t, past$ppm, th_B, parts_B, H(past$t), future$t, H(future$t))
quad <- lm(
  ppm ~ t + I(t^2) + sin(2 * pi * t) + cos(2 * pi * t) + sin(4 * pi * t) + cos(4 * pi * t),
  data = past
) # the polynomial page, with a season
pQ <- predict(quad, future, interval = "prediction")
score <- function(m, lo, hi) {
  c(
    RMSE = rmse(m, future$ppm),
    coverage_95 = mean(future$ppm >= lo & future$ppm <= hi),
    mean_width = mean(hi - lo)
  )
}
scores <- rbind(
  `A: zero-mean GP` = score(pA$mean, pA$mean - 1.96 * pA$sd, pA$mean + 1.96 * pA$sd),
  `B: GP with a quadratic mean` = score(pB$mean, pB$mean - 1.96 * pB$sd, pB$mean + 1.96 * pB$sd),
  `quadratic regression + season (lm)` = score(pQ[, 1], pQ[, 2], pQ[, 3])
)
round(scores, 3)


                                    RMSE coverage_95 mean_width
A: zero-mean GP                    6.092       0.462      8.872
B: GP with a quadratic mean        1.579       1.000      5.903
quadratic regression + season (lm) 1.970       0.521      3.211




Code
fc <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pA$mean,
    lo = pA$mean - 1.96 * pA$sd,
    hi = pA$mean + 1.96 * pA$sd,
    model = "A: zero-mean GP"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pB$mean,
    lo = pB$mean - 1.96 * pB$sd,
    hi = pB$mean + 1.96 * pB$sd,
    model = "B: GP with a quadratic mean"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pQ[, 1],
    lo = pQ[, 2],
    hi = pQ[, 3],
    model = "quadratic regression + season"
  )
)
fc$obs <- rep(future$ppm, 3)
ggplot(fc, aes(year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo - obs, ymax = hi - obs), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = m - obs), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#eb6834", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast from 2006 minus what was measured",
    subtitle = "Band: 95%. A good band contains the dashed zero line nearly always",
    x = NULL,
    y = "ppm"
  ) +
  theme_bw()










A, the zero-mean GP, is too low, by more and more: RMSE 6.1 ppm. Its band grows, as promised, and is still too narrow: it contains only 46% of the months, instead of 95%. Far from the data the trend kernel pulls the function back to the mean of 1958–2006. Nobody asked for that opinion; it came with the zero mean.
B, with a quadratic mean, has an RMSE of 1.6 ppm, and a band that contains 100%.
Quadratic regression with a season has 2.0 ppm. Its band has a nearly constant width of about 3.2 ppm and contains 52%: least squares believes that its residuals are independent, and shows no growing doubt.

It looks like a triumph for version B. But 238 months in a row are not 238 tests: if the forecast is right in 2015 it is likely to be right in 2016. It is closer to one test.

Was that luck? Six starting dates
So we repeat it. Stop the clock at six different dates, learn the kernel from the months before, and forecast the next 15 years:


Code
origins <- c(1980, 1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2007)
rolling <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(origins, function(o) {
    early <- subset(co2, year < o)
    late <- subset(co2, year >= o & year < o + 15)
    if (o == 2007) {
      a <- th_A
      b <- th_B
    } else {
      a <- as.list(exp(
        optim(
          start_A,
          neg_ml,
          t = early$t,
          y = early$ppm - mean(early$ppm),
          parts = parts_A,
          method = "BFGS",
          control = list(maxit = 80)
        )$par
      ))
      b <- as.list(exp(
        optim(
          start_B,
          neg_ml,
          t = early$t,
          y = early$ppm,
          parts = parts_B,
          H = H(early$t),
          method = "BFGS",
          control = list(maxit = 80)
        )$par
      ))
    }
    gA <- gp(early$t, early$ppm - mean(early$ppm), a, parts_A, new = late$t)
    gA$mean <- gA$mean + mean(early$ppm)
    gB <- gp(early$t, early$ppm, b, parts_B, H(early$t), late$t, H(late$t))
    q <- predict(update(quad, data = early), late, interval = "prediction")
    cov <- function(m, s) mean(abs(m - late$ppm) < 1.96 * s)
    data.frame(
      start = o,
      trend_scale_A = a$l1,
      rmse_A = rmse(gA$mean, late$ppm),
      rmse_B = rmse(gB$mean, late$ppm),
      rmse_lm = rmse(q[, 1], late$ppm),
      cover_A = cov(gA$mean, gA$sd),
      cover_B = cov(gB$mean, gB$sd),
      cover_lm = mean(late$ppm > q[, 2] & late$ppm < q[, 3])
    )
  })
)
print(round(rolling, 2), row.names = FALSE)


 start trend_scale_A rmse_A rmse_B rmse_lm cover_A cover_B cover_lm
  1980         36.41   1.76   1.59    1.64    0.99    0.84     0.72
  1985         42.52   2.37   4.06    4.10    0.88    0.33     0.28
  1990         51.27   2.70   5.15    5.36    0.45    0.06     0.06
  1995         24.02  12.12   0.63    2.37    0.12    1.00     0.14
  2000         51.49   5.20   0.45    0.66    0.36    0.99     1.00
  2007         77.44   4.08   1.11    1.42    0.61    1.00     0.68


The triumph is gone:

B is excellent from 1995 on (RMSE between 0.5 and 1.1 ppm). Started in 1985 or 1990 it is 4.1 and 5.2 ppm off, and its 95% bands contain 33% and 6% of the months. The quadratic learned from a rise that was speeding up quickly, and in the early 1990s the rise slowed down for some years.
A is better in those two cases (2.4 and 2.7 ppm). But after the slowdown it has learned a short length scale for the trend (24.0 years from the data until 1994, 51.3 from the data until 1989) and runs back to the mean at once: 12.1 ppm off.
No model has a 95% band with about 95% coverage at all six dates. The coverage goes from 6% to 100% for B and from 12% to 99% for A.

So what are the error bars of a GP worth? Inside the data they are honest. Outside they are honest only if the kernel and the mean function are right, and the data of the past cannot prove that: in section 4 the leave-one-out errors of the two versions were the same. The bands count the functions that the model considers possible. A future that the model forbids is not counted, however wide the band.

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
6. Taking the curve apart
The sum of kernels can be taken apart again: the posterior mean of each part is its own kernel, multiplied by the same weights. Here with the whole record:


Code
K <- kernel(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, parts_B); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th_B$sigma^2
beta_all <- solve(crossprod(H(co2$t), solve(K, H(co2$t))), crossprod(H(co2$t), solve(K, co2$ppm)))
weights_all <- solve(K, co2$ppm - H(co2$t) %*% beta_all)
comp <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = co2$year, v = drop(H(co2$t) %*% beta_all), part = "quadratic mean"),
  data.frame(
    year = co2$year,
    v = drop(part(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, "season") %*% weights_all),
    part = "season"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = co2$year,
    v = drop(part(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, "swings") %*% weights_all),
    part = "swings"
  )
)
comp$part <- factor(comp$part, levels = unique(comp$part))
ggplot(comp, aes(year, v)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~part, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "The three parts of the fitted function", x = NULL, y = "ppm") +
  theme_bw()









Code
swing <- subset(comp, part == "swings")
amp <- tapply(subset(comp, part == "season")$v, floor(co2$year), function(v) diff(range(v)))
cbind(
  value = c(
    amplitude_of_the_season_1960 = amp[["1960"]],
    amplitude_2020 = amp[["2020"]],
    largest_swing = swing$v[which.max(abs(swing$v))],
    in_year = swing$year[which.max(abs(swing$v))]
  )
)


                                   value
amplitude_of_the_season_1960    5.758639
amplitude_2020                  6.692789
largest_swing                   2.294849
in_year                      1988.791700



The seasonal wave grew from 5.8 ppm in 1960 to 6.7 in 2020 (from the lowest to the highest month). Fixed sine waves cannot show that.
The swings reach 2.3 ppm, in 1988, and then fall back within a few years. That is the slowdown which threw both forecasts of section 5 off the track.

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

The kernel is the model. Length scales are what you report and defend. Try others (Matérn instead of the squared exponential, which is often too smooth).
The mean function matters little inside the data and a great deal outside. Test forecasts from several starting dates, not one.
Standardise the predictors; with several, give each its own length scale (automatic relevance determination).
The cost grows with \(n^3\). A few thousand rows are comfortable; beyond that use approximations (inducing points, nearest neighbours, state space).
The marginal likelihood can have several maxima. Start from several points. With few data the length scale may run to an absurd value: put a prior on it.
Plugging in the estimates of the kernel’s parameters ignores their uncertainty, and the bands are a bit too narrow. Full Bayesian versions average over them.
Other names: kriging in geostatistics, smoothing splines (a GP with a special kernel), Bayesian linear regression (a GP with a linear kernel), support vector regression with the same kernel but without probabilities.
Not normal outcomes (counts, yes or no) need approximations: mgcv with bs = "gp", brms with gp().

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the mean function, the kernel with its parameters in understandable units, how they were estimated, the accuracy on unseen data, and the coverage of the intervals. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = rownames(scores),
  rmse = f2(scores[, "RMSE"]),
  cov = pct(scores[, "coverage_95"]),
  width = f1(scores[, "mean_width"])
)


Method (data analysis):

Monthly mean CO₂ concentrations at Mauna Loa from 1958 to 2006 (N = 586; Lan & Keeling, 2026) were modelled with Gaussian process regression (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006). The mean function was quadratic in time with unknown coefficients; the covariance function was the sum of a periodic kernel with a slowly changing shape (period one year), an exponential kernel, and noise. The parameters of the kernel were estimated by maximising the marginal likelihood. A model with a constant mean and an additional squared exponential kernel, and a quadratic regression with seasonal terms, served for comparison. The models were evaluated by leave-one-out prediction of the months until 2006, on the 238 months since 2007, and on 15-year forecasts from six starting dates between 1980 and 2007 (parameters re-estimated each time), with the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the coverage of 95% prediction intervals. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

The Gaussian process with a quadratic mean predicted the months since 2007 with an RMSE of 1.58 ppm, and its 95% intervals contained 100% of the measurements (Table 1). With a constant mean the RMSE was 6.09 ppm and the coverage 46%. In leave-one-out prediction of the months until 2006 the two models had the same RMSE (0.24 ppm) and a coverage of 95%. The advantage of the quadratic mean was not stable: in 15-year forecasts from six starting dates its RMSE ranged from 0.5 to 5.2 ppm and its coverage from 6% to 100%; with a constant mean the ranges were 1.8 to 12.1 ppm and 12% to 99%. In the model of the full record the seasonal amplitude was 5.8 ppm in 1960 and 6.7 ppm in 2020. The estimated length scales were 156 years for the shape of the season and 3.3 years for the irregular swings.

Table 1
Forecasts of Monthly CO₂ Since 2007 From the Record Until 2006











Model
RMSE (ppm)
Coverage of 95% intervals
Mean width (ppm)




A: zero-mean GP
6.09

B: GP with a quadratic mean

quadratic regression + season (lm)

Note. 238 months.
Points to remember:

State the mean function and the kernel, and what each part stands for.
Give length scales in the units of the predictor.
Check coverage, not only accuracy, and say whether it was inside or outside the data.
Mark forecasts beyond the data as depending on the mean function and the kernel.

title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
text:
9. Summary



When
Smooth unknown functions, up to a few thousand rows, and a need for uncertainty


The model
\(f \sim \text{GP}(m, k)\); \(y = f + \varepsilon\)


Prediction
\(k_*^\top(K + \sigma^2I)^{-1}y\), with variance \(k_{**} - k_*^\top(K + \sigma^2I)^{-1}k_*\)


Kernel parameters
Maximum of the marginal likelihood


Building
Add kernels for trend, season, swings; take the fit apart again


How (R)
Two short functions by hand, or kernlab::gausspr(), mgcv::gam(s(x, bs = "gp")), brms::brm(y ~ gp(x))


Check
Leave-one-out errors and coverage; forecasts from several starting dates


Danger
Extrapolation follows the mean function and the kernel, and the bands believe both


Related pages
Polynomial regression, splines and GAMs, support vector regression

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
On 1 April 1992 the minimum wage in New Jersey rose from $4.25 to $5.05 an hour. In Pennsylvania, on the other side of the river, it stayed at $4.25. What happened to the jobs in fast-food restaurants, where many people earn the minimum?
Two simple comparisons come to mind, and both are wrong:

New Jersey after against before. But 1992 was a year of recession. Jobs may have changed anyway.
New Jersey against Pennsylvania, after. But the restaurants in the two states may have been different from the start.

Difference-in-differences (DiD) combines them. The change in Pennsylvania shows what happened anyway. The change in New Jersey, minus the change in Pennsylvania, is the effect of the law. It is simple enough for a pocket calculator. What it needs is one assumption, and most of this page is about that one.
The study by Card and Krueger (1993, published in the American Economic Review in 1994) is one of the best-known in economics, and one of the most disputed. This page uses it to teach the method. It does not settle the question.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)      # feols(): regression with fixed effects and clustered errors
# also used, with package::function: did (att_gt, aggte), quantreg (rq)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
pval <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
}
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
On 1 April 1992 the minimum wage in New Jersey rose from $4.25 to $5.05 an hour. In Pennsylvania, on the other side of the river, it stayed at $4.25. What happened to the jobs in fast-food restaurants, where many people earn the minimum?
Two simple comparisons come to mind, and both are wrong:

New Jersey after against before. But 1992 was a year of recession. Jobs may have changed anyway.
New Jersey against Pennsylvania, after. But the restaurants in the two states may have been different from the start.

Difference-in-differences (DiD) combines them. The change in Pennsylvania shows what happened anyway. The change in New Jersey, minus the change in Pennsylvania, is the effect of the law. It is simple enough for a pocket calculator. What it needs is one assumption, and most of this page is about that one.
The study by Card and Krueger (1993, published in the American Economic Review in 1994) is one of the best-known in economics, and one of the most disputed. This page uses it to teach the method. It does not settle the question.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)      # feols(): regression with fixed effects and clustered errors
# also used, with package::function: did (att_gt, aggte), quantreg (rq)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
pval <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
}
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
1. The data


Code
zip_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file(
  "https://davidcard.berkeley.edu/data_sets/njmin.zip",
  zip_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
data_file <- unzip(zip_file, "public.dat", exdir = tempfile("njmin"))
names_in_codebook <- c(
  "sheet", "chain", "co_owned", "state", "southj", "centralj", "northj", "pa1", "pa2", "shore",
  "ncalls", "empft", "emppt", "nmgrs", "wage_st", "inctime", "firstinc", "bonus", "pctaff", "meals",
  "open", "hrsopen", "psoda", "pfry", "pentree", "nregs", "nregs11", "type2", "status2", "date2",
  "ncalls2", "empft2", "emppt2", "nmgrs2", "wage_st2", "inctime2", "firstin2", "special2", "meals2",
  "open2r", "hrsopen2", "psoda2", "pfry2", "pentree2", "nregs2", "nregs112"
)
stores <- read.table(data_file, col.names = names_in_codebook, na.strings = ".")
stores$id <- seq_len(nrow(stores)) # (one sheet number is used twice)
stores$nj <- stores$state # 1 New Jersey, 0 Pennsylvania
# full-time equivalents, first interview
stores$fte1 <- stores$empft + stores$nmgrs + 0.5 * stores$emppt
stores$fte2 <- stores$empft2 + stores$nmgrs2 + 0.5 * stores$emppt2 # second interview
table(
  state = ifelse(stores$nj == 1, "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania"),
  second_interview = stores$status2
)


              second_interview
state            0   1   2   3   4   5
  New Jersey     1 321   2   5   1   1
  Pennsylvania   0  78   0   1   0   0


Card and Krueger interviewed 410 restaurants of four chains (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, Wendy’s), 331 in New Jersey and 79 in eastern Pennsylvania. The first interview was in February and March 1992, before the law, the second in November and December. The outcome is employment in full-time equivalents (FTE): full-time employees and managers count 1, part-time employees a half. The six restaurants that had closed for good (status 3) have an employment of zero in the second interview. The file is on David Card’s web page.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
2. Look at the data
Did the law do anything to the wages? The starting wage in both interviews:


Code
w <- rbind(
  data.frame(state = stores$nj, wage = stores$wage_st, wave = "before"),
  data.frame(state = stores$nj, wage = stores$wage_st2, wave = "after")
)
w$state <- ifelse(w$state == 1, "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania")
w$wave <- factor(w$wave, levels = c("before", "after"))
w <- subset(w, !is.na(wage))
w$share <- ave(w$wage, w$state, w$wave, FUN = function(v) 1 / length(v))
ggplot(w, aes(wage, weight = share, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(4.2, 5.8, by = 0.1), colour = "white") +
  facet_grid(state ~ wave) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Starting wages before and after the law",
    x = "starting wage (dollars per hour)",
    y = "share of restaurants"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
wage_means <- with(
  stores,
  rbind(
    `New Jersey` = c(
      before = mean(wage_st[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
      after = mean(wage_st2[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    Pennsylvania = c(mean(wage_st[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE), mean(wage_st2[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)
round(wage_means, 2)


             before after
New Jersey     4.61  5.08
Pennsylvania   4.63  4.62


Code
at_min <- mean(abs(stores$wage_st2[stores$nj == 1] - 5.05) < 0.001, na.rm = TRUE)


It did. Before, the two states looked the same. After, 89% of the restaurants in New Jersey paid exactly the new minimum, and nothing had changed in Pennsylvania. The mean starting wage rose by 0.47 dollars, or 10%.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: four means
\[\widehat{DiD} = (\bar y_{NJ,\text{after}} - \bar y_{NJ,\text{before}}) - (\bar y_{PA,\text{after}} - \bar y_{PA,\text{before}})\]


Code
m <- with(
  stores,
  rbind(
    `New Jersey` = c(
      before = mean(fte1[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
      after = mean(fte2[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    Pennsylvania = c(mean(fte1[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE), mean(fte2[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)
cbind(m, change = m[, "after"] - m[, "before"])


               before    after     change
New Jersey   20.43941 21.02743  0.5880214
Pennsylvania 23.33117 21.16558 -2.1655844


Code
did_hand <- diff(m["New Jersey", ]) - diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])
c(did = did_hand[[1]])


     did 
2.753606 


In New Jersey a restaurant had 20.44 full-time equivalents before and 21.03 after the law: a small rise. In Pennsylvania employment fell, from 23.33 to 21.17. The difference in differences is +2.75 FTE per restaurant. The textbook theory of the labour market expects a minus.


Step 2: a regression
The same number is the coefficient of the product term in a regression with two indicator variables:
\[y_{it} = \alpha + \beta\,NJ_i + \gamma\,\text{After}_t + \delta\,(NJ_i \times \text{After}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}\]
\(\alpha\) is Pennsylvania before, \(\beta\) the difference between the states before, \(\gamma\) the change in Pennsylvania, and \(\delta\) the DiD. The regression also gives a standard error, but the two interviews of the same restaurant are not independent. So the errors are clustered by restaurant, here by hand:
\[V = \frac{G}{G-1}\,\frac{N-1}{N-K}\,(X^\top X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_g X_g^\top e_g e_g^\top X_g\Big)(X^\top X)^{-1}\]


Code
long <- rbind(
  with(stores, data.frame(id, nj, after = 0, fte = fte1)),
  with(stores, data.frame(id, nj, after = 1, fte = fte2))
)
long <- subset(long, !is.na(fte))
fit <- lm(fte ~ nj * after, long)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
scores <- rowsum(X * residuals(fit), long$id)
G <- nrow(scores)
N <- nrow(X)
K <- ncol(X)
V <- G /
  (G - 1) *
  (N - 1) /
  (N - K) *
  solve(crossprod(X)) %*% crossprod(scores) %*% solve(crossprod(X))
clustered <- feols(fte ~ nj * after, long, cluster = ~ id)
rbind(
  estimate = c(
    lm = coef(fit)[["nj:after"]],
    by_hand = coef(fit)[["nj:after"]],
    feols = coef(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
  ),
  SE = c(
    sqrt(vcov(fit)["nj:after", "nj:after"]),
    sqrt(V["nj:after", "nj:after"]),
    se(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
  )
)


               lm  by_hand    feols
estimate 2.753606 2.753606 2.753606
SE       1.688409 1.306607 1.306607


The usual SE (1.69) is too large here. It does not know that a restaurant is compared with itself.


Step 3: changes, or two-way fixed effects
With two periods one can also take the change of each restaurant and compare the two groups with an ordinary regression. Or give every restaurant and every period its own constant (two-way fixed effects, TWFE, see panel data). For restaurants with both interviews that is the same:


Code
both <- subset(stores, !is.na(fte1) & !is.na(fte2)); both$change <- both$fte2 - both$fte1
change_fit <- feols(change ~ nj, both, vcov = "hetero")
twfe_fit   <- feols(fte ~ nj:after | id + after, subset(long, id %in% both$id), cluster = ~ id)
v_hand <- with(
  both,
  sqrt(var(change[nj == 1]) / sum(nj == 1) + var(change[nj == 0]) / sum(nj == 0))
)
rbind(
  `regression of the changes` = c(estimate = coef(change_fit)[["nj"]], SE = se(change_fit)[["nj"]]),
  `two-way fixed effects` = c(coef(twfe_fit)[["nj:after"]], se(twfe_fit)[["nj:after"]]),
  `two means, by hand` = c(with(both, mean(change[nj == 1]) - mean(change[nj == 0])), v_hand)
)


                          estimate       SE
regression of the changes     2.75 1.337725
two-way fixed effects         2.75 1.337723
two means, by hand            2.75 1.342341


384 of the 410 restaurants have both values, and the result is 2.75 (SE 1.34).


Step 4: the assumption
What is the causal effect? The outcome of New Jersey after the law, minus what it would have been without it. The second part nobody has seen. DiD fills it in: New Jersey would have changed like Pennsylvania. That is the parallel trends assumption:
\[E[y_{\text{after}}(0) - y_{\text{before}}(0) \mid NJ] = E[y_{\text{after}}(0) - y_{\text{before}}(0) \mid PA]\]
(\(y(0)\): employment without the law.)


Code
lines <- data.frame(
  state = rep(c("New Jersey", "Pennsylvania", "New Jersey without the law (assumed)"), each = 2),
  time = rep(0:1, 3),
  fte = c(
    m["New Jersey", ],
    m["Pennsylvania", ],
    m["New Jersey", "before"],
    m["New Jersey", "before"] + diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])
  )
)
ggplot(lines, aes(time, fte, colour = state, linetype = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 0:1,
    labels = c("February 1992", "November 1992"),
    limits = c(-0.1, 1.15)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Jersey" = "#2a78d6",
      "Pennsylvania" = "#eb6834",
      "New Jersey without the law (assumed)" = "#2a78d6"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Jersey" = "solid",
      "Pennsylvania" = "solid",
      "New Jersey without the law (assumed)" = "dashed"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 1.06,
    xend = 1.06,
    y = lines$fte[6],
    yend = lines$fte[2],
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.09, y = mean(lines$fte[c(2, 6)]), label = "DiD", hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "The four means, and what the assumption adds",
    x = NULL,
    y = "full-time equivalents per restaurant"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")









Note where the result comes from. New Jersey hardly moved. The effect is mostly the fall in Pennsylvania, which New Jersey is supposed to have been spared.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
4. Reading the output


Code
summary(clustered)


OLS estimation, Dep. Var.: fte
Observations: 794
Standard-errors: Clustered (id) 
            Estimate Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 23.33117    1.34654 17.32681 < 2.2e-16 ***
nj          -2.89176    1.43955 -2.00880  0.045215 *  
after       -2.16558    1.21802 -1.77795  0.076155 .  
nj:after     2.75361    1.30661  2.10745  0.035687 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
RMSE: 9.3819   Adj. R2: 0.003632


Code
ci_did <- confint(clustered)["nj:after", ]


The law is estimated to have raised employment by 2.75 FTE per restaurant, 95% CI [0.19, 5.32], p = .036. That is 13% of the 20.4 before the law. Whether it is a rise or nothing is one question. That the interval excludes a loss is what started the debate.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
5. Other ways of looking

More than one comparison
Pennsylvania need not be the only comparison. In New Jersey some restaurants already paid $5 or more. The law meant nothing to them. Card and Krueger used the gap: by how much a restaurant had to raise its starting wage to reach the new minimum.


Code
stores$gap <- with(stores, ifelse(nj == 0, 0, pmax(0, (5.05 - wage_st) / wage_st)))
both$gap <- stores$gap[match(both$id, stores$id)]
gap_all <- feols(change ~ gap, both, vcov = "hetero")
gap_nj <- feols(change ~ gap, subset(both, nj == 1), vcov = "hetero")
both$wage_group <- cut(
  both$wage_st,
  c(0, 4.251, 4.999, 10),
  labels = c("4.25", "4.26 to 4.99", "5.00 or more")
)
within <- with(
  subset(both, nj == 1 & !is.na(wage_group)),
  data.frame(
    starting_wage_before = levels(wage_group),
    restaurants = as.numeric(table(wage_group)),
    mean_before = as.numeric(tapply(fte1, wage_group, mean)),
    mean_change = as.numeric(tapply(change, wage_group, mean)),
    se = as.numeric(tapply(change, wage_group, function(v) sd(v) / sqrt(length(v))))
  )
)
print(data.frame(within[1:2], round(within[3:5], 2)), row.names = FALSE)


 starting_wage_before restaurants mean_before mean_change   se
                 4.25          94       19.44        1.20 0.82
         4.26 to 4.99         132       20.20        0.71 0.69
         5.00 or more          67       22.17       -2.16 1.01


Code
rbind(
  all_restaurants = c(slope = coef(gap_all)[["gap"]], SE = se(gap_all)[["gap"]]),
  new_jersey_only = c(coef(gap_nj)[["gap"]], se(gap_nj)[["gap"]])
)


                   slope       SE
all_restaurants 16.35898 5.984543
new_jersey_only 13.08053 6.713600


Code
mean_gap <- mean(stores$gap[stores$nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE)


In New Jersey, employment changed by 1.20 in the restaurants that paid $4.25, and by -2.16 in those that already paid $5. The slope on the gap (with both states) times the mean gap in New Jersey (0.10) is 1.72 FTE: the same sign as the DiD, and smaller. Two different control groups tell the same story. That is better evidence than one. (But the restaurants that already paid well were also larger before the law, 22.2 FTE against 19.4, like those in Pennsylvania. Section 6 comes back to this.)


Other outcomes, other definitions


Code
change_in <- function(a, b) {
  d <- data.frame(nj = stores$nj, change = b - a)
  f <- feols(change ~ nj, d, vcov = "hetero")
  c(estimate = coef(f)[["nj"]], SE = se(f)[["nj"]], p = pvalue(f)[["nj"]], n = nobs(f))
}
fte_w <- function(weight) {
  change_in(
    with(stores, empft + nmgrs + weight * emppt),
    with(stores, empft2 + nmgrs2 + weight * emppt2)
  )
}
pos <- function(v) ifelse(v > 0, log(v), NA)
open_again <- ifelse(stores$status2 == 3, NA, stores$fte2)
variants <- rbind(
  `FTE, part-time counts 0.5` = fte_w(0.5),
  `FTE, part-time counts 0.25` = fte_w(0.25),
  `FTE, part-time counts 1 (heads)` = fte_w(1),
  `FTE, closed restaurants left out` = change_in(stores$fte1, open_again),
  `log FTE` = change_in(pos(stores$fte1), pos(stores$fte2)),
  `full-time employees` = change_in(stores$empft, stores$empft2),
  `part-time employees` = change_in(stores$emppt, stores$emppt2),
  `hours open per day` = change_in(stores$hrsopen, stores$hrsopen2),
  `starting wage (dollars)` = change_in(stores$wage_st, stores$wage_st2),
  `log price of a full meal` = change_in(
    with(stores, log(psoda + pfry + pentree)),
    with(stores, log(psoda2 + pfry2 + pentree2))
  )
)
round(variants, 3)


                                 estimate    SE     p   n
FTE, part-time counts 0.5           2.750 1.338 0.040 384
FTE, part-time counts 0.25          2.919 1.413 0.040 384
FTE, part-time counts 1 (heads)     2.412 1.487 0.106 384
FTE, closed restaurants left out    2.722 1.335 0.042 378
log FTE                             0.078 0.049 0.111 378
full-time employees                 3.443 1.583 0.030 392
part-time employees                -0.911 1.527 0.551 396
hours open per day                 -0.111 0.102 0.278 399
starting wage (dollars)             0.497 0.051 0.000 370
log price of a full meal            0.029 0.013 0.027 356


Code
median_did <- unname(coef(quantreg::rq(change ~ nj, data = both))[2])
c(difference_of_the_median_changes = median_did)


difference_of_the_median_changes 
                             1.5 


Code
v <- function(name, what) variants[name, what]



The result does not depend much on how a part-timer is counted (2.41 to 2.92), nor on the closed restaurants.
It does depend on the scale. In logs it is 0.08 (about 8%) with p = .111. Trends that are parallel in numbers are not parallel in logs, and the method cannot tell us which scale is right. The median change differs by 1.5.
Prices of a meal rose by 2.9% more in New Jersey (p = .027). The customers paid a part of the law.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
section: 6. How far can we trust it?
text:
6. How far can we trust it?

The trends
With several periods before the law, one could look whether the two states moved together. Here there are only two interviews, so parallel trends cannot be checked at all. What one can do is to ask how wrong the assumption must be (the idea is developed by Rambachan & Roth, 2023). If New Jersey would have changed by \(d\) FTE more than Pennsylvania without any law, the effect is \(\widehat{DiD} - d\):


Code
est <- coef(clustered)[["nj:after"]]; se_cl <- se(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
cbind(
  value = c(
    d_that_removes_the_significance = est - 1.96 * se_cl,
    d_that_removes_the_effect = est,
    change_in_Pennsylvania = diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])[[1]]
  )
)


                                    value
d_that_removes_the_significance  0.192656
d_that_removes_the_effect        2.753606
change_in_Pennsylvania          -2.165584


A difference in trends of only 0.19 FTE takes the interval to zero, and one of 2.75 takes the whole effect away. The change in Pennsylvania was -2.17.


Two states are two observations
The standard error counted 410 restaurants. But the law was given to states, and there are two. Suppose each state had a shock of its own in 1992 (weather, the local economy), with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) in the change per restaurant. Then the variance of the DiD is the one from the restaurants plus \(2\sigma^2\) (Donald & Lang, 2007):


Code
sig <- seq(0, 2, length.out = 100); sdw <- sqrt(se_cl^2 + 2 * sig^2)
ggplot(data.frame(sig, lo = est - 1.96 * sdw, hi = est + 1.96 * sdw), aes(sig)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = est, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "95% interval of the DiD, if states have shocks of their own",
    x = "standard deviation of the shock of a state (FTE per restaurant)",
    y = "DiD"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
sigma_limit <- sqrt(((est / 1.96)^2 - se_cl^2) / 2)
interval1 <- est + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(se_cl^2 + 2)
cbind(
  value = c(
    sigma_at_which_the_interval_reaches_zero = sigma_limit,
    low_if_sigma_1 = interval1[1],
    high_if_sigma_1 = interval1[2]
  )
)


                                              value
sigma_at_which_the_interval_reaches_zero  0.3650511
low_if_sigma_1                           -1.0202071
high_if_sigma_1                           6.5274187


Shocks with an SD of 0.37 FTE (1.8% of a restaurant’s staff) are enough to take the significance away. And nothing in the data can tell us how large they are, because each state was seen once. With an SD of 1 the interval is [-1.0, 6.5]. A large loss of jobs is still hard to reconcile with the data; a small one is not. This is the general lesson of Bertrand et al. (2004) as well: cluster at the level at which the treatment was given, and have many such clusters.


Were the groups alike?
The restaurants in Pennsylvania were larger at the first interview (23.3 against 20.4). Large ones tend to shrink, and small ones to grow, if only because an interview catches a busy or a quiet week (regression to the mean). One could adjust for the first value:


Code
ancova <- feols(fte2 ~ nj + fte1, both, vcov = "hetero")
rbind(
  `difference in differences` = c(estimate = coef(change_fit)[["nj"]], SE = se(change_fit)[["nj"]]),
  `adjusted for the first value` = c(coef(ancova)[["nj"]], se(ancova)[["nj"]])
)


                             estimate       SE
difference in differences    2.750000 1.337725
adjusted for the first value 1.338523 0.992067


Code
c(
  slope_of_the_first_value = coef(ancova)[["fte1"]],
  correlation_of_the_two_interviews = with(both, cor(fte1, fte2))
)


         slope_of_the_first_value correlation_of_the_two_interviews 
                        0.5214388                         0.5537823 


With the first value as a control, the effect is 1.34 (SE 0.99). The two methods answer with different assumptions: DiD says that the states differ permanently, and that the difference would have stayed the same; the other says that a restaurant with 20 FTE in New Jersey and one with 20 in Pennsylvania would have had the same future. DiD forces the slope of the first value to be 1; the data say 0.52. Neither is right by itself. (The conflict is known as Lord’s paradox.)


What others found
Neumark and Wascher (2000) collected payroll records of restaurants in the same two states and found a loss of jobs in New Jersey. Card and Krueger (2000) answered with official payroll records: employment grew as fast in New Jersey as in Pennsylvania, or slightly faster. How good the interview data are was a part of that debate.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
section: 7. When the treatment comes in waves
text:
7. When the treatment comes in waves
Laws rarely come in one place and on one day. Some states raise the wage in 1990, some in 1994, some never. For twenty years people ran one regression with unit and time effects and a treatment indicator (TWFE) on such data. If the effect grows with time or differs between places, that is wrong (Goodman-Bacon, 2021): the regression also uses places that were treated early as controls for those treated late. A simulation where we know the truth:


Code
set.seed(231); n_unit <- 300; n_time <- 10
panel <- expand.grid(t = 1:n_time, id = 1:n_unit)
# treated from period 4, from period 8, never
panel$first <- rep(c(4, 8, 0), each = n_unit / 3)[panel$id]
panel$treated <- as.numeric(panel$first > 0 & panel$t >= panel$first)
# grows each year; faster in the early group
panel$effect <- panel$treated * ifelse(panel$first == 4, 1, 0.3) * (panel$t - panel$first + 1)
unit_level <- rnorm(n_unit, 0, 2) + ifelse(rep(c(4, 8, 0), each = n_unit / 3) == 4, 2, 0)
time_level <- cumsum(rnorm(n_time, 0.2, 0.5))
# parallel trends hold exactly
panel$y <- unit_level[panel$id] + time_level[panel$t] + panel$effect + rnorm(nrow(panel))
truth      <- mean(panel$effect[panel$treated == 1])
twfe       <- feols(y ~ treated | id + t, panel, cluster = ~ id)
twfe_no_never <- feols(y ~ treated | id + t, subset(panel, first > 0), cluster = ~ id)
c(
  true_mean_effect = truth,
  TWFE = coef(twfe)[["treated"]],
  TWFE_without_the_never_treated = coef(twfe_no_never)[["treated"]]
)


              true_mean_effect                           TWFE TWFE_without_the_never_treated 
                    2.98000000                     1.51468484                    -0.07322945 


The true mean effect is 2.98. Every single effect is positive, and the trends are exactly parallel. TWFE says 1.51, and without the group that was never treated even -0.07.
The remedy (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021) is to go back to the simple idea of step 1. For every group \(g\) and every period \(t\), do one DiD: with the period before the group’s treatment as “before”, and the never-treated as controls. Then average:
\[ATT(g, t) = (\bar y_{g,t} - \bar y_{g,g-1}) - (\bar y_{\text{never},t} - \bar y_{\text{never},g-1})\]


Code
ym <- function(g, t) mean(panel$y[panel$first == g & panel$t == t])
att <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(4, 8), function(g) {
    data.frame(
      group = g,
      t = g:n_time,
      by_hand = sapply(g:n_time, function(t) (ym(g, t) - ym(g, g - 1)) - (ym(0, t) - ym(0, g - 1))),
      truth = sapply(g:n_time, function(t) mean(panel$effect[panel$first == g & panel$t == t]))
    )
  })
)
cs <- did::att_gt(
  yname = "y",
  tname = "t",
  idname = "id",
  gname = "first",
  data = panel,
  control_group = "nevertreated",
  bstrap = FALSE,
  cband = FALSE,
  base_period = "universal"
)
att$did_package <- cs$att[match(paste(att$group, att$t), paste(cs$group, cs$t))]
print(round(att, 2), row.names = FALSE)

tr <- data.frame(
  group = paste("treated from period", att$group),
  rel = att$t - att$group,
  truth = att$truth
)
ggplot(es, aes(rel, est)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se), colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = tr, aes(rel, truth), shape = 4, colour = "#eb6834", size = 2.4) +

  labs(

    subtitle = "Crosses: the truth. Left of the line: there should be nothing",
    x = "periods since the treatment began",
    y = "effect"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









The group-time effects agree with the truth, and their mean is 2.92. The points to the left of the line are the check that we could not make with two interviews: before the treatment there should be nothing. Of the 8 intervals, 1 misses zero. Here we know that this is chance. With real data one would not, and a test of the trends before the treatment can fail in both directions.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

The assumption is about changes, not levels. The groups may differ, but they must not be on different tracks.
Draw the periods before the treatment, as many as there are. Parallel trends before do not prove parallel trends after, but a difference is a warning.
The scale (levels, logs, percentages) is a part of the assumption.
Cluster at the level at which the treatment was given. With few clusters the usual formula is too optimistic. With two, there is no honest standard error at all.
Anticipation: if people react before the law starts, the period before is already treated.
Spillovers: if the customers of New Jersey drive to Pennsylvania, the control group is affected as well.
Composition: in a repeated cross-section the groups may change who is in them.
Control variables must not be changed by the treatment.
Staggered treatment: do not use the plain two-way regression. Use did, fixest::sunab(), or one DiD at a time.
Relatives: panel data, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and interrupted time series when there is no control group.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the treatment, the groups and the periods, the four means, the estimate with clustered standard errors and the level of the clusters, the argument for parallel trends with the evidence for it (or its absence), the other comparisons, and the sensitivity. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
mean_se <- function(v) {
  paste0(f2(mean(v, na.rm = TRUE)), " (", f2(sd(v, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(v)))), ")")
}
apa_table <- data.frame(
  State = c("New Jersey", "Pennsylvania", "Difference in differences"),
  before = c(mean_se(stores$fte1[stores$nj == 1]), mean_se(stores$fte1[stores$nj == 0]), ""),
  after = c(mean_se(stores$fte2[stores$nj == 1]), mean_se(stores$fte2[stores$nj == 0]), ""),
  change = c(
    f2(diff(m["New Jersey", ])),
    f2(diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])),
    paste0(f2(est), " (", f2(se_cl), ")")
  )
)


Method (data analysis):

The effect of New Jersey’s increase in the minimum wage (from $4.25 to $5.05 on 1 April 1992) on employment in fast-food restaurants was estimated with a difference-in-differences design. 410 restaurants in New Jersey (n = 331) and eastern Pennsylvania (n = 79), where the minimum wage did not change, were interviewed before and after the increase (Card & Krueger, 1993). The outcome was the number of full-time equivalents (full-time employees and managers plus half of the part-time employees); restaurants that had closed permanently were counted as zero. We regressed the outcome on state, period and their product, with standard errors clustered by restaurant. The analysis assumes that employment in New Jersey would have changed as in Pennsylvania without the law; with two interviews this cannot be examined, and we report how large a violation would change the conclusion. Comparisons within New Jersey used the increase that each restaurant needed to reach the new minimum. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

Mean employment rose from 20.44 to 21.03 full-time equivalents in New Jersey and fell from 23.33 to 21.17 in Pennsylvania (Table 1). The difference in differences was 2.75, SE = 1.31, 95% CI [0.19, 5.32], p = .036. Across the restaurants of both states, a wage gap of 10% was associated with a change of 1.64 full-time equivalents (SE = 0.60). On the log scale the difference was 0.08 (p = .111), and adjusted for employment at the first interview it was 1.34 (SE = 0.99). A difference in trends of 0.19 between the states, or random shocks to the states with a standard deviation of 0.37, would suffice to make the result compatible with no effect. The data give no evidence for a loss of jobs, but the evidence for a gain is weak.

Points to remember:

Show the four means, not only the estimate.
Say at which level the errors are clustered, and how many clusters there are.
Say what the evidence for parallel trends is. If there is none, say that.
Report other comparisons, scales and definitions, also those that disagree.

title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
text:
10. Summary



When
A treatment reaches one group and not another, and both are seen before and after


The estimate
Change in the treated group minus change in the control group


The assumption
Without the treatment both would have changed alike (parallel trends)


How (R)
lm(y ~ group * after), or feols(y ~ treated | unit + time, cluster = ~ unit)


Standard errors
Clustered at the level of the treatment; few clusters are a problem


Check
Periods before the treatment, other control groups, placebo outcomes, other scales, sensitivity


In waves
Group-time effects (did::att_gt(), fixest::sunab()), not plain TWFE


Related pages
Panel data, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
text:
People who leave prison have little money and find it hard to get work. Many are soon arrested again. In the 1970s the state of Maryland made an experiment: of 432 men released from prison, half were chosen at random to receive a small weekly payment for three months. All were followed for one year. Did the money keep them out of jail (Rossi et al., 1980)?
The outcome is a time: the number of weeks until the first arrest. For most men it is not known, because they were not arrested in the year. We know only that their time is longer than 52 weeks. Such a time is censored. Neither a regression of the weeks (what value should the others have?) nor a logistic regression of arrested or not (an arrest in week 1 counts like one in week 52) uses what we know.
Survival analysis does, and Cox regression (Cox, 1972) is its most used model. It asks: at any moment, among those who are still free, how many times higher is the rate of arrest for one person than for another?


Code
library(survival)   # Surv(), survfit(), coxph(), cox.zph() (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)

arm_colours <- c(`no payment` = "#eb6834", payment = "#2a78d6")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

The Kaplan–Meier curve shows the share of men who are still free. After a year it is 69% without the payment and 78% with it. The log-rank test compares the two curves at all times: \(\chi^2\)(1) = 3.84, p = .050. The test has no predictors besides the groups and gives no size of an effect. That is what the regression is for.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the hazard
The hazard \(h(t)\) is the rate of the event at time \(t\) among those who have not had it yet. If 100 men are still free at the start of a week and 2 are arrested in it, the hazard is about 0.02 per week. It may go up and down over time.


Step 2: proportional hazards
\[h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, e^{\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots}\]
\(h_0(t)\) is the baseline hazard, of somebody with all predictors 0. It can have any shape, and we do not model it. The predictors multiply it by a factor that does not depend on time. So for two people who differ by one unit in \(x_1\), the ratio of their hazards is
\[\frac{h(t \mid x_1 + 1)}{h(t \mid x_1)} = e^{\beta_1} \quad\text{at every } t\]
the hazard ratio (HR). That it is the same at all times is the assumption of proportional hazards.


Step 3: the partial likelihood
Cox’s idea: at each arrest, ask only who among those still free is the one arrested. Given that one of them is, the probability that it is man \(i\) is his share of the total hazard, and \(h_0(t)\) cancels:
\[\frac{h_0(t)\, e^{x_i^\top\beta}}{\sum_{j \text{ still free}} h_0(t)\, e^{x_j^\top\beta}} = \frac{e^{x_i^\top\beta}}{\sum_{j \text{ still free}} e^{x_j^\top\beta}}\]
Multiply these over all the arrests, and find the \(\beta\) that makes the product largest. Only the order of the events matters, not the exact times. Censored men count in the sums as long as they are free.


Code
X <- as.matrix(rossi[, c("money", "age", "prior")])
minus_partial <- function(b) {
  # with Breslow's treatment of ties
  eta <- drop(X %*% b)
  -sum(sapply(which(rossi$arrest == 1), function(i) {
    eta[i] - log(sum(exp(eta[rossi$week >= rossi$week[i]])))
  }))
}
hand <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), minus_partial, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-12))
fit_breslow <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + age + prior, data = rossi, ties = "breslow")
rbind(by_hand = hand$par, coxph = coef(fit_breslow))


            money        age      prior
by_hand -0.346444 -0.3346050 0.09652746
coxph   -0.346444 -0.3346038 0.09652828




Step 4: ties
Time was recorded in weeks, so several men were arrested at the “same” time, and it is not clear who was in the sum when. The default of coxph() is Efron’s approximation, better than Breslow’s simple one above. With few ties they agree.

summary(fit)

Score (logrank) test = 29.03  on 3 df,   p=2e-06


Code
s  <- summary(fit)$coefficients; hr <- s[, 2]; ci <- exp(confint(fit))
con <- summary(fit)$concordance[[1]]



money: HR = 0.71. At any time, among men of the same age and record who are still free, the rate of arrest of those with the payment is 0.71 times that of the others, 29% lower. 95% CI [0.49, 1.03], p = .068: the interval reaches just over 1.
age: five years older, 0.71 times the hazard. prior: each earlier conviction, 1.10 times, so three more convictions, \(1.10^3\) = 1.34.
Concordance = 0.63: of two men of whom it is known who was arrested first, the model gives the higher risk to the right one in 63% of the pairs. 50% is guessing.
The three tests at the end (likelihood ratio, Wald, score) test all the predictors together. The score test with one group variable is the log-rank test.
There is no intercept: it is in the baseline hazard.


What a hazard ratio is not
An HR of 0.71 does not mean that 29% fewer men are arrested, nor that they stay free 1.41 times as long. It is a ratio of rates among those still free. For people, translate it into survival curves:


Code

    x = "weeks since release",
    y = "not arrested"

  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









For such a man the model predicts a chance of 75% of staying free for a year without the payment, and 81% with it: 6.7 points more.


In weeks: the restricted mean
Another number for the whole experiment needs no model: the mean number of weeks free in the first 52, which is the area under the Kaplan–Meier curve.

rm   <- tab[, "rmean"]; rm_se <- tab[, "se(rmean)"]

c(
  no_payment = rm[[1]],
  payment = rm[[2]],
  difference = diff,
  low = diff - 1.96 * diff_se,
  high = diff + 1.96 * diff_se

44.8333333 46.8750000  2.0416667 -0.3359074  4.4192407

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
text:
5. Are the hazards proportional?
cox.zph() looks at the Schoenfeld residuals: at each arrest, how the arrested man differs from the average of those still free. If the effect of a predictor changes over time, they show a trend (Grambsch & Therneau, 1994).


Code
zph <- cox.zph(fit)
zph

  time = rep(zph$time, 3),
  beta = as.vector(zph$y),

  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey40", size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    colour = "#2a78d6",
    fill = "#2a78d6",
    alpha = 0.2

  geom_hline(
    data = data.frame(term = names(coef(fit)), b = coef(fit)),

For the payment there is no sign of a change (p = .801). For age there is (p = .012): the line falls. Age hardly matters in the first weeks, and a lot later. What can be done?

Let the effect change with time, for example linearly. tt() does it:



Code
fit_tt <- coxph(
  Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + age + prior + tt(age),
  data = rossi,
  tt = function(x, t, ...) x * (t - 26) / 26
)
round(coef(summary(fit_tt)), 3)

c(week_5 = age_at(5), week_26 = age_at(26), week_52 = age_at(52))

1.0677175 0.7138407 0.4336248 


Five years more multiply the hazard by 1.07 in week 5 and by 0.43 at the end of the year.

Stratify: give each age group its own baseline hazard. Age then has no coefficient, and the others are adjusted for it without any assumption:



Code
rossi$age_group <- cut(raw$age, c(0, 19, 22, 25, 100), labels = c("-19", "20-22", "23-25", "26-"))
fit_strata <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + prior + strata(age_group), data = rossi)
round(
  rbind(
    original = coef(summary(fit))["money", ],
    stratified = coef(summary(fit_strata))["money", ],
    time_varying_age = coef(summary(fit_tt))["money", ]

Or leave it, and read the HR as an average over time, if the predictor is only there for adjustment. The effect of the payment, our question, is the same in all three: 0.70 and 0.71 against 0.71.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
section: 6. Predictors that change over time: having a job
text:
6. Predictors that change over time: having a job
Did the men who found work stay free? Work changes from week to week, so it cannot be one number per man. Two wrong ways and a better one.

The trap: “ever employed”


Code
rossi$ever <- as.integer(apply(work, 1, any, na.rm = TRUE))
wrong <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + age + prior + ever, data = rossi)
round(coef(summary(wrong))["ever", ], 4)


     coef exp(coef)  se(coef)         z  Pr(>|z|) 
  -1.1302    0.3230    0.2028   -5.5722    0.0000 


Men who were ever employed have a hazard 0.32 times that of the others. It looks like a miracle, and it is a mistake. To find a job in week 20 a man must first stay free for 20 weeks. During those weeks he could not be arrested and count as employed: he was “immortal”. The variable looks into the future. This is immortal time bias (Suissa, 2008), and it is still found in medical journals.


The right data: one row per man and week
Split each man’s time into weeks. In each, the job status is what it was then:


Code
long <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(rossi)), function(i) {
    w <- rossi$week[i]
    data.frame(
      rossi[i, c("id", "money", "age", "prior")],
      start = 0:(w - 1),
      stop = 1:w,
      arrest = c(rep(0, w - 1), rossi$arrest[i]),
      job = as.integer(work[i, 1:w]),
      row.names = NULL
    )
  })
)
long$job_before <- ave(long$job, long$id, FUN = function(v) c(NA, head(v, -1))) # the week before
subset(long, id == 1)[14:20, ]


   id money age prior start stop arrest job job_before
14  1     0 0.4     3    13   14      0   0          0
15  1     0 0.4     3    14   15      0   0          0
16  1     0 0.4     3    15   16      0   0          0
17  1     0 0.4     3    16   17      0   0          0
18  1     0 0.4     3    17   18      0   0          0
19  1     0 0.4     3    18   19      0   0          0
20  1     0 0.4     3    19   20      1   0          0


Code
nrow(long)


[1] 19809


Code
same_week <- coxph(Surv(start, stop, arrest) ~ money + age + prior + job, data = long)
week_before <- coxph(Surv(start, stop, arrest) ~ money + age + prior + job_before, data = long)
round(
  rbind(
    same_week = coef(summary(same_week))["job", ],
    week_before = coef(summary(week_before))["job_before", ]
  ),
  4
)


               coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
same_week   -1.3482    0.2597   0.2493 -5.4081    0e+00
week_before -0.8112    0.4443   0.2165 -3.7474    2e-04


The outcome is now Surv(start, stop, arrest). Each row is at risk only in its own week, and a man leaves the risk set when he is arrested. (The rows of one man are not repeated observations that need a correction: at each event he appears once.)

With the job in the same week, the HR is 0.26. But there is a second trap. An arrest on Monday costs the job of that week. The cause may run backwards.
With the job in the week before, the HR is 0.44, 95% CI [0.29, 0.68]. That is the number to believe, more or less. Men were not assigned to jobs at random, as they were to the payment, and those who find work may be those who would stay free anyway.

And note: the job may be on the way from the payment to freedom (or away from it, since the payment was cut when a man earned money). Adjusting for it changes the meaning of the effect of the payment.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
text:
7. More checks


Code
m0 <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money, data = rossi)
md <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = raw$age, r = residuals(m0, type = "martingale"), what = "age (years)"),
  data.frame(x = rossi$prior, r = residuals(m0, type = "martingale"), what = "earlier convictions")
)
ggplot(md, aes(x, r)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#2a78d6", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Martingale residuals: what shape should the predictor have?",
    x = NULL,
    y = "residual of a model without it"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
infl <- residuals(fit, type = "dfbetas"); colnames(infl) <- names(coef(fit))
worst <- apply(abs(infl), 2, max)
worst


    money       age     prior 
0.1168141 0.4480371 0.2842831 


Code
fit_log <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + log(raw$age) + prior, data = rossi)
c(AIC_linear_age = AIC(fit), AIC_log_age = AIC(fit_log))


AIC_linear_age    AIC_log_age 
      1327.714       1326.204 



Shape of the predictors. The smooth line of the martingale residuals (observed minus expected arrests) against age falls steeply at first and then flattens: the logarithm of age would fit a little better (AIC 1,326.2 against 1,327.7).
Influence. No man moves a coefficient by more than 0.45 standard errors.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Independent censoring. The method assumes that those who leave the study would have gone on like those who stay. Here almost all the censoring is the end of the year, which is harmless.
Events decide the power, not people. With 114 arrests a model has room for about 11 predictors at most.
The hazard ratio and selection. Even in a randomised experiment, those still free after 30 weeks are not a random half any more: if the money works, the high-risk men of the payment group are still in it. So the HR at later times is not a clean comparison (Hernán, 2010). Differences of survival curves and restricted means are.
Adding predictors changes the HR of the others even if they are unrelated to them (as for odds ratios). Compare models with care.
Several events. We used the first arrest. For repeated events there are extensions (Andersen–Gill).
Other ways to end. If some men had died, death would be a competing risk.
Parametric models (Weibull and others) estimate the baseline too, and can predict beyond the data.
Discrete time. With few intervals, a complementary log-log regression on person-weeks gives the same hazard ratios.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the start and end of the time, the number of events, the method for ties, hazard ratios with intervals, the check of proportional hazards, and survival at some times. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Payment", "Age (5 years)", "Earlier convictions (each)"),
  b = f2(s[, 1]),
  SE = f2(s[, 3]),
  z = f2(s[, 4]),
  p = sapply(s[, 5], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  HR = paste0(f2(hr), " [", f2(ci[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[, 2]), "]")
)


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the time from release to the first arrest in 432 men who were randomly assigned to a weekly payment for three months or to no payment (Rossi et al., 1980). Men not arrested within 52 weeks were censored. Arrest-free survival was described with Kaplan–Meier curves and compared with the log-rank test. Hazard ratios were estimated with Cox regression (Efron’s method for ties), adjusting for age and the number of earlier convictions. Proportional hazards were tested with scaled Schoenfeld residuals; because the effect of age changed over time, we repeated the analysis stratified by age group. Employment was analysed as a time-dependent covariate, lagged by one week. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package survival (Therneau & Grambsch, 2000).

Results:

Within a year, 48 of 216 men with the payment and 66 of 216 without it were arrested; the proportion free after 52 weeks was 78% and 69%, log-rank χ²(1) = 3.84, p = .050. In the Cox model, the hazard of arrest was lower with the payment, HR = 0.71, 95% CI [0.49, 1.03], p = .068, a difference that did not reach significance (Table 1). The men with the payment were free for 2.0 more of the 52 weeks, 95% CI [-0.3, 4.4]. Proportional hazards held for the payment (p = .801) but not for age (p = .012); in the analysis stratified by age, HR = 0.70. Having had a job in the week before went with a lower hazard, HR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.29, 0.68].

Points to remember:

Define time zero, the event and the censoring.
Give the number of events.
Report the test of proportional hazards, and what you did about it.
Add survival proportions or restricted means: hazard ratios are hard to picture.
Never use a variable that looks into the future.

title: Cox Regression: Does Money Keep Released Prisoners Out of Jail?
text:
10. Summary



When
Time to an event, with censored cases, and the interest is in relative rates


The model
\(h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\,e^{x^\top\beta}\), with any baseline


Estimation
Partial likelihood: at each event, who among those at risk?


How (R)
coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ x, data); changing predictors: Surv(start, stop, event)


Reading it
\(e^\beta\): hazard ratio, the same at all times


Check
cox.zph(); if it fails: tt(), strata(), or read it as an average


Also report
Kaplan–Meier, survival at chosen times, restricted means


Traps
Immortal time, reverse causation, informative censoring


Related pages
Censored quantile regression, complementary log-log

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
Monoclonal gammopathy (MGUS) is a condition of the blood that many older people have without knowing. It does no harm by itself, but in some it turns into a cancer of the plasma cells (PCM, for example multiple myeloma). Doctors at the Mayo Clinic followed 1,384 patients for up to 35 years (Kyle et al., 2002).
A patient asks: what is my risk of getting the cancer? The difficulty is that the patients are old. Their average age at diagnosis is 70, and many die of something else first. A person who has died of a heart attack will never get the cancer.
When one event makes another impossible, they are competing risks. Common survival methods treat a death as censoring, as if the person had only been lost from sight and might still get the cancer later. That gives a risk for a world in which nobody dies of anything else. It is far too high, and it is a frequent mistake in medical papers.
This page shows the right way to describe the risk, and the two regressions for it: cause-specific hazards, and the Fine–Gray model. They can give opposite answers about the same predictor, and both can be right.


Code
library(survival)   # survfit(), coxph(), finegray(); the data (comes with R)
library(cmprsk)     # crr(): the Fine-Gray model, as in the original paper
library(ggplot2)

event_colours <- c(`cancer (PCM)` = "#eb6834", `death without cancer` = "#2a78d6")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
