text:
1. The data
The data come with R, in the package survival:


Code
mgus <- subset(mgus2, !is.na(mspike))
# years until the first event, or the end
mgus$time <- with(mgus, ifelse(pstat == 1, ptime, futime)) / 12
mgus$event <- factor(
  with(mgus, ifelse(pstat == 1, 1, 2 * death)),
  0:2,
  c("censored", "PCM", "death")
)
mgus <- subset(mgus, time > 0)
mgus$age10 <- (mgus$age - 70) / 10; mgus$male <- as.integer(mgus$sex == "M")
nrow(mgus)


[1] 1373


Code
table(mgus$event)



censored      PCM    death 
     404      115      854 


Code
c(mean_age = mean(mgus$age), longest_follow_up = max(mgus$time))


         mean_age longest_follow_up 
         70.45521          35.33333 


Each patient has one first event: the cancer (PCM), or death without it, or neither until the end of the study (censored). age10 is the age at diagnosis in decades from 70, male the sex, and mspike the size of the abnormal protein in the blood (grams per decilitre), which is known to predict the cancer. Of 1,373 patients, 115 got the cancer, 854 died without it. (The other 11 of the 1,384 are left out, because their M-spike was not measured.)

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
2. One minus Kaplan–Meier is wrong
The tempting calculation: call the cancer the event, treat deaths as censored, and take one minus the Kaplan–Meier curve.


Code
km <- survfit(Surv(time, event == "PCM") ~ 1, data = mgus) # deaths treated as censored: wrong
cif <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = mgus) # event is a factor with several outcomes: right
at  <- c(5, 10, 20, 25)
risk <- rbind(`1 - Kaplan-Meier`        = 1 - summary(km, times = at)$surv,
              `cumulative incidence`    = summary(cif, times = at)$pstate[, 2],
              `death without cancer`    = summary(cif, times = at)$pstate[, 3])
colnames(risk) <- paste(at, "years"); round(risk, 3)


                     5 years 10 years 20 years 25 years
1 - Kaplan-Meier       0.042    0.096    0.210    0.261
cumulative incidence   0.034    0.064    0.100    0.110
death without cancer   0.319    0.532    0.723    0.762




Code
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(time = km$time, risk = 1 - km$surv, what = "1 − Kaplan–Meier (deaths as censored)"),
  data.frame(time = cif$time, risk = cif$pstate[, 2], what = "cumulative incidence of the cancer")
)
ggplot(curves, aes(time, risk, colour = what)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey55", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(100 * v, "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(
    title = "Two answers to: what is the risk of the cancer?",
    x = "years since diagnosis",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









After 25 years the first method says 26.1%, and the truth about these patients is 11.0%. The difference is the patients who died: 76.2% of them in 25 years. Kaplan–Meier assumes that they would have got the cancer at the same rate as the survivors, if they had only lived. They did not live. The Kaplan–Meier answer is about an imaginary world, and even there only if those who died and those who did not had the same risk, which nobody can check.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: cause-specific hazards
For each event \(k\) there is a hazard: the rate of this event among those who have had none of them yet,
\[h_k(t) = \text{rate of event } k \text{ at } t, \text{ given no event before } t\]


Step 2: cumulative incidence
The cumulative incidence of event \(k\) is the probability of having had it by time \(t\):
\[F_k(t) = \int_0^t S(u)\, h_k(u)\, du\]
where \(S(u)\) is the probability of still being free of any event. At each moment, the share still free, times the rate of event \(k\). So the risk of the cancer depends on both hazards: a high rate of death empties the pool. The sum of all the cumulative incidences and of those still free is 1.
By hand (the Aalen–Johansen estimate):


Code
times <- sort(unique(mgus$time)); S <- 1; F1 <- F2 <- 0; out <- NULL
for (t in times) {
  at_risk <- sum(mgus$time >= t)
  d1 <- sum(mgus$time == t & mgus$event == "PCM")
  d2 <- sum(mgus$time == t & mgus$event == "death")
  F1 <- F1 + S * d1 / at_risk
  F2 <- F2 + S * d2 / at_risk # the share still free just before t, times the two rates
  S <- S * (1 - (d1 + d2) / at_risk)
  out <- rbind(out, c(t, F1, F2, S))
}
i <- max(which(out[, 1] <= 20))
c(
  by_hand = out[i, 2],
  survfit = summary(cif, times = 20)$pstate[, 2],
  sum_of_all_three = sum(out[i, 2:4])
)


         by_hand      survfit.PCM sum_of_all_three 
       0.1002904        0.1002904        1.0000000 




Step 3: two kinds of regression
Cause-specific. A Cox model for each event, with the other event as censoring. Its hazard ratios are about rates among those still free: how does \(x\) act on the process?
Fine–Gray. A model directly for the cumulative incidence. Fine and Gray (1999) defined a subdistribution hazard, whose relation to \(F_k\) is the usual one, \(1 - F_k(t) = \exp\{-\int_0^t \tilde h_k(u)\,du\}\), and put a proportional model on it:
\[\tilde h_k(t \mid x) = \tilde h_{k0}(t)\, e^{x^\top\beta}\]
The trick is who is at risk: in the subdistribution, those who died stay in the risk set, for ever, with no chance of the event. It sounds absurd, and it is a bookkeeping device. If many die early, they stay in the denominator and keep the risk low, as it is in reality. If \(\beta > 0\), the cumulative incidence is higher. That is all its coefficients say; they are not effects on a rate among people who could have the event.


Step 4: with censoring
People who die stay in the risk set, but for how long would they have been followed? Fine and Gray give them a weight that falls with time, the probability of not yet having been censored. finegray() builds the data set with these weights, and an ordinary Cox model with weights does the rest.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
4. The regressions


Code
# cause-specific: the cancer
cs_pcm <- coxph(Surv(time, event == "PCM") ~ age10 + male + mspike, data = mgus)
# cause-specific: death
cs_death <- coxph(Surv(time, event == "death") ~ age10 + male + mspike, data = mgus)

fg_data <- finegray(Surv(time, event) ~ ., data = mgus, etype = "PCM") # the weighted data set
fg_pcm <- coxph(
  Surv(fgstart, fgstop, fgstatus) ~ age10 + male + mspike,
  weights = fgwt,
  data = fg_data
)
fg_dead  <- finegray(Surv(time, event) ~ ., data = mgus, etype = "death")

Read age in the panel of the cancer.

Cause-specific: HR = 1.18, 95% CI [1.00, 1.39]. Among people who are alive and free of cancer, the rate is if anything a little higher in older ones.
Fine–Gray: HR = 0.84, [0.76, 0.94]. The risk of ever getting it is clearly lower in older people.

Both are right. Ten years more multiply the rate of death by 1.92. Older people are not protected from the cancer. They have less time to get it.
The protein (mspike) acts on the cancer itself: 2.42 and 2.43 are nearly the same, because it hardly changes the rate of death (0.94). In the Fine–Gray model for death its ratio is 0.86: a larger protein “protects” from dying without cancer. Not because it keeps people alive, but because more of them get the cancer first.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
5. Which one to use?







Question
Model




Why does it happen? Does \(x\) act on the biological process? (etiology, effect of a treatment on the disease)
Cause-specific hazards, for all the events


How many will have it? What is the risk of this patient? (prognosis, planning, costs)
Cumulative incidence; Fine–Gray, or predictions from the cause-specific models together



This division of labour is the usual advice (Austin et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2009). Latouche et al. (2013) recommend to report both: the cause-specific hazards of all the events, and the cumulative incidences. One without the others can mislead, as the two results for age show. In particular, never report a Fine–Gray ratio as an effect on the disease.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
6. Predicted risks
The two routes to the risk of one patient: from the Fine–Gray model directly, and from the two cause-specific models, put together with the formula of step 2 (a multi-state model; survfit() does it).


Code
new <- data.frame(age10 = c(-1, 1, -1, 1), male = 1, mspike = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 2))
new$who <- c(
  "60 years, M-spike 0.5", "80 years, M-spike 0.5", "60 years, M-spike 2", "80 years, M-spike 2"
)
sf_fg <- survfit(fg_pcm, newdata = new)
# both cause-specific models at once
multi <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age10 + male + mspike, data = mgus, id = id)
sf_cs <- survfit(multi, newdata = new)
risk_at <- function(t) {
  data.frame(
    who = new$who,
    FineGray = 1 - summary(sf_fg, times = t)$surv[1, ],
    cause_specific = summary(sf_cs, times = t)$pstate[1, , 2],
    death_first = summary(sf_cs, times = t)$pstate[1, , 3]
  )
}
r20 <- risk_at(20)
print(cbind(who = r20$who, round(r20[, -1], 3)), row.names = FALSE)

   60 years, M-spike 2    0.185          0.205       0.560

  rbind,
  lapply(1:4, function(j) {
    rbind(
      data.frame(

        time = sf_cs$time,

A man of 60 with a large protein has a 20-year risk of the cancer of 21%; a man of 80 with the same protein, 12%, because 87% of such men die of something else within 20 years. The two routes agree to within 2.0 points.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
7. Checking the model


Code
rbind(
  cause_specific_PCM = cox.zph(cs_pcm)$table[, "p"],
  cause_specific_death = cox.zph(cs_death)$table[, "p"],
  fine_gray_PCM = cox.zph(fg_pcm)$table[, "p"]
)


                            age10      male    mspike       GLOBAL
cause_specific_PCM   9.359611e-02 0.6266840 0.8992740 3.867087e-01
cause_specific_death 1.149011e-08 0.3447954 0.5521883 1.903550e-07
fine_gray_PCM        5.064391e-06 0.6208059 0.7698267 1.036011e-04


Proportional hazards can be checked for each model in the usual way. If the cause-specific hazards are proportional, the subdistribution hazards in general cannot be, and the other way round: the two models cannot both be exactly right. In practice both are approximations. That is what we see. For the cause-specific hazard of the cancer no predictor fails. For death, age does: its effect on mortality changes over 30 years of follow-up, as one would expect. And in the Fine–Gray model age fails as well: the subdistribution hazard mixes the two processes, and the competing deaths of the old come at other times than those of the young. Its single ratio for age is an average over the follow-up. For the risks of section 6, where this could matter, the two routes gave similar answers.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Decide what the events are before the analysis, and make them complete: everybody has exactly one first event, or is censored.
Censoring and competing events are not the same. A censored person may still have the event, outside our view. A person with a competing event may not.
Combined endpoints (cancer or death) avoid the problem, and answer another question.
Few events. With 115 cancers there is room for a few predictors only.
The Fine–Gray hazard ratio is not a ratio of risks either. An HR of 0.83 does not mean 17% less risk; report the cumulative incidences.
Time-dependent predictors do not work in Fine–Gray models: after a death they have no value.
In trials, a treatment that kills people early can “reduce” the incidence of everything else. Always look at all the causes.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the events and their numbers, cumulative incidences, the cause-specific hazard ratios of all the events, and, for prognosis, the subdistribution hazard ratios, clearly labelled. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
cell <- function(e, m) {
  sapply(c("age (10 years)", "male", "M-spike (g/dl)"), function(t) {
    paste0(f2(get(t, e, m)), " [", f2(get(t, e, m, "low")), ", ", f2(get(t, e, m, "high")), "]")
  })
}
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Age (10 years)", "Male", "M-spike (g/dl)"),
  a = cell("cancer", "cause-specific"),
  b = cell("death", "cause-specific"),
  c = cell("cancer", "Fine–Gray"),
  row.names = NULL
)


Method (data analysis):

We followed 1,373 patients with monoclonal gammopathy (Kyle et al., 2002) until progression to a plasma cell malignancy, death without it, or the end of the study. Death was treated as a competing event. Cumulative incidences were estimated with the Aalen–Johansen method. Cause-specific hazards of both events were analysed with Cox models, and the cumulative incidence of malignancy with the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard model (Fine & Gray, 1999); predictors were age, sex and the size of the M-spike. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages survival and cmprsk.

Results:

During follow-up 115 patients progressed to a malignancy and 854 died without it. The cumulative incidence of malignancy was 6.4% after 10 and 10.0% after 20 years (one minus the Kaplan–Meier estimate, which treats deaths as censored, would be 21.0% after 20 years), and that of death without malignancy 72.3% after 20 years. A larger M-spike was associated with a higher rate of malignancy, cause-specific HR = 2.42, 95% CI [1.75, 3.35]. Older patients had a slightly higher rate, HR = 1.18 per 10 years, 95% CI [1.00, 1.39], but a lower cumulative incidence, subdistribution HR = 0.84, 95% CI [0.76, 0.94], because of their higher mortality (Table 1).

Note. N = 1,373. Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Points to remember:

Never report one minus Kaplan–Meier as a risk when there are competing events.
Report the numbers of all the events.
Give the cause-specific hazard ratios of all the events.
Call Fine–Gray ratios subdistribution hazard ratios, and use them for risk, not for causes.

title: Competing Risks (Fine–Gray): Will It Be Cancer, or Something Else First?
text:
10. Summary



When
A first event of several kinds, where one prevents the others


Describe with
Cumulative incidence: survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1), with event a factor whose first level is censoring


Not with
1 − Kaplan–Meier (too high)


Rates
Cause-specific Cox models, one per event


Risks
Fine–Gray: finegray() + coxph(..., weights = fgwt), or cmprsk::crr()


They differ when
A predictor acts on the competing event


Predicted risk
From all the cause-specific models together, or from Fine–Gray


Related pages
Cox, Weibull and AFT

title: Beta Regression: How Closely Did the Brexit Vote Follow Education?
text:
In June 2016 the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, with 52% for Leave. But the country was divided. In some districts three quarters voted Leave, in others one fifth. What kind of districts were they? Education is the best-known answer: the more people with a degree, the fewer votes for Leave. How close is the relation, and what is left for age and for the share of people born abroad?
The outcome is a share, a number between 0 and 1. Ordinary regression has three problems with it. Its straight line leaves the range from 0 to 1 sooner or later. Its errors are supposed to have the same spread everywhere, but shares near 0 or 1 have no room to vary. And near the limits the distribution is skewed.
Beta regression (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004) is the regression for shares, rates and proportions that are not counts of yes and no: the share of income spent on food, the share of a leaf that is ill, a test score as a fraction of the maximum, an election result.


Code
library(betareg)    # betareg()
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL(): standard errors for districts of the same region

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

text:
1. The data
The Electoral Commission publishes the result of every district. The 2011 census, through the service Nomis of the Office for National Statistics, has their people. Both are free and need no login:


Code
votes <- read.csv(
  "https://www.electoralcommission.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-07/EU-referendum-result-data.csv"
)
census <- function(table, cells) {

    "https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/api/v01/dataset/",
    table,
    ".data.csv?date=latest&geography=TYPE464",

    cells,
    "&measures=20301&select=geography_code,cell,obs_value"
  ))
  aggregate(OBS_VALUE ~ GEOGRAPHY_CODE, data = d, FUN = sum)
}
degree <- census("NM_623_1", "6") # highest qualification: level 4 or more (degree), % of 16+
old    <- census("NM_145_1", "13,14,15,16")                         # aged 65 and over

brexit <- merge(
  votes[, c("Area_Code", "Area", "Region", "Leave", "Valid_Votes")],
  degree,
  by.x = "Area_Code",
  by.y = "GEOGRAPHY_CODE"
)
names(brexit)[6] <- "degree"
brexit$age65  <- old$OBS_VALUE[match(brexit$Area_Code, old$GEOGRAPHY_CODE)]
brexit$abroad <- 100 - uk$OBS_VALUE[match(brexit$Area_Code, uk$GEOGRAPHY_CODE)]
brexit$leave  <- brexit$Leave / brexit$Valid_Votes

title: Beta Regression: How Closely Did the Brexit Vote Follow Education?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the beta distribution
A beta variable lies between 0 and 1. Written with its mean \(\mu\) and a precision \(\phi\):
\[E(y) = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(y) = \frac{\mu(1 - \mu)}{1 + \phi}\]
The variance is largest in the middle, and goes to zero at 0 and 1. The larger \(\phi\), the less the values scatter around the mean.


Code
grid <- seq(0.002, 0.998, by = 0.002)
shapes <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.85), function(mu) {
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(c(5, 20, 80), function(phi) {
        data.frame(
          y = grid,
          d = dbeta(grid, mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi),
          mean = paste("mean", mu),
          precision = paste0("φ = ", phi)
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
shapes$precision <- factor(shapes$precision, levels = paste0("φ = ", c(5, 20, 80)))
ggplot(shapes, aes(y, d, colour = precision)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~mean) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#2a78d6", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Beta distributions", x = "y", y = "density") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Step 2: the mean depends on predictors, through a link
As in logistic regression, the logit keeps the mean between 0 and 1:
\[\log\frac{\mu_i}{1 - \mu_i} = x_i^\top\beta\]
\(e^{\beta}\) is an odds ratio for the mean share. The word “odds” is used as for probabilities: a share of 60% has odds of 60/40 = 1.5.


Step 3: the precision may depend on predictors, too
\[\log \phi_i = z_i^\top\gamma\]
The simplest model has one \(\phi\) for all. Modelling it lets some districts scatter more than others.


Step 4: maximum likelihood, by hand
The density is \(\frac{\Gamma(\phi)}{\Gamma(\mu\phi)\,\Gamma((1-\mu)\phi)}\, y^{\mu\phi - 1}(1 - y)^{(1-\mu)\phi - 1}\), which R knows as dbeta(y, mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi):


Code
brexit$deg10 <- (brexit$degree - 27) / 10
brexit$old10 <- (brexit$age65 - 17) / 10
brexit$abr10 <- (brexit$abroad - 10) / 10 # per 10 points
X <- model.matrix(~ deg10 + old10 + abr10, data = brexit); y <- brexit$leave
minus_loglik <- function(par) {
  mu <- plogis(drop(X %*% par[1:4])); phi <- exp(par[5])
  -sum(dbeta(y, mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi, log = TRUE))
}
hand <- optim(
  c(0, 0, 0, 0, 4),

6. Against the alternatives


Code
ols   <- lm(leave ~ deg10 + old10 + abr10, data = brexit)
logit <- lm(qlogis(leave) ~ deg10 + old10 + abr10, data = brexit)
binom <- glm(
  cbind(Leave, Valid_Votes - Leave) ~ deg10 + old10 + abr10,
  family = binomial,
  data = brexit
)
quasi <- glm(
  cbind(Leave, Valid_Votes - Leave) ~ deg10 + old10 + abr10,
  family = quasibinomial,
  data = brexit
)
effects <- rbind(`beta regression`       = c(coef(fit)["deg10"], sqrt(vcov(fit)["deg10", "deg10"])),
                 `OLS on the logit`      = coef(summary(logit))["deg10", 1:2],
                 `binomial (wrong)`      = coef(summary(binom))["deg10", 1:2],
                 `quasi-binomial`        = coef(summary(quasi))["deg10", 1:2])
colnames(effects) <- c("b (logit scale)", "SE")
round(effects, 4)


                 b (logit scale)     SE
beta regression          -0.4313 0.0147
OLS on the logit         -0.4301 0.0147
binomial (wrong)         -0.4395 0.0006
quasi-binomial           -0.4395 0.0155


Code
c(OLS_effect_in_points = 100 * coef(ols)[["deg10"]], beta_effect_in_points = 100 * ame[["deg10"]])


 OLS_effect_in_points beta_effect_in_points 
            -10.22701             -10.35527 


Code
dispersion <- summary(quasi)$dispersion
dispersion


[1] 641.9004



OLS on the share gives -10.2 points for 10 points of degrees, and the beta regression -10.4 on average. Between 30% and 70% a logit is almost straight, so the two agree. With shares near 0 or 1 they would not.
OLS on the logit of the share agrees with the beta regression here. It describes the mean of the logit, not the logit of the mean, and to come back to shares it needs a correction, like the smearing of gamma regression.
Binomial regression treats every voter as an independent observation. With millions of votes its standard error is 24.0 times smaller than that of the beta regression, and it is nonsense: the dispersion is 642 instead of 1. Voters of one district share their district.
Quasi-binomial corrects the standard errors by this factor, and gives the larger districts more weight. It is a good alternative when the numerator and the denominator are known. Its variance, \(\mu(1-\mu)\phi/n\), shrinks with the number of voters, while the beta regression gives every district the same precision.

Which is right? The chance variation of 86,386 votes is tiny. What makes districts differ is everything that the model does not contain. That does not shrink with the size, which speaks for the beta regression.

title: Beta Regression: How Closely Did the Brexit Vote Follow Education?
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

The ecological fallacy. The rows are districts, not people. That districts with more graduates voted less for Leave does not prove that graduates did. (Surveys of voters show that they did, but this page cannot.) Robinson (1950) is the classic warning.
Exactly 0 or 1 has no place in a beta distribution. A common fix is \((y(n - 1) + 0.5)/n\) (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006); better is a model with extra parts for the zeros and ones (zero-or-one-inflated beta), or the extended-support versions in recent versions of betareg.
Is it a share of a whole that was counted? With successes out of a small known number of trials, use binomial or beta-binomial regression. The beta regression is for shares without a meaningful number of trials, or with a number so large that it does not matter.
Several shares that add up to 1 (votes for five parties) need Dirichlet regression, or log-ratios.
Scales. Scores of a questionnaire divided by their range are a frequent use (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006). Remember that the units are then “share of the range”.
Links. The logit is the default. Others can be compared by AIC: link = "loglog" etc.
The precision is part of the model. A wrong model for it makes the standard errors wrong. Use sandwich errors (vcov = sandwich) if in doubt.

title: Beta Regression: How Closely Did the Brexit Vote Follow Education?
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its range, the links of the mean and of the precision, odds ratios or effects in points with intervals, the precision, and the unit of analysis. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
sm  <- summary(fit_phi)$coefficients$mean; cim <- confint(fit_phi)
ame2 <- sm[-1, 1] * mean(fitted(fit_phi) * (1 - fitted(fit_phi)))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Intercept", "Degree (10 points)", "Aged 65+ (10 points)", "Born abroad (10 points)"
  ),
  b = f3(sm[, 1]),
  SE = f3(sm[, 2]),
  z = f2(sm[, 3]),
  p = sapply(sm[, 4], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  OR = paste0(f2(exp(sm[, 1])), " [", f2(exp(cim[1:4, 1])), ", ", f2(exp(cim[1:4, 2])), "]"),
  ame = c("—", f1(100 * ame2))
)


Method (data analysis):

The share of valid votes for Leave in the 2016 referendum in the 348 districts of England and Wales (Electoral Commission, 2019) was analysed with beta regression (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004), with a logit link for the mean and a log link for the precision. Predictors of the mean were the percentages of residents with a degree-level qualification, aged 65 and over, and born outside the United Kingdom (2011 census; Office for National Statistics, 2013), centred and in units of 10 percentage points; the precision depended on the first and the third. Models were compared with likelihood-ratio tests. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package betareg (Cribari-Neto & Zeileis, 2010).

Results:

The share of Leave votes ranged from 21.4% to 75.6% (M = 54.4%). Districts with more graduates voted less for Leave, OR = 0.65 per 10 points, 95% CI [0.64, 0.67], p < .001, on average 10.2 percentage points (Table 1). The scatter around the mean differed between districts, χ²(2) = 10.0, p = .007. Adding the regions improved the model, χ²(9) = 95.2, p < .001, so the districts are not independent and the standard errors are too small. The results concern districts and not individual voters.

title: Beta Regression: How Closely Did the Brexit Vote Follow Education?
text:
11. Summary



When
The outcome is a continuous share between 0 and 1 (not 0 or 1 exactly)


The model
\(y \sim \text{Beta}\) with mean \(\mu\) and precision \(\phi\); \(\text{logit}(\mu) = x^\top\beta\)


Variance
\(\mu(1 - \mu)/(1 + \phi)\)


How (R)
betareg(y ~ x1 + x2 | z, data): after the bar, the precision


Reading it
\(e^\beta\): odds ratio of the mean share; better, average marginal effects


Alternatives
OLS (shares in the middle), quasi-binomial (counts known), zero-or-one-inflated beta


Checks
Quantile residuals, precision, groups of rows


Related pages
Generalized linear models, gamma regression, probit

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
On 31 January 1983 wearing a seat belt became compulsory for drivers and front-seat passengers in Great Britain. Did it save lives? The government asked two statisticians to find out (Harvey & Durbin, 1986).
There is no control group. The law came for everybody on the same day. All there is are the numbers of casualties, month by month, for years before and two years after. The question is whether the series stepped down at the date of the law, by more than its usual ups and downs.
A regression with a dummy variable for “after the law” seems to do it. But months that follow each other are not independent: a bad autumn affects several months, the economy goes in waves, and every December is worse than every June. Ordinary least squares takes neighbouring months for new information, and its standard errors are wrong.
Regression with ARIMA errors (often called ARIMAX) has two parts: a regression for what we want to know, and an ARIMA model for how the rest moves over time. Used for a question like this, it is called interrupted time series or intervention analysis (Box & Tiao, 1975).


Code
library(forecast)   # Arima(), auto.arima(), forecast()
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

The data come with R, as the time series Seatbelts: 192 months, from January 1969 to December 1984.

y <- log(Seatbelts[, "drivers"]) # log of the car drivers killed or seriously injured

                192                  23 


drivers is the number of car drivers killed or seriously injured in the month, rear the same for rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern. kms is the distance driven, PetrolPrice the price of petrol, and law is 1 from February 1983. We take logarithms: effects on casualties are percentages, and a seasonal swing that grows with the level becomes constant.

section: 3. Why least squares is not enough
text:
3. Why least squares is not enough


Code
month <- factor(cycle(y))
ols <- lm(y ~ X[, "law"] + X[, "petrol"] + X[, "km"] + month)
round(coef(summary(ols))[2:4, ], 3)


              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
X[, "law"]      -0.161      0.023  -7.121    0.000
X[, "petrol"]   -0.403      0.057  -7.111    0.000
X[, "km"]       -0.157      0.046  -3.427    0.001


Code
r_acf <- acf(resid(ols), plot = FALSE, lag.max = 24)$acf[-1]
round(r_acf[1:12], 2)


 [1] 0.45 0.38 0.26 0.20 0.27 0.21 0.18 0.09 0.16 0.10 0.20 0.20


Code
lb_ols <- Box.test(resid(ols), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box"); lb_ols$p.value


[1] 0


With a dummy for each month of the year, OLS finds an effect of the law of -0.16 on the log scale. But the residuals correlate with those of the next month at 0.45, and with those of two months later at 0.38. The Ljung–Box test of the first 24 autocorrelations has p < .001. The standard errors are too small, and they cannot be repaired by a formula that does not know how the series moves.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
section: 4. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
4. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: regression with errors that remember
\[y_t = \beta_1\,\text{law}_t + \beta_2\,\text{petrol}_t + \beta_3\,\text{km}_t + n_t\]
\(n_t\) is everything else, and it follows a time-series model. The \(\beta\)’s have their usual meaning.


Step 2: ARIMA, three ingredients

AR(p): today’s value depends on the last ones, \(n_t = \phi_1 n_{t-1} + \dots + e_t\).
MA(q): today’s value depends on the last shocks, \(n_t = e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \dots\).
I(d): the series is differenced \(d\) times to remove a drift, \(n_t - n_{t-1}\).



Step 3: the season
The same three for the same month of last year, with capital letters: ARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12}\). A seasonal difference (\(D = 1\)), \(n_t - n_{t-12}\), compares each month with the same month a year ago. It removes the yearly wave even if it changes slowly. When the errors are differenced, the regression is too: the law is compared as a change.


Step 4: what the estimate does
With AR(1) errors, the likelihood is that of the regression on quasi-differenced data, \(y_t - \phi y_{t-1}\) against \(x_t - \phi x_{t-1}\) (see generalized least squares). The new information of each month is only what the last month did not already say. By hand, for AR(1) errors and month dummies:


Code
months <- model.matrix(~ month)[, -1]; Xm <- matrix(X, ncol = 3, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(X)))
Z  <- cbind(months, Xm); XX <- cbind(1, Z); n <- length(y)
profile_ll <- function(phi) {
  # exact likelihood for a given phi (Prais-Winsten)
  q <- function(v) c(sqrt(1 - phi^2) * v[1], v[-1] - phi * v[-n])
  f <- lm.fit(apply(XX, 2, q), q(as.numeric(y)))
  s2 <- mean(f$residuals^2)
  -n / 2 * (log(2 * pi * s2) + 1) + 0.5 * log(1 - phi^2)
}
phi_hat <- optimize(profile_ll, c(-0.99, 0.99), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
q <- function(v) c(sqrt(1 - phi_hat^2) * v[1], v[-1] - phi_hat * v[-n])
hand <- setNames(
  lm.fit(apply(XX, 2, q), q(as.numeric(y)))$coefficients,
  c("(Intercept)", colnames(Z))
)
ar1 <- arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = Z, method = "ML")
rbind(
  by_hand = c(phi = phi_hat, hand[c("law", "petrol", "km")]),
  arima = coef(ar1)[c("ar1", "law", "petrol", "km")]
)


             phi        law     petrol         km
by_hand 0.452686 -0.1731235 -0.3780838 -0.1324072
arima   0.452697 -0.1731300 -0.3780785 -0.1324141

text:
5. Choosing the order


Code
# searches over the orders, with the AICc
auto <- auto.arima(y, xreg = X, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
auto


Series: y 
Regression with ARIMA(1,0,3)(0,1,1)[12] errors 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1     ma2      ma3     sma1      law   petrol      km
      0.9818  -0.7106  0.0566  -0.1851  -0.8536  -0.2219  -0.3083  0.1077
s.e.  0.0184   0.0753  0.0982   0.0815   0.0789   0.0419   0.0946  0.1187

sigma^2 = 0.005586:  log likelihood = 208.25
AIC=-398.49   AICc=-397.43   BIC=-369.75


Code
candidates <- list(
  `(1,0,0)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 0),
  `(1,0,1)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 1),
  `(2,0,1)(0,1,1)` = c(2, 0, 1),
  `(0,1,1)(0,1,1)` = c(0, 1, 1),
  `(1,0,3)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 3)
)
fits <- lapply(candidates, function(o) Arima(y, order = o, seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), xreg = X))
comp <- t(sapply(fits, function(m) {
  c(
    AICc = m$aicc,
    law = coef(m)[["law"]],
    SE = sqrt(vcov(m)["law", "law"]),
    Ljung_Box_p = Box.test(resid(m), 24, fitdf = length(coef(m)) - 3, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
  )
}))
round(comp, 3)


                   AICc    law    SE Ljung_Box_p
(1,0,0)(0,1,1) -381.611 -0.175 0.034       0.000
(1,0,1)(0,1,1) -395.050 -0.224 0.049       0.012
(2,0,1)(0,1,1) -395.573 -0.223 0.042       0.006
(0,1,1)(0,1,1) -389.272 -0.244 0.047       0.005
(1,0,3)(0,1,1) -397.432 -0.222 0.042       0.038


auto.arima() chooses the smallest AICc among many models. (AICs can only be compared between models with the same differences: the one with \(d = 1\) is in another league.) What matters more than the winner is the column law: whatever the order, the effect is between -0.24 and -0.18. The OLS estimate of -0.16 was smaller, probably because the month dummies and the straight regression could not follow the slow drifts. We take the winner.


Code
fit <- auto
b <- coef(fit)[c("law", "petrol", "km")]; se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[c("law", "petrol", "km")]
tab <- cbind(b, SE = se, z = b / se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(b / se)), effect = exp(b) - 1)
round(tab, 4)


             b     SE       z      p  effect
law    -0.2219 0.0419 -5.2909 0.0000 -0.1990
petrol -0.3083 0.0946 -3.2602 0.0011 -0.2653
km      0.1077 0.1187  0.9069 0.3645  0.1137


Code
ci <- exp(b[["law"]] + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se[["law"]]) - 1



law = -0.222: the number of drivers killed or seriously injured was \(e^{-0.222}\) = 0.80 times what it would have been, a fall of 20%, 95% CI [13%, 26%].
petrol = -0.31: 10% higher petrol prices go with about 2.9% fewer casualties, with the distance held constant.
km is not clearly different from zero once the season and the memory are in the model.
The first coefficients (ar1, ma1, …, sma1) describe the memory. They are not effects, and nobody reports them one by one.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
6. Checking the model
If the model is right, the residuals are white noise: no pattern left.


Code
res <- data.frame(date = road$date, r = as.numeric(resid(fit)))[-(1:13), ]
a <- acf(res$r, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 24)
pa <- ggplot(res, aes(date, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Residuals", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
pb <- ggplot(data.frame(lag = a$lag[-1], r = a$acf[-1]), aes(lag, r)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(res)),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Their autocorrelations", x = "lag (months)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)









Code
lb <- Box.test(resid(fit), lag = 24, fitdf = length(coef(fit)) - 3, type = "Ljung-Box")
c(Ljung_Box = lb$statistic, p = lb$p.value, Shapiro_p = shapiro.test(res$r)$p.value)


Ljung_Box.X-squared                   p           Shapiro_p 
        31.26106668          0.03778711          0.26997021 


The Ljung–Box test has p = .038, so the residuals are not perfectly white: two or three autocorrelations at long lags (18 and 22 months) lie just outside the dashed limits, where one in twenty does by chance. Compared with the OLS residuals, nearly all of the memory is in the model. The other orders of the table do no better, and the effect of the law is nearly the same in all of them.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
7. The world without the law
Fit the model to the months before the law only, and let it forecast the two years after, with the petrol prices and distances that really occurred:


Code
last   <- c(1983, 1)
y_pre  <- window(y, end = last)
X_pre <- window(X[, c("petrol", "km")], end = last)
X_post <- window(X[, c("petrol", "km")], start = c(1983, 2))
pre    <- Arima(y_pre, order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3], seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6], xreg = X_pre)
fc     <- forecast(pre, xreg = X_post, level = 95)
post   <- subset(road, law == 1)
cf <- data.frame(
  date = post$date,
  observed = post$drivers,
  expected = exp(as.numeric(fc$mean)),
  low = exp(as.numeric(fc$lower)),
  high = exp(as.numeric(fc$upper))
)
saved  <- sum(cf$expected - cf$observed)
c(
  observed = sum(cf$observed),
  expected = sum(cf$expected),
  difference = saved,
  share = saved / sum(cf$expected)
)


    observed     expected   difference        share 
3.039900e+04 3.697005e+04 6.571046e+03 1.777397e-01 


Code
below <- mean(cf$observed < cf$low)
below


[1] 0.5652174




Code
ggplot(subset(road, date >= 1978), aes(date, drivers)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = cf,
    aes(date, ymin = low, ymax = high),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2a78d6",
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = cf, aes(date, expected), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1983 + 1 / 12, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#eb6834") +
  labs(
    title = "Observed (grey), and forecast from the years before the law (blue, 95% band)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "drivers killed or seriously injured"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))









In the 23 months the forecast expected 36,970 casualties, and 30,399 happened: 6,571 fewer, or 18%. In 57% of the months the number was below the 95% band.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
8. Attacks on the result

A control: the rear seats
If the fall came from better weather, better roads or less traffic, the rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern, would have profited too:


Code
y_rear <- log(Seatbelts[, "rear"]); y_front <- log(Seatbelts[, "front"])
same_order <- function(v) {
  Arima(v, order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3], seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6], xreg = X)
}
rear  <- same_order(y_rear); front <- same_order(y_front)
eff <- function(m) {
  bb <- coef(m)[["law"]]
  s <- sqrt(vcov(m)["law", "law"])
  100 * c(effect = exp(bb) - 1, low = exp(bb - 1.96 * s) - 1, high = exp(bb + 1.96 * s) - 1)
}
controls <- rbind(
  drivers = eff(fit),
  `front-seat passengers` = eff(front),
  `rear-seat passengers` = eff(rear)
)
round(controls, 1)


                      effect   low  high
drivers                -19.9 -26.2 -13.0
front-seat passengers  -28.1 -34.6 -21.1
rear-seat passengers     2.5  -7.3  13.4


The effect in percent: drivers -20, front-seat passengers -28, rear-seat passengers 3, 95% CI [-7, 13]. Those whom the law did not concern saw no change that can be told from zero.


Placebo laws
Pretend that the law came at other dates, in the years before it existed, and estimate the “effect” each time:


Code
dates <- seq(1971, 1981, by = 0.5)
placebo <- sapply(dates, function(d) {
  fake <- as.numeric(time(y_pre) >= d)
  m <- try(
    Arima(
      y_pre,
      order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3],
      seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6],
      xreg = cbind(law = fake, X_pre)
    ),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  if (inherits(m, "try-error")) NA else coef(m)[["law"]]
})
pl <- data.frame(
  date = c(dates, 1983.08),
  b = c(placebo, b[["law"]]),
  kind = c(rep("invented dates", length(dates)), "the real law")
)
ggplot(pl, aes(date, 100 * (exp(b) - 1), fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey65", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "The 'effect' of invented laws, and of the real one",
    x = NULL,
    y = "change of casualties (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
larger <- sum(placebo <= b[["law"]], na.rm = TRUE)
c(placebos = sum(!is.na(placebo)), as_large_as_the_law = larger)


           placebos as_large_as_the_law 
                 21                   0 


None of the invented dates should give much. A group of them does: those of the middle of the 1970s, after the oil crisis of the winter of 1973–74 had brought speed limits and empty roads. But 0 of the 21 invented dates gave a fall as large as the law’s. The method finds any step, whatever its cause. That the step of February 1983 is the law, and not something else that happened at the same time, is an argument from outside the model, and the rear seats are its best support.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

Two models share the name ARIMAX. Regression with ARIMA errors (here, and in arima(xreg = )) has coefficients with the usual meaning. Models with lags of \(y\) next to \(x\) (transfer functions) have not: there \(\beta\) is only the immediate effect.
Spurious regression. Two unrelated series that drift will correlate. Two random walks:



Code
set.seed(131)
spur <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- cumsum(rnorm(100))
  b <- cumsum(rnorm(100))
  c(
    levels = summary(lm(a ~ b))$coefficients[2, 4] < .05,
    differences = summary(lm(diff(a) ~ diff(b)))$coefficients[2, 4] < .05
  )
})
rowMeans(spur)


     levels differences 
      0.752       0.050 



OLS finds a “significant” relation between two independent random walks in 75% of the cases; after differencing, in 5%. With series that drift, difference or model the drift.
Shape of the effect. We assumed a sudden, permanent step. A law may work slowly, fade, or change the slope. Think first; a step is only the simplest shape.
Few points after the change make it hard to tell a step from the beginning of something else.
Anticipation. People may change before the date. Here many put on their belts in January 1983.
Covariates must not be changed by the intervention, and for forecasts their future values must be known.
Counts. These are large, so logs of them are fine. For small counts use time-series models for counts.
Structural models (level, slope and season that evolve) are the alternative that Harvey and Durbin used. They found a similar effect.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the series and its length, the transformation, the order of the ARIMA model and how it was chosen, the checks, the effect with its interval, and the evidence that it is the intervention. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Seat belt law", "Petrol price (log)", "Distance driven (log)"),
  b = f3(tab[, "b"]),
  SE = f3(tab[, "SE"]),
  z = f2(tab[, "z"]),
  p = sapply(tab[, "p"], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  CI = paste0("[", f3(b - 1.96 * se), ", ", f3(b + 1.96 * se), "]")
)
order_text <- paste0(
  "ARIMA(",
  paste(arimaorder(fit)[1:3], collapse = ","),
  ")(",
  paste(arimaorder(fit)[4:6], collapse = ","),
  ")"
)


Method (data analysis):

The monthly number of car drivers killed or seriously injured in Great Britain, January 1969–December 1984 (192 months; Harvey & Durbin, 1986), was analysed on the log scale with a regression with ARIMA errors (interrupted time series; Schaffer et al., 2021). The seat belt law was coded as a step from February 1983; the log petrol price and the log distance driven were covariates. The order of the ARIMA model was chosen with the corrected AIC (Hyndman & Khandakar, 2008); residuals were checked with the Ljung–Box test. As controls we analysed front- and rear-seat passengers, invented dates before the law, and the forecast of the period after the law from the period before it. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package forecast.

Results:

The selected model was ARIMA(1,0,3)(0,1,1)12; its residuals showed little autocorrelation, Ljung–Box Q(24) = 31.3, p = .038. The law was followed by a fall of 20% in the number of drivers killed or seriously injured, b = -0.222, SE = 0.042, 95% CI for the change [-26%, -13%] (Table 1). The forecast from the years before the law expected 6,571 more casualties in 23 months than were observed (18%). For rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern, the change was 3%, 95% CI [-7%, 13%].

Points to remember:

Say what shape of effect was assumed (step, slope, pulse) and that it was chosen beforehand.
Report the order, the selection and the residual check, and how the effect changes with other orders.
Give the effect in percent, with an interval.
Show a control series or placebo dates.

title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
text:
11. Summary



When
One long time series, predictors or an intervention, and errors that remember


The model
\(y_t = x_t^\top\beta + n_t\), with \(n_t\) an ARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s\) process


How (R)
forecast::auto.arima(y, xreg = X), or arima(y, order, seasonal, xreg)


Choosing
AICc (same differences), then white-noise residuals


Reading it
\(\beta\) as in any regression; on logs, \(e^\beta - 1\) is a percentage


Checks
ACF of the residuals, Ljung–Box


For interventions
Forecast without the intervention, control series, placebo dates


Danger
Spurious regression of drifting series


Related pages
Generalized least squares, panel data

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
text:
When the economy grows, the party in the White House is said to win the next election. Douglas Hibbs (2000) made a model of it, “bread and peace”: the growth of personal income during the term predicts the vote. How strong is the connection, and what does it say about an election in which growth is 2%?
There is a difficulty: there have been few elections. With 16 rows an ordinary regression gives a line and a wide interval, and nothing else. A Bayesian regression does two things more.

It starts with a prior: a distribution that says what we consider possible before we see the data. (A growth of 1% does not move the vote by 40 points.) The data then change the prior into the posterior.
Its answers are probabilities of the things we want to know: the probability that the slope is above 2, or that the party keeps the White House. An ordinary confidence interval does not say that, although everybody reads it that way.

The price is that one has to state the prior, and to say what happens with another. This page writes everything by hand, and gets the same numbers from the package rstanarm.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(rstanarm)    # stan_glm(): Bayesian regression with Stan behind it
# also used, with package::function: loo (loo, loo_compare), posterior (rhat, ess_bulk)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
# a probability from draws is never exactly 1
ptop <- function(p) if (p > 0.999) "over 99.9%" else pct(p, 1)
# APA: no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: Bayes’ rule
\[\underbrace{p(\theta \mid y)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(y \mid \theta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}}, \qquad y_i \sim N(\alpha + \beta\,(x_i - \bar x),\ \sigma^2)\]
The likelihood says how well values of the parameters explain the data. Multiplied with the prior, it gives the probability of the values after seeing the data. The sign \(\propto\) means “up to a constant that makes the total 1”.


Step 2: one parameter on a grid
To see how it works, pretend that \(\alpha\) and \(\sigma\) are known (the values of least squares), so that only the slope \(\beta\) is unknown. Take a prior that is sceptical: a normal distribution around 0 with SD 1. Compute the three curves at many values of \(\beta\):


Code
beta_grid <- seq(-3, 6, length.out = 400); a_hat <- mean(y); s_hat <- sigma(ls_fit)
prior_d <- dnorm(beta_grid, 0, 1)
lik <- exp(sapply(beta_grid, function(b) sum(dnorm(y, a_hat + b * xc, s_hat, log = TRUE))))
lik <- lik / sum(lik) / diff(beta_grid[1:2])
post_d  <- prior_d * lik; post_d <- post_d / sum(post_d) / diff(beta_grid[1:2])
gd <- data.frame(
  beta = rep(beta_grid, 3),
  density = c(prior_d, lik, post_d),
  curve = factor(
    rep(c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"), each = 400),
    levels = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior")
  )
)
ggplot(gd, aes(beta, density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#1baf7a", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "A sceptical prior, the data, and the result",
    x = "slope: points of the vote per 1% of growth",
    y = "density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
prec <- c(prior = 1, data = sum(xc^2) / s_hat^2)
c(
  mean_of_the_posterior_on_the_grid = sum(beta_grid * post_d) * diff(beta_grid[1:2]),
  precision_weighted_mean = sum(prec * c(0, coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]])) / sum(prec)
)


mean_of_the_posterior_on_the_grid           precision_weighted_mean 
                         2.061243                          2.061243 


The posterior lies between the prior and the data. For normal distributions its mean is the mean of the two, weighted with their precision (1/variance):
\[E(\beta \mid y) = \frac{\text{prec}_{\text{prior}} \cdot \text{prior mean} + \text{prec}_{\text{data}} \cdot \hat\beta}{\text{prec}_{\text{prior}} + \text{prec}_{\text{data}}}\]
The data weigh 2.1 here, the prior 1. So this prior counts as much as 7.8 further elections would, next to the 16 that we have.


Step 3: the whole model in closed form
For the linear model there is a prior with which everything can be computed with a formula: the normal–inverse-gamma prior, \(\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(m_0, \sigma^2 V_0)\), \(\sigma^2 \sim IG(a_0, b_0)\). The posterior is of the same kind, with
\[V_n = (V_0^{-1} + X^\top X)^{-1}, \qquad m_n = V_n(V_0^{-1}m_0 + X^\top y),\]
\[a_n = a_0 + \tfrac n2, \qquad b_n = b_0 + \tfrac12\left(y^\top y + m_0^\top V_0^{-1}m_0 - m_n^\top V_n^{-1}m_n\right)\]
and each coefficient has a t distribution with \(2a_n\) degrees of freedom. With \(V_0^{-1} \to 0\), \(a_0 = -p/2\) and \(b_0 = 0\) (a flat prior) one gets the numbers of least squares:


Code
nig <- function(X, y, m0, V0inv, a0, b0) {
  Vn <- solve(V0inv + crossprod(X))
  mn <- drop(Vn %*% (V0inv %*% m0 + crossprod(X, y)))
  an <- a0 + length(y) / 2
  bn <- b0 + (sum(y^2) + drop(t(m0) %*% V0inv %*% m0) - drop(t(mn) %*% solve(Vn, mn))) / 2
  data.frame(
    mean = mn,
    low = mn - qt(0.975, 2 * an) * sqrt(bn / an * diag(Vn)),
    high = mn + qt(0.975, 2 * an) * sqrt(bn / an * diag(Vn))
  )
}
X <- cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, growth = xc)
rbind(
  flat_prior_by_hand = nig(X, y, c(0, 0), diag(0, 2), -1, 0)["growth", ],
  least_squares = c(coef(ls_fit)["growth"], confint(ls_fit)["growth", ])
)


                       mean      low     high
flat_prior_by_hand 3.060528 1.567169 4.553887
least_squares      3.060528 1.567169 4.553887


With a flat prior the 95% credible interval is the 95% confidence interval. The numbers are the same, and what one may say about them is different.


Step 4: sampling
For most models there is no formula. Then one draws from the posterior. The oldest method (Metropolis et al., 1953) is a walk: propose a small random step; if the posterior is higher there, go; if it is lower, go with a probability equal to the ratio. The places visited are draws from the posterior, after a while. The constant in Bayes’ rule cancels in the ratio, so nobody needs to know it.
The priors (for the centred predictor):

\(\alpha \sim N(50, 5)\): with average growth the incumbent party gets about half of the votes, very probably between 40 and 60.
\(\beta \sim N(0, 5)\): 1% of growth changes the vote by less than 10 points, in an unknown direction. That is a weak statement, which is only to keep out absurd values.
\(\sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1/5)\): elections deviate from the line by a few points, 5 on average.



Code
log_posterior <- function(th, yy = y, xx = xc, prior_b = c(0, 5), t_errors = FALSE) {
  # th = (alpha, beta, log sigma)
  s <- exp(th[3])
  mu <- th[1] + th[2] * xx
  loglik <- if (t_errors) {
    sum(dt((yy - mu) / s, 4, log = TRUE) - log(s))
  } else {
    sum(dnorm(yy, mu, s, log = TRUE))
  }
  loglik +
    dnorm(th[1], 50, 5, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(th[2], prior_b[1], prior_b[2], log = TRUE) +
    dexp(s, 1 / 5, log = TRUE) +
    th[3] # + th[3]: because we walk on log sigma
}
metropolis <- function(draws, start, step, logp, ...) {
  out <- matrix(0, draws, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("alpha", "beta", "sigma")))
  now <- start
  lp <- logp(now, ...)
  for (i in seq_len(draws)) {
    candidate <- now + step * rnorm(3)
    lp_new <- logp(candidate, ...)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_new - lp) {
      now <- candidate
      lp <- lp_new
    }
    out[i, ] <- now
  }
  out[, 3] <- exp(out[, 3])
  out
}
set.seed(241); steps <- c(1.3, 1, 0.3); warm <- 2000; keep <- 20000
chains <- lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  metropolis(
    warm + keep,
    c(rnorm(1, 50, 8), rnorm(1, 0, 8), log(4) + rnorm(1)),
    steps,
    log_posterior
  )
})
hand <- do.call(rbind, lapply(chains, function(m) m[-(1:warm), ]))
summ <- function(v) {
  c(mean = mean(v), sd = sd(v), low = quantile(v, 0.025)[[1]], high = quantile(v, 0.975)[[1]])
}
t(apply(hand, 2, summ))


           mean        sd       low      high
alpha 51.966981 0.9900795 49.980349 53.913527
beta   2.993196 0.7523957  1.499903  4.464881
sigma  4.014293 0.8194796  2.770954  5.972682


Four chains, each from a different, deliberately bad start, and the first 2,000 steps of each thrown away (warm-up).


Code
tr <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:4, function(k) {
    data.frame(i = 1:400, beta = chains[[k]][1:400, "beta"], chain = factor(k))
  })
)
ggplot(tr, aes(i, beta, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "The first 400 steps of four chains",
    subtitle = "They start in different places and meet",
    x = "step",
    y = "slope"
  ) +
  theme_bw()











Step 5: the same with a package
stan_glm() uses a much better sampler than ours (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) and the same model and priors. prior_intercept is for the centred predictor, like our \(\alpha\).


Code
fit <- stan_glm(
  vote ~ growth,
  data = hibbs,
  prior = normal(0, 5),
  prior_intercept = normal(50, 5),
  prior_aux = exponential(1 / 5),
  seed = 242,
  refresh = 0,
  iter = 10000
)
stan <- as.matrix(fit) # columns: (Intercept) at growth 0, growth, sigma
stan_tab <- rbind(
  alpha = summ(stan[, "(Intercept)"] + stan[, "growth"] * mean(hibbs$growth)),
  beta = summ(stan[, "growth"]),
  sigma = summ(stan[, "sigma"])
)
round(cbind(hand = t(apply(hand, 2, summ)), stan = stan_tab), 2)


       mean   sd   low  high  mean   sd   low  high
alpha 51.97 0.99 49.98 53.91 51.97 1.00 49.97 53.95
beta   2.99 0.75  1.50  4.46  3.00 0.75  1.50  4.50
sigma  4.01 0.82  2.77  5.97  4.00 0.82  2.76  5.90


Code
difference <- max(abs(t(apply(hand, 2, summ))[, c("mean", "sd")] - stan_tab[, c("mean", "sd")]))


(First four columns: our walk; last four: rstanarm.) They agree: the largest difference in a mean or SD is 0.02.


Did the chains arrive?
The check is the R-hat of Gelman and Rubin: the variance of all draws together, against the variance within each chain. If the chains are in different places the first is larger. By hand, with every chain cut in two halves, so that a drift within a chain also shows:
\[\hat R = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{m-1}{m}W + \frac 1m B}{W}}\]
(\(m\): length of a half; \(W\): mean of the variances within the halves; \(B\): \(m\) times the variance of the means of the halves. Values above 1.01 are suspicious; Vehtari et al., 2021, recommend a version based on ranks.)


Code
halves <- function(cs) {
  do.call(
    cbind,
    lapply(cs, function(v) {
      m <- length(v) / 2
      cbind(v[1:m], v[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
    })
  )
}
rhat_hand <- function(cs) {
  h <- halves(cs)
  m <- nrow(h)
  W <- mean(apply(h, 2, var))
  B <- m * var(colMeans(h))
  sqrt(((m - 1) / m * W + B / m) / W)
}
get <- function(p) lapply(chains, function(m) m[-(1:warm), p])
diag_tab <- sapply(c("alpha", "beta", "sigma"), function(p) {
  c(
    R_hat_by_hand = rhat_hand(get(p)),
    R_hat_rank = posterior::rhat(do.call(cbind, get(p))),
    effective_draws = posterior::ess_bulk(do.call(cbind, get(p)))
  )
})
round(diag_tab, 4)


                    alpha      beta     sigma
R_hat_by_hand      1.0004    1.0005    1.0002
R_hat_rank         1.0004    1.0005    1.0002
effective_draws 6597.7163 6964.2780 7363.7930


Code
rhat_first <- rhat_hand(lapply(chains, function(m) m[1:100, "beta"]))
c(R_hat_of_the_first_100_steps = rhat_first)


R_hat_of_the_first_100_steps 
                    2.307847 


Code
ess_stan <- posterior::ess_bulk(matrix(stan[, "growth"], ncol = 4))


R-hat is 1.00 for all. (With only the first 100 steps it is 2.31.) The effective number of draws tells how many independent draws the walk is worth: 6,964 out of 80,000 for the slope. rstanarm gets 16,141 out of 20,000.

Code

                 2.5%     97.5%
(Intercept) 42.794880 49.754346
growth       1.501168  4.499976
sigma        2.761800  5.904736


Code
b <- hand[, "beta"]
c(P_slope_above_0 = mean(b > 0), P_slope_above_2 = mean(b > 2), P_slope_above_4 = mean(b > 4))


P_slope_above_0 P_slope_above_2 P_slope_above_4 
      0.9995875       0.9105875       0.0857000 


The median is the middle of the posterior, the MAD_SD a robust SD. What we may say now:

The slope is probably between 1.5 and 4.5 (95% credible interval), with a mean of 3.0.
The probability that growth goes with more votes is over 99.9%. The probability that the slope is above 2 is 91%, above 4 9%.
Those are probabilities given the model and the prior. They say nothing about whether the line is a good model.


A forecast
In 2016 income was growing by about 2% (Gelman et al., 2020). The forecast for a new election uses all the uncertainty: for every draw of the parameters, draw a new vote.
\[p(y^* \mid y) = \int p(y^* \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta\]


Code
set.seed(243)
line_2 <- hand[, "alpha"] + hand[, "beta"] * (2 - mean(hibbs$growth))
vote_2 <- line_2 + rnorm(nrow(hand), 0, hand[, "sigma"])
cbind(
  value = c(
    mean = mean(vote_2),
    low = quantile(vote_2, 0.025)[[1]],
    high = quantile(vote_2, 0.975)[[1]],
    P_incumbent_party_above_50 = mean(vote_2 > 50),
    P_line_above_50 = mean(line_2 > 50)
  )
)

    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(38, 66)) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast for an election with 2% growth",
    x = "vote of the party in the White House (%)",
    y = "density"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The expected vote is 52.3%. The line is above 50 at this growth with a probability of 99%, but a single election is much less certain: the probability of more than half is 72%. (The book gets 72%.) The result of 2016 was 51.1% for the candidate of the party in the White House, close to the middle of the distribution. (Hillary Clinton had more votes and lost the election. The model is about votes.)

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
text:
5. Is the model any good?

Simulate the data that the model expects
If the model is right, data simulated from it should look like the real ones. For every tenth draw of the parameters make 16 new elections, and compare the largest deviation from the line:


Code
pick <- seq(1, nrow(hand), by = 10); set.seed(244)
biggest <- function(v) max(abs(residuals(lm.fit(X, v))))
rep_stat <- apply(hand[pick, ], 1, function(p) biggest(p[1] + p[2] * xc + rnorm(n, 0, p[3])))
obs_stat <- biggest(y)
c(observed = obs_stat, P_simulated_at_least_as_large = mean(rep_stat >= obs_stat))


                     observed P_simulated_at_least_as_large 
                     8.992915                      0.259750 


Code
ggplot(data.frame(rep_stat), aes(rep_stat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_stat, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Largest deviation from the line in simulated elections",
    subtitle = "Orange: in the real data",
    x = "points of the vote",
    y = "simulations"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









The real data have one election (1952) that is 9.0 points from the line. The model makes one at least as far in 26% of the simulations, so this alone is no reason to doubt the normal errors.


Leave one out
How well does the model predict an election that it has not seen? For every election, take it out, sample again, and compute the log density of the real result. Then the sum, called elpd. One can also get it without sampling again, from the draws (by reweighting them), which is what loo() does, in a refined version:


Code
set.seed(245)
exact <- sapply(1:n, function(i) {
  d <- metropolis(7000, c(52, 3, log(4)), steps, log_posterior, yy = y[-i], xx = xc[-i])[
    -(1:1000),
  ]
  log(mean(dnorm(y[i], d[, 1] + d[, 2] * xc[i], d[, 3])))
})
weighted <- sapply(1:n, function(i) {
  -log(mean(1 / dnorm(y[i], hand[, 1] + hand[, 2] * xc[i], hand[, 3])))
})
loo_growth <- suppressWarnings(loo(fit))
fit0 <- stan_glm(
  vote ~ 1,
  data = hibbs,
  prior_intercept = normal(50, 5),
  prior_aux = exponential(1 / 5),
  seed = 246,
  refresh = 0,
  iter = 10000
)
loo_none <- suppressWarnings(loo(fit0))
c(
  exact_by_hand = sum(exact),
  reweighting_by_hand = sum(weighted),
  loo_package = loo_growth$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"],
  without_growth = loo_none$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"]
)


      exact_by_hand reweighting_by_hand         loo_package      without_growth 
          -46.37669           -46.14305           -46.30613           -51.59044 


Code
point_diff <- loo_growth$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loo_none$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
elpd_diff <- sum(point_diff)
elpd_se <- sqrt(n) * sd(point_diff)
k_bad <- which(loo::pareto_k_values(loo_growth) > 0.7)
c(difference = elpd_diff, se = elpd_se); c(influential_elections = hibbs$year[k_bad])


difference         se 
  5.284311   3.899148 


influential_elections 
                 1952 


The three ways of computing the elpd of the model with growth agree within 0.23. Growth improves the prediction by 5.3 (SE 3.9): more than its standard error, but less than two of them. With 16 elections, even a strong connection is hard to prove in new data. The package warns that the weights are unreliable for 1952, an election with a large influence (Vehtari et al., 2017). That is what the exact version is for.


Fat tails: change the likelihood
Two elections were decided by wars. A model that expects an outlier now and then has errors with a t distribution (4 degrees of freedom). In our sampler that is a switch:


Code
set.seed(247)
robust <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:4, function(k) {
    metropolis(warm + keep, c(52, 3, log(3)), steps, log_posterior, t_errors = TRUE)[-(1:warm), ]
  })
)
rbind(`normal errors` = summ(hand[, "beta"]), `t errors, 4 df` = summ(robust[, "beta"]))


                   mean        sd      low     high
normal errors  2.993196 0.7523957 1.499903 4.464881
t errors, 4 df 3.273493 0.6106044 1.942135 4.389692


The slope is 3.27 instead of 2.99, and its SD is 0.61 instead of 0.75. The two elections of the wars do not make the result; they pull it down a little. (See robust regression.)

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
section: 6. How much does the prior matter?
text:
6. How much does the prior matter?
Six persons, six priors for the slope, the same sixteen elections:


Code
priors <- list(
  `no opinion: N(0, 50)` = c(0, 50),
  `ours: N(0, 5)` = c(0, 5),
  `careful: N(0, 2)` = c(0, 2),
  `sceptic: N(0, 0.5)` = c(0, 0.5),
  `believer: N(4, 0.5)` = c(4, 0.5),
  `contrarian: N(-2, 0.5)` = c(-2, 0.5)
)
set.seed(248)
sens <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(priors), function(p) {
    d <- metropolis(22000, c(52, 1, log(4)), steps, log_posterior, prior_b = priors[[p]])[
      -(1:2000),
      "beta"
    ]
    data.frame(
      prior = p,
      prior_mean = priors[[p]][1],
      prior_sd = priors[[p]][2],
      mean = mean(d),
      low = quantile(d, 0.025)[[1]],
      high = quantile(d, 0.975)[[1]],
      P_above_0 = mean(d > 0)
    )
  })
)
print(data.frame(prior = sens$prior, round(sens[, 4:7], 2)), row.names = FALSE)


                  prior  mean   low  high P_above_0
   no opinion: N(0, 50)  3.05  1.52  4.62      1.00
          ours: N(0, 5)  2.97  1.47  4.44      1.00
       careful: N(0, 2)  2.71  1.26  4.05      1.00
     sceptic: N(0, 0.5)  0.70 -0.29  1.61      0.92
    believer: N(4, 0.5)  3.69  2.90  4.53      1.00
 contrarian: N(-2, 0.5) -1.34 -2.36 -0.34      0.00


Code
sens$prior <- factor(sens$prior, levels = rev(sens$prior))
ggplot(sens, aes(y = prior)) +
  geom_linerange(
    aes(
      xmin = pmax(-4, prior_mean - 1.96 * prior_sd),
      xmax = pmin(7, prior_mean + 1.96 * prior_sd)
    ),
    colour = "#eda100",
    linewidth = 2.4,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean), colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior (yellow) and posterior (blue) of the slope",
    subtitle = "95% ranges, cut at -4 and 7. Dashed: least squares",
    x = "points of the vote per 1% of growth",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")









Code
se_ <- function(p, w) sens[[w]][sens$prior == p]



With the three weak priors the result is nearly the same (mean between 2.7 and 3.0).
The strong opinions stay: the sceptic moves only to 0.7, the believer ends at 3.7 and the contrarian at -1.3. A prior with an SD of 0.5 counts as much as 31 elections, twice as many as there have been in the data.
So sixteen elections are not enough to convince a person with a strong opinion in the other direction.

So the prior is a part of the result, and it is reported. A prior that comes from outside (other countries, other elections) is knowledge. A prior that is made to get a result is a cheat, and it can be seen in this plot.

Bayes factors depend on it even more
A Bayes factor compares two hypotheses, here “the slope is 0” with “the slope is something, distributed like the prior”. It asks how well each predicted the data, so a very wide prior (a slope of 80 is possible) predicts badly. With flat priors for \(\alpha\) and \(\log\sigma\), the likelihood of the slope alone has a formula, \(L(\beta) \propto \left(S + S_{xx}(\beta - \hat\beta)^2\right)^{-(n-1)/2}\), and one integral does the rest:


Code
S <- sum(residuals(ls_fit)^2); Sxx <- sum(xc^2); b_hat <- coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]]
L  <- function(b) (1 + Sxx * (b - b_hat)^2 / S)^(-(n - 1) / 2)
bf <- data.frame(prior_sd = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 20, 100, 1000))
bf$bayes_factor_for_an_effect <- sapply(bf$prior_sd, function(s) {
  integrate(function(b) L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8, rel.tol = 1e-9)$value / L(0)
})
bf$posterior_mean <- sapply(bf$prior_sd, function(s) {
  den <- integrate(function(b) L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8)$value
  integrate(function(b) b * L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8)$value / den
})
print(round(bf, 2), row.names = FALSE)


 prior_sd bayes_factor_for_an_effect posterior_mean
    5e-01                       2.75           0.70
    1e+00                      19.04           1.90
    2e+00                      79.24           2.69
    5e+00                      77.91           2.99
    2e+01                      23.36           3.06
    1e+02                       4.73           3.06
    1e+03                       0.47           3.06


From an SD of 5 to one of 1,000 the posterior of the slope hardly changes (mean 2.99 and 3.06). The Bayes factor goes from 77.9 in favour of an effect to 0.47, which is against one. A default, very wide prior makes the “no effect” win in the end, whatever the data say (the Lindley paradox). Use Bayes factors only with priors that you would defend.

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
text:
7. What “calibrated” means
A credible interval is right on average over the prior: if the true values really came from the prior, 95% of the 95% intervals contain them. It is not right for every single true value. We can check both, with the formula of step 3 (here with a narrow prior for the slope, \(\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(0, (\sigma/2)^2)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim IG(5, 60)\)):


Code
set.seed(249); V0inv <- diag(c(1 / 4, 4)); m0 <- c(50, 0); a0 <- 5; b0 <- 60
sim_once <- function(beta_fixed = NULL) {
  s2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, a0, b0)
  a <- rnorm(1, 50, sqrt(4 * s2))
  bt <- if (is.null(beta_fixed)) rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(s2 / 4)) else beta_fixed * sqrt(s2 / 4)
  r <- nig(X, a + bt * xc + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(s2)), m0, V0inv, a0, b0)["growth", ]
  r$low < bt && bt < r$high
}
cal <- c(
  `true slope drawn from the prior` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once())),
  `true slope 1 prior SD from 0` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once(1))),
  `true slope 3 prior SDs from 0` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once(3)))
)
cbind(coverage = round(cal, 3))


                                coverage
true slope drawn from the prior    0.948
true slope 1 prior SD from 0       0.949
true slope 3 prior SDs from 0      0.897


Drawn from the prior: 94.8%. For a true slope that the prior considers very unlikely (3 SDs away) it is 89.7%. A frequentist confidence interval has its 95% for every value, and does not use any knowledge. Choose what you need, and say which.

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Write down the prior before you look, in units that a reader understands. Simulate from it (a prior predictive check) and see if it expects absurd data.
Centre the predictors: then the prior of the intercept is about the outcome at average values.
Report what the result looks like with other priors, at least a wider and a narrower one.
Check R-hat and the effective draws for every parameter, and look at the trace plots. rstanarm gives warnings about divergent transitions: do not ignore them.
The posterior is conditional on the model. Check it as you would any regression: simulated data, residuals, leave-one-out.
Probabilities of hypotheses (“99% that the slope is positive”) need the prior. Do not present them as a p value.
With many rows the prior hardly matters. With few, it does, and that is exactly when it helps.
Multilevel models are where Bayesian methods shine, because they estimate variances of small groups without trouble: stan_glmer() or brms::brm(). See multilevel models.
Relatives: the normal prior is ridge regression as a probability, and a prior on functions is a Gaussian process.

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the model with the distribution of the errors, every prior, the software with the number of chains and draws, the diagnostics, the posterior (mean or median, interval), checks of the model, and how the result changes with the prior (see the guidelines of Kruschke, 2021). The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
row_of <- function(label, m, se, lo, hi) {
  data.frame(
    Parameter = label,
    mean = f2(m),
    sd = f2(se),
    ci = paste0("[", f2(lo), ", ", f2(hi), "]")
  )
}
apa_table <- rbind(
  row_of(
    "Vote at average growth (%)",
    stan_tab["alpha", "mean"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "sd"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "low"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "high"]
  ),
  row_of(
    "Growth (points of the vote per 1%)",
    stan_tab["beta", "mean"],
    stan_tab["beta", "sd"],
    stan_tab["beta", "low"],
    stan_tab["beta", "high"]
  ),
  row_of(
    "Residual SD (points)",
    stan_tab["sigma", "mean"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "sd"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "low"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "high"]
  )
)
p_pos_stan <- mean(stan[, "growth"] > 0)
max_rhat <- max(apply(stan, 2, function(v) posterior::rhat(matrix(v, ncol = 4))))


Method (data analysis):

The vote share of the party holding the White House in the 16 presidential elections from 1952 to 2012 was regressed on the growth of real personal income per head during the term (Gelman et al., 2020; Hibbs, 2000), centred at its mean, with a Bayesian linear model with normal errors. The priors were N(50, 5) for the vote share at average growth, N(0, 5) for the slope (points per 1% of growth), and Exponential(1/5) for the residual standard deviation. The posterior was sampled with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (R package rstanarm; four chains of 10,000 iterations, half of them warm-up); convergence was judged with R-hat and the effective number of draws. We report posterior means, standard deviations and 95% credible intervals, the model was checked with posterior predictive simulations and leave-one-out cross-validation (Vehtari et al., 2017), and the sensitivity to the prior of the slope was examined with six priors and with t-distributed errors. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

All chains converged (R-hat ≤ 1.000; at least 16,100 effective draws for the slope). One percentage point of growth was associated with 3.0 points more of the vote (posterior SD = 0.75, 95% credible interval [1.5, 4.5]; posterior probability of a positive slope over 99.9%; Table 1). The residual standard deviation was 4.0 points. Growth improved the expected log predictive density by 5.3 (SE = 3.9). For a growth of 2% the predicted share was 52.3% (95% prediction interval [43.9, 60.6]), with a probability of 72% of exceeding one half. The posterior mean of the slope was between 2.7 and 3.0 for weak priors and between -1.3 and 3.7 for strong ones; with t-distributed errors it was 3.3.

Points to remember:

Give every prior and the reason for it.
Report R-hat and the effective draws.
Say “credible interval”, and say that probabilities are given the model and the prior.
Show what other priors would give.

title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
text:
10. Summary



When
Few data, knowledge from outside, probabilities of the parameters and forecasts wanted, hierarchical models


The rule
Posterior \(\propto\) likelihood × prior


Linear model
Closed form (normal–inverse-gamma), or sampling


Sampling
Metropolis (by hand), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan)


How (R)
stan_glm(y ~ x, prior = normal(0, 5), prior_intercept = normal(50, 5), prior_aux = exponential(0.2))


Read
Mean or median, credible interval, probabilities, forecasts


Check
R-hat, effective draws, simulated data, leave-one-out, other priors


Danger
Strong priors with few data, Bayes factors with default priors


Related pages
Simple regression, regularized regression, multilevel models, Gaussian processes

title: Censored Quantile Regression: How Long Do People Stay Off Drugs?
text:
Two residential programmes treat people who are addicted to drugs. One is short, the other is longer. Patients were assigned to them at random. The outcome is the number of days until a patient returns to drugs. Does the longer programme keep people off drugs for longer?
For about one patient in five the time is not known. They had not returned to drugs when the study lost sight of them, so we know only that their time is longer than some value. Such times are censored.
The usual answer is a survival model, such as the Cox model, which gives one number, a hazard ratio, for the whole time. But a programme may do nothing for the patients who relapse in the first weeks, and a lot for those who hold out. One number hides that. And “the hazard is 22% lower” is hard to explain to a patient. Quantile regression answers in days: by how much does the longer programme move the median time? The time by which a quarter of the patients have relapsed? Or three quarters?
Quantile regression needs complete data. Censored quantile regression is the version for times that are only partly known.


Code
library(quantreg)   # crq(): censored quantile regression; the data are also in this package
library(survival)   # Kaplan-Meier, Weibull and Cox models (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
