title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
text:
1. The data
The experiment is in the package languageR, the companion of Baayen (2008): 21 people decided for 79 English nouns (animals and plants) whether they are words. We read it from its copy on GitHub:


Code
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rda")
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cran/languageR/master/data/lexdec.rda",
  path,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
load(path)
words <- with(
  lexdec,
  data.frame(
    subject = Subject,
    word = Word,
    rt = exp(RT), # the file has the log of the milliseconds
    correct = Correct == "correct",
    foreign = as.integer(NativeLanguage == "Other"),
    freq = Frequency - mean(Frequency),
    length = Length - mean(Length)
  )
)
c(trials = nrow(words), wrong = sum(!words$correct))


trials  wrong 
  1659     65 


Code
words <- subset(words, correct) # the usual practice: correct answers only
c(
  trials = nrow(words),
  subjects = length(unique(words$subject)),
  words = length(unique(words$word))
)


  trials subjects    words 
    1594       21       79 


Code
summary(words$rt)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  365.0   502.2   571.0   610.0   663.0  1709.0 


rt is the reaction time in milliseconds. freq is the logarithm of the frequency of the word in a large collection of texts, centred: one unit more means about 2.7 times as frequent. foreign is 1 for the participants whose native language is not English, length the number of letters, centred. There are 1,594 correct answers.

2. Look at the data

pa <- ggplot(words, aes(rt)) +

  labs(title = "Reaction times", x = "milliseconds", y = "answers") +

bysub <- aggregate(rt ~ subject + foreign, data = words, FUN = function(v) {
  c(mean = mean(v), sd = sd(v))
})
bysub <- data.frame(
  mean = bysub$rt[, "mean"],
  sd = bysub$rt[, "sd"],
  native = ifelse(bysub$foreign == 1, "other", "English")
)

  geom_point(size = 2.6) +

    values = c(English = "#2a78d6", other = "#eb6834"),

  ) +

  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)









Code
power <- coef(lm(log(sd) ~ log(mean), data = bysub))[[2]]
power


[1] 1.389799


The distribution has a long right tail, and slow people are more variable: the SD grows with the mean, and faster than in proportion. On a log–log scale the slope is 1.4 (a slope of 1 would be proportional, as for the gamma; 1.5 is the inverse Gaussian).

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a story about a decision
Imagine that the brain collects evidence. It starts at zero, drifts upwards with speed \(v\), and shakes randomly on the way. When it reaches a threshold \(a\), the button is pressed. The time of the first passage through the threshold has an inverse Gaussian distribution (also called the Wald distribution; Folks & Chhikara, 1978), with
\[\mu = \frac{a}{v} \;\text{(mean)}, \qquad \lambda = a^2 \;\text{(shape)}\]
A simulation of such random walks:


Code
set.seed(101)
v <- 0.1
a <- 30
steps <- 1500 # drift per millisecond, threshold
walk <- function() {
  w <- cumsum(v + rnorm(steps))
  hit <- which(w >= a)[1]
  list(path = w, time = hit)
}
times <- replicate(4000, walk()$time)
few <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:6, function(i) {
    w <- walk()
    n <- if (is.na(w$time)) steps else w$time
    data.frame(walk = i, t = 1:n, x = w$path[1:n])
  })
)
pa <- ggplot(few, aes(t, x, group = walk, colour = factor(walk))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = a, linetype = "dashed") +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(title = "Six decisions: evidence until the threshold", x = "milliseconds", y = "evidence") +
  theme_bw()
dig <- function(x, mu, lambda) {
  sqrt(lambda / (2 * pi * x^3)) * exp(-lambda * (x - mu)^2 / (2 * mu^2 * x))
} # the density
curve_data <- data.frame(t = 10:1200); curve_data$d <- dig(curve_data$t, a / v, a^2)
pb <- ggplot(data.frame(times), aes(times)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    binwidth = 25,
    fill = "grey80",
    colour = "white",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(t, d), colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "4,000 such times, and the inverse Gaussian density",
    x = "milliseconds",
    y = "density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)









Code
c(mean_of_simulation = mean(times, na.rm = TRUE), theory = a / v)


mean_of_simulation             theory 
          304.4593           300.0000 




Step 2: the variance
\[E(y) = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(y) = \frac{\mu^3}{\lambda} = \phi\,\mu^3\]
The variance grows with the cube of the mean. Compare: constant for the normal, \(\mu\) for Poisson, \(\mu^2\) for the gamma, \(\mu^3\) for the inverse Gaussian. Slow conditions are much more variable, and have a longer tail.


Step 3: the mean, and its link
\[\mu_i = x_i^\top\beta \;\;\text{(identity link)} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \log\mu_i = x_i^\top\beta \;\;\text{(log link)}\]
With the identity link, effects are in milliseconds and add up. With the log link they are percentages and multiply. (The textbook link is \(1/\mu^2\), which nobody can read.) The choice is about how effects combine, and it decides what “no interaction” means.


Step 4: the weights
The likelihood equations weight each observation by the inverse of its variance, \(1/\mu^3\). The slow, noisy conditions count less. By hand, for the identity link, this is a repeated weighted least squares:


Code
X <- model.matrix(~ freq * foreign, data = words); y <- words$rt
beta <- coef(lm(rt ~ freq * foreign, data = words))                    # start from OLS
for (it in 1:50) {
  mu <- drop(X %*% beta)
  new <- coef(lm.wfit(X, y, w = 1 / mu^3)) # identity link: plain weighted least squares
  if (max(abs(new - beta)) < 1e-9) {
    break
  }
  beta <- new
}
fit <- glm(
  rt ~ freq * foreign,
  family = inverse.gaussian(link = "identity"),
  data = words,
  start = coef(lm(rt ~ freq * foreign, data = words))
)
rbind(by_hand = beta, glm = coef(fit))


        (Intercept)      freq  foreign freq:foreign
by_hand    568.8714 -19.77006 99.88254    -20.07592
glm        568.8714 -19.77006 99.88244    -20.07548


(glm() needs starting values with the identity link. The coefficients of OLS are good ones.)

    data = words, start = coef(lm(rt ~ freq * foreign, data = words)))

Coefficients:

freq          -19.770      3.416  -5.787 8.62e-09 ***
foreign        99.882      7.859  12.709  < 2e-16 ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for inverse.gaussian family taken to be 9.39331e-05)

    Null deviance: 0.14780  on 1593  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 0.12241  on 1590  degrees of freedom
AIC: 19959

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 3


Code
b <- coef(fit); s <- coef(summary(fit))
phi <- summary(fit)$dispersion



(Intercept): 569 ms, the mean for a native speaker and a word of average frequency.
freq: -19.8: for native speakers, each unit of log frequency saves 19.8 ms.
foreign: the others are 100 ms slower at average frequency.
freq:foreign: -20.1: for them, one unit of frequency saves 20.1 ms more, that is 39.8 ms in all.
Dispersion = 9.39e-05: \(\phi = 1/\lambda\). The predicted SD at a mean of \(\mu\) is \(\sqrt{\phi\mu^3}\): 108 ms at 500 ms and 179 ms at 700 ms.

These standard errors treat the 1,594 answers as independent. They are not, and section 6 repairs that. First, the distribution.

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
text:
5. Which distribution, and which scale?


Code
start_ms <- coef(lm(rt ~ freq * foreign, data = words))
fams <- list(
  `normal, identity` = glm(rt ~ freq * foreign, family = gaussian, data = words),
  `gamma, identity` = glm(
    rt ~ freq * foreign,
    family = Gamma("identity"),
    data = words,
    start = start_ms
  ),
  `inverse Gaussian, identity` = fit,
  `inverse Gaussian, log` = glm(rt ~ freq * foreign, family = inverse.gaussian("log"), data = words)
)
logs <- lm(log(rt) ~ freq * foreign, data = words)
# on the scale of milliseconds
aics <- c(sapply(fams, AIC), `log-normal` = AIC(logs) + 2 * sum(log(words$rt)))
cbind(AIC = sort(round(aics, 1)))


                               AIC
inverse Gaussian, log      19958.5
inverse Gaussian, identity 19959.1
log-normal                 19988.1
gamma, identity            20103.1
normal, identity           20545.5


The inverse Gaussian describes the reaction times best, then the log-normal and the gamma, and the normal distribution is far behind: an AIC 586 points larger. Between the two links there is little to choose.

The interaction depends on the scale
Does frequency help the foreign speakers more? Ask in four ways:


Code
inv <- lm(I(-1000 / rt) ~ freq * foreign, data = words)
int <- rbind(
  `milliseconds (inverse Gaussian, identity)` = s["freq:foreign", 1:4],
  `ratios (inverse Gaussian, log link)` = coef(summary(fams[[4]]))["freq:foreign", 1:4],
  `log(RT), least squares` = coef(summary(logs))["freq:foreign", 1:4],
  `-1000/RT, least squares` = coef(summary(inv))["freq:foreign", 1:4]
)
colnames(int) <- c("estimate", "SE", "t", "p")
round(int, 4)


                                          estimate     SE       t      p
milliseconds (inverse Gaussian, identity) -20.0755 6.0761 -3.3040 0.0010
ratios (inverse Gaussian, log link)        -0.0269 0.0097 -2.7604 0.0058
log(RT), least squares                     -0.0262 0.0087 -3.0215 0.0026
-1000/RT, least squares                    -0.0316 0.0137 -2.3153 0.0207


In milliseconds the interaction is clear, t = -3.3. On the log scale it is weaker, t = -3.0, and for the reciprocal weaker again, t = -2.3. It is the same data. Slow people have larger differences of every kind, in milliseconds. A transformation that compresses long times compresses this too. Here the interaction survives; in other data it disappears, or even turns round. So the scale must be chosen for a reason: a theory in milliseconds (stages that add up) needs milliseconds. Whether the times look normal is no argument, because a generalized linear model does not need them to.


Code
grid <- expand.grid(freq = seq(-2.8, 3, by = 0.1), foreign = 0:1)
grid$rt <- predict(fit, grid, type = "response")
grid$native <- ifelse(grid$foreign == 1, "other", "English")
bins <- aggregate(
  rt ~ cut(freq, quantile(freq, 0:6 / 6), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE) + foreign,
  data = words,
  FUN = mean
)
bins$freq <- aggregate(
  freq ~ cut(freq, quantile(freq, 0:6 / 6), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE) + foreign,
  data = words,
  FUN = mean
)$freq
bins$native <- ifelse(bins$foreign == 1, "other", "English")
ggplot(grid, aes(freq, rt, colour = native)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = bins, size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(English = "#2a78d6", other = "#eb6834"),
    name = "native language"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean reaction time and word frequency",
    subtitle = "Lines: inverse Gaussian model. Points: means in sixths of the frequency",
    x = "log frequency (centred)",
    y = "milliseconds"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
section: 6. People and words: a mixed model
text:
6. People and words: a mixed model
Each person answered many times, and each word was answered by many people. Fast people are fast for all words, hard words are hard for everybody. The answers are crossed in subjects and words, and both are samples from larger populations. A generalized linear mixed model has a random intercept for each (Baayen et al., 2008; Lo & Andrews, 2015):
\[\mu_{ij} = x_{ij}^\top\beta + u_i + w_j, \qquad u_i \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), \quad w_j \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)\]


Code
mixed <- glmer(
  rt ~ freq * foreign + (1 | subject) + (1 | word),
  data = words,
  family = inverse.gaussian(link = "identity"),
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)
sm <- coef(summary(mixed))
round(sm, 4)


             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  568.0473    17.6888 32.1134    0e+00
freq         -17.7037     3.8056 -4.6521    0e+00
foreign       98.3724    24.6420  3.9921    1e-04
freq:foreign -18.6494     4.1338 -4.5115    0e+00


Code
VarCorr(mixed)


 Groups  Name        Std.Dev.
 word    (Intercept) 33.227  
 subject (Intercept) 77.999  




Code
compare <- data.frame(
  term = names(b),
  glm = b,
  SE_glm = s[, 2],
  mixed = sm[, 1],
  SE_mixed = sm[, 2],
  row.names = NULL
)
print(cbind(term = compare$term, round(compare[, -1], 2)), row.names = FALSE)


         term    glm SE_glm  mixed SE_mixed
  (Intercept) 568.87   4.35 568.05    17.69
         freq -19.77   3.42 -17.70     3.81
      foreign  99.88   7.86  98.37    24.64
 freq:foreign -20.08   6.08 -18.65     4.13


Code
linear <- lmer(rt ~ freq * foreign + (1 | subject) + (1 | word), data = words)
loglin <- lmer(log(rt) ~ freq * foreign + (1 | subject) + (1 | word), data = words)
t_int <- c(
  inverse_gaussian = sm["freq:foreign", 3],
  normal = coef(summary(linear))["freq:foreign", 3],
  log_normal = coef(summary(loglin))["freq:foreign", 3]
)
t_int


inverse_gaussian           normal       log_normal 
       -4.511453        -4.834974        -4.216698 


Code
t_lang <- c(glm = s["foreign", 3], mixed = sm["foreign", 3])
t_lang


     glm    mixed 
12.70901  3.99207 



The difference between the two language groups is about the same (98 ms), but its standard error is 3.1 times as large: it compares 12 with 9 people, not hundreds of answers. The t falls from 12.7 to 4.0.
The effect of frequency compares words: its standard error grows a little.
The interaction is a comparison within people and words, and it becomes more precise, because the mixed model removes their differences: SE 4.1 instead of 6.1.
People differ by an SD of 78 ms, words by 33 ms.

The standard errors of glmer() with this family are known to be rough, and Lo and Andrews recommend it nevertheless for the fit. With only 21 people, treat a z of 2 as weak evidence. Random slopes (a personal effect of frequency) would be the next step.

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
text:
7. Checking the model


Code
pig <- function(x, mu, lambda) {
  pnorm(sqrt(lambda / x) * (x / mu - 1)) +
    exp(2 * lambda / mu) * pnorm(-sqrt(lambda / x) * (x / mu + 1))
} # the distribution function
quantile_res <- function(y, mu, phi) qnorm(pmin(pmax(pig(y, mu, 1 / phi), 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12))
phi_m  <- sum(residuals(mixed, type = "pearson")^2) / (nrow(words) - 6)
chk <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    r = quantile_res(words$rt, fitted(fit), phi),
    model = "inverse Gaussian, no random effects"
  ),
  data.frame(r = quantile_res(words$rt, fitted(mixed), phi_m), model = "inverse Gaussian, mixed"),
  data.frame(
    r = rstandard(lm(rt ~ freq * foreign, data = words)),
    model = "normal, no random effects"
  ),
  data.frame(r = as.numeric(scale(resid(linear))), model = "normal, mixed")
)
chk <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(split(chk, chk$model), function(d) cbind(d, q = qqnorm(d$r, plot.it = FALSE)$x))
)
ggplot(chk, aes(q, r)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Quantile residuals against the normal distribution",
    x = "normal quantile",
    y = "residual"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









Code
tail_share <- tapply(chk$r, chk$model, function(v) mean(v > 3))
cbind(percent_above_3_SD = round(100 * tail_share, 2))


                                    percent_above_3_SD
inverse Gaussian, mixed                           1.07
inverse Gaussian, no random effects               0.75
normal, mixed                                     1.51
normal, no random effects                         1.88


If the model is right, the points lie on the line. The normal models have a long right tail: 1.5% of the residuals of the mixed normal model are above 3 SD, where 0.13% are expected. The inverse Gaussian models follow the line better over most of the range, and their tail is shorter (1.1% for the mixed one), but still too long: a few very slow answers (lapses of attention) remain. They are usually cut off by a rule that is fixed before looking at the results.

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

The theory of the single threshold is a simplification. Reaction times also contain the time to see and to press. Adding a constant gives the shifted Wald, and a normal or exponential part the ex-Wald (Heathcote, 2004). Two thresholds, with errors, lead to the diffusion model.
Use it as a convenient shape, not as proof of the theory. The log-normal or the gamma may fit as well in other data.
Identity link: watch the sign. Nothing keeps the mean positive. With reaction times it is never a problem; with small means it is.
Choose the link and the scale before you see the interaction. An interaction that exists on one scale only is removable: say so, and say which scale your theory speaks.
Outliers and cut-offs. Report the rule and how many answers it removed.
Errors. We left out wrong answers. If one condition has more of them, speed and accuracy must be analysed together.
Random effects for people and items. Averaging over words first, or over people, hides one of the two.
Starting values are needed for the identity link. Scale and centre the predictors, or glmer() will not converge.

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the distribution and the link with reasons, the exclusions, the random effects, the estimates in milliseconds, and the comparison with other distributions if the choice matters. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
ci_low <- sm[, 1] - 1.96 * sm[, 2]; ci_high <- sm[, 1] + 1.96 * sm[, 2]
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Term = c(
    "Intercept", "Frequency (log, centred)", "Native language other than English",
    "Frequency × native language"
  ),
  b = f1(sm[, 1]),
  SE = f1(sm[, 2]),
  CI = paste0("[", f1(ci_low), ", ", f1(ci_high), "]"),
  z = f2(sm[, 3]),
  p = sapply(sm[, 4], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p)))
)


Method (data analysis):

Reaction times of correct lexical decisions (1,594 answers of 21 participants to 79 words; Baayen, 2008) were analysed with a generalized linear mixed model with an inverse Gaussian distribution and an identity link (Lo & Andrews, 2015), so that effects are in milliseconds. The inverse Gaussian was preferred to the normal, gamma and log-normal distributions by the AIC. Fixed effects were log word frequency (centred), native language (English or other) and their interaction; participants and words had random intercepts. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015).

Results:

Native speakers recognised words of average frequency in 568 ms. More frequent words were recognised faster, b = -17.7 ms per log unit, SE = 3.8, z = -4.65, p < .001, and participants with another native language were slower, b = 98.4 ms, SE = 24.6, z = 3.99, p < .001. They also gained more from frequency, b = -18.6 ms, SE = 4.1, z = -4.51, p < .001 (Table 1). The interaction had the same sign on the log scale (t = -4.22).

title: Inverse Gaussian Regression: How Much Faster Do We Recognise Common Words?
text:
10. Summary



When
Positive, right-skewed outcomes whose variance grows very fast with the mean: reaction times, times to a threshold


The distribution
Time of the first passage of a drifting random walk; \(\text{Var} = \phi\mu^3\)


How (R)
glm(y ~ x, family = inverse.gaussian("identity"), start = ...); mixed: lme4::glmer()


Links
Identity: milliseconds that add; log: ratios that multiply


Against transforming
Keeps the mean and the unit; interactions depend on the scale


Against the gamma
The variance grows with \(\mu^3\) instead of \(\mu^2\)


Checks
Quantile residuals, AIC against gamma and log-normal


Related pages
Gamma regression, multilevel models, generalized linear models

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
How do you find out what a house is worth? You look at what similar houses nearby were sold for, and take something like the average. Estate agents call these houses comparables. No formula, no coefficients.
k-nearest neighbours (kNN) is this, done by a computer. To predict a case, find the \(k\) most similar cases in the data and average their outcomes. It is the simplest method of machine learning, more than 70 years old (Fix and Hodges described it in 1951; Cover & Hart, 1967, worked out how good it can be), and it has no training at all. The whole model is the data.
All the difficulty is in two words: how many (k), and what is similar. Is a house of the same size at a distance of 3 km more similar than a house twice as large next door?


Code
library(FNN)        # knn.reg(), get.knnx(): fast neighbours
library(mgcv)       # bam(), for comparison (comes with R)
library(ranger)     # random forest, for comparison
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
1. The data
The county around Seattle (King County, Washington) publishes every sale of a house. This file has the sales from May 2014 to May 2015, and OpenML (2019) serves it as CSV:


Code
raw <- read.csv("https://www.openml.org/data/get_csv/21578898/house_sales.arff")
house <- with(
  raw,
  data.frame(
    price = price,
    logp = log10(price),
    date = as.Date(substr(date, 1, 8), "%Y%m%d"),
    east = (long + 122.2) * 111.32 * cos(47.56 * pi / 180),
    north = (lat - 47.56) * 111.32, # kilometres from a point in the middle
    lsize = log2(sqft_living),
    grade,
    built = yr_built,
    llot = log2(sqft_lot),
    view,
    water = as.integer(waterfront),
    zip = factor(zipcode)
  )
)
nrow(house)


[1] 21613


Code
range(house$date)


[1] "2014-05-02" "2015-05-27"


Code
quantile(house$price, c(0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99))


       1%       25%       50%       75%       99% 
 153500.4  321950.0  450000.0  645000.0 1964400.0 


There are 21,613 sales. east and north are the position in kilometres, lsize the living space (log base 2, so one unit is a doubling), grade the county’s grade of the building (1 to 13), built the year, llot the land (log), view (0 to 4) and water (on the waterfront). Prices are skewed, so we predict \(\log_{10}\) of the price; an error of 0.04 is about 10%.
The use of such a model is to value houses that are sold later. So we learn from the sales until January 2015, choose the settings with those of February and March, and test with April and May:


Code
train <- subset(house, date < as.Date("2015-02-01"))
valid <- subset(house, date >= as.Date("2015-02-01") & date < as.Date("2015-04-01"))
test  <- subset(house, date >= as.Date("2015-04-01"))
c(train = nrow(train), validation = nrow(valid), test = nrow(test))


     train validation       test 
     15611       3125       2877

2. Look at the data

  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +

    option = "C",

Place matters, and not in a way that a straight line could follow: there are expensive shores, cheap corridors and sharp borders.

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
section: 3. The method step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a distance
The usual one is Euclidean. With the predictors \(x_1, \dots, x_p\),
\[d(x, x') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2\, (x_j - x'_j)^2}\]
The weights \(w_j\) are part of the method, whether one chooses them or not. If a predictor is measured in other units, its weight changes.


Step 2: the neighbours, and their mean
Let \(N_k(x)\) be the \(k\) training cases with the smallest distance to \(x\). The prediction is
\[\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(x)} y_i\]
By hand, for the first house of the validation set, with place and size only:


Code
new <- valid[1, ]
d <- sqrt(
  (train$east - new$east)^2 + (train$north - new$north)^2 + (2 * (train$lsize - new$lsize))^2
) # a doubling of the size counts as 2 km
near <- order(d)[1:5]
cbind(
  distance = round(d[near], 2),
  km = round(sqrt((train$east[near] - new$east)^2 + (train$north[near] - new$north)^2), 2),
  train[near, c("price", "built", "grade")],
  size = round(2^train$lsize[near])
)


      distance   km  price built grade size
16518     0.90 0.78 304000  1972     7  900
6006      0.94 0.67 300000  1982     7  970
16644     0.97 0.31 335000  1967     7 1060
6767      1.03 0.67 350000  1967     7 1010
17242     1.04 0.93 300000  1971     7  910


Code
c(predicted = 10^mean(train$logp[near]), sold_for = new$price)


predicted  sold_for 
 317136.2  180000.0 




Step 3: the choice of \(k\)
With \(k = 1\) the prediction jumps from house to house and copies every accident of a single sale: no bias, much variance. With \(k = n\) it is the mean of all houses: no variance, much bias. In between is the best value, and it must be found by trying.


Step 4: no training, slow prediction
There is nothing to estimate. But for each new case all the distances must be computed. Programs use search trees (FNN does) that avoid most of the work in few dimensions.

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
4. What is similar? Scaling
Try three definitions, each with several \(k\), on the validation sales:


Code
vars <- c("east", "north", "lsize", "grade", "built", "llot", "view", "water")
centre <- colMeans(train[, vars]); spread <- apply(train[, vars], 2, sd)
Z <- function(d, w = rep(1, length(vars))) {
  sweep(sweep(sweep(as.matrix(d[, vars]), 2, centre), 2, spread, "/"), 2, w, "*")
} # standardise with the training data, then weight
knn <- function(Ztr, Zte, k, y = train$logp) knn.reg(Ztr, Zte, y, k = k)$pred
ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 35, 60, 100)
place <- c("east", "north")
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(train[, place], valid[, place], k), valid$logp)),
    what = "place only"
  ),
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(train[, vars], valid[, vars], k), valid$logp)),
    what = "all predictors, raw units"
  ),
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(Z(train), Z(valid), k), valid$logp)),
    what = "all predictors, standardised"
  )
)
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(curves, curves$what), function(d) d[which.min(d$rmse), ]))
best


                              k       rmse                         what
all predictors, raw units     5 0.10989469    all predictors, raw units
all predictors, standardised 12 0.09012174 all predictors, standardised
place only                    8 0.12973096                   place only




Code
ggplot(curves, aes(k, rmse, colour = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = ks) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Error on later sales, by the number of neighbours",
    x = "k (log scale)",
    y = "RMSE of log10(price)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










The classic U-shape: too few neighbours are noisy, too many are not similar.
With place only, 0.130 at best.
With all the predictors in raw units, 0.110. The year of construction runs over a hundred units and the waterfront over one, so the years decide who is a neighbour.
Standardised, 0.090. Each predictor has the same weight now.


Weights for the predictors
But why the same weight? Place matters more than the size of the garden. We can search for better weights on the validation set, one predictor at a time, doubling or halving its weight as long as it helps:


Code
w <- setNames(rep(1, length(vars)), vars)
score <- function(w, k = 8) rmse(knn(Z(train, w), Z(valid, w), k), valid$logp)
current <- score(w); history <- data.frame(step = 0, changed = "start", rmse = current)
for (round in 1:4) {
  for (v in vars) {
    for (f in c(2, 0.5)) {
      repeat {
        trial <- w
        trial[v] <- trial[v] * f
        s <- score(trial)
        if (s < current - 1e-5) {
          w <- trial
          current <- s
          history <- rbind(history, data.frame(step = nrow(history), changed = v, rmse = s))
        } else {
          break
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
w


 east north lsize grade built  llot  view water 
 8.00  4.00  2.00  1.00  0.25  1.00  0.25  1.00 


Code
k_w <- ks[which.min(sapply(ks, function(k) score(w, k)))]
c(standardised = best["all predictors, standardised", "rmse"], weighted = score(w, k_w), k = k_w)


standardised     weighted            k 
  0.09012174   0.08359334   8.00000000 


The search gives the most weight to east, north, lsize, and the error falls to 0.084. The weights are the model. They were tuned on the validation sales, so that error is too good; the test set will tell. (Weighting the neighbours themselves by their distance is another refinement, which helps a little.)

5. The comparables of one house
An advantage that few other methods of machine learning have: the prediction can be shown.

one <- 3

  cbind(what = "to be valued", test[one, ]),

  sqft = round(2^show$lsize),

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
6. Against other methods


Code
learn <- rbind(train, valid) # the test may use everything before April
Zl <- sweep(sweep(sweep(as.matrix(learn[, vars]), 2, centre), 2, spread, "/"), 2, w, "*")
knn_pred <- knn.reg(Zl, Zn, learn$logp, k = k_w)$pred
lin  <- lm(logp ~ east + north + lsize + grade + built + llot + view + water, data = learn)
# each postal code its own level
linz <- lm(logp ~ zip + lsize + grade + built + llot + view + water, data = learn)
gm <- bam(
  logp ~ s(east, north, k = 150) +
    s(lsize, k = 6) +
    s(grade, k = 6) +
    s(built, k = 8) +
    s(llot, k = 6) +
    view +
    water,
  data = learn
)
set.seed(161)
rf <- ranger(
  logp ~ east + north + lsize + grade + built + llot + view + water,
  data = learn,
  num.trees = 500
)
# a regression for the house, and kNN for the place: the mean residual of the nearest houses
res_learn <- resid(lin)
local <- knn.reg(learn[, place], test[, place], res_learn, k = 15)$pred
preds <- list(
  `Linear regression` = predict(lin, test),
  `Regression + postal codes` = predict(linz, test),
  `kNN, standardised` = knn.reg(
    Z(learn),
    Z(test),
    learn$logp,
    k = best["all predictors, standardised", "k"]
  )$pred,
  `kNN, weighted` = knn_pred,
  `GAM with a map` = as.numeric(predict(gm, test)),
  `Random forest` = predict(rf, test)$predictions,
  `Regression + kNN of its residuals` = predict(lin, test) + local
)
results <- data.frame(
  model = names(preds),
  rmse = sapply(preds, rmse, b = test$logp),
  median_error = sapply(preds, function(p) median(abs(10^(p - test$logp) - 1))),
  row.names = NULL
)
results <- results[order(results$rmse), ]
print(
  transform(results, rmse = round(rmse, 4), median_error = round(median_error, 3)),
  row.names = FALSE
)


                             model   rmse median_error
                    GAM with a map 0.0813        0.109
                     kNN, weighted 0.0857        0.112
                     Random forest 0.0858        0.106
         Regression + postal codes 0.0894        0.118
                 kNN, standardised 0.0903        0.115
 Regression + kNN of its residuals 0.0922        0.125
                 Linear regression 0.1195        0.168


Code
get <- function(m, col = "rmse") results[results$model == m, col]




Code
results$model <- factor(results$model, levels = rev(results$model))
ggplot(results, aes(median_error, model)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = median_error, yend = model), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(100 * v, "%"), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median error on the sales of April and May 2015",
    x = "half of the predictions are closer than this",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")










Plain linear regression misses half of the houses by more than 17%; the weighted kNN by more than 11%. Knowing the neighbours is worth a lot.
A regression with postal codes comes close to kNN (RMSE 0.089 against 0.086). It uses a simple formula for what is simple (size, grade, age), and the neighbourhood for the rest.
The same idea without postal codes: a regression for the house and kNN for the place, that is, the linear regression plus the average residual of the 15 nearest houses. A few lines of code take the RMSE of the regression from 0.120 to 0.092. It does not reach the weighted kNN, because the formula of the regression is too simple for the rest, too.
The GAM with a smooth map and smooth curves has the smallest error, 0.081, and the random forest has 0.086.

Where kNN loses, it is because it cannot learn that a doubling of the size adds a certain share of the price everywhere. It must find, for every place and grade, houses of the right size. The GAM adds up one map and one curve per predictor, and learns each of them from all the sales.

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
7. The curse of dimensionality
In many dimensions nothing is near. Add predictors that mean nothing (random numbers), and watch:


Code
set.seed(162)
extra <- c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)
noise <- matrix(
  rnorm((nrow(learn) + nrow(test)) * max(extra)),
  ncol = max(extra),
  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise", seq_len(max(extra))))
)
in_learn <- seq_len(nrow(learn)); in_test <- nrow(learn) + seq_len(nrow(test))
curse <- sapply(extra, function(m) {
  A <- cbind(Z(learn), noise[in_learn, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])
  B <- cbind(Z(test), noise[in_test, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])
  rmse(knn.reg(A, B, learn$logp, k = 8)$pred, test$logp)
})
lm_noise <- sapply(extra, function(m) {
  L <- cbind(learn[, c("logp", vars)], noise[in_learn, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])
  Te <- cbind(test[, vars], noise[in_test, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])
  rmse(predict(lm(logp ~ ., data = L), Te), test$logp)
})
rbind(noise_predictors = extra, kNN = round(curse, 4), linear_regression = round(lm_noise, 4))


                    [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]   [,5]    [,6]
noise_predictors  0.0000 1.0000 2.0000 4.0000 8.0000 16.0000
kNN               0.0902 0.0959 0.0995 0.1047 0.1150  0.1288
linear_regression 0.1195 0.1195 0.1195 0.1195 0.1196  0.1196


Code
dist_ratio <- sapply(c(2, 8, 24), function(p) {
  set.seed(163)
  u <- matrix(runif(2000 * p), ncol = p)
  d <- sqrt(colSums((t(u[-1, ]) - u[1, ])^2))
  min(d) / max(d)
})
setNames(round(dist_ratio, 2), paste(c(2, 8, 24), "dimensions"))


 2 dimensions  8 dimensions 24 dimensions 
         0.02          0.21          0.35 


With 16 useless predictors the error of kNN goes from 0.090 to 0.129. Linear regression hardly notices (0.120 and 0.120): it gives them coefficients near zero. kNN cannot ignore a predictor; each one has its weight in the distance. The second output shows the geometry: among 2,000 random points, the nearest is at 2% of the distance of the farthest in 2 dimensions, and at 35% in 24. “Nearest” loses its meaning (Beyer et al., 1999).

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
section: 8. How sure is the prediction? Conformal intervals
text:
8. How sure is the prediction? Conformal intervals
kNN has no standard errors. Conformal prediction gives intervals for any method, with one simple idea: look at the errors on sales that were not used, and take their 90% quantile (Lei et al., 2018). Here: predict the validation sales from the training sales, and use those errors for the test.


Code
err   <- abs(knn(Z(train, w), Z(valid, w), k_w) - valid$logp)
q90   <- sort(err)[ceiling(0.9 * (length(err) + 1))]
inside <- abs(knn_pred - test$logp) <= q90
c(half_width_log10 = q90, factor = 10^q90, coverage_in_test = mean(inside))


half_width_log10           factor coverage_in_test 
       0.1338998        1.3611305        0.8953771 


Code
cheap <- cut(
  knn_pred,
  quantile(knn_pred, 0:4 / 4),
  include.lowest = TRUE,
  labels = c("cheapest quarter", "2", "3", "most expensive quarter")
)
round(tapply(inside, cheap, mean), 3)


      cheapest quarter                      2                      3 most expensive quarter 
                 0.863                  0.910                  0.928                  0.882 


The 90% interval goes from the prediction divided by 1.36 to the prediction times 1.36. In the test 89.5% of the houses were inside. The coverage is right on average, and not in every group: it ranges from 86% to 93% across the quarters of the predicted price, because the interval has the same width everywhere.

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
text:
9. Things to keep in mind

Scale, then weight. Both decide the result. Use the training data for the centre and the spread.
Choose \(k\) by validation, on cases that resemble the future. An odd \(k\) has no meaning in regression.
At the edges kNN is biased: the neighbours of the largest house are all smaller. The prediction can never leave the range of the data.
Few, strong predictors. With many weak ones use other methods, or reduce them first.
Categories need a distance of their own (0 if equal, 1 if not, times a weight).
Dependence: the same house sold twice, flats of the same building. Keep them on the same side of the split.
Distance in space is not distance in life. Two houses on the opposite shores of a lake are near on the map.
It is a smoother. kNN with one predictor is a rough cousin of LOESS, which fits a line instead of a mean and has less bias at the ends.

title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
section: 10. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
10. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the predictors and their scaling, the distance and the weights, \(k\) and how it was chosen, the split, the errors in understandable units, and simpler alternatives. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
r <- results[order(results$rmse), ]
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = as.character(r$model),
  rmse = f3(r$rmse),
  med = pct(r$median_error, 1)
)


Method (data analysis):

We predicted the log price of 2,877 houses sold in King County, Washington, in April and May 2015 from 18,736 earlier sales (May 2014–March 2015) with k-nearest neighbours regression. Predictors were the position (km), log living space, grade, year of construction, log lot size, view and waterfront, standardised with the training data. The number of neighbours and the weights of the predictors in the Euclidean distance were chosen with the sales of February and March 2015. Linear regression with and without postal codes, a generalized additive model with a smooth of the position, a random forest, and a regression corrected by the residuals of neighbouring houses served for comparison. Prediction intervals are split-conformal (Lei et al., 2018). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package FNN.

Results:

With k = 8 and weighted predictors, half of the predictions were within 11.2% of the price (RMSE of log10 price = 0.086), compared with 16.8% for linear regression (Table 1). A linear regression corrected by the mean residual of the 15 nearest houses had a median error of 12.5%. The 90% conformal intervals (predicted price divided or multiplied by 1.36) contained 89.5% of the prices.

Points to remember:

Report the scaling and the weights: they are the model.
Say how \(k\) was chosen.
Test on later cases if the use is prediction.
Give errors in percent, not only in logs.

text:
11. Summary



When
Prediction with few, strong predictors and much data, especially positions


The method
The mean outcome of the \(k\) nearest cases


How (R)
FNN::knn.reg(train, test, y, k); neighbours: get.knnx()


Choices
Predictors, scaling, weights, \(k\)


\(k\)
Small: noisy. Large: biased. Choose by validation


Strength
No assumptions, and every prediction can be shown


Weakness
Many predictors, edges, sparse regions


A useful mixture
Correct a regression by the mean residual of the nearest cases

LOESS, random forest, support vector regression

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
A company surveys 1,000 employees about their weekly working hours, their sleep quality and their wellbeing. We want two numbers: the average wellbeing, and how much wellbeing goes down with every extra hour of work. But 30% of the employees skipped the wellbeing page, and 10% did not give their hours.
What happens next depends on why the answers are missing. Rubin (1976) named three cases:








Mechanism
In words
In the survey




MCAR: missing completely at random
Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with any variable
A batch of questionnaires was lost in the post


MAR: missing at random
Whether a value is missing depends on other, observed variables
People who sleep badly skip the wellbeing page more often, and we know their sleep


MNAR: missing not at random
Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself
People with low wellbeing skip the wellbeing page, because of their low wellbeing



The names are confusing: “missing at random” does not mean random. It means random once we take the observed variables into account: among people with the same sleep quality, who skipped the page is random.
Most software, R included, handles missing values by quietly dropping every incomplete row (listwise deletion). This page shows when that is harmless, when it is not, why the popular quick fixes are worse, and how multiple imputation does better. Because we simulate the data, we know the true answers and can check every method against them.


Code
library(mice)       # multiple imputation by chained equations
library(MASS)       # mvrnorm(): correlated normal data
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
1. Simulate the complete data
Hours, sleep quality and wellbeing are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with these means, standard deviations and correlations:



Variable
Mean
SD
Correlation with hours
with sleep




hours (per week)
40
8




sleep (quality, 0 to 10)
6
1.5
−0.20



wellbeing (0 to 100)
60
12
−0.30
0.60





Code
means <- c(hours = 40, sleep = 6, wellbeing = 60)
sds   <- c(hours = 8, sleep = 1.5, wellbeing = 12)
corr  <- matrix(c( 1.00, -0.20, -0.30,
                  -0.20,  1.00,  0.60,
                  -0.30,  0.60,  1.00), 3, dimnames = list(names(means), names(means)))
Sigma <- diag(sds) %*% corr %*% diag(sds)          # the covariance matrix
dimnames(Sigma) <- dimnames(corr)

true_mean  <- 60
true_slope <- unname(corr["hours", "wellbeing"] * sds["wellbeing"] / sds["hours"])   # r * SD_y / SD_x
true_slope


[1] -0.45


Code
make_people <- function(n) as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, means, Sigma))
set.seed(2026)
full <- make_people(1000)
fit_full <- lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = full)
c(mean_wellbeing = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"]))


mean_wellbeing          slope 
    59.7983421     -0.4648238 


In the population, wellbeing drops by 0.45 points per extra hour of work (\(b = r \times SD_y / SD_x = -0.30 \times 12 / 8\)). Our sample of 1,000 gives 59.80 and -0.465: these are the answers we would get without missing data, the benchmark for every method below.
Sleep is not part of our question. It plays the role of an auxiliary variable: measured in the same survey, related to wellbeing, and (section 5) very useful.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
2. Three ways to lose data
The function below removes about 30% of the wellbeing values, in one of the three ways, and 10% of the hours completely at random:

MCAR: 300 wellbeing values chosen at random, with generate_missing() of the rwf package.
MAR: the chance of missing wellbeing depends on sleep: \(P(\text{missing}) = \text{logistic}(a - 1.5\,z_{\text{sleep}})\), where \(z\) is the standardised sleep score and \(a\) is set to give 30% missing. People who sleep badly skip it more often.
MNAR: the same, but with \(z_{\text{wellbeing}}\): the lower the wellbeing, the more likely it is missing.



Code
add_missing <- function(complete, mechanism, share = 0.30) {
  d <- complete
  n <- nrow(d)
  z <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  p_missing <- function(lp) {                         # choose the intercept a that gives the wanted share
    a <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + lp)) - share, c(-10, 10))$root
    plogis(a + lp)
  }
  if (mechanism == "MCAR") d$wellbeing <- generate_missing(d$wellbeing, missing = round(share * n))
  if (mechanism == "MAR")  d$wellbeing[runif(n) < p_missing(-1.5 * z(d$sleep))] <- NA
  if (mechanism == "MNAR") d$wellbeing[runif(n) < p_missing(-1.5 * z(d$wellbeing))] <- NA
  d$hours <- generate_missing(d$hours, missing = round(0.10 * n))   # 10% of hours: completely at random
  d
}

set.seed(1)
data_mcar <- add_missing(full, "MCAR")
data_mar  <- add_missing(full, "MAR")
data_mnar <- add_missing(full, "MNAR")


In real data we never see the missing values. Here we do, so we can look at who went missing:


Code
mech <- rbind(data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mcar$wellbeing), mechanism = "MCAR: at random"),
              data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mar$wellbeing),  mechanism = "MAR: depends on sleep"),
              data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mnar$wellbeing), mechanism = "MNAR: depends on wellbeing"))
mech$mechanism <- factor(mech$mechanism, levels = unique(mech$mechanism))
ggplot(mech, aes(sleep, wellbeing, colour = missing)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("observed", "missing")) +
  labs(title = "Which wellbeing values went missing", x = "sleep quality", y = "wellbeing", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










MCAR: the red points are scattered everywhere.
MAR: they gather on the left, among people who sleep badly. Since bad sleepers also have lower wellbeing, the missing values are mostly low ones.
MNAR: they gather at the bottom: the low wellbeing values themselves are missing.

What happens if we simply analyse the observed values?


Code
round(sapply(list(complete = full, MCAR = data_mcar, MAR = data_mar, MNAR = data_mnar), function(d)
  c(share_missing  = mean(is.na(d$wellbeing)),
    mean_wellbeing = mean(d$wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE),
    slope          = unname(coef(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d))["hours"]))), 3)


               complete   MCAR    MAR   MNAR
share_missing     0.000  0.300  0.323  0.318
mean_wellbeing   59.798 59.757 62.145 63.878
slope            -0.465 -0.505 -0.409 -0.373


Under MCAR the observed values are a random subset, so the estimates are fine, only less precise. Under MAR and MNAR the people who stayed are happier than the people who left, so the average wellbeing is too high, and the slope is too flat.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 3. Look at the missing data first
text:
3. Look at the missing data first

The missing-data pattern
md.pattern() counts the combinations of observed and missing values:


Code
md.pattern(data_mar, plot = FALSE)


    sleep hours wellbeing    
608     1     1         1   0
292     1     1         0   1
69      1     0         1   1
31      1     0         0   2
        0   100       323 423


How to read it: each row is a pattern, with 1 for observed and 0 for missing. The row name is the number of people with that pattern, and the last column the number of missing values in it. The last row gives the number of missing values per variable. Here 608 people answered everything, and 392 (39%) have at least one hole, so listwise deletion would drop more than a third of the sample. The same pattern as a picture:


Code
pat <- md.pattern(data_mar, plot = FALSE)
counts <- as.numeric(rownames(pat)[-nrow(pat)])
tiles <- expand.grid(pattern = seq_along(counts), variable = colnames(pat)[-ncol(pat)])
tiles$observed <- as.vector(pat[-nrow(pat), -ncol(pat)]) == 1
tiles$label <- factor(paste0(counts, " people")[tiles$pattern], levels = rev(paste0(counts, " people")))
ggplot(tiles, aes(variable, label, fill = observed)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#0082c8", `FALSE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("missing", "observed")) +
  labs(title = "Missing-data patterns (MAR data)", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)











Is it MCAR?
We can check whether missingness is related to observed variables: a logistic regression of “wellbeing is missing” on sleep.


Code
missing_vs_sleep <- function(d) summary(glm(is.na(wellbeing) ~ sleep, family = binomial, data = d))$coefficients["sleep", ]
round(rbind(MCAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mcar), MAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mar), MNAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mnar)), 4)


     Estimate Std. Error  z value Pr(>|z|)
MCAR  -0.0287     0.0464  -0.6186   0.5362
MAR   -1.0246     0.0742 -13.8029   0.0000
MNAR  -0.5264     0.0546  -9.6483   0.0000


Under MCAR sleep does not predict missingness. Under MAR it does strongly, so the data are not MCAR. But look at the MNAR row: sleep predicts missingness there too, because sleep is correlated with the wellbeing that drives it. No test can tell MAR from MNAR, because the difference lies in the values we do not have. That choice rests on knowledge of how the data were collected, and on the sensitivity analysis of section 6.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 4. The quick fixes, and what they do
text:
4. The quick fixes, and what they do
From here on we use the MAR data, the realistic case. Four common approaches:

Listwise deletion: analyse only the complete rows (R’s default).
Mean imputation: fill each hole with the mean of the variable.
Regression imputation: fill each hole with the value predicted from the other variables.
Stochastic regression imputation: the same, plus a random error, so the imputed values scatter like real ones.

mice() can do all three imputations once (m = 1), with method = "mean", "norm.predict" and "norm.nob":


Code
single <- function(method) complete(mice(data_mar, m = 1, method = method, maxit = if (method == "mean") 1 else 5,
                                         printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1))
filled <- list("complete data (benchmark)" = full,
               "listwise deletion"         = na.omit(data_mar),
               "mean imputation"           = single("mean"),
               "regression imputation"     = single("norm.predict"),
               "stochastic regression"     = single("norm.nob"))
describe_fit <- function(d) {
  f <- lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d)
  c(n = nobs(f), mean = mean(d$wellbeing), sd = sd(d$wellbeing), r = cor(d$hours, d$wellbeing),
    slope = unname(coef(f)["hours"]), se = summary(f)$coefficients["hours", "Std. Error"])
}
quick <- t(sapply(filled, describe_fit))
round(quick, 3)


                             n   mean     sd      r  slope    se
complete data (benchmark) 1000 59.798 11.910 -0.301 -0.465 0.047
listwise deletion          608 62.414 11.175 -0.277 -0.409 0.058
mean imputation           1000 62.145  9.298 -0.211 -0.267 0.039
regression imputation     1000 59.705 10.546 -0.363 -0.518 0.042
stochastic regression     1000 59.867 11.839 -0.316 -0.483 0.046




Code
shown <- c("mean imputation", "regression imputation", "stochastic regression")
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(shown, function(nm)
  data.frame(filled[[nm]][, c("hours", "wellbeing")], imputed = is.na(data_mar$wellbeing), method = nm)))
pts$method <- factor(pts$method, levels = shown)
ggplot(pts, aes(hours, wellbeing, colour = imputed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("observed", "imputed")) +
  labs(title = "Where the imputed wellbeing values land", x = "weekly hours", y = "wellbeing", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Row by row:

Listwise deletion keeps 608 of 1,000 people. Its mean (62.41) is too high, because the bad sleepers, who are less happy, are the ones who left.
Mean imputation is the worst. Every hole gets the same value: the horizontal red line in the plot, and the vertical blue line of people whose hours were filled with the mean. So the mean stays as biased as with deletion, the SD shrinks (9.30 against 11.91), and the correlation and slope are pulled towards 0 (-0.267). On top of that, R treats the 1,000 rows as real data, so the standard error is too small.
Regression imputation uses sleep, so the mean is nearly right. But each imputed value is an exact prediction from hours and sleep, with none of the scatter of real data around the prediction, so in the middle plot the red points are packed more tightly than the blue ones. The SD is too small, the correlation too strong (-0.363 against -0.301), and the standard error too small.
Stochastic regression adds random scatter, so the mean, SD, correlation and slope all come out about right. Only the standard error is still wrong: R thinks the imputed values are as certain as observed ones, but they are guesses. The next section fixes that.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
5. Multiple imputation
Multiple imputation (Rubin, 1987) does stochastic imputation not once but \(m\) times, creating \(m\) complete datasets that differ only in the imputed values. Each dataset is analysed as usual, and the \(m\) results are combined. The differences between the \(m\) results show how uncertain the imputations are, and that uncertainty goes into the standard errors.
mice (multivariate imputation by chained equations; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) imputes one variable at a time from all the others, cycling through the variables a few times. Its default for numeric variables is predictive mean matching (pmm): for each missing value it predicts a value from the other variables, finds the five observed cases whose predictions are closest, and borrows the real value of one of them at random. The imputed values are therefore always values that really occur in the data.


Code
imp <- mice(data_mar, m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
imp


Class: mids
Number of multiple imputations:  40 
Imputation methods:
    hours     sleep wellbeing 
    "pmm"        ""     "pmm" 
PredictorMatrix:
          hours sleep wellbeing
hours         0     1         1
sleep         1     0         1
wellbeing     1     1         0


How to read it:

Number of multiple imputations: \(m\) = 40 completed datasets (why 40: see below).
Imputation methods: pmm for the two incomplete variables; "" for sleep, which has nothing to impute.
PredictorMatrix: which variables (columns) predict which (rows). By default every variable predicts every other. Include the variables of the analysis (the outcome too), and auxiliary variables such as sleep.

Analyse each completed dataset with with(), and combine with pool():


Code
fits   <- with(imp, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))
pooled <- pool(fits)
summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE)


         term   estimate  std.error statistic       df      p.value      2.5 %     97.5 %   conf.low  conf.high
1 (Intercept) 78.0165217 2.41001487 32.371801 175.4128 6.810418e-76 73.2601643 82.7728791 73.2601643 82.7728791
2       hours -0.4548743 0.06113269 -7.440771 150.5196 7.120770e-12 -0.5756633 -0.3340853 -0.5756633 -0.3340853


Code
pooled_mean <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)   # the mean of wellbeing
pooled_mean


         term estimate std.error statistic      df       p.value    2.5 %   97.5 % conf.low conf.high
1 (Intercept) 59.81394 0.4377225  136.6481 295.041 8.576632e-269 58.95248 60.67539 58.95248  60.67539


The columns are read like a regression table: estimate, std.error, statistic (t), df, p.value and the 95% confidence interval. The pooled mean of wellbeing is 59.81, against 59.80 in the complete data and 62.41 after listwise deletion.

Rubin’s rules, by hand
With \(m\) estimates \(\hat Q_1, \dots, \hat Q_m\) and their squared standard errors \(U_1, \dots, U_m\):

Pooled estimate: the average, \(\bar Q = \frac{1}{m}\sum \hat Q_j\)
Within-imputation variance: the average squared standard error, \(\bar U = \frac{1}{m}\sum U_j\). The uncertainty we would have if the data were complete.
Between-imputation variance: the variance of the estimates, \(B = \frac{1}{m-1}\sum (\hat Q_j - \bar Q)^2\). The extra uncertainty caused by the missing values.
Total variance: \(T = \bar U + \left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right) B\), and the pooled standard error is \(\sqrt{T}\).

Three summaries of how much the missing data cost:

Relative increase in variance: \(r = \dfrac{(1 + 1/m)\,B}{\bar U}\)
Proportion of variance due to missingness: \(\lambda = \dfrac{(1 + 1/m)\,B}{T}\)
Fraction of missing information: \(\text{FMI} = \dfrac{r + 2/(\nu + 3)}{r + 1}\), where \(\nu\) is the degrees of freedom (Barnard & Rubin, 1999).



Code
est <- sapply(fits$analyses, function(f) coef(f)[["hours"]])
u   <- sapply(fits$analyses, function(f) vcov(f)["hours", "hours"])
m   <- length(est)
q_bar  <- mean(est)
u_bar  <- mean(u)
b      <- var(est)
t_var  <- u_bar + (1 + 1 / m) * b
riv    <- (1 + 1 / m) * b / u_bar
lambda <- (1 + 1 / m) * b / t_var
df_com <- nrow(data_mar) - 2                                    # the df if the data were complete
df_old <- (m - 1) / lambda^2
df_obs <- (df_com + 1) / (df_com + 3) * df_com * (1 - lambda)
df     <- df_old * df_obs / (df_old + df_obs)                   # Barnard-Rubin degrees of freedom
fmi    <- (riv + 2 / (df + 3)) / (riv + 1)
by_hand <- c(estimate = q_bar, ubar = u_bar, b = b, t = t_var, df = df, riv = riv, lambda = lambda, fmi = fmi)
from_pool <- unlist(pooled$pooled[pooled$pooled$term == "hours", names(by_hand)])
signif(rbind(by_hand, from_pool), 4)


          estimate     ubar        b        t    df    riv lambda    fmi
by_hand    -0.4549 0.002109 0.001588 0.003737 150.5 0.7717 0.4356 0.4429
from_pool  -0.4549 0.002109 0.001588 0.003737 150.5 0.7717 0.4356 0.4429


The two rows agree. For the slope, \(\lambda\) = 0.44: about 44% of its variance comes from not knowing the missing values, and the FMI says about 44% of the information about it was lost.
The FMI is not simply the share of missing values. The better the other variables predict the missing values, the smaller it is: with a perfect predictor nothing would be lost. Sleep predicts wellbeing only moderately (r = 0.60), and here the FMI ends up a little above the share of people with an incomplete row (39%).


Checking the imputations
Convergence. mice iterates; the mean of the imputed values should settle down and the separate runs (chains) should mix, with no trend:


Code
imp_trace <- mice(data_mar, m = 5, maxit = 20, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
chains <- imp_trace$chainMean["wellbeing", , ]                    # iterations x chains
trace_df <- data.frame(iteration = rep(seq_len(nrow(chains)), ncol(chains)), chain = factor(rep(seq_len(ncol(chains)), each = nrow(chains))),
                       mean = as.vector(chains))
c1 <- ggplot(trace_df, aes(iteration, mean, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Convergence of the\nimputed mean", x = "iteration", y = "mean of imputed wellbeing") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

imputed <- imp$imp$wellbeing                                     # one column per imputation
dens <- rbind(data.frame(value = data_mar$wellbeing[!is.na(data_mar$wellbeing)], set = "observed", draw = "0"),
              data.frame(value = unlist(imputed), set = "imputed", draw = rep(names(imputed), each = nrow(imputed))))
c2 <- ggplot(dens, aes(value, group = draw, colour = set, linewidth = set)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(observed = "#0082c8", imputed = "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(observed = 1.4, imputed = 0.2)) +
  labs(title = "Observed and imputed wellbeing\n(one red line per imputation)", x = "wellbeing", y = "density",
       colour = NULL, linewidth = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
c1 + c2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.3))










Left: the chains wander around the same level from the first iterations, with no trend. Five iterations (the default) are enough here.
Right: the imputed values (red) lie lower than the observed ones (blue). That is not a fault. Under MAR the people with missing wellbeing sleep worse, so their wellbeing is expected to be lower. A difference between observed and imputed values is a problem only if it makes no sense; impossible values (say, below 0) would be one.



How many imputations?
The old advice was 5. With 5, the results change noticeably every time you run the imputation with another seed. A useful rule is to use at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases (White et al., 2011): here 39%, so about 40. The spread of the pooled slope and its standard error over 10 runs with different seeds:


Code
spread <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 20, 40), function(mm) do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, function(s) {
  p <- summary(pool(with(mice(data_mar, m = mm, seed = s, printFlag = FALSE), lm(wellbeing ~ hours))))
  data.frame(m = mm, estimate = p$estimate[2], se = p$std.error[2])
}))))
round(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread, spread$m), function(s)
  c(m = s$m[1], estimate_mean = mean(s$estimate), estimate_sd = sd(s$estimate),
    se_mean = mean(s$se), se_sd = sd(s$se)))), 4)


    m estimate_mean estimate_sd se_mean  se_sd
5   5       -0.4681      0.0146  0.0599 0.0097
20 20       -0.4635      0.0080  0.0576 0.0034
40 40       -0.4619      0.0055  0.0579 0.0021


The averages hardly change, but the run-to-run spread (estimate_sd, se_sd) shrinks as \(m\) grows. With 40 imputations a second run would give practically the same numbers.


Auxiliary variables
The data are MAR given sleep. What if we leave sleep out of the imputation model?


Code
imp_no_aux <- mice(data_mar[, c("hours", "wellbeing")], m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
mi_summary <- function(im) c(mean  = summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))))$estimate,
                             slope = summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))))$estimate[2])
aux <- rbind("complete data (benchmark)" = c(mean = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"])),
             "listwise deletion"         = quick["listwise deletion", c("mean", "slope")],
             "MI without sleep"          = mi_summary(imp_no_aux),
             "MI with sleep"             = mi_summary(imp))
round(aux, 3)


                            mean  slope
complete data (benchmark) 59.798 -0.465
listwise deletion         62.414 -0.409
MI without sleep          61.949 -0.406
MI with sleep             59.814 -0.455


Without sleep, multiple imputation is no better than deletion: from the point of view of a model that does not know sleep, the data are not MAR. With sleep, it recovers the benchmark. So put in the imputation model every variable that predicts the missing values or the missingness, even if it is not part of the analysis (the “inclusive strategy”; Collins et al., 2001).
The same holds for any analysis that compares models: every step of a Hierarchical Regression must use the same people, which multiple imputation gives you without dropping anyone. Fit each step in each imputed dataset and pool them; for example pool.r.squared(fits) pools \(R^2\):


Code
pool.r.squared(fits)


           est      lo 95     hi 95       fmi
R^2 0.08949307 0.05018298 0.1374607 0.4134909

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 6. MNAR: when imputation is not enough
text:
6. MNAR: when imputation is not enough
Multiple imputation assumes MAR. With the MNAR data:


Code
imp_mnar <- mice(data_mnar, m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
mnar_tab <- rbind("complete data (benchmark)" = c(mean = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"])),
                  "listwise deletion"         = c(mean = mean(na.omit(data_mnar)$wellbeing),
                                                  slope = unname(coef(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = data_mnar))["hours"])),
                  "multiple imputation"       = mi_summary(imp_mnar))
round(mnar_tab, 3)


                            mean  slope
complete data (benchmark) 59.798 -0.465
listwise deletion         64.054 -0.373
multiple imputation       62.552 -0.406


Imputation helps a little, because sleep carries some information about the missing wellbeing values, but the mean is still too high. The data cannot tell us how much lower the missing values are.
What we can do is a sensitivity analysis: ask how the results change if the missing people are worse off than MAR predicts. The delta adjustment (van Buuren, 2018) subtracts a fixed amount \(\delta\) from every imputed wellbeing value, through the post argument of mice():


Code
deltas <- c(0, -2, -4, -6, -8, -10)
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(deltas, function(delta) {
  post <- make.post(data_mnar)
  post["wellbeing"] <- paste("imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] +", delta)      # shift every imputed value by delta
  im <- mice(data_mnar, m = 20, method = "pmm", post = post, seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
  pm <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)
  ps <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))), conf.int = TRUE)
  data.frame(delta, mean = pm$estimate, mean_low = pm$`2.5 %`, mean_high = pm$`97.5 %`,
             slope = ps$estimate[2], slope_low = ps$`2.5 %`[2], slope_high = ps$`97.5 %`[2])
}))
round(sens, 3)


  delta   mean mean_low mean_high  slope slope_low slope_high
1     0 62.479   61.738    63.220 -0.407    -0.514     -0.300
2    -2 61.792   60.991    62.592 -0.431    -0.537     -0.325
3    -4 61.212   60.460    61.964 -0.442    -0.554     -0.330
4    -6 60.538   59.709    61.367 -0.472    -0.585     -0.358
5    -8 59.933   59.082    60.783 -0.481    -0.599     -0.363
6   -10 59.273   58.399    60.146 -0.519    -0.643     -0.395




Code
s1 <- ggplot(sens, aes(delta, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(full$wellbeing), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_low, ymax = mean_high), fill = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Mean wellbeing", x = "delta (shift of the imputed values)", y = "pooled estimate, 95% CI")
s2 <- ggplot(sens, aes(delta, slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"]), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = slope_low, ymax = slope_high), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Slope of hours", x = "delta (shift of the imputed values)", y = NULL)
s1 + s2 + plot_annotation(caption = "Dashed line: the complete-data value, which real data never show")









As \(\delta\) grows, the estimated mean falls, and somewhere around \(\delta\) = -8 it reaches the complete-data value (which in real life we would not know). The slope moves less and stays clearly negative for every \(\delta\) tried.
In practice, report the analysis under MAR and then the range of results for plausible values of \(\delta\), chosen with subject knowledge (for example, “people who skip a wellbeing page score up to 5 points lower than similar people who answer it”). If the conclusion survives the whole range, it is robust; if it flips at some \(\delta\), say where.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
7. A simulation: bias and coverage
One dataset can be lucky. We repeat everything 100 times for each mechanism (500 people per sample) and record, for every method, the average error of the estimates (bias) and how often its 95% confidence interval contains the true value (coverage, which should be 95%). The truth is the population value: a mean of 60 and a slope of -0.45. To keep the page fast, multiple imputation uses 5 imputations here.


Code
ci_lm <- function(f, term) {
  e <- coef(f)[[term]]; se <- summary(f)$coefficients[term, "Std. Error"]; q <- qt(0.975, df.residual(f))
  c(estimate = e, low = e - q * se, high = e + q * se)
}
both <- function(d) rbind(mean = ci_lm(lm(wellbeing ~ 1, data = d), "(Intercept)"),
                          slope = ci_lm(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d), "hours"))
one_run <- function(mechanism, n = 500) {
  d <- add_missing(make_people(n), mechanism)
  out <- list("listwise deletion"     = both(na.omit(d)),
              "mean imputation"       = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, maxit = 1, method = "mean", printFlag = FALSE))),
              "regression imputation" = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, method = "norm.predict", printFlag = FALSE))),
              "stochastic regression" = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, method = "norm.nob", printFlag = FALSE))))
  im <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "pmm", printFlag = FALSE)
  pm <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)
  ps <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))), conf.int = TRUE)
  out[["multiple imputation"]] <- rbind(mean  = c(pm$estimate, pm$`2.5 %`, pm$`97.5 %`),
                                        slope = c(ps$estimate[2], ps$`2.5 %`[2], ps$`97.5 %`[2]))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(out), function(nm) data.frame(mechanism, method = nm, estimand = c("mean", "slope"),
                                                            estimate = out[[nm]][, 1], low = out[[nm]][, 2], high = out[[nm]][, 3])))
}
set.seed(11)
sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"), function(mech) do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_run(mech), simplify = FALSE))))
sim$truth   <- ifelse(sim$estimand == "mean", true_mean, true_slope)
sim$covered <- sim$low <= sim$truth & sim$truth <= sim$high
res <- aggregate(cbind(bias = estimate - truth, coverage = covered) ~ mechanism + method + estimand, data = sim, FUN = mean)
res$mechanism <- factor(res$mechanism, levels = c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"))
res$method <- factor(res$method, levels = rev(c("listwise deletion", "mean imputation", "regression imputation",
                                                "stochastic regression", "multiple imputation")))
res <- res[order(res$estimand, res$mechanism, -as.integer(res$method)), ]
rownames(res) <- NULL
res

Code
# one number from the table, for the text below
get <- function(mech, meth, est, what) res[res$mechanism == mech & res$method == meth & res$estimand == est, what]




Code
long <- rbind(data.frame(res[, c("mechanism", "method")], panel = paste("Bias of the", res$estimand), value = res$bias),
              data.frame(res[, c("mechanism", "method")], panel = paste("Coverage of the", res$estimand), value = res$coverage))
long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = c("Bias of the mean", "Bias of the slope", "Coverage of the mean", "Coverage of the slope"))
refs <- data.frame(panel = factor(levels(long$panel), levels = levels(long$panel)), x = c(0, 0, 0.95, 0.95))
ggplot(long, aes(value, method, colour = mechanism)) +
  geom_vline(data = refs, aes(xintercept = x), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MCAR = "#0082c8", MAR = "#f39c12", MNAR = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "100 samples per mechanism: average error and 95% CI coverage\n(dashed: no bias, 95% coverage)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"))









What the simulation shows (the true slope is negative, so a positive bias of the slope means a slope that is too flat):

Listwise deletion is fine under MCAR: no bias, and coverage of 0.97 for the mean and 0.90 for the slope (with 100 samples, coverage is itself uncertain by about ±0.04). Under MAR and MNAR its mean is too high, by 2.4 and 3.9 points, and its intervals almost never contain the true mean.
Mean imputation pulls the slope towards 0 even under MCAR (a bias of 0.14), and its intervals contain the true slope only 31% of the time or less.
Regression imputation gets the mean nearly right under MAR, but makes the slope too steep (a bias of -0.05), and its intervals are too narrow (coverage of the slope 0.79).
Stochastic regression is about as accurate as multiple imputation here, since the simulated data are exactly normal, which suits it. But its intervals are too narrow, because one imputation hides the uncertainty of the guesses: coverage between 0.89 and 0.94 under MCAR and MAR.
Multiple imputation is nearly unbiased under MCAR and MAR (for the mean under MAR, 0.20 points, against 2.42 for deletion), with coverage between 0.91 and 0.97. Under MNAR every method is biased; only a sensitivity analysis (section 6) shows how much it could matter.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report should give the amount and pattern of missing data, the assumed mechanism and why, how the imputation was done, and the pooled results (Enders, 2022; van Buuren, 2018). We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
sp  <- summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE)
row <- sp[sp$term == "hours", ]
pf  <- pooled$pooled[pooled$pooled$term == "hours", ]
mis_test <- missing_vs_sleep(data_mar)

f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))


Method (missing data):

Of the 1,000 participants, 32.3% had missing wellbeing scores and 10% missing working hours; 39.2% had at least one missing value. Missing wellbeing was more likely among participants reporting poorer sleep quality, b = -1.02, p < .001, so the data were not missing completely at random. We assumed that they were missing at random given the observed variables, and handled them with multiple imputation by chained equations in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the mice package (Version 3.19.0; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011). Missing values were imputed with predictive mean matching, using wellbeing, working hours and sleep quality (an auxiliary variable) as predictors. We created 40 imputed datasets, analysed each separately, and combined the results with Rubin’s rules.

Results:

Across the imputed datasets, mean wellbeing was 59.81, 95% CI [58.95, 60.68]. Each additional weekly working hour was associated with lower wellbeing, b = -0.45, SE = 0.06, t(150.5) = -7.44, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.33]. The fraction of missing information for this coefficient was .44.

Points to remember:

Report how much is missing, per variable and in total (the share of incomplete cases), and the main patterns.
Say which mechanism you assume and why, and what you checked (which observed variables predict missingness).
Describe the imputation model: the method, the number of imputations and iterations, and all the variables in it, auxiliary ones included.
Report pooled estimates with their standard errors or confidence intervals; the FMI shows how much the missing data cost.
If MNAR is plausible, add a sensitivity analysis, such as the delta adjustment, and report how far the conclusions hold.
Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("mice") in R give the exact references.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
9. Summary







MCAR
Missingness unrelated to anything: deletion is unbiased, only less precise


MAR
Missingness depends on observed variables: deletion is biased; multiple imputation that uses those variables is not


MNAR
Missingness depends on the missing values: no method fixes it from the data alone; use a sensitivity analysis


Telling them apart
Observed variables that predict missingness rule out MCAR; nothing in the data can rule out MNAR


Mean imputation
Never: shrinks variances, distorts correlations, too-small standard errors


Regression imputation
Imputed values on a line: correlations too strong, standard errors too small


One stochastic imputation
Estimates fine, standard errors too small


Multiple imputation
imp <- mice(d, m = 40); pool(with(imp, lm(...))): valid estimates and standard errors under MAR


Rubin’s rules
\(T = \bar U + (1 + 1/m)B\); FMI = the share of information lost


How many imputations
At least the percentage of incomplete cases


Imputation model
All analysis variables, the outcome included, plus auxiliary variables


Check
Convergence of the chains; imputed values that make sense
