title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
1. The data
The Bike Sharing Dataset (Fanaee-T & Gama, 2014) comes from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. It describes the Capital Bikeshare system in Washington, DC, for 2011 and 2012: one row for each hour. It is free, needs no login, and is released under a CC BY 4.0 licence (cite the paper). The zip file is 280 KB and downloads in about two seconds.


Code
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/275/bike+sharing+dataset.zip",
              zip, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
folder <- tempfile()
unzip(zip, files = "hour.csv", exdir = folder)
raw <- read.csv(file.path(folder, "hour.csv"))
dim(raw)


[1] 17379    17


The outcome is cnt, the number of rentals in the hour. The file also has casual and registered, the same count split by type of customer: they add up to the outcome, so they are not used as predictors. The weather variables come scaled to 0 to 1; we put them back in degrees and percentages.







Predictor
Meaning




year, month, hour
When: 2011 or 2012; 1 to 12; 0 to 23


weekday
Day of the week, 0 (Sunday) to 6


holiday, workingday
A public holiday; neither weekend nor holiday


weather
1 clear or few clouds, 2 mist or cloud, 3 light rain or snow, 4 heavy rain or snow


temp
Temperature, in degrees Celsius


feels
“Feels like” temperature, in degrees Celsius


humidity
Relative humidity, %


wind
Wind speed, on the scale of the data (0 to 67; the documentation gives no unit)





Code
d <- data.frame(
  date       = as.Date(raw$dteday),
  rentals    = raw$cnt,
  year       = factor(raw$yr + 2011),
  month      = raw$mnth,
  hour       = raw$hr,
  weekday    = raw$weekday,
  holiday    = raw$holiday,
  workingday = raw$workingday,
  weather    = raw$weathersit,
  temp       = raw$temp * 41,
  feels      = raw$atemp * 50,
  humidity   = raw$hum * 100,
  wind       = raw$windspeed * 67)
predictors <- c("year", "month", "hour", "weekday", "holiday", "workingday", "weather",
                "temp", "feels", "humidity", "wind")
formula_rf <- reformulate(predictors, "rentals")
sum(is.na(d))


[1] 0


There are 17,379 hours and no missing values. A random forest needs no scaling and no dummy variables: it only asks of each predictor whether a value is above or below a cut-point.

Split the data by day, not by hour
To judge a model we keep some data out of the fitting and test on it. The obvious way is to put a random 25% of the hours in a test set. Here that would be a mistake. The hours of one day are almost copies of each other: the same weather, the same day type, the same season. A test hour with its neighbours in the training set is easy to predict, and the test error would be too optimistic.
So we cut by day: 25% of the days, with all their hours, go to the test set.


Code
set.seed(1)
all_days  <- unique(d$date)
test_days <- sample(all_days, round(0.25 * length(all_days)))
in_test   <- d$date %in% test_days
tr <- d[!in_test, ]   # training set
te <- d[in_test, ]    # test set, kept out until section 6
c(training = nrow(tr), test = nrow(te))


training     test 
   13015     4364 


The training set has 13,015 hours and the test set 4,364, from 183 days that the model never sees.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
summary(d$rentals)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    1.0    40.0   142.0   189.5   281.0   977.0 


The median hour has 142 rentals, the mean 189 and the maximum 977: a right-skewed count. Now the hour of the day, for working days and for other days:


Code
by_hour <- aggregate(rentals ~ hour + workingday, tr, mean)
by_hour$day <- factor(ifelse(by_hour$workingday == 1, "Working day", "Weekend or holiday"),
                      levels = c("Working day", "Weekend or holiday"))
peak_work <- by_hour[by_hour$workingday == 1, ][which.max(by_hour$rentals[by_hour$workingday == 1]), ]
morning   <- by_hour[by_hour$workingday == 1 & by_hour$hour < 12, ][which.max(by_hour$rentals[by_hour$workingday == 1 & by_hour$hour < 12]), ]
peak_off  <- by_hour[by_hour$workingday == 0, ][which.max(by_hour$rentals[by_hour$workingday == 0]), ]

ggplot(by_hour, aes(hour, rentals, colour = day)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(blue, orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +
  labs(title = "Rentals by hour of the day", x = "hour", y = "mean rentals per hour", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









On working days there are two peaks, the commute: the morning one at 8:00 (472 rentals) and the higher evening one at 17:00 (520). At the weekend there is one broad hill with its top at 13:00 (371 rentals). The same hour has a different effect on a working day and on a weekend day, so hour and day type interact.


Code
ggplot(tr, aes(temp, rentals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, colour = blue, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"), colour = orange, se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Rentals and temperature", x = "temperature (°C)", y = "rentals per hour") +
  theme_bw()









Code
cor_temp <- cor(d$temp, d$feels)


Warmer hours have more rentals, up to a point. The cloud is very wide at every temperature, because the hour of the day matters as much. Note also that temp and feels carry almost the same information: their correlation is .988. This will matter for the importance of the predictors in section 7.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a single regression tree
A regression tree splits the predictor space in boxes by a series of questions (“is the hour before 7?”). It predicts the mean outcome of the training hours in each box. At each split it looks for the predictor and cut-point that reduce the sum of squared errors the most. A tree grown deep fits the training data closely, and changes a lot if the data change a little: it has a low bias and a high variance. (The decision tree example shows this in detail.)


Step 2: bagging, an average of trees on bootstrap samples
Draw \(B\) bootstrap samples from the \(n\) training hours: each takes \(n\) hours at random with replacement. Grow a tree \(T_b\) on each. The prediction is the average:
\[\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x)\]
This is bagging (bootstrap aggregating; Breiman, 1996). Averaging reduces variance and leaves the bias almost unchanged, so deep, unpruned trees (high variance, low bias) are the best things to average.


Step 3: why averaging helps only as far as the trees differ
If the \(B\) trees each had variance \(\sigma^2\) and were independent, the average would have variance \(\sigma^2 / B\). But trees grown on overlapping samples of the same data are correlated. If each pair has correlation \(\rho\), the variance of the average is
\[\text{Var}\big(\hat f(x)\big) = \rho \sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\,\sigma^2\]
The second term disappears as \(B\) grows. The first does not: more trees cannot push the variance below \(\rho\sigma^2\). To gain more, the trees must become less alike. The chart shows the formula for \(\sigma^2 = 1\):


Code
variance <- expand.grid(B = c(1:10, seq(15, 500, 5)), rho = c(0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8))
variance$var <- with(variance, rho + (1 - rho) / B)
variance$rho <- factor(variance$rho)

ggplot(variance, aes(B, var, colour = rho)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette) +
  labs(title = "Variance of an average of B trees",
       subtitle = "Each tree has variance 1; rho is the correlation between two trees",
       x = "number of trees, B (log scale)", y = "variance of the average", colour = "rho") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Step 4: random predictor subsets make the trees less alike
If one predictor is much stronger than the others (here: the hour), every bagged tree splits on it first, and the trees come out similar: \(\rho\) stays high. The random forest adds a second source of randomness: at each split the tree may choose only among mtry predictors drawn at random from the \(p\) available. A split on the hour is then not available at many of the splits, so other predictors get their chance, and the trees differ.

mtry = \(p\): no restriction, which is plain bagging.
A smaller mtry: less correlation between the trees (lower \(\rho\)) but each tree is a little weaker (higher bias). The best value is somewhere in between, and is found by tuning (section 5).
The defaults: ranger() uses \(\lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor\); the package randomForest uses \(p/3\) for regression.

The other settings are the minimum node size (a node with fewer hours is not split further; small = deep trees) and the number of trees, \(B\).


Step 5: out-of-bag error, a free test set
A bootstrap sample leaves out a fraction
\[\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \to e^{-1} \approx .368\]
of the hours: about a third. For each hour \(i\), average only the trees that did not see it, to get its out-of-bag (OOB) prediction \(\hat f_{\text{oob}}(x_i)\). The OOB error is
\[\text{RMSE}_{\text{oob}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - \hat f_{\text{oob}}(x_i)\big)^2}\]
It needs no separate test set, and comes with the fit. It works when the rows are independent. Here they are not (see the warning in section 1), and section 5 shows what that does.


Step 6: the full algorithm

For \(b = 1, \dots, B\): draw a bootstrap sample; grow a deep tree on it, and at every split choose the best cut among mtry randomly drawn predictors.
Predict with the average of the \(B\) trees.
No pruning is needed: the average takes care of the variance.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
4. Fitting a first forest


Code
set.seed(2)
first <- ranger(formula_rf, data = tr, num.trees = 500, seed = 2)
first


Ranger result

Call:
 ranger(formula_rf, data = tr, num.trees = 500, seed = 2) 

Type:                             Regression 
Number of trees:                  500 
Sample size:                      13015 
Number of independent variables:  11 
Mtry:                             3 
Target node size:                 5 
Variable importance mode:         none 
Splitrule:                        variance 
OOB prediction error (MSE):       3403.594 
R squared (OOB):                  0.8962956 


With ranger() the formula is the usual one, num.trees is \(B\), and mtry and min.node.size default to 3 and 5. The printout reports the OOB prediction error (MSE) and an OOB \(R^2\).


Code
oob_rmse_first  <- sqrt(first$prediction.error)
test_rmse_first <- rmse(te$rentals, predict(first, te)$predictions)


The OOB RMSE is 58.3 rentals per hour. We have not looked at the test set yet; to see what the OOB figure is worth, we compare it with the test RMSE now (once, and not to choose anything): 68.7. The OOB error is too optimistic. Every hour is OOB for a third of the trees, but the other hours of the same day are in the bootstrap sample of those trees and help to predict it. For tuning we need an error that respects the days.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 5. Tuning: mtry, minimum node size and the number of trees
text:
5. Tuning: mtry, minimum node size and the number of trees

Cross-validation by day
We use 5-fold cross-validation with whole days in the folds: fit on four fifths of the training days, predict the fifth that was left out, and average the RMSE of the five folds. The OOB error is computed alongside, to see how far it is from the cross-validated one.


Code
set.seed(3)
train_days <- sort(unique(tr$date))
fold_of    <- setNames(sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(train_days))), train_days)
fold       <- fold_of[as.character(tr$date)]   # the fold of every training hour

tune <- function(mtry, min.node.size, num.trees) {
  cv <- sapply(1:5, function(k) {
    m <- ranger(formula_rf, tr[fold != k, ], num.trees = num.trees, mtry = mtry,
                min.node.size = min.node.size, seed = 1)
    rmse(tr$rentals[fold == k], predict(m, tr[fold == k, ])$predictions)
  })
  oob <- ranger(formula_rf, tr, num.trees = num.trees, mtry = mtry,
                min.node.size = min.node.size, seed = 1)$prediction.error
  c(cv = mean(cv), oob = sqrt(oob))
}

grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 4, 8, 11), min.node.size = c(1, 5, 20))
grid[c("cv", "oob")] <- t(mapply(tune, grid$mtry, grid$min.node.size, num.trees = 200))
best <- grid[which.min(grid$cv), ]
best


  mtry min.node.size       cv      oob
7    8             5 50.96688 42.37292


A small grid, 4 values of mtry by 3 minimum node sizes, with 200 trees per forest. The best cross-validated RMSE is 51.0, at mtry = 8 and a minimum node size of 5.


Code
grid$node <- factor(grid$min.node.size)
ggplot(grid, aes(mtry, cv, colour = node)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(grid$mtry)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-validated error over the tuning grid",
       x = "mtry: predictors tried at each split (11 = bagging)", y = "cross-validated RMSE",
       colour = "minimum node size") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
oob_best <- grid[which.min(grid$oob), ]



mtry matters most. With mtry = 2 the error is 84.8: the trees are too weak and often cannot use the hour. With mtry = 11 (bagging) it is 51.7: the trees are too alike. The best value is in between.
Minimum node size matters little, up to 20 hours; deep trees are fine, as the theory says. A very large value would make the trees shallow and add bias.
The OOB error says the same about the ranking, but not about the level. Its best value is 42.2, at mtry = 8; the cross-validated error of the same setting is 51.1. The OOB figure for the chosen setting, 42.4, is much lower than its cross-validated 51.0.



The number of trees
More trees never hurt (the variance only falls), but at some point they stop helping. They only cost time.


Code
trees <- data.frame(B = c(10, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000))
res <- sapply(trees$B, function(B) tune(best$mtry, best$min.node.size, B))
trees <- rbind(data.frame(B = trees$B, RMSE = res["cv", ], error = "Cross-validated by day"),
               data.frame(B = trees$B, RMSE = res["oob", ], error = "Out-of-bag"))

ggplot(trees, aes(B, RMSE, colour = error)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(blue, orange)) +
  labs(title = "Error against the number of trees", x = "number of trees, B (log scale)",
       y = "RMSE", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
cv_trees <- trees[trees$error == "Cross-validated by day", ]


The cross-validated RMSE falls from 54.1 with 10 trees to 51.0 with 200 and 51.0 with 1,000: after a few hundred trees nothing is gained. We use 500 trees. The OOB curve is lower all the way, the gap that section 4 explained.
Cross-validated hyperparameters are a choice made on the training data. The test set has not been used for any of it.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 6. The test set: forest, linear regression and single tree
text:
6. The test set: forest, linear regression and single tree
The final forest is fitted on the whole training set with the settings found above. Two baselines go with it, fitted on the same hours:

A linear regression with the same predictors. It is given every help that a linear model can use: the hour, the month, the weekday and the weather as categories (one coefficient for each value), temperature, humidity and wind as numbers. It has no interactions: it does not know that the hours work differently on working days. (feels is left out of it, as it duplicates temp.)
A single regression tree with rpart, pruned by cross-validation (see the decision tree example).



Code
set.seed(4)
forest <- ranger(formula_rf, data = tr, num.trees = 500, mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size,
                 importance = "impurity", quantreg = TRUE, seed = 4)

linear <- lm(rentals ~ year + factor(month) + factor(hour) + factor(weekday) + holiday + workingday +
               factor(weather) + temp + humidity + wind, data = tr)

set.seed(5)
big_tree <- rpart(formula_rf, tr, control = rpart.control(cp = 0.0005, xval = 10))
cp_best  <- big_tree$cptable[which.min(big_tree$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
tree     <- prune(big_tree, cp = cp_best)
leaves   <- sum(tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")

pred <- data.frame(forest = predict(forest, te)$predictions,
                   linear = predict(linear, te),
                   tree   = predict(tree, te))
results <- t(sapply(pred, function(p) metrics(te$rentals, p)))
results <- results[c("linear", "tree", "forest"), ]
data.frame(Model = c("Linear regression", paste0("Single tree (", leaves, " leaves)"), "Random forest"),
           round(results, 2), row.names = NULL)


                     Model   RMSE   MAE   R2
1        Linear regression 102.64 76.13 0.68
2 Single tree (103 leaves)  65.91 44.61 0.87
3            Random forest  50.32 30.75 0.92




Code
long <- data.frame(model = factor(rep(c("Linear regression", "Single tree", "Random forest"), each = nrow(te)),
                                  levels = c("Linear regression", "Single tree", "Random forest")),
                   observed  = te$rentals,
                   predicted = c(pred$linear, pred$tree, pred$forest))
ggplot(long, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7, colour = blue) +
  geom_abline(colour = orange, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Predicted and observed rentals in the test set",
       subtitle = "The orange line is a perfect prediction", x = "predicted rentals per hour", y = "observed rentals per hour") +
  theme_bw()









On 4,364 hours that none of the models has seen:

The random forest is wrong by 50.3 rentals per hour (RMSE) and by 30.8 on average (MAE), and explains 92.4% of the variance (\(R^2\)).
The single tree has an RMSE of 65.9: 31% worse. It has 103 leaves, and it is still less accurate: one tree is noisy, the average of 500 is not.
The linear regression has an RMSE of 102.6, 104% worse than the forest, \(R^2\) = .68. In the chart it predicts negative rentals for some hours, and it misses the peaks: it cannot give the morning and evening peaks without an interaction of hour and day type.
The cross-validated RMSE of the chosen forest (51.0) is close to its test RMSE (50.3). The OOB RMSE (42.3) is not.

RMSE is in the units of the outcome (rentals per hour) and punishes large errors; MAE is the typical error; \(R^2\) is the share of the variance of the test hours that the model explains. Always give the baselines together with the model: a number such as \(R^2\) = .92 means little on its own.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
7. Which predictors matter? Permutation importance

Two kinds of importance

Impurity importance (also called Gini importance, or for regression the total reduction in squared error): add up, over all trees, how much each predictor’s splits reduced the error. It comes free with the fit (importance = "impurity").
Permutation importance: take a data set that the model did not train on, shuffle one predictor, which breaks its link with the outcome, and see how much worse the predictions get:

\[\text{VI}_j = \text{RMSE}\big(\text{data with } x_j \text{ shuffled}\big) - \text{RMSE}\big(\text{data}\big)\]
A predictor the model relies on makes the error jump; one that it ignores leaves it where it was. It is easy to compute by hand on the test set, and we repeat the shuffle five times and take the mean:


Code
set.seed(6)
base_rmse <- rmse(te$rentals, predict(forest, te)$predictions)
permutation <- sapply(predictors, function(v) {
  mean(replicate(5, {
    shuffled <- te
    shuffled[[v]] <- sample(shuffled[[v]])
    rmse(te$rentals, predict(forest, shuffled)$predictions)
  })) - base_rmse
})
perm <- data.frame(predictor = names(permutation), increase = as.numeric(permutation))
perm$predictor <- factor(perm$predictor, levels = perm$predictor[order(perm$increase)])

ggplot(perm, aes(increase, predictor)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Permutation importance in the test set",
       x = "increase in RMSE when the predictor is shuffled", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()









Code
top <- names(sort(permutation, decreasing = TRUE))



hour dominates: shuffling it adds 167 rentals to the RMSE, 3.2 times more than the second predictor, workingday (52).
The next are year (43) and temp (21): a rise from 2011 to 2012, and temperature.
wind and holiday do almost nothing (0.2 and -0.2). The holiday is already in workingday.

This ranks the predictors by how much this model needs them for prediction. It does not say how large the effect is, or whether it is a cause (see the end of this section).


Caveat 1: impurity importance favours continuous predictors
Splits on a predictor with many distinct values have more possible cut-points to choose from, and so more chances to find a cut that reduces the error by luck. Impurity importance rewards this. To see it, we add a column of pure noise, noise, a random number between 0 and 1 for each hour, unrelated to the outcome, and refit:


Code
set.seed(7)
tr_noise <- cbind(tr, noise = runif(nrow(tr)))
noisy <- ranger(reformulate(c(predictors, "noise"), "rentals"), data = tr_noise, num.trees = 500,
                mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size,
                importance = "impurity", seed = 7)
noisy_perm <- ranger(reformulate(c(predictors, "noise"), "rentals"), data = tr_noise, num.trees = 500,
                     mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size,
                     importance = "permutation", seed = 7)
both <- data.frame(predictor = rep(names(noisy$variable.importance), 2),
                   share = c(noisy$variable.importance / sum(noisy$variable.importance),
                             pmax(noisy_perm$variable.importance, 0) / sum(pmax(noisy_perm$variable.importance, 0))),
                   kind = rep(c("Impurity", "Permutation (out-of-bag)"), each = length(noisy$variable.importance)))
order_by <- both$predictor[both$kind == "Permutation (out-of-bag)"][order(both$share[both$kind == "Permutation (out-of-bag)"])]
both$predictor <- factor(both$predictor, levels = order_by)
noise_imp  <- both$share[both$predictor == "noise" & both$kind == "Impurity"]
noise_perm <- both$share[both$predictor == "noise" & both$kind == "Permutation (out-of-bag)"]
beaten <- as.character(both$predictor[both$kind == "Impurity" & both$share < noise_imp & both$predictor != "noise"])
beaten_text <- paste0("`", beaten, "`", collapse = " and ")

ggplot(both, aes(share, predictor, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(blue, orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Impurity and permutation importance, with a noise predictor",
       x = "share of the total importance", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The noise predictor gets 1.4% of the impurity importance, more than the real predictors holiday and wind; its permutation importance is 0.0%. A predictor with no information should have none. The shares add up to 100%, so every predictor is shown against the others. For this reason, prefer permutation importance, ideally computed on data that the forest has not seen, as we did above.


Caveat 2: correlated predictors share their importance
temp and feels have a correlation of .988. If we shuffle temp alone, the forest can still use feels, which has nearly the same information, so the error barely rises, and neither predictor looks important on its own. Shuffling the pair together (the same permutation for both) shows what they are worth together:


Code
set.seed(8)
pair <- mean(replicate(5, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(te)); shuffled <- te
  shuffled$temp <- te$temp[idx]; shuffled$feels <- te$feels[idx]
  rmse(te$rentals, predict(forest, shuffled)$predictions)
})) - base_rmse


Shuffled alone, temp adds 21.4 to the RMSE and feels 7.6. Shuffled together they add 48.6: more than the two numbers added up (29.0). The temperature is more important than the table seems to say, and its importance is split between two columns. With a group of related predictors, shuffle the group, or keep one of them.


Caveat 3: importance is not causation
Importance describes the model, not the world. hour is the most important predictor because the model needs it to predict; it does not mean that changing the hour changes the demand. A predictor can also be important only because it stands in for something that is not in the data (the year stands in for the growth of the company). And a causal effect can be hidden behind a correlated predictor, as above.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 8. What does the forest learn? Partial dependence
text:
8. What does the forest learn? Partial dependence
A forest has no coefficients. The partial dependence (Friedman, 2001) shows the average prediction as one predictor changes. For a predictor \(x_j\) and a value \(v\), set \(x_j = v\) in every row of the data, predict, and average:
\[\text{PD}_j(v) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat f\big(x_{ij} = v,\; \mathbf{x}_{i,-j}\big)\]
Do this for a grid of values and plot. No package is needed:


Code
set.seed(9)
sample_rows <- tr[sample(nrow(tr), 1000), ]   # 1,000 hours are enough, and fast

# the average prediction for each value in `values`, with `change` building the changed data
partial <- function(values, change, data = sample_rows) {
  sapply(values, function(v) mean(predict(forest, change(data, v))$predictions))
}



The hour, for working days and for other days


Code
hours <- 0:23
pd_hour <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 0), function(w)
  data.frame(hour = hours, day = ifelse(w == 1, "Working day", "Weekend or holiday"),
             rentals = partial(hours, function(x, v) { x$hour <- v; x$workingday <- w; x }))))
pd_hour$day <- factor(pd_hour$day, levels = c("Working day", "Weekend or holiday"))

ggplot(pd_hour, aes(hour, rentals, colour = day)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(blue, orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence on the hour", x = "hour", y = "predicted rentals per hour", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
pk <- tapply(pd_hour$rentals, pd_hour$day, max)


The forest has found the interaction without being told: two commuter peaks on working days, up to 454 rentals, and one afternoon hill at the weekend, up to 320. This is the shape that the linear regression could not draw.


Temperature, humidity and wind
For temperature there is a trap. If we set temp to 30 °C but leave feels as it was (say, 10 °C), the forest sees an hour that cannot occur. The two columns have to move together, so we also shift feels by the same amount:


Code
temp_grid <- seq(0, 35, by = 1)
hum_grid  <- seq(20, 100, by = 4)
wind_grid <- seq(0, 40, by = 2)

pd_weather <- rbind(
  data.frame(variable = "Temperature (°C)", x = temp_grid, version = "Naive: temp only",
             y = partial(temp_grid, function(x, v) { x$temp <- v; x })),
  data.frame(variable = "Temperature (°C)", x = temp_grid, version = "temp and feels together",
             y = partial(temp_grid, function(x, v) { x$feels <- x$feels + (v - x$temp); x$temp <- v; x })),
  data.frame(variable = "Humidity (%)", x = hum_grid, version = "temp and feels together",
             y = partial(hum_grid, function(x, v) { x$humidity <- v; x })),
  data.frame(variable = "Wind speed", x = wind_grid, version = "temp and feels together",
             y = partial(wind_grid, function(x, v) { x$wind <- v; x })))
pd_weather$version <- factor(pd_weather$version, levels = c("temp and feels together", "Naive: temp only"))
pd_weather$variable <- factor(pd_weather$variable, levels = c("Temperature (°C)", "Humidity (%)", "Wind speed"))

ggplot(pd_weather, aes(x, y, colour = version)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(blue, orange)) +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence on the weather", x = NULL, y = "predicted rentals per hour", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
tt <- subset(pd_weather, variable == "Temperature (°C)" & version == "temp and feels together")
tn <- subset(pd_weather, variable == "Temperature (°C)" & version == "Naive: temp only")
hh <- subset(pd_weather, variable == "Humidity (%)")



Temperature (blue line): predicted rentals rise from 97 at 0 °C to 244 at 29 °C, and fall again at the hottest hours. The naive version (orange line) moves much less (142 to 223): feels still says “cold” when temp is changed, and the forest follows feels. This is the importance problem of section 7 again.
Humidity: rentals fall from 205 at 20% to 160 at 100%. Humid hours are rainy ones.
Wind: a weak effect, as the importance already said.

Partial dependence averages over the other predictors, and so hides the differences between hours: the hour chart showed that the same predictor can work differently in two groups. It also assumes that the predictor can be changed independently of the others, which is false for correlated ones, as the temperature showed. Read it as a description of the model, not as the effect of a change in the world.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 9. How sure is one prediction? Quantile regression forests
text:
9. How sure is one prediction? Quantile regression forests
The average of the trees is a single number. A quantile regression forest (Meinshausen, 2006) keeps more: for a new hour, it collects the observed outcomes of the training hours that share a leaf with it, in all the trees, and takes their quantiles. The 5% and 95% quantiles are a 90% prediction interval. In ranger() it is quantreg = TRUE when fitting (done above), and type = "quantiles" when predicting.


Code
q <- predict(forest, te, type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))$predictions
covered <- te$rentals >= q[, 1] & te$rentals <= q[, 3]
width   <- median(q[, 3] - q[, 1])

# two test days, one working and one not, in 2012 and with clear weather
pick <- function(w) {
  days <- aggregate(weather ~ date, te[te$workingday == w & te$year == "2012", ], max)
  min(days$date[days$weather == 1])
}
show_days <- c(pick(1), pick(0))
shown <- do.call(rbind, lapply(show_days, function(day) {
  rows <- te$date == day
  data.frame(day = format(as.Date(day), "%a %d %b %Y"), hour = te$hour[rows], observed = te$rentals[rows],
             lower = q[rows, 1], middle = q[rows, 2], upper = q[rows, 3])
}))
shown$day <- factor(shown$day, levels = unique(shown$day))

ggplot(shown, aes(hour)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = "90% interval"), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = middle, colour = "Median prediction"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed, colour = "Observed"), size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ day) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = blue) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Median prediction" = blue, "Observed" = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Prediction intervals for two test days", x = "hour", y = "rentals per hour", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The interval is wide when the model is unsure, at the commuter peaks, and narrow at night. Over the 4,364 test hours, 91.5% of the observed values fall inside their 90% interval: close to the 90% that it should be. The median interval is 122 rentals wide. The coverage was checked on days that the forest had not seen, which is what makes it trustworthy: the same check on the training hours would flatter the model.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 10. The limits: a forest cannot extrapolate
text:
10. The limits: a forest cannot extrapolate
Each tree predicts the mean of the training hours in a leaf. So the forest can only predict values that lie within what it has seen, and for a predictor value beyond the training range it carries on with the prediction of the nearest edge. A linear regression, in contrast, draws the line on.
To see it, we fit a forest and a linear regression only on the cooler hours of the training set, up to 20 °C, and draw their partial dependence on temperature (section 8) over the whole range, with feels moved together with temp. The grey line is the forest fitted on all the training hours, which has seen the warm ones:


Code
limit <- 20
cool <- tr[tr$temp <= limit, ]
set.seed(10)
forest_cool <- ranger(formula_rf, cool, num.trees = 500, mtry = best$mtry, min.node.size = best$min.node.size, seed = 10)
# no month in the linear model here: July and August are all warmer than 20 degrees, and would have no coefficient
linear_cool <- lm(rentals ~ year + factor(hour) + factor(weekday) + holiday + workingday +
                    factor(weather) + temp + humidity + wind, data = cool)

grid_t <- seq(0, 36, by = 1)
shift  <- function(x, v) { x$feels <- x$feels + (v - x$temp); x$temp <- v; x }
pd_with <- function(predict_fun) sapply(grid_t, function(v) mean(predict_fun(shift(sample_rows, v))))
extra <- data.frame(temp = rep(grid_t, 3),
                    model = factor(rep(c("Forest, all hours", "Forest, cool hours only", "Linear regression, cool hours only"),
                                       each = length(grid_t)),
                                   levels = c("Forest, all hours", "Forest, cool hours only", "Linear regression, cool hours only")),
                    rentals = c(pd_with(function(x) predict(forest, x)$predictions),
                                pd_with(function(x) predict(forest_cool, x)$predictions),
                                pd_with(function(x) predict(linear_cool, x))))

ggplot(extra, aes(temp, rentals, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = limit, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Forest, all hours" = "grey60", "Forest, cool hours only" = blue,
                                 "Linear regression, cool hours only" = orange)) +
  annotate("text", x = limit - 0.5, y = max(extra$rentals), label = "training data end", hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence on temperature, fitted on cool hours",
       x = "temperature (°C)", y = "predicted rentals per hour", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))









Code
at <- function(m, t) extra$rentals[extra$model == m & extra$temp == t]


The forest fitted on cool hours is flat beyond 20 °C: from 188 rentals at 20 °C to 190 at 35 °C. It carries on with the prediction of the warmest leaf it knows. The forest that saw the warm hours goes from 203 to 227, so about 37 rentals are missing from the forest that could not extrapolate. The linear regression draws its line on, to 312 at 35 °C: it can go beyond the data, whether or not it is right (here the real curve levels off, so it is not). The difference is in kind: a line may be right beyond the data, and a forest cannot be. The same happens over time: a forest fitted on 2011 cannot predict the growth of 2012.
Two practical rules follow. Check that new data lie in the range of the training data before trusting a forest, and do not use it to forecast a trend: model the trend first (for example with a linear term) and give the forest the residuals, or use a method that can extrapolate.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
section: 11. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
11. Reporting the results in APA style
A report of a predictive model (APA 7th edition) needs the data and how they were split, the model and its settings, how they were chosen, the error on held-out data against baselines, and what the importance and the partial dependence show. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
n_all   <- nrow(d)
r2_f    <- results["forest", "R2"]


Method (data analysis):

We predicted the number of bicycle rentals per hour from the hour, day type, season, year and weather, using the 17,379 hourly records of the Capital Bikeshare system in Washington, DC, for 2011 and 2012 (Fanaee-T & Gama, 2014). Because the hours of a day are strongly dependent, 183 randomly chosen days (25%; n = 4,364 hours) were held out as a test set, and all tuning used 5-fold cross-validation with whole days in the folds. We fitted a random forest (Breiman, 2001) of 500 trees with the ranger package (Wright & Ziegler, 2017). The number of predictors tried at each split (mtry = 8) and the minimum node size (5) were chosen from a grid by cross-validated root mean squared error (RMSE). The forest was compared on the test set with a linear regression and a single regression tree pruned by cross-validation (rpart; Therneau & Atkinson, 2023). Variable importance was the increase in test RMSE after permuting each predictor, and the relation to the main predictors was described with partial dependence. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

On the held-out days the random forest predicted hourly rentals with an RMSE of 50.3 and a mean absolute error of 30.8, R² = .92. A linear regression with the same predictors was clearly less accurate (RMSE = 102.6, R² = .68), as was a single pruned tree (RMSE = 65.9, R² = .87; Table 1). The hour of the day was by far the most important predictor, followed by workingday, year and temp (Table 2). Partial dependence showed separate peaks in the morning and the afternoon on working days, and a single afternoon peak at other days. The 90% quantile-forest prediction intervals contained 92% of the observed test values.

Points to remember:

Report the error on data that were not used for fitting or tuning, with a baseline (a linear model, and the mean). Say how the data were split, and split by the unit that makes rows dependent (here the day).
Give the settings (mtry, minimum node size, number of trees), how you chose them, and the package and the seed.
Do not report the OOB error as a test error when the rows are not independent.
Describe importance as importance for the prediction, name the kind (permutation, impurity), and say what you did about correlated predictors.
Do not use causal wording for importance or partial dependence.
Cite R and the packages: citation("ranger") gives the reference.

title: Random Forest Regression: How Many Bikes Will People Rent This Hour?
text:
12. Summary







When
A continuous outcome, with nonlinear effects and interactions that you do not want to specify in advance, and enough data (hundreds of rows or more)


How it works
The average of many deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample, each split choosing among mtry random predictors


Why it works
Averaging cuts the variance to \(\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B\); random predictor subsets lower \(\rho\)


How (R)
ranger::ranger(y ~ ., data, num.trees = 500, mtry, min.node.size); predict(fit, newdata)$predictions


Tuning
mtry first, minimum node size second, then enough trees (a few hundred); cross-validate by the unit that makes rows dependent


Out-of-bag error
A free estimate of the test error, only for independent rows


Importance
Prefer permutation importance on held-out data to impurity importance; shuffle correlated predictors together


Shape of effects
Partial dependence, by hand in a few lines


Uncertainty
quantreg = TRUE and predict(..., type = "quantiles")


Limits
No extrapolation beyond the training range; importance is not causation; a black box with no coefficients

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Ordinary least squares (OLS) picks coefficients \(\beta\) that minimize the residual sum of squares (RSS): \(\sum(y_i - X_i\beta)^2\). That works fine until predictors are correlated with each other (multicollinearity) or there are many predictors relative to observations — then OLS coefficients become unstable: tiny changes in the data can swing them wildly, and the model overfits.
Regularized regression fixes this by adding a penalty on the size of the coefficients to the loss function, so the optimizer is discouraged from letting any coefficient get too large. Which penalty you choose gives you a different member of the same family:









Method
Penalty added to RSS
glmnet alpha
Effect




Ridge
\(\lambda \sum \beta_j^2\) (L2)
0
Shrinks coefficients toward zero, never exactly zero


Lasso
\(\lambda \sum \lvert\beta_j\rvert\) (L1)
1
Shrinks and can zero coefficients out (variable selection)


Elastic Net
a weighted mix of L1 and L2
0–1
Compromise: some sparsity, handles correlated predictors better than pure lasso



All of these introduce one new tuning parameter, \(\lambda\) (how strong the penalty is), which has to be chosen — that choice is a running theme through this script.
The dataset throughout is the built-in mtcars: predicting mpg (miles per gallon) from the other car characteristics (cylinders, weight, horsepower, etc.), several of which are strongly correlated (e.g. wt and disp) — exactly the setting where ridge/lasso earn their keep over plain lm().


Code
# y is centered; X is standardized inside glmnet for the CV/IC fits (standardize = TRUE);
# the coefficient-path plots and hridge use raw X (standardize = FALSE)
y <- as.matrix(scale(mtcars$mpg, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE))
X <- as.matrix(mtcars[, !names(mtcars) %in% "mpg"])
dim(X)

Code

Elastic Net
a weighted mix of L1 and L2
0–1
Compromise: some sparsity, handles correlated predictors better than pure lasso



All of these introduce one new tuning parameter, \(\lambda\) (how strong the penalty is), which has to be chosen — that choice is a running theme through this script.
The dataset throughout is the built-in mtcars: predicting mpg (miles per gallon) from the other car characteristics (cylinders, weight, horsepower, etc.), several of which are strongly correlated (e.g. wt and disp) — exactly the setting where ridge/lasso earn their keep over plain lm().


Code
# y is centered; X is standardized inside glmnet for the CV/IC fits (standardize = TRUE);
# the coefficient-path plots and hridge use raw X (standardize = FALSE)
y <- as.matrix(scale(mtcars$mpg, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE))
X <- as.matrix(mtcars[, !names(mtcars) %in% "mpg"])
dim(X)


[1] 32 10


Code
colnames(X)


 [1] "cyl"  "disp" "hp"   "drat" "wt"   "qsec" "vs"   "am"   "gear" "carb"

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Ridge regression

Fitting ridge and choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation
glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, ...) — alpha = 0 is what tells glmnet “this is ridge, not lasso.” The function needs a value (or grid) of lambda to try. Rather than guess one, cv.glmnet() performs k-fold cross-validation: it fits ridge on each grid value of \(\lambda\), holds out folds to measure prediction error, and reports which \(\lambda\) generalizes best (lambda.min).


Code
lambdas_to_try <- 10^seq(-3, 5, length.out = 100)

ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try,
                       standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
plot(ridge_cv)









The plot shows cross-validated MSE (y-axis) against \(-\log(\lambda)\) (x-axis, so penalty strength decreases from left to right). Too large a \(\lambda\) underfits (left), too small overfits (right). The two dotted vertical lines mark lambda.min (minimum CV error) and lambda.1se (the largest \(\lambda\) whose CV error is within one standard error of that minimum).


Code
lambda_cv <- ridge_cv$lambda.min
lambda_cv


[1] 2.983647


Code
model_cv <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_cv, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_cv <- predict(model_cv, X)
rsq_ridge_cv <- cor(y, y_hat_cv)^2
rsq_ridge_cv


            s0
[1,] 0.8524086




Choosing \(\lambda\) by information criteria (AIC/BIC) instead
Cross-validation isn’t the only way to pick \(\lambda\). This section computes AIC and BIC directly for every candidate \(\lambda\), as an alternative to CV.
The subtlety: AIC/BIC need a “degrees of freedom” value, and in ridge regression that isn’t just the number of predictors (since coefficients are shrunk, not freely estimated) — it’s the trace of the ridge hat matrix \(H = X(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\), which continuously decreases from \(p\) (at \(\lambda=0\), same as OLS) toward 0 as \(\lambda \to \infty\).
One caveat: glmnet minimizes \(\frac{1}{2N}\text{RSS} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum\beta_j^2\) (and scales \(y\) internally), so its \(\lambda\) is not on the same scale as the \(\lambda\) in \(X^\top X + \lambda I\). The df computed here is therefore an approximation, not the exact effective df of each glmnet fit. The residuals come from the actual glmnet predictions, and BIC uses the usual \(\text{df} \cdot \log(n)\) penalty.


Code
X_scaled <- scale(X)
aic <- bic <- c()

for (lambda in seq(lambdas_to_try)) {
  model <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try[lambda], standardize = TRUE)
  resid <- y - predict(model, X)

  # Ridge hat matrix and its trace = effective degrees of freedom
  ld <- lambdas_to_try[lambda] * diag(ncol(X_scaled))
  H <- X_scaled %*% solve(t(X_scaled) %*% X_scaled + ld) %*% t(X_scaled)
  df <- tr(H)  # tr() comes from the psych package

  aic[lambda] <- nrow(X_scaled) * log(t(resid) %*% resid) + 2 * df
  bic[lambda] <- nrow(X_scaled) * log(t(resid) %*% resid) + df * log(nrow(X_scaled))
}

plot(log(lambdas_to_try), aic, col = "orange", type = "l", ylim = range(c(aic, bic)),
     ylab = "Information Criterion")
lines(log(lambdas_to_try), bic, col = "skyblue3")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = c("orange", "skyblue3"), legend = c("AIC", "BIC"))









BIC penalizes model complexity (degrees of freedom) more heavily than AIC once you have more than a handful of observations, which is why it typically prefers a larger \(\lambda\) (a simpler, more shrunk model) than AIC does — visible here as the skyblue curve’s minimum (at \(\lambda \approx\) 5.21) sitting to the right of the orange curve’s (at \(\lambda \approx\) 2.48).


Code
lambda_aic <- lambdas_to_try[which.min(aic)]
lambda_bic <- lambdas_to_try[which.min(bic)]
c(lambda_aic = lambda_aic, lambda_bic = lambda_bic)


lambda_aic lambda_bic 
  2.477076   5.214008 


Code
model_aic <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_aic, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_aic <- predict(model_aic, X)
rsq_ridge_aic <- cor(y, y_hat_aic)^2

model_bic <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_bic, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_bic <- predict(model_bic, X)
rsq_ridge_bic <- cor(y, y_hat_bic)^2

c(rsq_ridge_aic = rsq_ridge_aic, rsq_ridge_bic = rsq_ridge_bic)


rsq_ridge_aic rsq_ridge_bic 
    0.8536968     0.8481806 




Visualizing the shrinkage itself
This is the most direct illustration of what ridge actually does. Each line is one predictor’s coefficient, traced across every value of \(\lambda\) tried. The x-axis is \(-\log(\lambda)\), so \(\lambda\) grows from right to left. Follow any single line from right (small \(\lambda\), close to the unpenalized OLS coefficient) to left (large \(\lambda\)): it bends toward zero, but — unlike lasso below — none of the lines ever reaches zero and stays there.


Code
plot(glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = FALSE), xvar = "lambda")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = 1:6, legend = colnames(X), cex = 0.7)

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
section: Heteroscedastic ridge: penalizing each coefficient differently
text:
Heteroscedastic ridge: penalizing each coefficient differently
Plain ridge penalizes every coefficient equally (\(\lambda \sum \beta_j^2\), same \(\lambda\) for every \(j\)). But if some predictors are inherently noisier than others, treating them identically may not be ideal. Heteroscedastic ridge instead gives each coefficient its own penalty weight \(w_j\), derived from that predictor’s own simple (univariate) regression:
\[\text{minimize} \quad \sum(y_i - X_i\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum w_j \beta_j^2\]
Predictors whose univariate slope has a larger standard error get a larger \(w_j\) and are shrunk more. Because \(X\) is not standardized here, these weights largely reflect each predictor’s units (e.g. disp, measured in cubic inches, gets a tiny weight), so standardize \(X\) first if you want \(w_j\) to reflect uncertainty.


Code
# w_j = variance of the coefficient from a simple regression of y on X[,j] alone
weights <- sapply(seq(ncol(X)), function(predictor) {
  uni_model <- lm(y ~ X[, predictor])
  summary(uni_model)$coefficients[2, 2]^2  # squared standard error
})
names(weights) <- colnames(X)
weights


         cyl         disp           hp         drat           wt         qsec           vs           am         gear         carb 
1.039475e-01 2.220137e-05 1.024003e-04 2.270160e+00 3.125940e-01 3.127160e-01 2.664632e+00 3.113184e+00 1.711206e+00 3.232441e-01 




Code
hridge_loss <- function(betas, y, X, lambda, weights) {
  sum((y - X %*% betas)^2) + lambda * sum(weights * betas^2)
}

hridge <- function(y, X, lambda, weights) {
  # Regular ridge gives a sensible starting point for the numerical optimizer
  model_init <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = lambda, standardize = FALSE)
  betas_init <- as.vector(model_init$beta)

  # Pass lambda/weights explicitly so the loss never picks up a global variable;
  # BFGS converges here, while the default Nelder-Mead stops at maxit for 10 parameters
  coef <- optim(betas_init, hridge_loss, y = y, X = X, lambda = lambda,
                weights = weights, method = "BFGS")$par
  fitted <- X %*% coef
  rsq <- cor(y, fitted)^2
  names(coef) <- colnames(X)
  list(coef = coef, fitted = fitted, rsq = rsq)
}

hridge_model <- hridge(y, X, lambda = 0.001, weights = weights)
rsq_hridge_0001 <- hridge_model$rsq
hridge_model$coef


        cyl        disp          hp        drat          wt        qsec          vs          am        gear        carb 
-0.40433235  0.01319901 -0.02206732  0.50014598 -3.64524339  0.58652650  0.39718262  2.31882063  0.40427348 -0.15931827 


Choosing \(\lambda\) here could use the same cross-validation or AIC/BIC strategies shown above for plain ridge — not implemented here, but see momisc::hridge for a fuller implementation.

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Lasso: L1 penalty, sparse coefficients
Switching alpha from 0 to 1 changes the penalty from L2 (\(\sum\beta_j^2\)) to L1 (\(\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)). The geometry of the L1 penalty (a diamond-shaped constraint region vs. ridge’s circular one) means its corners often land exactly on an axis — i.e., some coefficients get shrunk all the way to zero. That makes lasso a built-in variable-selection method, not just a shrinkage method.


Code
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
plot(lasso_cv)









Code
lambda_cv_lasso <- lasso_cv$lambda.min
model_cv_lasso <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_cv_lasso, standardize = TRUE)
y_hat_cv_lasso <- predict(model_cv_lasso, X)
rsq_lasso_cv <- cor(y, y_hat_cv_lasso)^2
rsq_lasso_cv


            s0
[1,] 0.8424217




Code
res <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas_to_try, standardize = FALSE)
plot(res, xvar = "lambda")
legend("bottomright", lwd = 1, col = 1:6, legend = colnames(X), cex = 0.7)









Compare this plot to ridge’s coefficient path above: here, lines don’t just bend toward zero, they hit zero and stay there as \(\lambda\) grows (moving left on the \(-\log(\lambda)\) axis; the numbers along the top count the non-zero coefficients) — each one dropping out is lasso “deciding” that predictor isn’t worth keeping at that penalty strength.

Comparing R² across methods so far


Code
rsq <- cbind("R-squared" = c(rsq_ridge_cv, rsq_ridge_aic, rsq_ridge_bic,
                              rsq_hridge_0001, rsq_lasso_cv))
rownames(rsq) <- c("ridge cross-validated", "ridge AIC", "ridge BIC",
                    "hridge 0.001", "lasso cross-validated")
print(rsq)


                      R-squared
ridge cross-validated 0.8524086
ridge AIC             0.8536968
ridge BIC             0.8481806
hridge 0.001          0.8679368
lasso cross-validated 0.8424217


These are all in-sample R² (predicting on the same X used to fit), so they’re useful for comparing the methods to each other here, but shouldn’t be read as an estimate of real-world predictive accuracy — that’s what the cross-validation step is doing internally when picking \(\lambda\), just not reported as a final held-out number here.

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
section: Elastic net: mixing L1 and L2
text:
Elastic net: mixing L1 and L2
Elastic net adds both penalties at once, weighted by alpha between 0 (pure ridge) and 1 (pure lasso). In glmnet’s parameterization the penalty is:
\[\lambda \left[ \alpha \sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\sum\beta_j^2 \right]\]
It’s useful when you want lasso’s variable-selection behavior but have groups of correlated predictors — pure lasso tends to arbitrarily pick just one predictor out of a correlated group and zero out the rest, while elastic net’s ridge component lets correlated predictors share the credit more smoothly.
Here, caret::train() searches over both alpha and lambda simultaneously (method = "glmnet"), using repeated cross-validation to score each combination.
Note: building the data with cbind(y, X) would not work. scale() returns an unnamed column, so the first column is named "" (V1 once coerced to a data frame), and mpg ~ . fails with “object ‘mpg’ not found”. Naming the column explicitly avoids this:


Code
library(caret)
train_control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5,
                               search = "random", verboseIter = FALSE)

data_enet <- data.frame(mpg = as.vector(y), X)
elastic_net_model <- train(mpg ~ ., data = data_enet, method = "glmnet",
                            preProcess = c("center", "scale"), tuneLength = 25,
                            trControl = train_control)




Code
elastic_net_model$bestTune


       alpha   lambda
1 0.06072057 1.166075


Code
y_hat_enet <- predict(elastic_net_model, X)
rsq_enet <- cor(y, y_hat_enet)^2
rsq_enet


          [,1]
[1,] 0.8579053

title: Regularized Regression: Ridge, Heteroscedastic Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net
text:
Summary

All four methods (ridge, heteroscedastic ridge, lasso, elastic net) are OLS plus a penalty on coefficient size; they differ only in which penalty.
Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero — good for multicollinearity, keeps every predictor in the model.
Heteroscedastic ridge lets each predictor be penalized by its own confidence (via per-coefficient weights) instead of one blanket penalty.
Lasso (L1) shrinks and zeroes out coefficients — a built-in feature selector, at the cost of being less stable when predictors are correlated.
Elastic net mixes both, tunable via alpha, and is often the practical default when you’re not sure which of ridge or lasso suits your data.
In every case, the real modeling decision isn’t “ridge vs. lasso” alone — it’s how you choose \(\lambda\) (cross-validation vs. information criteria), since that controls the whole bias/variance trade-off.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
General Electric and Westinghouse were the two giants of electrical engineering in the United States. How much did each of them invest in new equipment every year, and what did it depend on? Grunfeld’s theory says: on the value of the firm (what the market expects of it) and on the capital that it already has (which must be replaced). So there is a regression for each firm:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{invest}_{GE,t} &= \beta_{1} + \beta_{2}\,\text{value}_{GE,t} + \beta_{3}\,\text{capital}_{GE,t} + \varepsilon_{GE,t} \\
\text{invest}_{W,t}  &= \gamma_{1} + \gamma_{2}\,\text{value}_{W,t} + \gamma_{3}\,\text{capital}_{W,t} + \varepsilon_{W,t}
\end{aligned}\]
The two equations have nothing in common. Different firms, different outcomes, different predictors, different coefficients. They seem unrelated. But both firms lived through the same years. A good year for the whole industry, which neither value nor capital explains, makes both errors positive. Then the error of one equation contains information about the error of the other.
Arnold Zellner (1962) showed how to use this information. His method, seemingly unrelated regressions (SUR), estimates the equations together and gets more precise coefficients than separate regressions. His example was this one, with these two firms.
SUR is the neighbour of multivariate regression. There, all equations have the same predictors, and joint estimation changes nothing. Here the predictors differ, and it does.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(systemfit)   # systems of equations: OLS, SUR and others
library(lmtest)      # dwtest(): autocorrelation

firm_colours <- c("General Electric" = "#2a78d6", "Westinghouse" = "#eb6834")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
f4   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
1. The data
Grunfeld’s data have been used in so many textbooks that several wrong versions went around. Kleiber and Zeileis (2010) went back to the original and corrected them. Their version is in the R package AER, and as a CSV file in the Rdatasets collection:

head(grunfeld[, c("firm", "year", "invest", "value", "capital")], 3)

[1] TRUE

years  from    to

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?

2. Look at the data


Code
both <- rbind(ge, wh)
ggplot(both, aes(year, invest, colour = firm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = firm_colours, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Investment of the two firms", x = NULL, y = "million dollars (constant prices)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









General Electric is the larger firm, and the two series move together. But do the errors of the two regressions move together? That is what matters.


Code
ols_ge <- lm(invest ~ value + capital, data = ge)
ols_wh <- lm(invest ~ value + capital, data = wh)
round(
  rbind(GE = coef(summary(ols_ge))["value", ], Westinghouse = coef(summary(ols_wh))["value", ]),
  4
)


             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
GE             0.0266     0.0156  1.7057   0.1063
Westinghouse   0.0529     0.0157  3.3677   0.0037


Code
r_errors <- cor(resid(ols_ge), resid(ols_wh))
r_errors


[1] 0.728965




Code
errors <- data.frame(year = ge$year, GE = resid(ols_ge), W = resid(ols_wh))
ggplot(errors, aes(GE, W)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_text(aes(label = year), size = 2.8, nudge_y = 1.4, colour = "grey40") +

  theme_bw()









They do: the residuals of the two regressions correlate at 0.73. In 1941 and 1947, for example, both firms invested more than their values and capitals explain, and in 1950 both invested less. The two regressions are not unrelated at all.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the errors of one year are correlated
Let \(m\) be the number of equations (firms) and \(T\) the number of years. Within a year, the errors of the equations have a covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). Between years, the errors are independent:
\[\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, \varepsilon_{jt}) = \sigma_{ij}, \qquad \text{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, \varepsilon_{js}) = 0 \;\text{ for } t \ne s\]


Step 2: stack the equations
Write the two outcomes one below the other, and the predictors in blocks:
\[\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} y_{GE} \\ y_W \end{pmatrix}}_{y} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} X_{GE} & 0 \\ 0 & X_W \end{pmatrix}}_{X} \begin{pmatrix} \beta \\ \gamma \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{GE} \\ \varepsilon_W \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \Sigma \otimes I_T\]
The Kronecker product \(\Sigma \otimes I_T\) is a matrix of \(2 \times 2\) blocks: in each block, \(\sigma_{ij}\) on the diagonal, because only errors of the same year are related. It is now one regression with correlated errors, which is generalized least squares (see this page):
\[\hat\beta_{SUR} = \big(X^\top (\Sigma^{-1} \otimes I)\, X\big)^{-1} X^\top (\Sigma^{-1} \otimes I)\, y, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\beta_{SUR}) = \big(X^\top (\Sigma^{-1} \otimes I)\, X\big)^{-1}\]


Step 3: \(\Sigma\) is unknown, so estimate it

Estimate each equation by OLS, and keep the residuals.
\(\hat\sigma_{ij} = \sum_t e_{it} e_{jt} / T\). (Dividing by \(T - k\) instead, with \(k\) coefficients per equation, is the other common choice.)
Put \(\hat\Sigma\) into the formula: feasible GLS.

The step from 1 to 3 can be repeated with the new residuals until nothing changes. The end is the maximum likelihood estimate for normal errors.


Step 4: where the gain comes from
Suppose the residual of General Electric in 1946 is large and positive. Because the errors correlate, we expect a positive error for Westinghouse in 1946, too. SUR takes that expected error out of Westinghouse’s investment before it looks for the slope. It is like a covariate that OLS does not have.


Step 5: when there is nothing to gain
Two cases give exactly the OLS estimates:

The errors are uncorrelated (\(\sigma_{ij} = 0\)): no information to pass on.
All equations have the same predictors: the covariate of step 4 would be orthogonal to the predictors by construction.

The gain is largest when the errors are highly correlated and the predictors are not.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
4. The estimates by hand


Code
X_ge <- model.matrix(ols_ge); X_wh <- model.matrix(ols_wh)
Tn <- nrow(X_ge); k <- ncol(X_ge)
Z  <- matrix(0, Tn, k)
X  <- rbind(cbind(X_ge, Z), cbind(Z, X_wh))                            # the block matrix of step 2
y  <- c(ge$invest, wh$invest)
colnames(X) <- c(
  paste0("GE_", c("intercept", "value", "capital")),
  paste0("W_", c("intercept", "value", "capital"))
)

E     <- cbind(GE = resid(ols_ge), W = resid(ols_wh))
Sigma <- crossprod(E) / Tn
round(Sigma, 1)


      GE     W
GE 660.8 176.4
W  176.4  88.7


Code
W     <- kronecker(solve(Sigma), diag(Tn))                             # inverse of Sigma ⊗ I
V_sur <- solve(t(X) %*% W %*% X)
b_sur <- drop(V_sur %*% t(X) %*% W %*% y)
cbind(OLS = c(coef(ols_ge), coef(ols_wh)), SUR = b_sur, SE_SUR = sqrt(diag(V_sur)))

value        0.02655119   0.03831021  0.01329011
capital      0.15169387   0.13903627  0.02303559

Covariance of the residuals used for estimation is \(\hat\Sigma\) from the OLS residuals, and ... correlations of the residuals shows the link between the equations, after the final fit.

McElroy R² is a single \(R^2\) for the whole system. The \(R^2\) of an equation can be lower than with OLS, because OLS makes each \(R^2\) as large as possible, and SUR does not aim for that.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
5. Tests

Are the equations related at all? The Breusch–Pagan test
The null hypothesis is that \(\Sigma\) is diagonal. Under it, \(T\) times the sum of the squared correlations of the OLS residuals follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with \(m(m-1)/2\) degrees of freedom (Breusch & Pagan, 1980). (This is another test than the Breusch–Pagan test for unequal variances.)


Code
lm_stat <- Tn * r_errors^2
c(LM = lm_stat, df = 1, p = pchisq(lm_stat, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))


          LM           df            p 
10.627798572  1.000000000  0.001114003 


The errors are related, \(\chi^2\)(1) = 10.63, p = .001.


Do the two firms invest alike?
The question of the title compares coefficients between equations. Separate regressions cannot do it properly: the two estimates are correlated. In the system it is an ordinary linear hypothesis, with the covariance matrix of all six coefficients:
\[H_0:\; \beta_2 = \gamma_2 \;\text{ and }\; \beta_3 = \gamma_3\]


Code
equal_slopes <- linearHypothesis(
  sur,
  c("GE_value_ge - W_value_wh = 0", "GE_capital_ge - W_capital_wh = 0"),
  test = "F"
)
equal_slopes


Linear hypothesis test (F statistic of a Wald test)

Hypothesis:
GE_value_ge - W_value_wh = 0
GE_capital_ge - W_capital_wh = 0

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: sur

  Res.Df Df      F Pr(>F)
1     36                 
2     34  2 2.0004 0.1509


Code
difference <- function(term_a, term_b) {
  d <- b[[term_a]] - b[[term_b]]
  s <- sqrt(vcov(sur)[term_a, term_a] + vcov(sur)[term_b, term_b] - 2 * vcov(sur)[term_a, term_b])
  c(difference = d, SE = s, t = d / s)
}
diffs <- rbind(
  value = difference("GE_value_ge", "W_value_wh"),
  capital = difference("GE_capital_ge", "W_capital_wh")
)
diffs

value   -0.01931959 0.01170707 -1.650250
capital  0.07505821 0.04514405  1.662638


We cannot say that the slopes differ, F(2, 34) = 2.00, p = .151. That is not evidence that they are the same: with 20 years the standard errors of the differences are large. If theory says that the slopes are equal, we can impose it, and estimate them with both firms’ data:


Code
restricted <- systemfit(
  equations,
  method = "SUR",
  data = wide,
  restrict.matrix = c("GE_value_ge - W_value_wh = 0", "GE_capital_ge - W_capital_wh = 0")
)

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
6. When does SUR help? Experiments

The same predictors: nothing happens
If each firm had all four predictors (its own and the other’s), the equations would have identical right-hand sides:


Code
same_rhs <- list(GE = invest_ge ~ value_ge + capital_ge + value_wh + capital_wh,
                 W  = invest_wh ~ value_ge + capital_ge + value_wh + capital_wh)
max(abs(
  coef(systemfit(same_rhs, method = "OLS", data = wide)) -
    coef(systemfit(same_rhs, method = "SUR", data = wide))
))


[1] 1.193534e-11


The largest difference between OLS and SUR is zero, up to rounding, although the errors are correlated. This is the case of multivariate regression.


A known truth: how large is the gain, and are the standard errors right?
We take the predictors of the real data, a truth equal to our SUR estimates, and errors with a chosen correlation. For each correlation we simulate 1,000 histories of 20 years, and compare the true spread of the estimates of one slope with the standard errors that the programs report:


Code
set.seed(12)
truth <- b_sur
sds   <- sqrt(diag(Sigma))
fit_both <- function(yy) {
  b_o <- c(qr.coef(qr(X_ge), yy[1:Tn]), qr.coef(qr(X_wh), yy[Tn + 1:Tn]))
  e <- matrix(yy - X %*% b_o, Tn)
  S <- crossprod(e) / (Tn - k) # the cautious version, with degrees of freedom
  Si <- solve(S)
  A <- rbind(
    cbind(Si[1, 1] * crossprod(X_ge), Si[1, 2] * crossprod(X_ge, X_wh)),
    cbind(Si[2, 1] * crossprod(X_wh, X_ge), Si[2, 2] * crossprod(X_wh))
  )
  y1 <- yy[1:Tn]
  y2 <- yy[Tn + 1:Tn]
  V <- solve(A)
  b_s <- V %*%
    c(
      Si[1, 1] * crossprod(X_ge, y1) + Si[1, 2] * crossprod(X_ge, y2),
      Si[2, 1] * crossprod(X_wh, y1) + Si[2, 2] * crossprod(X_wh, y2)
    )
  c(
    ols = b_o[[2]],
    sur = b_s[[2]],
    se_ols = sqrt(S[1, 1] * solve(crossprod(X_ge))[2, 2]),
    se_sur = sqrt(V[2, 2])
  )
}
rhos <- c(0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.73, 0.9)
experiment <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rhos, function(rho) {
  S0 <- diag(sds) %*% matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2) %*% diag(sds)
  L  <- t(chol(S0))
  r  <- replicate(1000, fit_both(drop(X %*% truth) + as.vector(t(L %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * Tn), 2)))))
  data.frame(rho, SD_OLS = sd(r["ols", ]), SD_SUR = sd(r["sur", ]),
             reported_OLS = mean(r["se_ols", ]), reported_SUR = mean(r["se_sur", ]))
}))
experiment$gain <- 1 - experiment$SD_SUR / experiment$SD_OLS
round(experiment, 4)

4 0.73 0.0142 0.0134       0.0142       0.0130  0.0589

sim_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(rho = rhos, sd = experiment$SD_OLS, what = "OLS: true spread"),
  data.frame(rho = rhos, sd = experiment$SD_SUR, what = "SUR: true spread"),
  data.frame(rho = rhos, sd = experiment$reported_SUR, what = "SUR: reported standard error")
)

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6", "#2a78d6"),
    name = NULL,
    breaks = c("OLS: true spread", "SUR: true spread", "SUR: reported standard error")
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("solid", "solid", "dashed"),
    name = NULL,
    breaks = c("OLS: true spread", "SUR: true spread", "SUR: reported standard error")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "The slope of value for General Electric, 1,000 simulations each",
    x = "correlation of the errors of the two equations",
    y = "standard deviation of the estimate"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")










With uncorrelated errors SUR gains nothing (-0.3%). It even loses a little, because it estimates a correlation that is zero.
With the correlation of our data (0.73) the estimates are 5.9% more precise, and with 0.9, 17.4%.
The reported standard errors of SUR are smaller than the true spread: 0.0130 against 0.0134 at 0.73. The formula takes \(\hat\Sigma\) for the true \(\Sigma\). With 20 years and two equations the error is small. It grows with the number of equations, as the third experiment shows.

With five firms there are 10 correlations to estimate from 20 years. They range from -0.27 to 0.73: the electrical firms and US Steel go together, the car makers hardly go with them. The reported standard errors of General Electric get smaller with more firms. Can we believe them?


Many equations: the standard errors stop being true
Again a known truth: the predictors of 2, 5 and 10 of the firms, their OLS coefficients, and errors that correlate at 0.4 between all the firms. How does the reported standard error of the slope of value (first firm) compare with the true spread of the estimates?


Code
set.seed(13)
firms <- setdiff(unique(grunfeld$firm), "American Steel")             # ten firms
many <- function(m, reps = 500) {
  d <- lapply(c("General Electric", setdiff(firms, "General Electric"))[1:m], function(f) {
    subset(grunfeld, firm == f)
  })
  Xs <- lapply(d, function(z) cbind(1, z$value, z$capital))
  fits <- lapply(seq_len(m), function(j) lm.fit(Xs[[j]], d[[j]]$invest))
  mu <- sapply(fits, function(f) f$fitted.values)
  s0 <- sapply(fits, function(f) sqrt(sum(f$residuals^2) / (Tn - k)))
  R <- matrix(0.4, m, m)
  diag(R) <- 1
  L <- t(chol(diag(s0) %*% R %*% diag(s0)))
  r <- replicate(reps, {
    Ys <- mu + t(L %*% matrix(rnorm(m * Tn), m))
    Es <- sapply(seq_len(m), function(j) lm.fit(Xs[[j]], Ys[, j])$residuals)
    Si <- solve(crossprod(Es) / (Tn - k))
    A <- do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:m, function(i) {
        do.call(cbind, lapply(1:m, function(j) Si[i, j] * crossprod(Xs[[i]], Xs[[j]])))
      })
    )
    v <- do.call(
      c,
      lapply(1:m, function(i) {
        rowSums(sapply(1:m, function(j) Si[i, j] * crossprod(Xs[[i]], Ys[, j])))
      })
    )
    V <- solve(A)
    c(est = sum(V[2, ] * v), se = sqrt(V[2, 2]))
  })
  data.frame(
    equations = m,
    covariances = m * (m + 1) / 2,
    true_spread = sd(r["est", ]),
    reported_SE = mean(r["se", ]),
    ratio = mean(r["se", ]) / sd(r["est", ])
  )
}
trap <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(2, 5, 10), many))
round(trap, 4)

2         5          15      0.0144      0.0124 0.8599
3        10          55      0.0144      0.0103 0.7110


With two equations the reported standard error is 1.03 times the true one, with five 0.86 and with ten 0.71. With ten firms and 20 years there are 55 variances and covariances to estimate, and the formula does not know how badly.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

Many equations, few years. \(\Sigma\) has \(m(m+1)/2\) elements. If \(m\) comes close to \(T\), the reported standard errors become far too small, as in the third experiment; with \(m > T\) the estimate of \(\Sigma\) cannot even be inverted. Beck and Katz (1995) showed this for panels of countries, and proposed to keep OLS and correct its standard errors instead (panel-corrected standard errors).
Autocorrelation. SUR allows errors to correlate between equations in the same year, not between years. Our residuals fail here:



Code
dw <- rbind(
  GE = unlist(dwtest(ols_ge)[c("statistic", "p.value")]),
  Westinghouse = unlist(dwtest(ols_wh)[c("statistic", "p.value")])
)
round(dw, 3)


             statistic.DW p.value
GE                  1.072   0.004
Westinghouse        1.413   0.037



The Durbin–Watson statistics (1.07 and 1.41, far below 2) show positive autocorrelation, so all the standard errors of this page, OLS and SUR, are too small. A serious analysis would add autoregressive errors to each equation (Parks’ method), or dynamics.
One wrong equation spoils the others. If the equation of one firm lacks an important predictor, its error goes through \(\Sigma\) into the estimates of the other firms. OLS keeps such damage inside its own equation. SUR is more precise when everything is right, and less robust when something is wrong.
Endogeneity. SUR does not help if a predictor depends on the errors, for example if investment raises the value of the firm in the same year. (Here the value is that of the beginning of the year.) Three-stage least squares combines SUR with instrumental variables: method = "3SLS".
Pooling. If the coefficients are the same in all equations, a panel model is simpler and more precise. SUR is for few units, many times and different coefficients.
In psychology and sociology the same model appears as a path model with correlated residuals. lavaan fits it with y1 ~ x1; y2 ~ x2; y1 ~~ y2, and with maximum likelihood it gives the iterated estimates. For categorical outcomes, the bivariate probit model is the relative of SUR.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the equations, why they are estimated together, the residual correlation and its test, the method and its variant, and the estimates. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
terms <- c("Intercept", "Value", "Capital")
fmt <- function(v) ifelse(rep(terms, 2) == "Intercept", f1(v), f3(v))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Equation  = c("General Electric", "", "", "Westinghouse", "", ""),
  Predictor = rep(terms, 2),
  ols  = fmt(coef(ols)), ols_se = fmt(se_ols),
  sur  = fmt(b), sur_se = fmt(se),
  t    = f2(b / se))


Method (data analysis):

We modelled the annual gross investment of General Electric and Westinghouse from 1935 to 1954 (T = 20 years, million dollars; Grunfeld’s data as corrected by Kleiber & Zeileis, 2010) with one equation per firm, with the market value of the firm and its stock of capital as predictors. Because both firms were exposed to the same economic conditions, the equations were estimated jointly by seemingly unrelated regressions (Zellner, 1962), using the residual covariance matrix of the OLS equations with a correction for degrees of freedom. Independence of the equations was tested with the Breusch–Pagan (1980) test, and equality of the slopes with an F test on the joint estimates. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package systemfit (Henningsen & Hamann, 2007).

Results:

The residuals of the two equations were correlated, r = .73, χ²(1) = 10.63, p = .001. In the joint estimates (Table 1), investment increased with the value of the firm both for General Electric, b = 0.038, SE = 0.014, t(17) = 2.66, and for Westinghouse, b = 0.058, SE = 0.015, t(17) = 3.96. The slopes of the two firms did not differ significantly, F(2, 34) = 2.00, p = .151. The residuals were autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson = 1.07 and 1.41), so the standard errors are probably too small.

Points to remember:

Report the residual correlations: they are the reason for the method.
Say how \(\hat\Sigma\) was computed (divisor, one step or iterated).
Show OLS next to SUR. If they differ by more than precision can explain, suspect a wrong equation.
Give the number of equations and of time points.

title: Seemingly Unrelated Regression: Do General Electric and Westinghouse Invest Alike?
text:
9. Summary



When
Several regressions with different predictors whose errors are correlated, such as firms in the same years or outcomes of the same people


The model
Stacked equations, errors with covariance \(\Sigma \otimes I\)


How (R)
systemfit(list(eq1 = y1 ~ x1, eq2 = y2 ~ x2), method = "SUR", data = wide)


The estimator
Feasible GLS: OLS, then \(\hat\Sigma\) from its residuals, then GLS; iterated = maximum likelihood


Gain
Large with correlated errors and different predictors


No gain
Uncorrelated errors, or the same predictors everywhere


Tests
Breusch–Pagan for \(\Sigma\) diagonal; linearHypothesis() between equations


Dangers
Many equations and few times; autocorrelation; one misspecified equation


Related pages
Multivariate regression, generalized least squares
