title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
In the 1880s Francis Galton offered prizes to families who would send him their measurements. He wanted to know how height passes from parents to children. One result puzzled him: very tall parents had tall children, but not as tall as themselves; very short parents had short children, but not as short. Children “regressed” towards the average. He called it regression towards mediocrity (Galton, 1886), and the name stuck to the method.
This page asks his question with his data: how much of a father’s extra height does his son get?
Simple linear regression answers with a straight line: one outcome \(y\) (the son’s height), one predictor \(x\) (the father’s height), and a line that goes through the cloud of points as closely as possible. All the other regressions on this site are extensions of it, so this page goes slowly through every number that R prints.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL(): standard errors for sons who share a father
library(lmtest)     # coeftest(), coefci(): tests and intervals with those standard errors

line_colours <- c("regression line" = "#2a78d6", "son = father" = "#eb6834")

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
1. The data
Galton’s notebooks were transcribed by James Hanley (2004). The table is in the R package HistData, and as a CSV file in the Rdatasets collection: one row per grown-up child.


Code
url <- "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/HistData/GaltonFamilies.csv"
galton <- read.csv(url)
head(galton[, c("family", "father", "mother", "gender", "childHeight")], 4)


  family father mother gender childHeight
1    001   78.5     67   male        73.2
2    001   78.5     67 female        69.2
3    001   78.5     67 female        69.0
4    001   78.5     67 female        69.0


Heights are in inches (1 inch = 2.54 cm), most of them rounded to the nearest half inch or inch. We keep the sons, one row each:


Code
sons <- subset(galton, gender == "male", select = c(family, father, childHeight))
names(sons)[3] <- "son"
# one row per couple
parents <- unique(subset(galton, gender == "male", select = c(family, father, mother)))
nrow(sons)


[1] 481


Code
length(unique(sons$family))   # how many fathers


[1] 179


Code
summary(sons[, c("father", "son")])


     father           son       
 Min.   :62.00   Min.   :60.00  
 1st Qu.:68.00   1st Qu.:67.50  
 Median :69.00   Median :69.20  
 Mean   :69.14   Mean   :69.23  
 3rd Qu.:70.50   3rd Qu.:71.00  
 Max.   :78.50   Max.   :79.00  


There are 481 sons of 179 fathers. Fathers average 69.1 inches (175.6 cm) and sons 69.2 (175.9 cm): the two generations are equally tall. A father with several sons appears several times, a point to which section 6 returns.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
ggplot(sons, aes(father, son)) +
  geom_abline(
    aes(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "son = father"),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.1, seed = 1),
    alpha = 0.4,
    colour = "grey30",
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = "regression line"), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = line_colours, name = NULL) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(61, 79), ylim = c(59, 80)) +
  labs(
    title = "Sons against fathers",
    x = "father's height (inches)",
    y = "son's height (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The cloud rises: taller fathers have taller sons. (The points are nudged a little, because the rounding puts many of them on the same spot.) If every son were as tall as his father, the points would lie along the dashed line. They do not. The regression line is flatter: on the right it lies below the dashed line, on the left above it. That is what Galton saw:


Code
tallest  <- sons$father >= 73
shortest <- sons$father <= 66
tails <- data.frame(group       = c("fathers of 73 inches or more", "fathers of 66 inches or less"),
                    n           = c(sum(tallest), sum(shortest)),
                    mean_father = c(mean(sons$father[tallest]), mean(sons$father[shortest])),
                    mean_son    = c(mean(sons$son[tallest]),    mean(sons$son[shortest])))
tails


                         group  n mean_father mean_son
1 fathers of 73 inches or more 29    73.98276 71.01034
2 fathers of 66 inches or less 63    65.31746 67.56825


The tallest fathers are on average 4.8 inches above the average father, but their sons are only 1.8 inches above the average son. The shortest fathers are 3.8 inches below; their sons, 1.7.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a line plus scatter
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\]

\(\beta_1\), the slope: how many inches taller, on average, are the sons of fathers who are one inch taller.
\(\beta_0\), the intercept: the average son of a father of height 0. Nobody has that height, so here it only fixes how high the line sits.
\(\varepsilon_i\), the error: how far son \(i\) is from the line. The mother, the food, the illnesses of childhood and luck are all in there.



Step 2: the least-squares line
Any line leaves residuals, \(e_i = y_i - (b_0 + b_1 x_i)\), the vertical distances from the points to the line. The least-squares line makes \(\sum_i e_i^2\) as small as possible. Setting the two derivatives of this sum to zero gives
\[b_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2} = \frac{\text{cov}(x, y)}{\text{var}(x)}, \qquad b_0 = \bar y - b_1 \bar x\]
The second formula says that the line goes through the point of the two means, \((\bar x, \bar y)\).


Code
x <- sons$father
y <- sons$son
n <- length(y)

b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
c(b0 = b0, b1 = b1)


        b0         b1 
38.3625810  0.4465226 




Step 3: the slope is a correlation in disguise
The correlation is the covariance divided by both standard deviations, and the slope divides by the variance of \(x\) only. So
\[b_1 = r \,\frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
In standard deviations, the rule is even shorter: a father who is 1 SD above the mean has sons who are, on average, \(r\) SDs above theirs.


Code
r <- cor(x, y)
c(r = r, s_x = sd(x), s_y = sd(y), slope = r * sd(y) / sd(x))


        r       s_x       s_y     slope 
0.3923835 2.3057667 2.6239049 0.4465226 




Step 4: why there is always regression to the mean
A correlation is never larger than 1, and in real data it is smaller. So a father 2 SDs above the mean has sons about \(2r\) = 0.78 SDs above it, closer to the mean. No force pulls the sons back. A very tall father is usually tall for two reasons, the genes he passes on and other causes that he does not (good food, luck, an error in the measurement). His sons inherit the first part and get their own share of the second, which is average on average.
The same holds in the other direction: very tall sons have fathers who are less tall than they are. Heights do not shrink to the mean from generation to generation; the spread of the sons (\(s\) = 2.62) is not smaller than that of the fathers (\(s\) = 2.31).


Step 5: how sure are we? The standard error of the slope
A different sample of families would give a different slope. If the errors are independent and have the same variance \(\sigma^2\), the spread of the slope from sample to sample is
\[SE(b_1) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}}, \qquad s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i e_i^2}{n - 2}}\]
\(s\) is the residual standard error, the typical distance of a son from the line; \(n - 2\) because two numbers, \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), were estimated. The slope is more precise when the points lie close to the line, when there are many of them, and when the fathers differ a lot in height. Then
\[t = \frac{b_1}{SE(b_1)} \quad\text{with } n - 2 \text{ degrees of freedom}, \qquad 95\%\ \text{CI} = b_1 \pm t_{0.975}\, SE(b_1)\]


Code
e     <- y - (b0 + b1 * x)                         # residuals
s     <- sqrt(sum(e^2) / (n - 2))                  # residual standard error
se_b1 <- s / sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2))
t_b1  <- b1 / se_b1
p_b1  <- 2 * pt(abs(t_b1), df = n - 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
ci_b1 <- b1 + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n - 2) * se_b1
c(s = s, SE = se_b1, t = t_b1, p = p_b1, lower = ci_b1[1], upper = ci_b1[2])


           s           SE            t            p        lower        upper 
2.415990e+00 4.782546e-02 9.336504e+00 3.737109e-19 3.525490e-01 5.404962e-01 




Step 6: how much is explained? R²
The total variation of the sons splits in two, the part that the line follows and the part left around it:
\[\underbrace{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\sum_i (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{\sum_i e_i^2}_{\text{left over}}, \qquad R^2 = \frac{\text{explained}}{\text{total}}\]
With one predictor, \(R^2 = r^2\): here \(0.392^2\) = 0.154.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output


Code
fit <- lm(son ~ father, data = sons)
summary(fit)



Call:
lm(formula = son ~ father, data = sons)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-9.3959 -1.5122  0.0413  1.6217  9.3808 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 38.36258    3.30837  11.596   <2e-16 ***
father       0.44652    0.04783   9.337   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.416 on 479 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.154, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1522 
F-statistic: 87.17 on 1 and 479 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Every number of section 3 is there. Part by part:








In the output
Meaning
Here




Residuals
Five numbers of the \(e_i\); they should be roughly symmetric around 0
half of the sons are between -1.5 and +1.6 inches from the line


Estimate, father
The slope \(b_1\)
0.447 inches of son for one inch of father


Estimate, (Intercept)
\(b_0\), the line at \(x = 0\)
38.4 inches: no meaning by itself


Std. Error
How uncertain the estimate is
0.048 for the slope


t value
Estimate / Std. Error
9.34


Pr(>|t|)
The chance of a \(t\) this far from 0 if the true slope were 0
far below .001


Residual standard error
\(s\), the typical distance from the line
2.42 inches


Multiple R-squared
\(R^2 = r^2\)
0.154


F-statistic
The test of the whole model. With one predictor, \(F = t^2\)
\(9.34^2\) = 87.2





Code
# the intercept becomes useful if we centre the father's height
centred <- lm(son ~ I(father - mean(father)), data = sons)
round(coef(summary(centred)), 3)


                         Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)                69.234      0.110 628.489        0
I(father - mean(father))    0.447      0.048   9.337        0


The model with the centred predictor is the same line with the same slope. Its intercept, 69.23, is now the average height of the sons of an average father.

What the slope says about Galton’s question
A father who is one inch taller than another has sons who are 0.45 inches taller on average, 95% CI [0.35, 0.54]. So a son gets somewhat less than half of his father’s extra height. Two hypotheses are tested by this one interval:

No link (\(\beta_1 = 0\)), the test that R prints: rejected, the interval is far from 0.
Sons equal to their fathers on average, whatever the father’s height (\(\beta_1 = 1\)): also rejected, the interval is far from 1. R does not print this test, but the t is easy: \((b_1 - 1)/SE = -11.6\).

Always ask which value of the slope is the interesting one. It is not always zero.


Two regressions, not one
Predicting fathers from sons is a different regression, and not the first line turned around:


Code
reverse <- lm(father ~ son, data = sons)
c(
  son_on_father = b1,
  father_on_son = coef(reverse)[["son"]],
  turned_around = 1 / coef(reverse)[["son"]]
)


son_on_father father_on_son turned_around 
    0.4465226     0.3448085     2.9001602 


Code
c(product_of_slopes = b1 * coef(reverse)[["son"]], r_squared = r^2)


product_of_slopes         r_squared 
        0.1539648         0.1539648 




Code
two <- rbind(
  data.frame(line = "son predicted from father", intercept = b0, slope = b1),
  data.frame(
    line = "father predicted from son",
    intercept = -coef(reverse)[[1]] / coef(reverse)[[2]],
    slope = 1 / coef(reverse)[[2]]
  )
)

ggplot(sons, aes(father, son)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.1, seed = 1),
    alpha = 0.25,
    colour = "grey40",
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_abline(data = two, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = line), linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = mean(x), y = mean(y), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("son predicted from father" = "#2a78d6", "father predicted from son" = "#1baf7a"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(61, 79), ylim = c(59, 80)) +
  labs(
    title = "Two regression lines through the same cloud",
    subtitle = "They cross at the two means (black point)",
    x = "father's height (inches)",
    y = "son's height (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Least squares measures vertical distances, the errors in what we predict. Swap the roles and the errors to make small are the horizontal ones, so the line changes. The product of the two slopes is \(r^2\), and the lines coincide only when \(r = \pm 1\). The choice of \(y\) is the choice of what to predict. When neither variable is the outcome, because both measure the same thing with error, use Deming regression.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
section: 5. Predictions: for the average son, or for one son?
text:
5. Predictions: for the average son, or for one son?
How tall will the sons of a father of 74 inches (188.0 cm) be? There are two questions in this one:

How tall are such sons on average? Only the line is uncertain: a confidence interval.
How tall will one such son be? The line is uncertain, and the son scatters around it: a prediction interval.

\[SE_{\text{mean}} = s\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0 - \bar x)^2}{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}}, \qquad SE_{\text{one}} = s\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0 - \bar x)^2}{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}}\]


Code
new <- data.frame(father = 74)
conf <- predict(fit, new, interval = "confidence")
pred <- predict(fit, new, interval = "prediction")
rbind(average_son = conf, one_son = pred)


       fit      lwr      upr
1 71.40525 70.89964 71.91086
1 71.40525 66.63116 76.17935


Code
# the same by hand, for the standard errors
h0 <- 1 / n + (74 - mean(x))^2 / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
c(se_mean = s * sqrt(h0), se_one = s * sqrt(1 + h0))


  se_mean    se_one 
0.2573177 2.4296545 


The average of such sons is 71.4 inches, 95% CI [70.9, 71.9]. One such son will be between 66.6 and 76.2 inches with 95% probability: a range of 24.3 cm. More families would shrink the first interval towards nothing. They would not shrink the second below about \(\pm 2s\).


Code
grid  <- data.frame(father = seq(62, 78.5, by = 0.25))
bands <- rbind(
  cbind(
    grid,
    predict(fit, grid, interval = "prediction"),
    band = "95% prediction interval: one son"
  ),
  cbind(
    grid,
    predict(fit, grid, interval = "confidence"),
    band = "95% confidence interval: the average son"
  )
)
bands$band <- factor(bands$band, levels = unique(bands$band))

ggplot(sons, aes(father, son)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = bands, aes(y = fit, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, fill = band), alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.1, seed = 1),
    alpha = 0.35,
    colour = "grey30",
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_line(data = cbind(grid, son = predict(fit, grid)), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#f3d19c", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The line is known well; one son is not",
       x = "father's height (inches)", y = "son's height (inches)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
inside <- predict(fit, interval = "prediction")
share_inside <- mean(sons$son >= inside[, "lwr"] & sons$son <= inside[, "upr"])


Of the sons in the data, 95.8% lie inside the prediction band, close to the 95% it promises. The line is only for fathers between 62 and 78.5 inches: the data say nothing beyond that.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
6. Checking the assumptions
The estimates need the line to be the right shape. The standard errors, t tests and intervals also need errors that are independent and equally spread. The prediction interval needs them to be roughly normal too. In order of importance:


Code
check <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(fit), resid = resid(fit), std = rstandard(fit))
check$q <- qqnorm(check$std, plot.it = FALSE)$x

pa <- ggplot(check, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.05, seed = 1),
    alpha = 0.4,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals against fitted values",
    x = "fitted height (inches)",
    y = "residual (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
pb <- ggplot(check, aes(q, std)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q plot", x = "normal quantile", y = "standardised residual") +
  theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)










Linearity. The orange curve stays near 0, with no U and no wave. The RESET test adds powers of the fitted values to the model and asks whether they help; they do not, p = .817. If there were a bend, see polynomial regression.
Equal spread. The band is equally wide from left to right. The Breusch–Pagan test finds nothing, p = .573. If the spread changed, see weighted least squares.
Normal errors. The points follow the line in the Q-Q plot, with a few sons further out than a normal distribution would put them. With 481 rows this matters little for the slope, but the prediction interval depends on it.
Influence. The largest Cook’s distance is 0.049, far below 1: no son moves the line by himself. If some did, see robust regression.
Independence. This one fails, and no plot above shows it.


Brothers are not independent
The 481 sons have only 179 fathers. Brothers share a mother, a kitchen and a childhood, so if one is taller than the line says, his brother probably is too:


Code
sons$resid <- resid(fit)
families   <- split(sons$resid, sons$family)
pairs      <- do.call(rbind, lapply(families[lengths(families) > 1], function(v) t(combn(v, 2))))
both_ways  <- rbind(pairs, pairs[, 2:1])              # each pair counted in both orders
brother_r  <- cor(both_ways)[1, 2]
c(pairs_of_brothers = nrow(pairs), correlation = brother_r)


pairs_of_brothers       correlation 
      605.0000000         0.2899052 


The residuals of two brothers correlate at 0.29. So 481 sons carry less information than 481 unrelated men, and the usual standard error is too small. Cluster-robust standard errors keep the line and allow any correlation within a family:


Code
v_cl    <- vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~ family)
robust  <- coeftest(fit, vcov = v_cl)
ci_cl   <- coefci(fit, vcov. = v_cl)
rbind(usual          = coef(summary(fit))["father", ],
      cluster_robust = robust["father", ])


                Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
usual          0.4465226 0.04782546 9.336504 3.737109e-19
cluster_robust 0.4465226 0.05546032 8.051209 6.537981e-15


The standard error of the slope goes from 0.048 to 0.055, 1.16 times as large, and the 95% CI from [0.35, 0.54] to [0.34, 0.56]. The conclusions do not change here, but the honest interval is the wider one. A model with a random intercept for each family is the other way (see multilevel models).

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

A slope is a difference between people, not an effect. Taller fathers differ from shorter ones in other ways too: their wives are a little taller, for example (the heights of the parents correlate at 0.11), and their families may have been better fed. The slope is what we should expect of a son when we know his father’s height, not what would happen if a father grew.
One parent is half of the story. Adding the mother’s height is a job for multiple regression (see hierarchical regression).
A measurement error in \(x\) flattens the slope. Families reported their own measurements, and most are rounded. Noise in \(x\) biases the slope towards 0 (attenuation), so part of the gap between 0.45 and 1 may be error; noise in \(y\) only widens the scatter.
Regression to the mean explains many “effects”. Choose the worst schools, the sickest patients or the best athletes of one year, and the next year they will be closer to average, whatever was done to them in between (Barnett et al., 2005). Compare with a control group chosen in the same way.
\(R^2\) is not the quality of the model. It is low here (0.15) because much besides the father decides a son’s height, and the line is nevertheless right. A high \(R^2\) can come with a wrong model, as with the CO₂ record in polynomial regression.
The sample is not the population. Galton’s families answered an advertisement with prizes, in England in the 1880s.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the variables and their units, the slope with its uncertainty, the test, and \(R^2\). The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
fs <- summary(fit)$fstatistic
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Intercept", "Father's height (inches)"),
  b   = f2(coef(fit)),
  SE  = f3(robust[, 2]),
  CI  = paste0("[", f2(ci_cl[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci_cl[, 2]), "]"),
  t   = f2(robust[, 3]),
  p   = sapply(robust[, 4], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  beta = c("—", nz(r, 2)))


Method (data analysis):

We analysed the heights of 481 adult sons of 179 fathers collected by Galton (1886) and transcribed by Hanley (2004). We regressed the son’s height on the father’s height, both in inches, by ordinary least squares. Because 302 of the sons had a brother earlier in the file, we report cluster-robust standard errors with families as clusters (Zeileis et al., 2020). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

Sons (M = 69.23, SD = 2.62) were as tall on average as their fathers (M = 69.14, SD = 2.31). Father’s height predicted son’s height, b = 0.45, 95% CI [0.34, 0.56], t(479) = 8.05, p < .001, R² = .15 (Table 1). For each additional inch of the father, sons were 0.45 inches taller on average. The slope was also below 1, showing regression to the mean: the sons of fathers 2 SD above the mean were expected to be 0.78 SD above it.

Points to remember:

Give b with its units, its confidence interval, the test with its degrees of freedom, and R².
Say which value the slope was tested against, if it was not zero.
The standardised slope β is the correlation when there is one predictor. Report it as well if readers will compare studies.
Say what one row is, and whether rows belong together.
Do not write “effect” or “leads to” for a difference between people who were not assigned to anything.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Do Tall Fathers Have Tall Sons?
text:
9. Summary



When
A continuous outcome and one predictor, related by a straight line


The model
\(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\)


The estimates
\(b_1 = \text{cov}(x, y)/\text{var}(x) = r\, s_y / s_x\); the line goes through \((\bar x, \bar y)\)


How (R)
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d), then summary(), confint(), predict()


Reading it
The slope is the average difference in \(y\) between units that differ by 1 in \(x\)


Regression to the mean
Extreme \(x\) go with less extreme \(y\) whenever \(|r| < 1\)


Prediction
interval = "confidence" for the average, interval = "prediction" for one case


Checks
Residuals against fitted values, Q-Q plot, Cook’s distance, and how the rows were collected


If it fails
Bend: polynomial. Unequal spread: WLS. Outliers: robust. Dependence: cluster-robust errors or multilevel models

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
text:
People die of heat, and people die of cold. Between the two there must be a temperature at which the fewest people die. What is it? And how much worse are the extremes?
No formula is known for this curve. It should be high on the left, low in the middle and high on the right, but it need not be a parabola: heat may act suddenly above some threshold, and cold slowly. So we want a method that finds the shape by itself. But we also need more than a smooth line through a cloud of points (as LOESS gives). In winter there are also influenza, short days and indoor air. The season must be in the model next to the temperature, like a covariate in a regression.
Splines are flexible curves made of ordinary regression columns. A generalized additive model (GAM) is a regression in which some predictors enter as splines:
\[\log E(\text{deaths}) = \beta_0 + s_1(\text{temperature}) + s_2(\text{time}) + \text{day of the week}\]
Each \(s\) is a smooth curve whose shape and wiggliness are estimated from the data. The rest is a generalized linear model, as in this page.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(mgcv)      # gam(): generalized additive models (comes with R)
library(splines)   # bs(), ns(): spline columns for any regression (comes with R)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
text:
1. The data
The data are the daily deaths in Chicago (accidents excluded) and the weather and air pollution of each day, from 1987 to 2000. They come from a large American study of mortality and air pollution (Samet et al., 2000), and the authors of the R package dlnm distribute them:


Code
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rda")
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gasparrini/dlnm/master/data/chicagoNMMAPS.rda",
              path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
load(path)
chicago <- chicagoNMMAPS[, c("date", "time", "dow", "death", "temp")]
nrow(chicago)


[1] 5114


Code
summary(chicago[, c("death", "temp")])


     death            temp        
 Min.   : 69.0   Min.   :-26.667  
 1st Qu.:105.0   1st Qu.:  1.667  
 Median :114.0   Median : 10.556  
 Mean   :115.4   Mean   : 10.107  
 3rd Qu.:124.0   3rd Qu.: 19.444  
 Max.   :411.0   Max.   : 33.333  


Code
chicago[order(-chicago$death), ][1:5, ]


           date time      dow death       temp
3118 1995-07-15 3118 Saturday   411 30.0000000
3119 1995-07-16 3119   Sunday   287 28.3333333
3120 1995-07-17 3120   Monday   228 25.8333333
3117 1995-07-14 3117   Friday   226 33.0555556
1096 1989-12-31 1096   Sunday   186 -0.8333333


There are 5,114 days. death is the number of deaths, temp the mean temperature of the day in °C, dow the day of the week and time counts the days. An average day has 115.4 deaths. The worst days are in July 1995: a heat wave, with 411 deaths on one day.
Cold may take days to act, for example through infections. So we also compute the mean temperature of the seven days before each day:


Code
# mean of today and the 6 days before
running <- as.numeric(stats::filter(chicago$temp, rep(1 / 7, 7), sides = 1))
chicago$week <- c(NA, running[-length(running)]) # moved by one day: the 7 days before today
chicago <- subset(chicago, !is.na(week))
nrow(chicago)


[1] 5107

2. Look at the data


Code
pa <- ggplot(chicago, aes(date, death)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4, colour = "grey30") +

  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(60, 240)) +
  labs(

    x = "temperature (°C)",
    y = "deaths"
  ) +

patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)









The first chart shows the seasons: every winter is a hill. The second one falls with the temperature, and turns up at the hot end. But part of the fall may be the winter itself, and not the cold.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
section: 3. Splines step by step, with formulas
text:
3. Splines step by step, with formulas

Step 1: polynomials in pieces
Cut the range of the temperature at some points, the knots, and use a cubic polynomial in each piece, joined so smoothly that the eye does not see the joints: equal value, slope and curvature on both sides. That is a cubic spline. It can bend where it is needed, and a bend on one side does not disturb the other side, as it would in a polynomial.


Step 2: a spline is a sum of columns
Any cubic spline can be written as a weighted sum of fixed curves, the basis functions:
\[s(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \beta_j\, B_j(x)\]
So once the knots are fixed, a spline is a linear model: each \(B_j(x)\) is a column, and least squares finds the \(\beta\)’s. The basis of B-splines has functions that are zero except over a few pieces:


Code
grid  <- seq(min(chicago$temp), max(chicago$temp), length.out = 300)
knots <- seq(-27, 34, length.out = 9)                                  # 8 pieces, for the drawing
B     <- splineDesign(c(rep(knots[1], 3), knots, rep(knots[9], 3)), grid, outer.ok = TRUE)
basis <- data.frame(
  temp = grid,
  value = as.vector(B),
  j = factor(rep(seq_len(ncol(B)), each = length(grid)))
)

ggplot(basis, aes(temp, value, group = j)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = j), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knots, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey60") +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(title = paste(ncol(B), "B-spline basis functions (the dotted lines are the knots)"),
       x = "temperature (°C)", y = "value of the column") +
  theme_bw()











Step 3: how many knots? Use many, and pay for the wiggles
With few knots the curve is stiff, with many it follows the noise. And where to put them? The modern answer is: take more than enough knots, and add a penalty for wiggliness to the sum of squares:
\[\sum_i \big[y_i - s(x_i)\big]^2 + \lambda \int s''(x)^2\, dx\]
\(s''\) is the curvature. \(\lambda\) decides the price: with \(\lambda = 0\) we get the wild curve of all the knots, with \(\lambda \to \infty\) a straight line. The penalty is a quadratic form in the coefficients, \(\lambda\, \beta^\top S \beta\), so the solution is still a formula, like ridge regression:
\[\hat\beta = (B^\top B + \lambda S)^{-1} B^\top y\]
For B-splines with equally spaced knots, a simple and good \(S\) makes neighbouring coefficients differ smoothly. It is built from their second differences (P-splines; Eilers & Marx, 1996):


Code
x <- chicago$temp; y <- chicago$death
n_basis <- 20
step  <- (max(x) - min(x)) / (n_basis - 3)
# equally spaced knots, beyond the ends too
ts <- seq(min(x) - 3 * step, max(x) + 3 * step, by = step)
B_    <- splineDesign(ts, x, outer.ok = TRUE)
D <- diff(diag(ncol(B_)), differences = 2) # second differences of the coefficients
S     <- crossprod(D)
fit_by_hand <- function(lambda) {
  A    <- solve(crossprod(B_) + lambda * S)
  beta <- A %*% crossprod(B_, y)
  edf  <- sum(diag(A %*% crossprod(B_)))                             # effective degrees of freedom
  rss  <- sum((y - B_ %*% beta)^2)
  list(beta = beta, edf = edf, GCV = length(y) * rss / (length(y) - edf)^2)
}
lambdas <- 10^seq(-2, 7, by = 0.25)
trials  <- lapply(lambdas, fit_by_hand)
gcv     <- sapply(trials, `[[`, "GCV")
best    <- which.min(gcv)
c(best_lambda = lambdas[best], edf = trials[[best]]$edf)


best_lambda         edf 
   3.162278   12.689426 




Step 4: effective degrees of freedom
The penalty ties the coefficients together, so 20 columns do not count as 20 parameters. The effective degrees of freedom (edf), the trace of the matrix that turns \(y\) into \(\hat y\), count how many parameters the curve really uses: 2 for a straight line, 20 for the unpenalised spline, and here 12.7.


Step 5: choosing \(\lambda\)
By hand we took the \(\lambda\) with the smallest GCV (generalised cross-validation), which imitates leaving out one day at a time. mgcv can do the same. The better default today is REML: the penalty is read as a statement that the coefficients come from a normal distribution, and \(\lambda\) becomes a variance ratio that is estimated like that of a mixed model. REML overfits less often (Wood, 2011).


Code
shown <- c(which(lambdas == 10^-2), best, length(lambdas))
B_grid <- splineDesign(ts, grid, outer.ok = TRUE)
curves <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(shown, function(k) {
    data.frame(
      temp = grid,
      death = drop(B_grid %*% trials[[k]]$beta),
      label = sprintf(
        "λ = %s, edf = %.1f",
        format(lambdas[k], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, digits = 2),
        trials[[k]]$edf
      )
    )
  })
)
curves$label <- factor(curves$label, levels = unique(curves$label))

ggplot(chicago, aes(temp, death)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.15, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(colour = label), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(80, 200)) +
  labs(
    title = "Too little penalty, the GCV choice, and too much",
    x = "temperature (°C)",
    y = "deaths"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
same <- gam(death ~ s(temp, bs = "ps", k = n_basis), data = chicago, method = "GCV.Cp")
c(edf_by_hand = trials[[best]]$edf, edf_mgcv = sum(same$edf))


edf_by_hand    edf_mgcv 
   12.68943    12.91523 


The same P-spline in mgcv has 12.9 edf: our grid of \(\lambda\) was only a little coarser than its search.


Step 6: from one spline to a GAM
A GAM puts several splines side by side, each with its own \(\lambda\), and a link function and distribution around them. The counts of deaths vary a bit more than a Poisson distribution allows, so we use the negative binomial (family = nb), which adds one parameter for the extra variation. The \(s\) curves are centred: each has mean zero over the data, and the intercept takes the level.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
section: 4. Fitting the models and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the models and reading the output

Model A: temperature alone


Code
model_a <- gam(death ~ s(temp) + dow, family = nb, data = chicago, method = "REML")
summary(model_a)



Family: Negative Binomial(198.233) 
Link function: log 

Formula:
death ~ s(temp) + dow

Parametric coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error  z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  4.728910   0.004362 1084.225  < 2e-16 ***
dowMonday    0.034737   0.006136    5.661 1.51e-08 ***
dowTuesday   0.027201   0.006144    4.427 9.55e-06 ***
dowWednesday 0.009819   0.006160    1.594 0.110926    
dowThursday  0.012516   0.006155    2.033 0.042007 *  
dowFriday    0.019083   0.006150    3.103 0.001916 ** 
dowSaturday  0.022355   0.006147    3.637 0.000276 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
          edf Ref.df Chi.sq p-value    
s(temp) 7.705  8.502   1115  <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

R-sq.(adj) =  0.178   Deviance explained = 18.9%
-REML =  20513  Scale est. = 1         n = 5107



Parametric coefficients are as in any GLM with a log link: \(e^{0.035}\) = 1.035, so Mondays have 3.5% more deaths than Sundays.
edf of s(temp) = 7.7: how wiggly the curve is. 1 would be a straight line.
p-value of a smooth tests whether the whole curve is flat. It is approximate, and with 5,107 days nearly everything is “significant”. Look at the curve instead.
Deviance explained plays the role of \(R^2\): 18.9%.

There is no table of coefficients for the curve. It has coefficients, but nobody reads them. A smooth is read as a picture.


Model B: add the season and the long-term trend
The smooth of time follows the slow changes from 1987 to 2000: winters, summers, a changing population. With 14 years and about 10 degrees of freedom a year it can follow the seasons but not single days: k = 150 gives it room, and REML decides how much to use.


Code
model_b <- gam(
  death ~ s(temp) + s(time, k = 150) + dow,
  family = nb,
  data = chicago,
  method = "REML"
)
summary(model_b)$s.table


               edf     Ref.df   Chi.sq p-value
s(temp)   7.288273   8.214878  154.777       0
s(time) 106.959544 125.862132 1333.443       0


Code
c(deviance_explained = summary(model_b)$dev.expl)


deviance_explained 
         0.3771583 




Model C: add the week before


Code
model_c <- gam(
  death ~ s(temp) + s(week) + s(time, k = 150) + dow,
  family = nb,
  data = chicago,
  method = "REML"
)
summary(model_c)$s.table


              edf     Ref.df   Chi.sq p-value
s(temp)  6.924380   7.938209 177.1123       0
s(week)  8.553357   8.933656 209.4865       0
s(time) 93.933745 113.094755 801.6846       0


Code
c(deviance_explained = summary(model_c)$dev.expl)


deviance_explained 
         0.3927253 


Code
AIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)


               df      AIC
model_a  16.02954 40953.02
model_b 123.88909 39858.20
model_c 119.87738 39724.88


The AIC falls by 1,094.8 when the season enters, and by another 133.3 with the week before. What happens to the temperature curve?


Code
# the curve of one or more smooths (in % of deaths, relative to the average of the curve), with its
# 95% band
curve_of <- function(model, terms, newdata) {
  X <- predict(model, newdata, type = "lpmatrix") # the columns of the model at these values
  # keep only these terms
  X[, !grepl(paste(gsub("([()])", "\\\\\\1", terms), collapse = "|"), colnames(X))] <- 0
  fit <- drop(X %*% coef(model))
  se <- sqrt(rowSums((X %*% vcov(model)) * X))
  data.frame(
    newdata,
    fit = 100 * (exp(fit) - 1),
    low = 100 * (exp(fit - 1.96 * se) - 1),
    high = 100 * (exp(fit + 1.96 * se) - 1)
  )
}
at <- data.frame(temp = seq(-22, 32, by = 0.5))
at$week <- 10
at$time <- 2500
at$dow <- "Wednesday" # the other terms are set to zero anyway
three <- rbind(cbind(curve_of(model_a, "s(temp)", at), model = "A: temperature alone"),
               cbind(curve_of(model_b, "s(temp)", at), model = "B: + season and trend"),
               cbind(curve_of(model_c, "s(temp)", at), model = "C: + the week before"))




Code
ggplot(three, aes(temp, fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Temperature of the day and deaths: s(temp) in the three models",
       x = "temperature of the day (°C)", y = "deaths, % above or below the average") +
  theme_bw()









Code
low_point <- sapply(split(three, three$model), function(d) d$temp[which.min(d$fit)])
low_point


 A: temperature alone B: + season and trend  C: + the week before 
                 21.5                   3.5                 -22.0 


Code
at_cold <- sapply(split(three, three$model), function(d) d$fit[d$temp == -15])


Alone (A), the curve is the one everybody expects: high in the cold, lowest at 21.5 °C, and up in the heat. But once the season is in the model (B), the cold side disappears: on a day of −15 °C the curve is at -2.4%, against 10.4% before. A cold day is not deadlier than a mild day of the same season. The heat side stays. The smooth of the week before shows where the cold went:


Code
at_week <- data.frame(week = seq(-17, 28, by = 0.5), temp = 10, time = 2500, dow = "Wednesday")
week <- curve_of(model_c, "s(week)", at_week)

ggplot(week, aes(week, fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = "#1baf7a", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1baf7a", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "The week before and deaths: s(week) in model C",
    x = "mean temperature of the seven days before (°C)",
    y = "deaths, % above or below the average"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









After a cold week more people die. Heat kills at once, cold kills with a delay. With the temperature of one day only, and the season as a smooth, the delayed effect of cold was taken for season.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
section: 5. The answer: the temperature with the fewest deaths
text:
5. The answer: the temperature with the fewest deaths
The question is about a temperature that lasts: a week and a day at the same temperature. In the additive model this is the sum of the two curves, \(s_1(x) + s_2(x)\), at the same \(x\). We compute it for a grid, find its lowest point, and express everything relative to it, as a relative risk (RR). The uncertainty of a difference between two points of a curve comes from the model matrix and the covariance matrix of the coefficients:
\[\log \text{RR}(x) = (X_x - X_{\min})\,\hat\beta, \qquad SE = \sqrt{(X_x - X_{\min})\, V\, (X_x - X_{\min})^\top}\]


Code
lasting <- function(model, from = -20, to = 31) {
  g <- data.frame(temp = seq(from, to, by = 0.5))
  g$week <- g$temp
  g$time <- 2500
  g$dow <- "Wednesday"
  X <- predict(model, g, type = "lpmatrix")
  X[, !grepl("s\\(temp\\)|s\\(week\\)", colnames(X))] <- 0
  f <- drop(X %*% coef(model))
  i <- which.min(f)
  d <- sweep(X, 2, X[i, ]) # each row minus the row of the minimum
  logrr <- drop(d %*% coef(model))
  se <- sqrt(rowSums((d %*% vcov(model)) * d))
  set.seed(3)
  draws <- rmvn(2000, coef(model), vcov(model)) # 2,000 curves that are compatible with the data
  minima <- g$temp[apply(X %*% t(draws), 2, which.min)]
  list(
    curve = data.frame(
      temp = g$temp,
      rr = exp(logrr),
      low = exp(logrr - 1.96 * se),
      high = exp(logrr + 1.96 * se)
    ),
    minimum = g$temp[i],
    interval = quantile(minima, c(0.025, 0.975))
  )
}
answer <- lasting(model_c)
rr <- function(t) answer$curve[answer$curve$temp == t, ]
c(minimum = answer$minimum, answer$interval)


minimum    2.5%   97.5% 
   22.5    22.0    23.0

  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +

The fewest people die at 22.5 °C, with an interval from 22 to 23 °C (from 2,000 simulated curves).
At 30 °C the risk is 1.32 times as high, 95% CI [1.25, 1.38]. At −15 °C, 1.17 times, [1.12, 1.22].
The two sides have different shapes: the cold side rises slowly over 40 degrees, the hot side turns up sharply above about 25 °C. A parabola would have missed both.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
text:
6. Checking the model

Was the basis large enough?
k is the upper limit of the wiggliness. If the edf come close to it, the curve was cut short, and k should be raised:


Code
k.check(model_c)


         k'       edf   k-index p-value
s(temp)   9  6.924380 0.9997614  0.4975
s(week)   9  8.553357 0.9912516  0.2875
s(time) 149 93.933745 0.9198874  0.0000


k' is the limit and edf what was used. The smooths of temperature are near their limit of 9, so we double the limit and see if the answer changes:


Code
model_k <- gam(
  death ~ s(temp, k = 20) + s(week, k = 20) + s(time, k = 150) + dow,
  family = nb,
  data = chicago,
  method = "REML"
)
answer_k <- lasting(model_k)
rbind(
  k10 = c(edf = summary(model_c)$s.table[1:2, "edf"], minimum = answer$minimum, AIC = AIC(model_c)),
  k20 = c(
    edf = summary(model_k)$s.table[1:2, "edf"],
    minimum = answer_k$minimum,
    AIC = AIC(model_k)
  )
)


    edf.s(temp) edf.s(week) minimum      AIC
k10    6.924380    8.553357    22.5 39724.88
k20    8.672946   14.819002    23.5 39698.30


The minimum moves from 22.5 to 23.5 °C, and the AIC changes by -26.6. So the simulated interval of section 5 was too narrow: it takes the basis as given. The smooth of time fails the test of k.check (its p value is small), which brings us to the next point.


Autocorrelation


Code
lag1 <- sapply(list(A = model_a, B = model_b, C = model_c), function(m) {
  acf(resid(m, type = "pearson"), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
})
lag1


        A         B         C 
0.2868245 0.1248022 0.1080386 


The residuals of neighbouring days correlate at 0.29 in model A and 0.11 in model C. What is left is small, but it makes the bands a little too narrow. If time were given many more degrees of freedom, it would take it all, and with it part of the effect of temperature. How smooth the season should be is a judgement in this kind of study, and the honest thing is to vary it:


Code
season <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(30, 60, 100, 150, 200), function(k) {
    m <- gam(
      death ~ s(temp) + s(week) + s(time, k = k) + dow,
      family = nb,
      data = chicago,
      method = "REML"
    )
    a <- lasting(m)
    data.frame(
      k,
      edf_time = summary(m)$s.table["s(time)", "edf"],
      minimum = a$minimum,
      RR_cold = a$curve$rr[a$curve$temp == -15],
      RR_hot = a$curve$rr[a$curve$temp == 30],
      AIC = AIC(m)
    )
  })
)
round(season, 2)


    k edf_time minimum RR_cold RR_hot      AIC
1  30    24.49    22.5    1.28   1.31 40067.11
2  60    43.64    22.5    1.26   1.32 39977.34
3 100    75.78    22.5    1.18   1.31 39787.67
4 150    93.93    22.5    1.17   1.32 39724.88
5 200   100.06    22.5    1.16   1.32 39713.10


The lowest point and the hot side do not depend on it. The cold side does: the relative risk at −15 °C goes from 1.28 with a stiff season to 1.16 with a flexible one. Heat comes in short bursts that no season can imitate; cold lasts, and shares its time with the winter.


Concurvity
In a GAM two smooths can carry the same information, as correlated predictors do. It is called concurvity, on a scale from 0 to 1:


Code
round(concurvity(model_c, full = FALSE)$estimate, 2)


        para s(temp) s(week) s(time)
para       1    0.00    0.00    0.00
s(temp)    0    1.00    0.73    0.00
s(week)    0    0.71    1.00    0.01
s(time)    0    0.73    0.85    1.00


Each column says how much of the smooth could be explained by the one in the row. The temperatures of the day and of the week before overlap, as they must, which makes their separate curves less certain than their sum. And the smooth of time could explain most of the weekly temperature, because the season sets it: what the model calls the effect of a cold week is learned from weeks that were colder than usual for their season.


The heat wave of July 1995
One week may decide the hot side of the curve. Without the week of 13 to 19 July 1995:


Code
no_wave  <- subset(chicago, date < as.Date("1995-07-13") | date > as.Date("1995-07-19"))
model_w <- gam(
  death ~ s(temp) + s(week) + s(time, k = 150) + dow,
  family = nb,
  data = no_wave,
  method = "REML"
)
answer_w <- lasting(model_w)
rr_w <- function(t) answer_w$curve[answer_w$curve$temp == t, ]
rbind(with_the_week = rr(30), without_it = rr_w(30))


              temp       rr      low     high
with_the_week   30 1.316046 1.254072 1.381083
without_it      30 1.141997 1.094650 1.191393


Code
c(minimum_without_it = answer_w$minimum)


minimum_without_it 
                22 


The relative risk at 30 °C falls from 1.32 to 1.14. Both numbers are true, and they answer different questions: the second is the risk of a hot week, the first includes one catastrophe. The lowest point moves only from 22.5 to 22 °C.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
section: 7. Splines without penalties, and other choices
text:
7. Splines without penalties, and other choices
Splines are just columns, so they work in any regression function. ns(x, df) makes a natural cubic spline, which is a straight line beyond the last knots, and is the usual choice when the number of degrees of freedom is fixed in advance:


Code
glm_ns <- glm(
  death ~ ns(temp, df = 4) + ns(week, df = 4) + ns(time, df = 7 * 14) + dow,
  family = quasipoisson,
  data = chicago
)
g <- data.frame(temp = seq(-20, 31, by = 0.5))
g$week <- g$temp
g$time <- 2500
g$dow <- "Wednesday"
p_ns <- predict(glm_ns, g)
g$temp[which.min(p_ns)]


[1] 18.5


With 4 degrees of freedom for each temperature and 7 per year for the season, the lowest point is at 18.5 °C, against 22.5 °C: four degrees of freedom are too stiff for the sharp turn at the hot end. This is the weakness of fixed degrees of freedom. The result depends on a number that somebody had to choose, and the penalised model estimates it.

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Additive means that the curve of one predictor is the same at all values of the others. If heat is worse after a hot week, the model needs an interaction, a surface: te(temp, week).
Beyond the data, a penalised spline continues roughly straight. It is an extrapolation like any other.
edf is not the number of bends, and the p value of a smooth does not say where the curve matters. Report the picture with its band, and differences between meaningful points.
The band is pointwise, for the curve around its mean. For a difference from a reference point, use the model matrix as in section 5: the band is zero wide at the reference.
Delays. We used one day and one week. Distributed lag models (dlnm) estimate a curve for every delay (Gasparrini, 2011).
Not causal by itself. Influenza epidemics come in cold weeks, and the smooth of time cannot remove an epidemic of two weeks. Part of the “cold” curve may be influenza.
Deaths of one city say what the city is used to. Such curves differ between climates: people in warm places are hurt by cold that others do not notice (Curriero et al., 2002).
Speed. For large data use bam() instead of gam().

title: Splines and GAMs: At What Temperature Do the Fewest People Die?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the family and link, every smooth with its basis dimension, how the smoothness was chosen, the edf, the picture, and some numbers read from the curve. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
st <- summary(model_c)$s.table
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Smooth = c("Temperature of the day", "Mean temperature of the 7 days before", "Time"),
  k      = c(10, 10, 150),
  edf    = f1(st[, "edf"]),
  chi    = f1(st[, "Chi.sq"]),
  p      = sapply(st[, "p-value"], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))))
rr_table <- data.frame(t = c(-15, -10, 0, 10, 20, 25, 28, 30))
rr_table <- cbind(
  rr_table,
  answer$curve[match(rr_table$t, answer$curve$temp), c("rr", "low", "high")]
)


Method (data analysis):

We modelled the daily number of deaths (accidents excluded) in Chicago from 1987 to 2000 (N = 5,107 days) with a generalized additive model with a negative binomial distribution and a log link. The predictors were smooth functions (thin plate regression splines; Wood, 2017) of the mean temperature of the day, of the mean temperature of the seven preceding days and of time (basis dimension 150, for season and trend), and the day of the week. Smoothness was selected by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The relative risk of a temperature that lasts is the sum of the two temperature curves, relative to the temperature at which it is lowest; its confidence interval is based on the covariance matrix of the coefficients, and that of the temperature of minimum mortality on 2,000 simulations from their distribution. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package mgcv (Wood, 2017).

Results:

Deaths were related to the temperature of the day and to that of the preceding week (Table 1); the model explained 39.3% of the deviance. The temperature with the lowest mortality was 22.5 °C, 95% CI [22.0, 23.0]. Compared with it, the relative risk was 1.17, 95% CI [1.12, 1.22], at −15 °C and 1.32, 95% CI [1.25, 1.38], at 30 °C (Table 2). Without the heat wave of 13–19 July 1995 the relative risk at 30 °C was 1.14, 95% CI [1.09, 1.19]. The lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals was 0.11.

text:
10. Summary



When
The relation is smooth, its shape is unknown, and there are other predictors


Spline
A sum of basis functions, \(\sum \beta_j B_j(x)\): a linear model with special columns


Penalty
\(\lambda \int s''^2\): more than enough knots, and a price for wiggles


edf
How many parameters the penalised curve really uses


How (R)
gam(y ~ s(x1) + s(x2, k = 20) + z, family = , method = "REML"); fixed df: glm(y ~ ns(x, 4))


Reading it
Pictures with bands; differences from predict(..., type = "lpmatrix")


Checks
k.check(), gam.check(), residual autocorrelation, concurvity()


Related pages
LOESS, polynomial regression, generalized linear models

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
When air flows over the blade of a fan, a wind turbine or a wing, it makes noise, even if nothing vibrates. In the 1980s NASA measured it in a wind tunnel: blades of different sizes, at different speeds and angles, and the sound level at many frequencies (Brooks et al., 1989). Can we predict the noise of a blade that was not measured?
The relation is smooth, and complicated: the noise has a peak at some frequency, and the peak moves with the size, the speed and the angle. A linear regression cannot follow it. Support vector regression (SVR; Cortes & Vapnik, 1995; Smola & Schölkopf, 2004) is one of the classic machine-learning methods for such problems. It has two ideas:

Errors below some size do not count. Only the points that lie outside a tube around the curve have a say.
Curves from distances. The prediction for a new case is a weighted sum of its similarities to some of the old ones.

This page also shows something that has nothing to do with SVR and decides whether any of the results are true: how the test data are separated from the training data.


Code
library(e1071)      # svm()
library(mgcv)       # gam(), for comparison (comes with R)
library(ranger)     # random forest, for comparison
library(ggplot2)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
1. The data


Code
zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file(
  "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/291/airfoil+self+noise.zip",
  zip,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
wing <- read.table(
  unz(zip, "airfoil_self_noise.dat"),
  col.names = c("freq", "angle", "chord", "speed", "thick", "db")
)
wing$lf <- log10(wing$freq) # frequency in factors of ten
wing$lt  <- log10(wing$thick)
# one experiment: the same blade, speed and angle
wing$run <- paste(wing$angle, wing$chord, wing$speed)
c(rows = nrow(wing), experiments = length(unique(wing$run)))


       rows experiments 
       1503         106 


Code
summary(wing$db)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  103.4   120.2   125.7   124.8   130.0   141.0 


The file is in the UCI machine learning repository. db is the sound level in decibels; the predictors are the frequency (log, lf), the angle of the blade (degrees), its length (chord, metres), the speed of the air (m/s) and the thickness of the boundary layer at the edge (log, lt), which is a property of the flow.
The 1,503 rows are not 1,503 experiments. Each experiment, one blade at one speed and angle, gave a whole spectrum of about 14 frequencies. There are 106 experiments.

Split by experiment, not by row
If we put single rows at random into the training and the test set, then for nearly every test row its neighbours in the same spectrum are in the training set. A method that only connects the dots would look brilliant. But the question is about blades that were not measured. So whole experiments go to one side or the other:


Code
set.seed(151)
runs  <- unique(wing$run)
test_runs <- sample(runs, round(0.25 * length(runs)))
train <- subset(wing, !(run %in% test_runs))
test  <- subset(wing, run %in% test_runs)
c(
  train_rows = nrow(train),
  test_rows = nrow(test),
  train_experiments = length(unique(train$run)),
  test_experiments = length(unique(test$run))
)


       train_rows         test_rows train_experiments  test_experiments 
             1127               376                80                26

shown <- subset(wing, run %in% sample(runs, 9))
ggplot(shown, aes(freq, db)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 1.3, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~run) +

  labs(
    title = "Nine experiments (angle, chord, speed)",
    x = "frequency (Hz, log scale)",
    y = "sound level (dB)"

Each spectrum is smooth, with one hump. The position and the height of the hump change from experiment to experiment.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
section: 3. The method step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a tube instead of a line
Least squares punishes every error, by its square. SVR does not punish errors smaller than \(\varepsilon\) at all, and larger ones only in proportion:
\[L_\varepsilon(e) = \max(0,\; |e| - \varepsilon)\]


Code
e <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.01)
losses <- rbind(
  data.frame(e, loss = e^2, kind = "squared (least squares)"),
  data.frame(e, loss = abs(e), kind = "absolute (median regression)"),
  data.frame(e, loss = pmax(0, abs(e) - 1), kind = "ε-insensitive, ε = 1 (SVR)")
)
ggplot(losses, aes(e, loss, colour = kind)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 4)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1baf7a", "#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three ways to count an error", x = "error", y = "loss") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Step 2: as flat as possible
For a linear function \(f(x) = w^\top x + b\), SVR minimises
\[\frac{1}{2}\lVert w \rVert^2 + C \sum_i L_\varepsilon\big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)\]
The first part asks for a flat function (a penalty like that of ridge regression), the second for small errors outside the tube. The cost \(C\) is the exchange rate: a large \(C\) follows the data, a small \(C\) stays flat.


Step 3: support vectors
The solution can be written with one weight per training case:
\[f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i\, (x_i^\top x) + b, \qquad -C \le \alpha_i \le C\]
Cases strictly inside the tube have \(\alpha_i = 0\): they could be deleted without changing anything. The others are the support vectors. In the formula the predictors appear only in products \(x_i^\top x\) of two cases.


Step 4: the kernel
So replace the product by any other measure of similarity, a kernel \(K(x_i, x)\). The most used is the radial one,
\[K(x_i, x) = \exp\!\left(-\gamma\, \lVert x_i - x \rVert^2\right)\]
which is 1 for identical cases and falls to 0 with the distance. Now \(f\) is a sum of bumps centred at the support vectors, and can take any smooth shape, without ever naming a formula. \(\gamma\) decides how wide the bumps are: a small \(\gamma\) gives a stiff function, a large one a wiggly function.


Step 5: check the formula by hand


Code
small <- svm(
  db ~ lf + angle + chord + speed + lt,
  data = train,
  cost = 10,
  gamma = 0.2,
  epsilon = 0.1
) # predictors and outcome are standardised inside
vars  <- c("lf", "angle", "chord", "speed", "lt")
Zt <- scale(
  as.matrix(test[, vars]),
  center = small$x.scale$`scaled:center`,
  scale = small$x.scale$`scaled:scale`
)
SV <- small$SV # the support vectors, standardised
# exp(-gamma * squared distance)
K <- exp(-0.2 * outer(rowSums(Zt^2), rowSums(SV^2), "+") + 2 * 0.2 * Zt %*% t(SV))
f_std <- drop(K %*% small$coefs) - small$rho
by_hand <- f_std * small$y.scale$`scaled:scale` + small$y.scale$`scaled:center`
max(abs(by_hand - predict(small, test)))


[1] 2.444267e-12


Code
c(support_vectors = small$tot.nSV, training_rows = nrow(train))


support_vectors   training_rows 
            684            1127 


The prediction is what step 4 says. 684 of the 1,127 training rows are support vectors.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
4. Tuning: cost, gamma, epsilon
The three settings are chosen by cross-validation in the training set, again by experiment:


Code
set.seed(153)
train_runs <- unique(train$run)
fold_of <- setNames(sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(train_runs))), train_runs)
fold <- fold_of[train$run]
form <- db ~ lf + angle + chord + speed + lt
cv_error <- function(cost, gamma, epsilon, folds = fold) {
  err <- unlist(lapply(1:5, function(k) {
    m <- svm(form, data = train[folds != k, ], cost = cost, gamma = gamma, epsilon = epsilon)
    predict(m, train[folds == k, ]) - train$db[folds == k]
  }))
  sqrt(mean(err^2))
}
grid <- expand.grid(cost = c(0.5, 2, 10, 50, 200), gamma = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1))
grid$rmse <- mapply(cv_error, grid$cost, grid$gamma, 0.1)
best <- grid[which.min(grid$rmse), ]
eps  <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4)
eps_rmse <- sapply(eps, function(e) cv_error(best$cost, best$gamma, e))
best_eps <- eps[which.min(eps_rmse)]
best; rbind(epsilon = eps, rmse = eps_rmse)


   cost gamma     rmse
13   10   0.1 2.858887


            [,1]     [,2]     [,3]     [,4]     [,5]
epsilon 0.010000 0.050000 0.100000 0.200000 0.400000
rmse    2.914118 2.918295 2.858887 2.929316 3.016123




Code
ggplot(grid, aes(factor(gamma), factor(cost), fill = rmse)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = f2(rmse)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#1baf7a", high = "white", name = "dB") +
  labs(title = "Cross-validated error, whole experiments left out", x = "γ", y = "cost C") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())









The best setting is \(C\) = 10, \(\gamma\) = 0.1 (error 2.86 dB), a fairly stiff function. Large \(\gamma\) with a large \(C\), the most flexible corner, is bad. \(\varepsilon\) matters little. (\(\varepsilon\) is in standard deviations of the outcome: 0.1 is 0.7 dB.)

The same tuning with rows at random


Code
set.seed(154)
random_fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train)))
grid$rmse_random <- mapply(
  cv_error,
  grid$cost,
  grid$gamma,
  0.1,
  MoreArgs = list(folds = random_fold)
)
best_random <- grid[which.min(grid$rmse_random), ]
best_random


   cost gamma     rmse rmse_random
29   50     1 3.243006    1.431678


If single rows are left out, the cross-validation promises an error of 1.43 dB, and chooses \(C\) = 50 and \(\gamma\) = 1: the most flexible model. Whose promise is kept?

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
5. The test


Code
svr      <- svm(form, data = train, cost = best$cost, gamma = best$gamma, epsilon = best_eps)
svr_rand <- svm(
  form,
  data = train,
  cost = best_random$cost,
  gamma = best_random$gamma,
  epsilon = 0.1
)
linear   <- lm(form, data = train)
poly2    <- lm(db ~ polym(lf, angle, chord, speed, lt, degree = 2, raw = TRUE), data = train)
gam_fit <- gam(
  db ~ te(lf, lt, k = 6) + s(angle, k = 6) + s(chord, k = 5) + speed,
  data = train,
  method = "REML"
)
set.seed(155)
forest   <- ranger(form, data = train, num.trees = 1000)
preds <- list(
  `Linear regression` = predict(linear, test),
  `Quadratic regression` = predict(poly2, test),
  `GAM` = predict(gam_fit, test),
  `Random forest` = predict(forest, test)$predictions,
  `SVR, tuned by experiment` = predict(svr, test),
  `SVR, tuned by rows at random` = predict(svr_rand, test)
)
results <- data.frame(
  model = names(preds),
  test_rmse = sapply(preds, rmse, b = test$db),
  R2 = sapply(preds, function(p) 1 - sum((test$db - p)^2) / sum((test$db - mean(train$db))^2)),
  row.names = NULL
)
# the uncertainty comes from the experiments: bootstrap whole experiments of the test set
set.seed(156)
boot <- replicate(1000, {
  pick <- sample(test_runs, replace = TRUE)
  rows <- unlist(lapply(pick, function(r) which(test$run == r)))
  sapply(preds, function(p) rmse(p[rows], test$db[rows]))
})
results$low <- apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.025); results$high <- apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.975)
print(
  transform(
    results,
    test_rmse = round(test_rmse, 2),
    R2 = round(R2, 2),
    low = round(low, 2),
    high = round(high, 2)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)


                        model test_rmse   R2  low high
            Linear regression      5.16 0.35 4.37 5.98
         Quadratic regression      3.37 0.72 2.89 3.82
                          GAM      3.83 0.64 3.03 4.52
                Random forest      2.75 0.82 2.31 3.18
     SVR, tuned by experiment      2.60 0.84 2.30 2.87
 SVR, tuned by rows at random      3.51 0.70 2.73 4.23


Code
get <- function(m, col = "test_rmse") results[results$model == m, col]




Code
results$model <- factor(results$model, levels = results$model[order(-results$test_rmse)])
ggplot(results, aes(test_rmse, model)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_random$rmse_random, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#eb6834") +
  labs(
    title = "Error on experiments that no model has seen",
    subtitle = "95% bootstrap intervals over experiments. Dashed: what tuning by rows at random promised",
    x = "root mean squared error (dB)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")










The SVR tuned by experiment misses new experiments by 2.60 dB, linear regression by 5.16.
The SVR tuned by rows had promised 1.43 and delivers 3.51.
The quadratic regression has 3.37, the GAM 3.83, and the random forest 2.75. The test set has 26 experiments, the intervals are wide and overlap, and the ranking of the good models is not certain.

With random splits, errors of 1 to 2 dB are easy to get on these data. They answer a question that nobody has: predicting a frequency of a spectrum of which the neighbouring frequencies are known.


Code
few <- test_runs[1:6]
show <- subset(test, run %in% few)
show$SVR <- predict(svr, show); show$linear <- predict(linear, show)
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(show[, c("run", "freq")], db = show$SVR, what = "SVR"),
  data.frame(show[, c("run", "freq")], db = show$linear, what = "linear regression")
)
ggplot(show, aes(freq, db)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(data = long, aes(colour = what), linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~run) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(SVR = "#2a78d6", `linear regression` = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 2000, 8000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Six experiments of the test set: measured (points) and predicted",
    x = "frequency (Hz, log scale)",
    y = "dB"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
6. What has the model learned?
SVR has no coefficients to read. Partial dependence shows the average prediction as one predictor changes:


Code
pd <- function(v, values) {
  sapply(values, function(x) {
    z <- train
    z[[v]] <- x
    mean(predict(svr, z))
  })
}
pd_data <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    list(
      c("lf", "log10 frequency"),
      c("angle", "angle (degrees)"),
      c("chord", "chord (m)"),
      c("speed", "speed (m/s)")
    ),
    function(p) {
      values <- seq(min(train[[p[1]]]), max(train[[p[1]]]), length.out = 25)
      data.frame(x = values, db = pd(p[1], values), what = p[2])
    }
  )
)
pd_data$what <- factor(pd_data$what, levels = unique(pd_data$what))
ggplot(pd_data, aes(x, db)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence of the sound level", x = NULL, y = "predicted dB") +
  theme_bw()









Code
range_of <- tapply(pd_data$db, pd_data$what, function(v) diff(range(v)))
round(range_of, 1)


log10 frequency angle (degrees)       chord (m)     speed (m/s) 
           20.3             7.0             8.2             3.0 


The frequency changes the prediction most (by 20.3 dB over its range), then the length of the blade (8.2 dB) and the angle (7.0), and the speed least (3.0). The peak that moves with the conditions is an interaction, which such averages hide.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
7. Scaling, outliers, size


Code
noscale <- svm(
  form,
  data = train,
  cost = best$cost,
  gamma = best$gamma,
  epsilon = best_eps,
  scale = FALSE
)
set.seed(157)
spoiled <- train
bad <- sample(nrow(spoiled), 20)
spoiled$db[bad] <- spoiled$db[bad] + 60 # 20 wrong measurements
out_svr <- svm(form, data = spoiled, cost = best$cost, gamma = best$gamma, epsilon = best_eps)
out_gam <- update(gam_fit, data = spoiled)
c(
  SVR = get("SVR, tuned by experiment"),
  SVR_unscaled = rmse(predict(noscale, test), test$db),
  SVR_with_outliers = rmse(predict(out_svr, test), test$db),
  GAM = get("GAM"),
  GAM_with_outliers = rmse(predict(out_gam, test), test$db)
)


              SVR      SVR_unscaled SVR_with_outliers               GAM GAM_with_outliers 
         2.602715          5.711961          2.543278          3.833790          4.111864 


Code
sv_share <- sapply(c(0.01, 0.1, 0.4, 0.8), function(e) {
  svm(form, data = train, cost = best$cost, gamma = best$gamma, epsilon = e)$tot.nSV / nrow(train)
})
setNames(round(sv_share, 2), paste("epsilon", c(0.01, 0.1, 0.4, 0.8)))


epsilon 0.01  epsilon 0.1  epsilon 0.4  epsilon 0.8 
        0.97         0.66         0.18         0.06 



Scale the predictors. The kernel adds squared distances. Without scaling, degrees of angle count thousands of times more than metres of chord, and the error rises to 5.7 dB. svm() scales by default; the same centre and scale must be used for new data, as predict() does.
Outliers count in proportion and not by their square. Twenty wrong values moved the error of the SVR to 2.54 and that of the GAM to 4.11 dB.
\(\varepsilon\) decides how many support vectors there are: 97% of the rows with 0.01, 18% with 0.4. Fewer support vectors make a smaller and faster model.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Keep together what belongs together: experiments, patients, schools, days. In the split and in the tuning.
Tune on a grid of factors (1, 10, 100, …), then refine. The three settings interact.
No intervals, no tests. SVR gives a number. For uncertainty use bootstrap, conformal prediction, or a Gaussian process, its probabilistic relative.
No extrapolation. Far from all support vectors the radial kernel gives 0 and the prediction returns to the constant \(b\).
Slow for large data: the time grows with the square to the cube of the rows. Above some ten thousand rows take boosting, forests or neural networks.
Categorical predictors must be coded as dummies, and they are then measured by the same distance as the rest.
Other kernels: linear (many predictors, few rows), polynomial. The radial one is the usual start.
A simple model is often close. Always fit one.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the unit of splitting, the preprocessing, the kernel, the tuning grid and its validation, the chosen settings, and the test error with its uncertainty and with simpler models. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
o <- order(results$test_rmse)
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = as.character(results$model)[o],
  rmse = f2(results$test_rmse[o]),
  ci = paste0("[", f2(results$low[o]), ", ", f2(results$high[o]), "]"),
  r2 = f2(results$R2[o])
)


Method (data analysis):

We predicted the sound level of airfoils (1,503 measurements from 106 wind tunnel experiments; Brooks et al., 1989) from log frequency, angle of attack, chord length, air speed and the log thickness of the boundary layer with support vector regression with a radial kernel (Smola & Schölkopf, 2004). Predictors and outcome were standardised with the training data. A random quarter of the experiments was the test set. Cost, γ and ε were chosen by five-fold cross-validation in the training set, with whole experiments in one fold. Linear and quadratic regression, a generalized additive model and a random forest served for comparison. Confidence intervals of the test error are from 1,000 bootstrap samples of experiments. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package e1071.

Results:

The selected settings were C = 10, γ = 0.1 and ε = 0.1 (cross-validated RMSE = 2.86 dB), with 742 support vectors. On 26 experiments that were not used for training, the RMSE was 2.60 dB, 95% CI [2.30, 2.87], compared with 5.16 for linear regression (Table 1). Cross-validation with single measurements left out at random would have suggested an RMSE of 1.43 dB, and the model chosen in this way had 3.51 dB on new experiments.

Points to remember:

Report the kernel, the grid and the chosen settings.

title: Support Vector Regression: How Loud Is This Wing?
text:
10. Summary



When
Prediction of a continuous outcome with smooth nonlinear relations, up to some ten thousand rows


Loss
Errors below \(\varepsilon\) are free, larger ones count in proportion


The function
\(f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i K(x_i, x) + b\), a sum over the support vectors


How (R)
e1071::svm(y ~ x, data, cost, gamma, epsilon)


Settings
Cost (fit against flatness), \(\gamma\) (width of the bumps), \(\varepsilon\) (width of the tube)


Needs
Scaling; tuning with independent units left out


Does not give
Coefficients, tests, intervals, extrapolation


Related pages
Regularized regression, random forest, gradient boosting, splines and GAMs
