title: Βαθμολόγηση Thurstonian IRT — Θεωρία
text:
Εξήγηση

Το μοντέλο Thurstonian IRT
Το Thurstonian Item Response Theory (TIRT) είναι ένα ψυχομετρικό μοντέλο για ερωτηματολόγια αναγκαστικής επιλογής (forced-choice), στα οποία ο εξεταζόμενος δεν βαθμολογεί κάθε πρόταση ανεξάρτητα, αλλά επιλέγει μεταξύ ζευγών ή ομάδων προτάσεων. Κάθε ζεύγος παράγει μια δυαδική απάντηση \(y \in \{0, 1\}\), ανάλογα με ποια πρόταση προτιμήθηκε.

Δομή του μοντέλου
Έστω:

\(\boldsymbol{\eta} = (\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_K)^\top\) : το διάνυσμα των \(K\) λανθανουσών ιδιοτήτων (latent traits) του εξεταζόμενου
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) : ο πίνακας παραμέτρων φόρτισης (\(N \times K\)), όπου \(\lambda_{ik}\) εκφράζει πόσο ισχυρά σχετίζεται το \(i\)-οστό ζεύγος με την \(k\)-οστή ιδιότητα
\(\tau_i\) : το κατώφλι (threshold) του \(i\)-οστού ζεύγους — αντιστοιχεί στη δυσκολία της επιλογής
\(\theta_i\) : η υπολειπόμενη διακύμανση (residual variance) του \(i\)-οστού ζεύγους
\(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) : ο πίνακας διακύμανσης-συνδιακύμανσης (\(K \times K\)) των λανθανουσών ιδιοτήτων



Μοντέλο πιθανότητας απάντησης (probit link)
Για κάθε δυαδική απάντηση \(y_i\), η πιθανότητα να επιλεγεί η πρώτη επιλογή (\(y_i = 1\)) δίνεται από:
\[P(y_i = 1 \mid \boldsymbol{\eta}) = \Phi(z_i)\]
όπου \(\Phi(\cdot)\) είναι η τυπική κανονική αθροιστική κατανομή (CDF) και
\[z_i = \frac{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\eta} - \tau_i}{\sqrt{\theta_i}}\]
Ο αριθμητής \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\eta} - \tau_i\) εκφράζει πόσο «εύκολο» είναι να επιλεγεί η πρώτη επιλογή για έναν εξεταζόμενο με ιδιότητες \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\). Η διαίρεση με \(\sqrt{\theta_i}\) κανονικοποιεί ώστε να ληφθεί υπόψη η μοναδικότητα του ζεύγους.




Εκτίμηση MAP (Maximum A Posteriori)
Ο στόχος είναι να βρούμε το διάνυσμα \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*\) που μεγιστοποιεί την εκ των υστέρων πιθανότητα (posterior probability) δεδομένου του παρατηρηθέντος μοτίβου απαντήσεων \(\mathbf{y}\).

Λογαριθμική πιθανοφάνεια (log-likelihood)
Υποθέτουμε, ως απλουστευτική παραδοχή, υπό συνθήκη ανεξαρτησία των δυαδικών απαντήσεων δεδομένου \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\)· η παραδοχή ισχύει ακριβώς για ζεύγη, ενώ για ομάδες 3 ή περισσότερων προτάσεων αγνοεί τις συσχετίσεις των σφαλμάτων εντός ομάδας, με αμελητέα επίδραση στις εκτιμήσεις (Brown & Maydeu-Olivares, 2011· Maydeu-Olivares & Brown, 2010). Τότε:
\[\ell(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ y_i \log \Phi(z_i) + (1 - y_i) \log\bigl(1 - \Phi(z_i)\bigr) \right]\]


Λογαριθμική εκ των προτέρων κατανομή (log-prior)
Υποθέτουμε πολυμεταβλητή κανονική εκ των προτέρων κατανομή για τις λανθάνουσες ιδιότητες:
\[\boldsymbol{\eta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, \boldsymbol{\Psi})\]
\[\log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\frac{1}{2}\, \boldsymbol{\eta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta} + \text{const}\]


Αντικειμενική συνάρτηση
Η εκτίμηση MAP ισοδυναμεί με ελαχιστοποίηση του αρνητικού λογαρίθμου της εκ των υστέρων κατανομής:
\[Q(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\ell(\boldsymbol{\eta}) - \log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\sum_{i} \left[ y_i \log \Phi(z_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\Phi(z_i)) \right] + \frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\eta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta}\]


Κλίση (gradient) για τον αλγόριθμο BFGS
Ο αναλυτικός υπολογισμός της κλίσης επιταχύνει σημαντικά τη βελτιστοποίηση. Ορίζουμε:
\[w_i = \frac{(y_i - \Phi(z_i))\,\phi(z_i)}{\Phi(z_i)\,(1-\Phi(z_i))\,\sqrt{\theta_i}}\]
όπου \(\phi(\cdot)\) είναι η τυπική κανονική πυκνότητα (PDF). Τότε η κλίση της \(Q\) ως προς \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) είναι:
\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\, Q(\boldsymbol{\eta}) = -\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}^\top \mathbf{w} + \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\eta}\]
όπου \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}\) περιέχει μόνο τις γραμμές του \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) για τις μη ελλείπουσες απαντήσεις (οι ελλείπουσες απλώς παραλείπονται από την πιθανοφάνεια).
Ο πρώτος όρος \(-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{obs}}^\top \mathbf{w}\) αντιστοιχεί στη συνεισφορά των παρατηρηθέντων απαντήσεων και το δεύτερο \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\eta}\) στην «έλξη» της εκ των προτέρων κατανομής προς το μηδέν.


Αναστροφή πίνακα (Gauss-Jordan)
Η αναστροφή του \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) υλοποιείται χειροκίνητα με απαλοιφή Gauss-Jordan με μερική οδήγηση (partial pivoting) (συνάρτηση compute_solve()), αντί της solve() της βασικής R:
\[[\boldsymbol{\Psi} \mid \mathbf{I}] \xrightarrow{\text{Gauss-Jordan}} [\mathbf{I} \mid \boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}]\]
Η μέθοδος υλοποιείται στις συναρτήσεις score_tirt() / score_tirt_pattern() του πακέτου rwf (εκτίμηση με stats::optim(method = "BFGS")).

title: Βαθμολόγηση Thurstonian IRT — Θεωρία
text:
Απλή Εξήγηση

Τι μετράμε;
Φανταστείτε ένα ψυχολογικό τεστ που δεν σας ζητά να βαθμολογήσετε κάθε πρόταση χωριστά («πόσο με εκφράζει αυτό;»), αλλά σας παρουσιάζει ζεύγη προτάσεων και σας ρωτά: «Ποια από τις δύο σε περιγράφει καλύτερα;»
Για παράδειγμα:

(Α) Μου αρέσει να εργάζομαι με ανθρώπους. (Β) Μου αρέσει να αναλύω δεδομένα.

Επιλέγετε ένα από τα δύο — αυτή είναι η αναγκαστική επιλογή. Το τεστ περιέχει δεκάδες τέτοια ζεύγη, και από το σύνολο των απαντήσεών σας θέλουμε να υπολογίσουμε πόσο ψηλά σκοράρετε σε κάθε χαρακτηριστικό (π.χ. κοινωνικότητα, αναλυτική σκέψη, κ.ο.κ.).



Πώς λειτουργεί η βαθμολόγηση;

Βήμα 1 — Τι ξέρουμε εκ των προτέρων
Ξεκινάμε με την παραδοχή ότι οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι είναι κοντά στον μέσο όρο για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό. Αυτό σημαίνει ότι, για να αποδώσουμε ακραίο σκορ, χρειαζόμαστε ισχυρές και συνεπείς ενδείξεις από το μοτίβο των επιλογών.


Βήμα 2 — Τι μας λένε οι απαντήσεις
Κάθε ζεύγος ερωτήσεων «φορτίζει» σε ένα ή περισσότερα χαρακτηριστικά. Για παράδειγμα, αν επιλέξετε «Μου αρέσει να εργάζομαι με ανθρώπους», αυτό αυξάνει το σκορ σας στην κοινωνικότητα. Αν επιλέξετε την άλλη, το μειώνει.
Η «δυσκολία» κάθε ζεύγους (threshold) καθορίζει πόσο σπάνια ή συνηθισμένη είναι η μία επιλογή έναντι της άλλης στον γενικό πληθυσμό.


Βήμα 3 — Εύρεση του «καλύτερου» σκορ
Ο αλγόριθμος δοκιμάζει διαφορετικούς συνδυασμούς σκορ για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό και ρωτά:

«Ποιος συνδυασμός σκορ είναι ο πιο πιθανός, λαμβάνοντας υπόψη τόσο τις απαντήσεις του εξεταζόμενου όσο και το ότι οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι βρίσκονται κοντά στον μέσο όρο;»

Αυτό γίνεται με έναν αλγόριθμο βελτιστοποίησης (BFGS) που «ανεβαίνει» στη βουνοκορφή της πιθανότητας — δηλαδή βρίσκει το σκορ που κάνει τις απαντήσεις πιο λογικές.


Βήμα 4 — Ισορροπία μεταξύ δεδομένων και εκ των προτέρων γνώσης
Το τελικό σκορ δεν βασίζεται μόνο στις απαντήσεις, αλλά και στη γνώση μας για τον πληθυσμό. Αν οι απαντήσεις ενός ατόμου είναι αντιφατικές ή ελλιπείς, το σκορ «τραβιέται» προς τον μέσο όρο — αυτό ονομάζεται συρρίκνωση (shrinkage) και αποτρέπει ακραίες εκτιμήσεις όταν τα δεδομένα δεν είναι αρκετά.




Σύνοψη σε μια εικόνα







Τεχνικός όρος
Απλά λόγια




Λανθάνουσα ιδιότητα (\(\eta\))
Το πραγματικό σκορ που θέλουμε να μετρήσουμε


Φόρτιση (\(\lambda\))
Πόσο «μαρτυράει» κάθε ζεύγος για κάθε χαρακτηριστικό


Κατώφλι (\(\tau\))
Πόσο «δύσκολο» είναι να επιλεγεί η μία πλευρά


Υπολειπόμενη διακύμανση (\(\theta\))
Πόσο «θορυβώδης» είναι η απάντηση


Πίνακας \(\Psi\)
Πώς σχετίζονται μεταξύ τους τα χαρακτηριστικά


MAP εκτίμηση
Το πιο πιθανό σκορ δεδομένων των απαντήσεων


BFGS
Ο αλγόριθμος αναζήτησης που βρίσκει το βέλτιστο σκορ




Βιβλιογραφία: Brown & Maydeu-Olivares (2011). Item response modeling of forced-choice questionnaires. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 71(3), 460–502.
Maydeu-Olivares & Brown (2010). Item response modeling of paired comparison and ranking data. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 45(6), 935–974.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
Historians learn how tall people were, and so how well they were fed, from the records of armies. But many armies had a minimum height. Shorter men were sent away, and nobody wrote them down. From such records the population looks too tall. And a regression on them, for example of a son’s height on his parents’ heights, gives wrong slopes, as we shall see.
A sample is truncated when the cases beyond a limit are missing altogether. We do not know who they were, nor how many. Other examples: an experiment that admits only families with an income below some limit (Hausman & Wise, 1977), a survey of firms with more than ten employees, the patients of a clinic that admits only those above some blood value.
Truncated regression tries to recover the line of the full population from the truncated sample. Can it? With real truncated data one never knows, because the truth is missing. So we use data for which we know the truth, Galton’s heights from simple linear regression, and make the truncated sample ourselves: an imaginary guard regiment that takes only sons of 68 inches (173 cm) or more.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(truncreg)   # truncreg(): truncated normal regression
library(survival)   # survreg(): the censored (Tobit) model, for comparison (comes with R)

line_colours <- c(
  "all sons (the truth)" = "grey25",
  "OLS, tall sons only" = "#eb6834",
  "truncated regression" = "#2a78d6"
)

# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
1. The data


Code
galton <- read.csv("https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/HistData/GaltonFamilies.csv")
sons   <- subset(galton, gender == "male", select = c(family, father, mother, childHeight))
names(sons)[4] <- "son"

minimum <- 68                                     # inches
guards  <- subset(sons, son >= minimum)           # all that the regiment's records contain
c(all_sons = nrow(sons), in_the_records = nrow(guards), missing = nrow(sons) - nrow(guards))


      all_sons in_the_records        missing 
           481            351            130 


Galton’s (1886) file has 481 adult sons with the heights of both parents, in inches. The records of our regiment contain 351 of them. The other 130 (27%) do not exist for it.
The truth that we want to recover is the regression on all the sons:


Code
full <- lm(son ~ father + mother, data = sons)
truth <- c(coef(full), sigma = sigma(full))
round(truth, 3)


(Intercept)      father      mother       sigma 
     19.313       0.418       0.329       2.295

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
naive <- lm(son ~ father + mother, data = guards)
sons$kept <- sons$son >= minimum
# lines against the father's height, at the mean of the mother's height
line_at <- function(b) c(intercept = b[[1]] + b[[3]] * mean(sons$mother), slope = b[[2]])
two <- rbind(line_at(coef(full)), line_at(coef(naive)))

ggplot(sons, aes(father, son)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(shape = kept, alpha = kept),
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.1, seed = 1),
    size = 1.6,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = minimum, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(
    aes(intercept = two[1, 1], slope = two[1, 2], colour = "all sons (the truth)"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    aes(intercept = two[2, 1], slope = two[2, 2], colour = "OLS, tall sons only"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.6, `FALSE` = 0.35), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = line_colours, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "The regiment sees only the points above the dashed line",
    x = "father's height (inches)",
    y = "son's height (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The orange line, fitted to the filled points only, is too flat. The reason can be seen at the left. Sons of short fathers are short on average, so only the unusually tall ones pass the limit: there the records contain only positive errors. Sons of tall fathers pass whatever their error is. So the errors of the men in the records are related to the father’s height, and least squares is biased.


Code
cbind(all_sons = coef(full), tall_sons_only = coef(naive))


              all_sons tall_sons_only
(Intercept) 19.3128130     39.4003147
father       0.4175562      0.2288268
mother       0.3287734      0.2350343


Code
c(SD_all = sigma(full), SD_tall = sigma(naive))


  SD_all  SD_tall 
2.295355 1.676011 


The slope of the father’s height falls from 0.42 to 0.23, that of the mother’s from 0.33 to 0.24, and the residual standard deviation from 2.30 to 1.68. A larger sample of tall sons would not help. It is the wrong population.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the line of the whole population
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, \text{father}_i + \beta_2\, \text{mother}_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]
We see case \(i\) only if \(y_i \ge c\), with \(c = 68\).


Step 2: the distribution of those we see
Among all the sons of such parents, the heights have a normal curve around \(\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{father}_i + \beta_2 \text{mother}_i\). Cut off the part below \(c\). What remains has an area of \(P(y_i \ge c) = \Phi\!\big(\frac{\mu_i - c}{\sigma}\big)\), less than 1. To be a distribution again it must be divided by that area. The result is the truncated normal density:
\[f(y_i \mid y_i \ge c) = \frac{\frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\sigma}\right)}{\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu_i - c}{\sigma}\right)}\]
(\(\phi\) is the height of the standard normal curve, dnorm(); \(\Phi\) the area to the left, pnorm().)


Code
shape <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(66.5, 69, 72), function(mu) {
    h <- seq(60, 80, by = 0.05)
    data.frame(
      h,
      whole = dnorm(h, mu, truth[["sigma"]]),
      seen = ifelse(
        h >= minimum,
        dnorm(h, mu, truth[["sigma"]]) / pnorm((mu - minimum) / truth[["sigma"]]),
        NA
      ),
      label = sprintf(
        "expected height %.1f: %s seen",
        mu,
        pct(pnorm((mu - minimum) / truth[["sigma"]]))
      )
    )
  })
)
ggplot(shape, aes(h)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(shape, !is.na(seen)), aes(y = seen), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = whole), colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = minimum, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ label, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "All the sons (line), and those in the records (blue), for three pairs of parents",
       x = "son's height (inches)", y = "density") +
  theme_bw()











Step 3: the average of those we see
The mean of the truncated normal is above the line:
\[E(y_i \mid y_i \ge c) = \mu_i + \sigma\, \lambda(\alpha_i), \qquad \lambda(\alpha) = \frac{\phi(\alpha)}{1 - \Phi(\alpha)}, \qquad \alpha_i = \frac{c - \mu_i}{\sigma}\]
\(\lambda\) is the inverse Mills ratio. It is large when most of the curve is cut off (\(\mu_i\) far below \(c\)) and goes to zero when nothing is. So the mean of the sons in the records is pushed up most where the parents are short. This term, which OLS does not know, is the bias.


Step 4: maximum likelihood
Add up the logarithms of the densities of step 2, and find the \(\beta\)’s and \(\sigma\) that make the sum as large as possible:
\[\log L = \sum_i \left[ \log \frac{1}{\sigma}\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\sigma}\right) - \log \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu_i - c}{\sigma}\right) \right]\]
The first part is the ordinary normal likelihood. The second is the correction. It says: take into account that I could not have seen it otherwise. The estimates are consistent if the model is right (Amemiya, 1973).


Code
X <- model.matrix(naive); y <- guards$son
minus_loglik <- function(par, X, y, cut) {
  # par: the coefficients, then log(sigma)
  mu <- drop(X %*% par[-length(par)])
  s <- exp(par[length(par)])
  -sum(dnorm(y, mu, s, log = TRUE) - pnorm((mu - cut) / s, log.p = TRUE))
}
start <- c(coef(naive), log(sigma(naive)))                      # start from OLS
hand  <- optim(start, minus_loglik, X = X, y = y, cut = minimum, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
               control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-12, parscale = c(10, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1)))
c(hand$par[-4], sigma = exp(hand$par[[4]]), logLik = -hand$value)


 (Intercept)       father       mother        sigma       logLik 
   6.5424749    0.4569973    0.4764748    2.4008651 -615.6717168

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
section: 4. Fitting the model and reading the output
text:
4. Fitting the model and reading the output


Code
fit <- truncreg(son ~ father + mother, data = guards, point = minimum, direction = "left")
summary(fit)



Call:
truncreg(formula = son ~ father + mother, data = guards, point = minimum, 
    direction = "left")

BFGS maximization method
99 iterations, 0h:0m:0s 
g'(-H)^-1g = 6.91E-06 
 


Coefficients :
            Estimate Std. Error t-value  Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 6.520213   9.590862  0.6798    0.4966    
father      0.457161   0.091847  4.9774 6.444e-07 ***
mother      0.476635   0.094281  5.0555 4.294e-07 ***
sigma       2.401141   0.193053 12.4377 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Log-Likelihood: -615.67 on 4 Df


Code
b <- coef(fit); se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))


point is the cut-off and direction = "left" says that the values below it are missing. The estimates agree with our own.

father, mother: the change in the full population’s expected height for one inch. These are the numbers we are after.
sigma: the residual standard deviation in the full population.
There is no \(R^2\), and the t tests are large-sample z tests.



Code
compare <- data.frame(
  term = c("Intercept", "Father", "Mother", "sigma"),
  truth = truth, OLS_tall = c(coef(naive), sigma(naive)),
  truncated = b, SE = se,
  z_from_truth = (b - truth) / se, row.names = NULL)
print(cbind(term = compare$term, round(compare[, -1], 3)), row.names = FALSE)


      term  truth OLS_tall truncated    SE z_from_truth
 Intercept 19.313   39.400     6.520 9.591       -1.334
    Father  0.418    0.229     0.457 0.092        0.431
    Mother  0.329    0.235     0.477 0.094        1.568
     sigma  2.295    1.676     2.401 0.193        0.548




Code
plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    term = c("Father", "Mother"),
    est = coef(full)[-1],
    se = coef(summary(full))[-1, 2],
    method = "all sons (the truth)"
  ),
  data.frame(
    term = c("Father", "Mother"),
    est = coef(naive)[-1],
    se = coef(summary(naive))[-1, 2],
    method = "OLS, tall sons only"
  ),
  data.frame(
    term = c("Father", "Mother"),
    est = b[2:3],
    se = se[2:3],
    method = "truncated regression"
  )
)
plot_data$method <- factor(plot_data$method, levels = rev(names(line_colours)))

ggplot(plot_data, aes(est, term, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = est - 1.96 * se, xmax = est + 1.96 * se),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = line_colours, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Slopes with 95% intervals", x = "inches of son per inch of parent", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The truncated regression brings the slopes back: 0.46 for the father (truth: 0.42) and 0.48 for the mother (truth: 0.33), and \(\sigma\) = 2.40 (truth: 2.30). The price is the standard error: 0.09 instead of the 0.05 of the full data. The intervals are honest: they are wide, and they contain the truth. The narrow OLS intervals do not.

Two kinds of effect
The slope \(\beta_1\) is the effect in the whole population. If the question is about the men in the regiment, it is the slope of \(E(y \mid y \ge c)\), which is smaller:
\[\frac{\partial E(y \mid y \ge c)}{\partial x} = \beta_1 \left[1 - \lambda(\alpha)\,\big(\lambda(\alpha) - \alpha\big)\right]\]


Code
mu    <- drop(X %*% b[1:3])
alpha <- (minimum - mu) / b[["sigma"]]
mills <- dnorm(alpha) / pnorm(alpha, lower.tail = FALSE)
shrink <- 1 - mills * (mills - alpha)                   # always between 0 and 1
cbind(
  value = c(
    average_factor = mean(shrink),
    effect_in_the_population = b[["father"]],
    effect_among_the_tall = b[["father"]] * mean(shrink),
    OLS = coef(naive)[["father"]]
  )
)


                             value
average_factor           0.4773988
effect_in_the_population 0.4571609
effect_among_the_tall    0.2182480
OLS                      0.2288268


Averaged over the men in the records, the factor is 0.48, so one inch of father goes with 0.22 inches among the tall sons: about what OLS found. OLS is not “wrong”. It answers the question about the regiment, and people read it as an answer about the population.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
5. Truncated or censored?
A censored sample is less damaged. There we know how many cases are beyond the limit, and their predictors; only the exact outcome is missing. Suppose that the regiment had written down the parents’ heights of the rejected sons, with the note “below 68”. That is the Tobit model:


Code
sons$recorded <- pmax(sons$son, minimum)
tobit <- survreg(
  Surv(recorded, son >= minimum, type = "left") ~ father + mother,
  data = sons,
  dist = "gaussian"
)
rbind(truth = truth[1:3], tobit = coef(tobit), truncated = b[1:3])


          (Intercept)    father    mother
truth       19.312813 0.4175562 0.3287734
tobit       20.470814 0.4125360 0.3182662
truncated    6.520213 0.4571609 0.4766347


Code
rbind(truth = coef(summary(full))[, 2], tobit = sqrt(diag(vcov(tobit)))[1:3], truncated = se[1:3])


          (Intercept)     father     mother
truth        4.095028 0.04561239 0.04530087
tobit        4.106565 0.04457759 0.04455023
truncated    9.590862 0.09184728 0.09428117











Truncated
Censored




Cases beyond the limit
missing
present, with the value “beyond the limit”


Their predictors
unknown
known


Their number
unknown
known


Model
truncated regression
Tobit


Standard error of the father’s slope here
0.092
0.045



The standard error of the Tobit slope is less than half as large. It is worth a lot to write down even those who are turned away. The most expensive mistake is to treat a censored sample as truncated, by deleting the cases at the limit.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
6. What can go wrong
The correction rests on three assumptions: we know the cut-off, the cut-off was applied strictly, and the errors are normal, right down to the tail that we cannot see. Each can fail.

Rounding moves the cut-off
Most of Galton’s heights are rounded to an inch or a half inch. A son written down as 68 may be 67.75. So the true limit of the records is a bit below 68:


Code
share_whole <- mean(guards$son %% 1 == 0)
cuts <- c(68, 67.75, 67.5)
moved <- t(sapply(cuts, function(cc) {
  m <- truncreg(son ~ father + mother, data = guards, point = cc, direction = "left")
  c(cut = cc, coef(m)[2:4])
}))
round(rbind(moved, truth = c(NA, truth[2:4])), 3)


        cut father mother sigma
      68.00  0.457  0.477 2.401
      67.75  0.375  0.389 2.165
      67.50  0.327  0.338 2.016
truth    NA  0.418  0.329 2.295


70% of the heights in the records are whole inches. Taking 67.75 or 67.5 as the limit changes the father’s slope from 0.46 to 0.38 and 0.33. A quarter of an inch matters that much, because the heights are densest near the limit and the correction depends on how the curve is cut there. The right treatment is a likelihood for intervals (“the son is between 67.5 and 68.5”). The smallest honest step is to report the results for more than one limit.


The errors must be normal
The model extends the curve that it sees into the part that it does not see. If the hidden tail has another shape, it is wrong. A simulation with the real parents’ heights and the true line, and three kinds of errors with the same standard deviation:


Code
set.seed(17)
Xf   <- model.matrix(full); line <- drop(Xf %*% truth[1:3]); s0 <- truth[["sigma"]]
kinds <- list(normal             = function(n) rnorm(n, 0, s0),
              `long tails (t, 4 df)` = function(n) rt(n, 4) * s0 / sqrt(2),
              `skewed (long to the right)` = function(n) (rgamma(n, 4) - 4) / 2 * s0)
reps <- 500
sim <- lapply(kinds, function(draw) {
  t(replicate(reps, {
    yy <- line + draw(length(line))
    keep <- yy >= minimum
    d <- data.frame(son = yy, father = Xf[, 2], mother = Xf[, 3])[keep, ]
    o <- coef(lm(son ~ father + mother, d))
    m <- try(
      suppressWarnings(truncreg(
        son ~ father + mother,
        data = d,
        point = minimum,
        direction = "left"
      )),
      silent = TRUE
    )
    c(OLS = o[["father"]], truncated = if (inherits(m, "try-error")) NA else coef(m)[["father"]])
  }))
})
bias <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(sim), function(k) {
    data.frame(
      errors = k,
      true = truth[["father"]],
      OLS = mean(sim[[k]][, "OLS"]),
      truncated = mean(sim[[k]][, "truncated"], na.rm = TRUE),
      SD_OLS = sd(sim[[k]][, "OLS"]),
      SD_truncated = sd(sim[[k]][, "truncated"], na.rm = TRUE),
      failed = sum(is.na(sim[[k]][, "truncated"]))
    )
  })
)
print(cbind(errors = bias$errors, round(bias[, -1], 3)), row.names = FALSE)

With normal errors the truncated regression is right on average (0.41, truth 0.42), and OLS is far off (0.23).
With long tails it gives 0.54, and with skewed errors 0.54. The correction is biased in both cases. With skewed errors it is off by 29%.
Even when it is right on average, it is imprecise: the spread of the estimates is 1.9 times that of OLS.

Our errors are close to normal (the full data allow us to check), so the method had a fair chance here. With a truly truncated sample this check is impossible: the tail that would show it is the missing one.


How much can be cut away?


Code
limits <- c(64, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70)
by_limit <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(limits, function(cc) {
    d <- subset(sons, son >= cc)
    m <- truncreg(son ~ father + mother, data = d, point = cc, direction = "left")
    data.frame(
      limit = cc,
      kept = nrow(d),
      share = nrow(d) / nrow(sons),
      OLS = coef(lm(son ~ father + mother, d))[["father"]],
      truncated = coef(m)[["father"]],
      SE = sqrt(vcov(m)["father", "father"])
    )
  })
)
round(by_limit, 3)

1    64  474 0.985 0.420     0.463 0.049
2    66  438 0.911 0.360     0.489 0.060
3    67  399 0.830 0.282     0.439 0.069

With a quarter of the sons missing (limit 68) the estimate is still usable. When more than half of them are missing (limit 70) the standard error is 0.25, more than half of the true slope. And OLS becomes flatter and flatter.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
section: 7. Borrowing a number: restricted maximum likelihood
text:
7. Borrowing a number: restricted maximum likelihood
The weak part of the estimation is \(\sigma\). From the cut curve alone it is hard to tell a wide distribution with a low mean from a narrow one with a high mean, and errors in \(\sigma\) carry over to the slopes. Height is a special case, because its spread is nearly the same in all populations that have been measured. A’Hearn (2004) proposed to fix \(\sigma\) at a known value and to estimate the rest:


Code
with_sigma <- function(s_fixed) {
  f <- function(par) minus_loglik(c(par, log(s_fixed)), X = X, y = y, cut = minimum)
  o <- optim(
    coef(naive),
    f,
    method = "BFGS",
    hessian = TRUE,
    control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-12, parscale = c(10, 0.1, 0.1))
  )
  list(b = o$par, se = sqrt(diag(solve(o$hessian))))
}
known <- with_sigma(truth[["sigma"]])
rbind(truth = truth[1:3], free_sigma = b[1:3], fixed_sigma = known$b)

truth         19.312813 0.4175562 0.3287734
free_sigma     6.520213 0.4571609 0.4766347
fixed_sigma    9.555659 0.4365355 0.4545173


Code

            (Intercept)     father     mother
free_sigma     9.590862 0.09184728 0.09428117
fixed_sigma    7.284649 0.07818965 0.07935915


Code
low <- with_sigma(0.9 * truth[["sigma"]]); high <- with_sigma(1.1 * truth[["sigma"]])
c(
  father_if_sigma_10pct_too_small = low$b[["father"]],
  father_if_sigma_10pct_too_large = high$b[["father"]]
)


father_if_sigma_10pct_too_small father_if_sigma_10pct_too_large 
                      0.3944664                       0.4819140 


With \(\sigma\) known, the standard error of the father’s slope falls from 0.092 to 0.078. But if the borrowed value is 10% too small or too large, the slope becomes 0.39 or 0.48. Here we cheated and took the true value. In practice the value comes from other studies, and it must be the spread given the predictors, not the plain one.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Is it really truncated? If you know how many cases are beyond the limit, it is censored: use Tobit. If the cases are missing because of another variable (people who did not answer, women who do not work), it is sample selection, the subject of the Heckman model.
Selecting on a predictor is harmless. Keeping only the sons of tall fathers does not bias the slope (it costs precision). Only selection on the outcome does.
The limit must be known and strict. In real armies, short volunteers were let in when soldiers were needed, and the density near the limit thins out gradually. Historians cut at a higher point, where the records are complete.
Normality cannot be checked where it matters. Try other distributions (crch::trch() has logistic and t errors) and report how much the answer moves.
The two limits can be on both sides: crch and gamlss.tr handle them.
Counts without zeros (the number of visits of those who visited) need the zero-truncated Poisson or negative binomial.
Standard errors here ignore that brothers share their parents. For the full data we used cluster-robust errors in simple linear regression; for the truncated model, bootstrap the families.
No miracle. The correction replaces missing information by an assumption. If the conclusion depends on it, say so.

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the limit and why it exists, the number of cases seen, the distribution that was assumed, the estimates with their uncertainty, and what they refer to. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
z  <- b / se
pv <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Intercept", "Father's height", "Mother's height", "σ"),
  full = paste0(f2(truth), c(paste0(" (", f2(coef(summary(full))[, 2]), ")"), "")),
  ols = paste0(
    f2(c(coef(naive), sigma(naive))),
    c(paste0(" (", f2(coef(summary(naive))[, 2]), ")"), "")
  ),
  tr = paste0(f2(b), " (", f2(se), ")"),
  ci = paste0("[", f2(b - 1.96 * se), ", ", f2(b + 1.96 * se), "]"),
  p = c(sapply(pv[1:3], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))), "—")
)


Method (data analysis):

Only sons with a height of at least 68 inches were in the sample (351 of the 481 sons in Galton’s records; the limit was imposed for this example). Because selection depended on the outcome, we regressed the son’s height on the heights of both parents with a truncated normal regression, estimated by maximum likelihood with a left truncation point of 68. The coefficients refer to the population without truncation. We examined the sensitivity to the truncation point (67.5 and 67.75 inches, because heights were rounded). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package truncreg (Croissant & Zeileis, 2026).

Results:

In the truncated regression, the son’s height increased with that of the father, b = 0.46, SE = 0.09, 95% CI [0.28, 0.64], z = 4.98, p < .001, and of the mother, b = 0.48, SE = 0.09, 95% CI [0.29, 0.66], z = 5.06, p < .001 (Table 1). Ordinary least squares on the same sample gave 0.23 and 0.24. With truncation points of 67.75 and 67.5 inches, the coefficient of the father’s height was 0.38 and 0.33.

Points to remember:

title: Truncated Regression: What If Only the Tall Sons Had Been Measured?
text:
10. Summary



When
Cases beyond a known limit of the outcome are missing from the sample


Why not OLS
The errors of those who remain are related to the predictors: slopes too flat


The model
Truncated normal: the normal density divided by the probability of being seen


How (R)
truncreg::truncreg(y ~ x, data, point = c, direction = "left")


Coefficients
For the whole population; for those in the sample, multiply by \(1 - \lambda(\lambda - \alpha)\)


Censored instead
If the number and predictors of the others are known: Tobit, much more precise


Assumptions
Known and strict limit, normal errors with constant variance


Weak points
Imprecise, and sensitive to rounding, the limit and the shape of the errors


Related pages
Tobit, simple linear regression

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
text:
The insulation of an electric motor ages with heat, and one day the motor fails. A motor is meant to run at 130 °C for years. Nobody wants to wait for years to know how long. So engineers test motors at higher temperatures, where they fail sooner, and calculate back. This is an accelerated life test.
Nelson and Hahn (1972) published a famous one: 40 motors at 150, 170, 190 and 220 °C. When the test was stopped, many had not failed, and at 150 °C none had. The question has three parts. How does life depend on the temperature? What is the distribution of the lifetimes? And what does it say about 130 °C, where nothing was measured?
The answer needs a model with a full distribution. The Cox model leaves the baseline open, and so it cannot say anything about times or temperatures outside the data. A parametric survival model can, at the price of an assumption. The accelerated failure time (AFT) model got its name here: the predictors make time itself run faster or slower.


Code
library(survival)   # survreg(): parametric survival regression (comes with R, as do the data)
library(ggplot2)

dist_colours <- c(
  weibull = "#2a78d6",
  lognormal = "#eb6834",
  loglogistic = "#1baf7a",
  exponential = "#eda100"
)

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the Weibull distribution
Weibull (1951) proposed a distribution for the strength of materials that has been used for lifetimes ever since. Its survival function and hazard are
\[S(t) = \exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{k}\right], \qquad h(t) = \frac{k}{\eta}\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{k-1}\]
\(\eta\) is the scale, the time at which 63% have failed. \(k\) is the shape: with \(k > 1\) the hazard rises (wear), with \(k < 1\) it falls (the weak ones go first), and with \(k = 1\) it is constant (the exponential distribution: no memory).


Code
grid <- seq(0.02, 3, by = 0.02)
shapes <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.7, 1, 1.5, 3), function(k) {
    data.frame(t = grid, h = k * grid^(k - 1), shape = paste("k =", k))
  })
)
ggplot(shapes, aes(t, h, colour = shape)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The hazard of the Weibull distribution (η = 1)", x = "time", y = "hazard") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Step 2: predictors stretch time
\[\log T = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma W\]
\(\log T\) is a line plus an error. If \(T\) is Weibull, \(W\) has the smallest extreme value distribution, and \(\sigma = 1/k\). With a normal \(W\), \(T\) is log-normal; with a logistic \(W\), log-logistic. In all of them, one unit more of \(x\) multiplies every quantile of the lifetime by \(e^{\beta_1}\), the time ratio. Life at 190 °C is life at 170 °C in fast motion.


Step 3: why \(1/T\)? The Arrhenius relation
Chemistry says that the speed of a reaction depends on the absolute temperature as \(e^{-E/(kT)}\). If ageing is such a reaction, the log of the lifetime is a straight line in 1 / absolute temperature. This is knowledge from outside the data, and the only thing that makes an extrapolation to 130 °C reasonable. (We use 1000/K, so the numbers are easy to read.)


Step 4: maximum likelihood with censoring
A failure at time \(t\) contributes the density \(f(t)\), a motor still running at time \(t\) contributes the survival probability \(S(t)\):
\[\log L = \sum_{\text{failed}} \log f(t_i) + \sum_{\text{running}} \log S(t_i)\]
By hand, with R’s Weibull functions (dweibull, pweibull):


Code
minus_loglik <- function(par) {
  # intercept, slope, log(sigma)
  eta <- exp(par[1] + par[2] * motors$x)
  k <- 1 / exp(par[3])
  -sum(ifelse(
    motors$status == 1,
    dweibull(motors$time, k, eta, log = TRUE),
    pweibull(motors$time, k, eta, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
  ))
}
hand <- optim(c(-12, 9, -1), minus_loglik, control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-14))
hand <- optim(hand$par, minus_loglik, control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-14))
fit  <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x, data = motors, dist = "weibull")
rbind(
  by_hand = c(`(Intercept)` = hand$par[1], x = hand$par[2], sigma = exp(hand$par[3]), logLik = -hand$value),
  survreg = c(coef(fit), fit$scale, logLik(fit))
)

x = 9.72: the slope of the Arrhenius line. Easier to say: going from 160 to 150 °C multiplies the lifetime by 1.70. An old rule of engineers says that 10 degrees less double the life.
Scale = 0.33 is \(\sigma\), so the shape is \(k = 1/\sigma\) = 3.07: well above 1. The hazard rises steeply: the insulation wears out.
Log(scale): its test asks whether \(\sigma = 1\), that is whether the exponential distribution would do. p < .001: it would not.
Loglik, Chisq: the likelihood-ratio test of all the predictors.
Do not confuse the scale of survreg (\(\sigma\)) with the scale of the Weibull distribution (\(\eta = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}\)).


Quantiles
The time by which a share \(p\) of the motors has failed:
\[t_p = \exp\big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma\, w_p\big), \qquad w_p = \log[-\log(1 - p)]\]

names(fits) <- dists
at130 <- data.frame(x = 1000 / (130 + 273.16))
interval <- function(m, p) {
  r <- predict(m, at130, type = "uquantile", p = p, se.fit = TRUE)
  est <- r$fit[[1]]; se <- r$se.fit[[1]]
  exp(c(estimate = est, low = est - 1.96 * se, high = est + 1.96 * se))
}
compare <- t(sapply(fits, function(m) {
  c(
    AIC = AIC(m),
    median_130 = interval(m, 0.5)[[1]],
    q10_130 = interval(m, 0.1)[[1]],
    q0.1_130 = interval(m, 0.001)[[1]]
  )
}))
round(compare)


            AIC median_130 q10_130 q0.1_130
weibull     299      42086   22797     5008
lognormal   303      47135   21937     7454
loglogistic 300      41805   22400     5880
exponential 315      88892   13512      128


By the AIC the Weibull (298.5) and the log-logistic (300.1) are best, the log-normal close, and the exponential is out. With 17 failures the data cannot say more. Now look at the predictions for 130 °C.

The median life is 42,086, 47,135 and 41,805 hours. These agree: about five years of running day and night.
The time when one in a thousand has failed, which matters for a guarantee, is 5,008, 7,454 and 5,880 hours. Here the distributions disagree by a factor of 1.5. Nothing in the data can decide, because there is no data in that tail. (The exponential distribution, which the data reject, would say 128 hours.)

  lapply(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), function(p) {
    r <- predict(fit, line, type = "uquantile", p = p, se.fit = TRUE)
    data.frame(
      temp = line$temp,
      est = exp(r$fit),
      low = exp(r$fit - 1.96 * r$se.fit),
      high = exp(r$fit + 1.96 * r$se.fit),
      q = paste0(100 * p, "% have failed")
    )
  })
)

ggplot(qs, aes(temp, est, colour = q)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = subset(qs, q == "50% have failed"),
    aes(ymin = low, ymax = high),
    fill = "#2a78d6",
    alpha = 0.15,
    colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(
    data = motors,
    aes(temp, time, shape = factor(status)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 1.8,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 130, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(`0` = 2, `1` = 16),
    labels = c("still running", "failed"),

  ) +

  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Weibull model: quantiles of the lifetime",
    subtitle = "Band: 95% interval of the median. Dashed line: the working temperature",
    x = "temperature (°C)",

  ) +

Code

The median at 130 °C is 42,086 hours, 95% CI [26,347, 67,226]. The interval is wide, and it contains only the uncertainty of the estimates. It does not contain the uncertainty about the Weibull, about the Arrhenius line, and about whether the same kind of failure happens at 130 °C at all. Meeker and Escobar (1998) list the ways in which such extrapolations go wrong.

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
text:
6. Checking the model

Is the spread the same at all temperatures?
The AFT model assumes one \(\sigma\). Let each temperature have its own (strata):


Code
# at 150 degrees nothing failed: no information about sigma
with_failures <- subset(motors, temp > 150)
one  <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x, data = with_failures, dist = "weibull")
many <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x + strata(temp), data = with_failures, dist = "weibull")
lr   <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(many)) - as.numeric(logLik(one)))
many$scale


 temp=170  temp=190  temp=220 
0.3483426 0.5717329 0.1115813 


Code
c(LR = lr, df = 2, p = pchisq(lr, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))


        LR         df          p 
7.44462238 2.00000000 0.02417802 


The scales are 0.35, 0.57, 0.11 at 170, 190 and 220 °C, and the test of equality gives p = .024. The spread is probably not the same: at 220 °C the failures were all found at two neighbouring inspections. With five to seven failures per group no estimate of a spread is reliable, but the assumption of one \(\sigma\) is doubtful, and again it is the highest temperature that stands out.


Is the line straight?


Code
curve <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x + I(x^2), data = motors, dist = "weibull")
free  <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ factor(temp), data = with_failures, dist = "weibull")
c(AIC_line = AIC(fit), AIC_curve = AIC(curve))


 AIC_line AIC_curve 
 298.5086  297.3267 


Code
c(AIC_line = AIC(one), AIC_each_temperature_free = AIC(free))


                 AIC_line AIC_each_temperature_free 
                 294.6898                  296.3326 


Code
lr_line <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(free)) - as.numeric(logLik(one)))
c(LR = lr_line, df = 1, p = pchisq(lr_line, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))


       LR        df         p 
0.3571972 1.0000000 0.5500670 


A bend (a squared term) lowers the AIC by only 1.2. Against a model where each of the three temperatures with failures has its own level, the Arrhenius line loses \(\chi^2\)(1) = 0.36, p = .550. The line is compatible with the data.


Code

m2 <- interval(no220, 0.5)
m2


 estimate       low      high 
 75516.69  26382.81 216154.80 


Without the motors tested at 220 °C the median at 130 °C becomes 75,517 hours, [26,383, 216,155], instead of 42,086. This is the size of the problem with extrapolation.


Residuals


Code
# standardised log times, censored like the times
z <- (log(motors$time) - predict(fit, type = "lp")) / fit$scale
km <- survfit(Surv(exp(z), motors$status) ~ 1)
resid_data <- data.frame(z = log(km$time), S = km$surv)
resid_data <- subset(resid_data, S > 0 & S < 1)
ggplot(resid_data, aes(z, log(-log(S)))) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(
    title = "Standardised residuals on Weibull paper",
    subtitle = "A straight line with slope 1 if the Weibull model is right",
    x = "residual",
    y = "log(-log(share not failed))"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
section: 7. The Weibull model is also a proportional hazards model
text:
7. The Weibull model is also a proportional hazards model
The Weibull is special. It is the only distribution that is both an AFT and a PH model. A time ratio of \(e^{\beta}\) is a hazard ratio of \(e^{-\beta/\sigma}\):
\[\text{HR} = e^{-\beta / \sigma} = e^{-\beta k}\]
We check it on the experiment of the Cox page, with 432 men released from prison, half of whom received money, and the weeks until the first arrest:


Code
rossi <- read.csv("https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/carData/Rossi.csv")
rossi$money <- as.integer(rossi$fin == "yes")
aft <- survreg(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + age + prio, data = rossi, dist = "weibull")
cox <- coxph(Surv(week, arrest) ~ money + age + prio, data = rossi)
tr  <- exp(coef(aft)[["money"]]); tr_ci <- exp(confint(aft)["money", ])
hr_weibull <- exp(-coef(aft) / aft$scale)[-1]
round(
  rbind(
    time_ratio = exp(coef(aft))[-1],
    hazard_ratio_Weibull = hr_weibull,
    hazard_ratio_Cox = exp(coef(cox))
  ),
  3
)

time_ratio           1.283 1.049 0.933
hazard_ratio_Weibull 0.705 0.935 1.103
hazard_ratio_Cox     0.707 0.935 1.102

The time ratio is 1.28, 95% CI [0.98, 1.68]: the payment stretches the time to the arrest by 28%. Many find this easier to understand than a ratio of hazards (Wei, 1992).

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
text:
8. Things to keep in mind

Extrapolation is the purpose and the danger. Say what it rests on: the distribution, the physical law, the same cause of failure.
Choose the distribution by theory and tradition as well as by AIC. The generalized gamma contains the exponential, Weibull and log-normal as special cases (flexsurv::flexsurvreg(dist = "gengamma")), and splines are more flexible still (Jackson, 2016).
Look at the hazard. If it falls after a peak (illness, infant mortality), the Weibull cannot follow it.
Censoring must be independent of the lifetime. Here it was fixed in advance.
Interval censoring. Failures found at inspections happened some time before. Surv(time1, time2, type = "interval2") does it properly.
Time that varies for predictors is harder in AFT models than in Cox.
A time ratio is an average stretch. If the effect is different for early and late events, use censored quantile regression, which has no such restriction.
Parameter names differ between programs. Check 1/scale, signs, and whether the coefficients are for log time or log hazard.

title: Weibull and Accelerated Failure Time Models: How Long Will a Motor Last?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the number of events and of censored cases, the distribution and why, the transformation of the predictors, time ratios or quantiles with intervals, and the basis of any extrapolation. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Intercept", "1000 / temperature (K)", "log σ"),
  b = f2(s[, 1]),
  SE = f2(s[, 2]),
  z = f2(s[, 3]),
  p = sapply(s[, 4], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p)))
)
pred_table <- data.frame(temp = c(130, 150, 170, 190, 220))
pred_table <- cbind(
  pred_table,
  t(sapply(pred_table$temp, function(tt) {
    r <- predict(
      fit,
      data.frame(x = 1000 / (tt + 273.16)),
      type = "uquantile",
      p = 0.5,
      se.fit = TRUE
    )
    exp(c(r$fit, r$fit - 1.96 * r$se.fit, r$fit + 1.96 * r$se.fit))
  }))
)
names(pred_table) <- c("temp", "med", "low", "high")


Method (data analysis):

The lifetimes of 40 motors tested at 150, 170, 190 and 220 °C (Nelson & Hahn, 1972) were analysed with a Weibull accelerated failure time model; 23 motors had not failed at the end of the test and were right-censored. The predictor was 1000 divided by the absolute temperature (Arrhenius relation). The Weibull distribution was compared with the exponential, log-normal and log-logistic distributions by the AIC, and the equality of the scale and the linearity of the relation were tested with likelihood-ratio tests. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package survival (Therneau, 2026).

Results:

Lifetimes were longer at lower temperatures, b = 9.72, SE = 0.70, z = 13.97, p < .001; 10 degrees less, from 160 to 150 °C, multiplied the lifetime by 1.70. The shape parameter was 3.07, an increasing hazard. The Weibull model had an AIC of 298.5 (log-logistic 300.1, log-normal 303.1, exponential 314.7). The extrapolated median lifetime at 130 °C was 42,086 hours, 95% CI [26,347, 67,226] (Table 1); without the tests at 220 °C it was 75,517 hours. These values rest on the Weibull distribution and the Arrhenius relation, which cannot be checked at 130 °C.

Points to remember:

Give the numbers of events and of censored cases at each condition.
Name the distribution and the parameterisation.
Report quantiles in real units, with intervals.
Mark extrapolations, and show how they change with other distributions.

text:
10. Summary



When
Times to an event, with censoring, and a need for full distributions, predictions or time ratios


The model
\(\log T = x^\top\beta + \sigma W\); Weibull: hazard \(\propto t^{k-1}\), \(k = 1/\sigma\)


How (R)
survreg(Surv(time, event) ~ x, data, dist = "weibull")


Reading it
\(e^\beta\): time ratio; for the Weibull also \(e^{-\beta/\sigma}\): hazard ratio


Quantiles
predict(fit, newdata, type = "quantile", p = c(.1, .5, .9))


Choosing
AIC, residual plots, theory of the hazard


Danger
Extrapolation in time and in the predictors


Related pages
Cox, censored quantile regression, Tobit (a survival model in disguise)

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
text:
Of 915 PhD students in biochemistry, 275 published no article in the last three years of their studies. Why not?
There may be two kinds of them. Some were never going to publish: they planned a career outside research, or their laboratory does not publish with students. For them the number is zero by nature. Others could have published, and worked on it, but it happened that nothing appeared in those three years. The data show the same 0 for both.
Zero-inflated models (Lambert, 1992) say exactly this: the zeros come from two sources. One part of the model says who is in the group of certain zeros. The other is an ordinary count model (Poisson or negative binomial) for everybody else, which produces zeros too. They are popular, easy to fit, and easy to over-interpret. Many zeros do not prove that there are two kinds of them. This page fits the models and then asks whether they are needed.


Code
library(pscl)       # zeroinfl(), hurdle(), vuong(); the data are also in this package
library(MASS)       # glm.nb(): negative binomial regression (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)

model_colours <- c(Poisson = "#eb6834", ZIP = "#eda100", NB = "#2a78d6", ZINB = "#1baf7a")

# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

2. Look at the data


Code
ggplot(phd, aes(articles)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:19) +
  labs(title = "Articles of 915 PhD students", x = "articles in three years", y = "students") +

Code
expected_zero <- dpois(0, mean(phd$articles)) * nrow(phd)
expected_zero


[1] 168.3471


The mean is 1.69. A Poisson distribution with this mean would have 168 zeros; there are 275. But it would also have a variance of 1.69, and the variance is 3.71, overdispersed. Too many zeros are one sign of overdispersion, and a long tail to the right is another. Both can come from the same cause: students differ in more ways than we have measured.

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
section: 3. The model step by step, with formulas
text:
3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: the count part
For the students who can publish, a count distribution with mean \(\mu_i = \exp(x_i^\top\beta)\). Either Poisson, or negative binomial with variance \(\mu + \mu^2/\theta\).


Step 2: the zero part
With probability \(\pi_i\) a student belongs to the group that never publishes (a structural zero):
\[\log\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i} = z_i^\top\gamma\]


Step 3: put together
\[P(y_i = 0) = \pi_i + (1 - \pi_i)\, f(0 \mid \mu_i), \qquad P(y_i = k) = (1 - \pi_i)\, f(k \mid \mu_i) \;\text{ for } k \ge 1\]
A zero can come from either source. Anything else can only come from the count part. The mean is \(E(y_i) = (1 - \pi_i)\,\mu_i\).


Step 4: the difference from a hurdle model
A hurdle model has one kind of zero, and its count part cannot produce zeros. So its zero part says “any article or none”, and the zero part of a zero-inflated model says “in the group that never publishes”. The signs are opposite, and the meanings differ. This is the most common mistake in reading the output.


Step 5: maximum likelihood, by hand


Code
X <- model.matrix(~ female + married + kids + prestige + mentor, data = phd)
y <- phd$articles
k <- ncol(X)
minus_loglik <- function(par) {                              # zero-inflated Poisson
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% par[1:k])); p <- plogis(drop(X %*% par[k + 1:k]))
  -sum(log(ifelse(y == 0, p + (1 - p) * dpois(0, mu), (1 - p) * dpois(y, mu))))
}
pois  <- glm(articles ~ female + married + kids + prestige + mentor, family = poisson, data = phd)
start <- c(coef(pois), -1, rep(0, k - 1))
hand  <- optim(start, minus_loglik, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-12))
zip <- zeroinfl(
  articles ~ female + married + kids + prestige + mentor,
  data = phd,
  dist = "poisson"
)
c(by_hand = -hand$value, zeroinfl = as.numeric(logLik(zip)))


  by_hand  zeroinfl 
-1604.773 -1604.773 


Code
both <- rbind(by_hand = hand$par[c(1:2, k + 6)], zeroinfl = unname(coef(zip))[c(1:2, k + 6)])
colnames(both) <- c("(Intercept)", "female", "zero part: (Intercept)")
round(both, 3)

zeroinfl       0.641 -0.209                 -0.134

Code
cnt <- summary(zinb)$coefficients$count; zer <- summary(zinb)$coefficients$zero
irr <- exp(cnt[, 1]); orz <- exp(zer[, 1])


The output has two tables.

Count model: the students who can publish. \(e^\beta\) is a ratio of expected counts. Women: 0.82 times as many articles as men (p = .010). Each child under 6: 0.86 times. Each article of the mentor: 1.025 times.
Zero-inflation model: who is in the group that never publishes. A positive coefficient means more likely to be a certain zero. The only clear one is the mentor: each of the mentor’s articles multiplies the odds of being a certain zero by 0.41 (p = .005). A student with an active mentor is hardly ever in that group.
Log(theta): \(\theta\) = 2.65. The smaller, the more the students still differ.

By the rest of the table we cannot say much about who the certain zeros are: the standard errors of the zero part are large. A student whose mentor published nothing and one whose mentor published ten articles:


Code
two <- data.frame(female = 0, married = 1, kids = 0, prestige = 3, mentor = c(0, 10))
pr <- data.frame(
  mentor = two$mentor,
  certain_zero = predict(zinb, two, type = "zero"),
  mean_if_not = predict(zinb, two, type = "count"),
  overall_mean = predict(zinb, two, type = "response"),
  chance_of_0 = predict(zinb, two, type = "prob")[, 1]
)
round(pr, 3)


  mentor certain_zero mean_if_not overall_mean chance_of_0
1      0        0.141       1.669        1.433       0.377
2     10        0.000       2.138        2.138       0.208

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
section: 5. Do we need it? Four ways to ask
text:
5. Do we need it? Four ways to ask

The zeros, and everything else


Code
hurdle_nb <- hurdle(
  articles ~ female + married + kids + prestige + mentor,
  data = phd,
  dist = "negbin"
)
zeros <- c(
  observed = sum(y == 0),
  Poisson = sum(dpois(0, fitted(pois))),
  ZIP = sum(predict(zip, type = "prob")[, 1]),
  NB = sum(dnbinom(0, mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta)),
  ZINB = sum(predict(zinb, type = "prob")[, 1])
)
round(zeros, 1)


observed  Poisson      ZIP       NB     ZINB 
   275.0    191.4    273.2    277.8    285.4 


Poisson expects 191 zeros instead of 275. But the plain negative binomial expects 278, without any zero inflation. It has one parameter more than Poisson, and it repairs the zeros and the tail at the same time. ZIP expects 273.
A rootogram compares all the counts (Kleiber & Zeileis, 2016). The bars are the observed frequencies, hanging from the expected ones, on a square-root scale. A bar that ends above the zero line means too few observed, one that goes below it too many.


Code
kmax <- 10
expected <- list(
  Poisson = sapply(0:kmax, function(j) sum(dpois(j, fitted(pois)))),
  ZIP     = colSums(predict(zip, type = "prob"))[1:(kmax + 1)],
  NB      = sapply(0:kmax, function(j) sum(dnbinom(j, mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta))),
  ZINB    = colSums(predict(zinb, type = "prob"))[1:(kmax + 1)])
observed <- sapply(0:kmax, function(j) sum(y == j))
roots <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(expected), function(m) {
    data.frame(
      model = m,
      count = 0:kmax,
      top = sqrt(expected[[m]]),
      bottom = sqrt(expected[[m]]) - sqrt(observed)
    )
  })
)
roots$model <- factor(roots$model, levels = names(model_colours))

ggplot(roots, aes(count)) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = count - 0.4, xmax = count + 0.4, ymin = bottom, ymax = top),
    fill = "grey75"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_line(aes(y = top, colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = top, colour = model), size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:kmax) +
  labs(
    title = "Rootograms: observed bars hanging from the expected curve",
    x = "articles",
    y = "square root of the frequency"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









The Poisson model fails everywhere. ZIP repairs the zero and misses the rest: it expects too few students with one article (the bar goes below the line), too many with three, and too few with six or seven. The NB and the ZINB both fit.


Information criteria


Code
models <- list(Poisson = pois, ZIP = zip, NB = nb, ZINB = zinb, `hurdle NB` = hurdle_nb)
crit <- data.frame(
  model = names(models),
  parameters = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  logLik = sapply(models, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),
  AIC = sapply(models, AIC),
  BIC = sapply(models, BIC),
  row.names = NULL
)
print(
  transform(crit, logLik = round(logLik, 1), AIC = round(AIC, 1), BIC = round(BIC, 1)),
  row.names = FALSE
)


     model parameters  logLik    AIC    BIC
   Poisson          6 -1651.1 3314.1 3343.0
       ZIP         12 -1604.8 3233.5 3291.4
        NB          7 -1561.0 3135.9 3169.6
      ZINB         13 -1550.0 3126.0 3188.6
 hurdle NB         13 -1552.6 3131.2 3193.8


Code
get <- function(m, col) crit[crit$model == m, col]


From Poisson to ZIP the AIC falls by 81. From Poisson to NB it falls by 178, with one parameter instead of six. The ZINB is 9.9 points better than the NB by AIC, and 19.0 points worse by BIC, which charges more for its six extra parameters. The two criteria disagree, and the evidence for a second kind of zero is weak.


Vuong’s test, and why not to use it here


Code
vt <- capture.output(vuong(nb, zinb))
cat(vt, sep = "\n")


Vuong Non-Nested Hypothesis Test-Statistic: 
(test-statistic is asymptotically distributed N(0,1) under the
 null that the models are indistinguishible)
-------------------------------------------------------------
              Vuong z-statistic             H_A  p-value
Raw                   -2.241831 model2 > model1 0.012486
AIC-corrected         -1.015385 model2 > model1 0.154961
BIC-corrected          1.939690 model1 > model2 0.026209


Vuong’s test compares two models that are not nested. It is printed in many papers as a “test of zero inflation”. But the NB is a special case of the ZINB (with \(\pi = 0\), which is at the edge of the possible values), so the conditions of the test do not hold, and its p value means little (Wilson, 2015). And the raw, AIC-corrected and BIC-corrected versions give three different answers.


A parametric bootstrap
The honest test simulates. Take the fitted NB (no inflation), generate new data from it, fit both models, and see how often the gain in likelihood is as large as ours by chance alone:


Code
gain <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(zinb)) - as.numeric(logLik(nb)))
set.seed(81)
gains <- replicate(200, {
  d <- phd
  d$articles <- rnbinom(nrow(d), mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta)
  a <- try(suppressWarnings(glm.nb(formula(nb), data = d)), silent = TRUE)
  z <- try(suppressWarnings(zeroinfl(formula(zinb), data = d, dist = "negbin")), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(a, "try-error") || inherits(z, "try-error")) {
    NA
  } else {
    2 * (as.numeric(logLik(z)) - as.numeric(logLik(a)))
  }
})
p_boot <- (1 + sum(gains >= gain, na.rm = TRUE)) / (1 + sum(!is.na(gains)))
cbind(
  value = c(
    our_gain = gain,
    mean_gain_without_inflation = mean(gains, na.rm = TRUE),
    p = p_boot,
    failed = sum(is.na(gains))
  )
)


                                 value
our_gain                    21.9349029
mean_gain_without_inflation  9.0123679
p                            0.0199005
failed                       0.0000000


Our gain is 21.9. Without any inflation the gain is 9.0 on average, and a gain as large as ours has the probability p = .020. So the ZINB describes something that the NB does not. The next section asks what.

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
section: 6. What does the zero part really say?
text:
6. What does the zero part really say?
The zero part depends almost entirely on the mentor. Students whose mentors published nothing are the “certain zeros”:


Code
grid <- data.frame(female = 0, married = 1, kids = 0, prestige = 3, mentor = 0:30)
grid$zero  <- predict(zinb, grid, type = "zero")
grid$ZINB  <- predict(zinb, grid, type = "response")
grid$NB    <- predict(nb, grid, type = "response")
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(mentor = grid$mentor, articles = grid$ZINB, model = "ZINB"),
  data.frame(mentor = grid$mentor, articles = grid$NB, model = "NB")
)
by_m <- aggregate(
  articles ~ cut(mentor, c(-1, 0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 80), labels = FALSE),
  data = phd,
  FUN = mean
)
by_m$mentor <- aggregate(
  mentor ~ cut(mentor, c(-1, 0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 80), labels = FALSE),
  data = phd,
  FUN = mean
)$mentor
ggplot(long, aes(mentor, articles, colour = model)) +
  geom_point(
    data = by_m,
    aes(mentor, articles),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(
    title = "Expected articles and the mentor's articles",
    subtitle = "Points: mean of all students in groups of mentors. Lines: a married man without children",
    x = "articles of the mentor",
    y = "articles of the student"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Code
certain <- sum(predict(zinb, type = "zero")) # expected number of certain zeros
# P(certain zero | 0 articles)
posterior <- predict(zinb, type = "zero") / predict(zinb, type = "prob")[, 1]
c(certain_zeros = certain, share_among_those_with_0 = mean(posterior[y == 0]))


           certain_zeros share_among_those_with_0 
              53.5428406                0.1947012 


By the ZINB, about 54 of the 915 students are certain zeros, which is 19% of those with no article. What the zero part has found may simply be a bend. The log of the expected count is not a straight line in the mentor’s articles: it rises quickly at first and then slowly. The NB has to use one slope for all, and the zero part offers a way to bend the curve near zero. Give the NB a bend of its own, and compare again:


Code
nb_bend <- glm.nb(articles ~ female + married + kids + prestige + log1p(mentor), data = phd)
zinb_bend <- zeroinfl(
  articles ~ female + married + kids + prestige + log1p(mentor),
  data = phd,
  dist = "negbin"
)
bend <- data.frame(
  model = c("NB, mentor", "ZINB, mentor", "NB, log(1 + mentor)", "ZINB, log(1 + mentor)"),
  parameters = c(7, 13, 7, 13),
  AIC = c(AIC(nb), AIC(zinb), AIC(nb_bend), AIC(zinb_bend)),
  BIC = c(BIC(nb), BIC(zinb), BIC(nb_bend), BIC(zinb_bend))
)
print(transform(bend, AIC = round(AIC, 1), BIC = round(BIC, 1)), row.names = FALSE)


                 model parameters    AIC    BIC
            NB, mentor          7 3135.9 3169.6
          ZINB, mentor         13 3126.0 3188.6
   NB, log(1 + mentor)          7 3118.9 3152.7
 ZINB, log(1 + mentor)         13 3121.1 3183.7


With the logarithm of the mentor’s articles, the plain NB has an AIC of 3,118.9, better than the ZINB with the straight line (3,126.0), with six parameters fewer. Adding zero inflation to it changes the AIC by 2.1. The “two kinds of zeros” have disappeared. They were a wrong curve.

A warning from simulation
What does one conclude who compares only Poisson with ZIP, when the truth is a negative binomial without any certain zeros?


Code
set.seed(82)
false_zip <- replicate(200, {
  d <- phd
  d$articles <- rnbinom(nrow(d), mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta)
  p0 <- glm(formula(pois), family = poisson, data = d)
  z0 <- suppressWarnings(zeroinfl(formula(zip), data = d))
  c(zip_wins = AIC(z0) < AIC(p0), certain_zeros = mean(predict(z0, type = "zero")))
})
rowMeans(false_zip)


     zip_wins certain_zeros 
    1.0000000     0.1787387 


ZIP beats Poisson in 100% of the data sets, and it declares 18% of the students to be certain zeros on average. There were none. Beating Poisson proves overdispersion, not two kinds of zeros.

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
text:
7. Things to keep in mind

First the negative binomial. Many zeros do not mean zero inflation (Warton, 2005). Use a zero-inflated model when theory says that there are certain zeros (people who do not own a car and car accidents, men and pregnancies), not because the bar at zero is high.
Check the curve of the predictors before you explain zeros.
Zero inflation or hurdle? If nobody can tell the two kinds of zeros apart in principle, the hurdle model is easier to explain. The fits are often the same.
Read the zero part with care. In zeroinfl() it models the probability of a certain zero; in hurdle() the probability of a positive count.
Say what you report. The coefficients of the count part are for those who can publish. The effect on the mean of everybody is another number: \(E(y) = (1 - \pi)\mu\).
Large standard errors in the zero part are the rule. With few zeros, or a large \(\mu\), the zero part is hardly identified.
Different predictors in the two parts are allowed: zeroinfl(y ~ x | z). With | 1 there is one constant probability.
Exposure: an offset(log(time)) goes into the count part.
Clustered data: glmmTMB fits zero-inflated models with random effects.

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) needs the distribution of the counts, the models that were compared and how, both parts of the chosen model, and the effects on the mean. The numbers come from the R objects:


Code
s_nb <- coef(summary(nb_bend)); ci_nb <- suppressMessages(confint(nb_bend))
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Intercept", "Female", "Married", "Children under 6", "Prestige of the department",
    "log(1 + mentor's articles)"
  ),
  b = f2(s_nb[, 1]),
  SE = f2(s_nb[, 2]),
  z = f2(s_nb[, 3]),
  p = sapply(s_nb[, 4], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  IRR = paste0(f2(exp(s_nb[, 1])), " [", f2(exp(ci_nb[, 1])), ", ", f2(exp(ci_nb[, 2])), "]")
)


Method (data analysis):

The number of articles of 915 PhD students (Long, 1990) had a mean of 1.69 and a variance of 3.71, and 275 students (30%) had none. We compared Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated Poisson and zero-inflated negative binomial regressions (Zeileis et al., 2008) with the AIC, the BIC, the expected number of zeros and rootograms, and tested zero inflation with a parametric bootstrap of the likelihood ratio (200 samples). The mentor’s articles entered linearly or as log(1 + x). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages pscl and MASS.

Results:

The Poisson model expected 191 students without an article and the negative binomial model 278, against 275 observed. With the mentor’s articles entered linearly, the zero-inflated negative binomial model fitted better than the negative binomial (bootstrap p = .020; AIC = 3,126.0 against 3,135.9), and the probability of a certain zero depended on the mentor’s articles. With log(1 + mentor’s articles) the negative binomial model without zero inflation had an AIC of 3,118.9, and zero inflation did not improve it (AIC = 3,121.1), so we report this model (Table 1). Women published fewer articles than men, IRR = 0.80, 95% CI [0.69, 0.92], as did students with young children, IRR = 0.84 per child, 95% CI [0.76, 0.93].

title: Zero-Inflated Poisson and Negative Binomial: Why Do Some PhD Students Publish Nothing?
text:
9. Summary



When
Counts with zeros from two sources: some units can never have a positive count


The model
\(P(0) = \pi + (1 - \pi) f(0)\), \(P(k) = (1 - \pi) f(k)\); \(E(y) = (1 - \pi)\mu\)


How (R)
pscl::zeroinfl(y ~ x | z, data, dist = "poisson") or "negbin"


Count part
\(e^\beta\): ratio of expected counts, for those who can


Zero part
Positive coefficient: more likely a certain zero


Compare with
The negative binomial: AIC, BIC, rootograms, parametric bootstrap


Warning
Overdispersion or a wrong curve can look like zero inflation

Hurdle models, generalized linear models (Poisson, negative binomial)

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
1. Theoretical Framework
Generalized Linear Models (GLMs; Nelder & Wedderburn, 1972) extend ordinary least squares regression to outcome variables whose conditional distribution belongs to the exponential family. A GLM is defined by three components:

Random component — the conditional distribution of \(Y | \mathbf{x}\) (e.g., Normal, Binomial, Poisson, Gamma)
Systematic component — a linear predictor \(\eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}\)
Link function \(g(\cdot)\) — a monotone differentiable function relating the conditional mean \(\mu_i = E[Y_i|\mathbf{x}_i]\) to the linear predictor: \(g(\mu_i) = \eta_i\)

The model is estimated via maximum likelihood, and inference relies on asymptotic normality of the MLE. Parameters are tested with Wald statistics (\(z = \hat\beta / \text{SE}\), asymptotically standard normal) or likelihood ratio tests (LRTs, asymptotically \(\chi^2\)).

Usual link

The links are the canonical ones, except the log for the Negative Binomial and Gamma families.

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
2. Gaussian GLM — Insurance Charges

2.1 Data and Rationale
Medical insurance charges are right-skewed and strictly positive. A log transformation induces approximate normality, making a Gaussian GLM with identity link on \(\log(\text{charges})\) appropriate. Alternatively, a Gamma GLM with log link directly models the original scale without requiring a transformation.


Code
p1 <- ggplot(df_insurance, aes(x=charges)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50, fill="#2166ac", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="Raw charges\n(right-skewed)", x="Charges (USD)")

p2 <- ggplot(df_insurance, aes(x=log_charges)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50, fill="#4dac26", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="Log-transformed charges\n(approx. normal)", x="log(Charges)")

plot_multiplot(p1, p2, cols=2)

We fit a full model with all main effects and the theoretically motivated smoker × bmi interaction (smoking amplifies the effect of obesity on health costs).

                    family=gaussian(link="identity"),
                    data=df_insurance)

m_gauss_main <- glm(log_charges ~ age + sex + bmi + children + smoker + region,
                    family=gaussian(link="identity"),

m_gauss_full <- glm(log_charges ~ age + sex + bmi + children + smoker + region +

text:
3. Binomial GLM — Graduate Admission

3.1 Data and Rationale
The df_admission dataset contains binary admission decisions (0/1) from a graduate programme alongside GRE score, GPA, and institutional rank. A binomial GLM with logit link — logistic regression — models the log-odds of admission as a linear function of the predictors.
\[\log\frac{P(\text{admit}=1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(\text{admit}=1|\mathbf{x})} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{gre} + \beta_2\,\text{gpa} + \beta_3\,\text{rank}\]

  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#2166ac","#d6604d"), labels=c("Rejected","Admitted")) +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="GRE by admission", fill=NULL)

  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#2166ac","#d6604d"), labels=c("Rejected","Admitted")) +
  theme_bw() + labs(title="GPA by admission", fill=NULL)

section: 4. Poisson and Negative Binomial GLM — Insurance Children
text:
4. Poisson and Negative Binomial GLM — Insurance Children

4.1 Rationale
The number of dependent children is a non-negative integer — a natural candidate for Poisson regression. A key assumption of the Poisson model is equidispersion (\(\text{Var}[Y] = \mu\)). When the variance exceeds the mean (overdispersion), the Negative Binomial GLM provides a robust alternative by introducing a dispersion parameter \(\alpha\) such that \(\text{Var}[Y] = \mu + \alpha\mu^2\).


4.2 Checking for Overdispersion


Code
cat("Mean of children:", round(mean(df_insurance$children), 4), "\n")


Mean of children: 1.0949 


Code
cat("Var  of children:", round(var(df_insurance$children),  4), "\n")


Var  of children: 1.4532 


Code

Dispersion ratio : 1.3272

  geom_bar(fill="#2166ac", colour="white") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title="Distribution of number of children", x="Children", y="Count")











4.3 Poisson Model

m_pois <- glm(children ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + region,
              family=poisson(link="log"),
              data=df_insurance)
summary(m_pois)

Rule of thumb for overdispersion: the ratio of the residual deviance to its degrees of freedom; values well above 1 suggest overdispersion.

4.4 Negative Binomial Model

               data=df_insurance)

Code
cat("\nEstimated dispersion parameter (theta):", round(m_nb$theta, 4), "\n")



Estimated dispersion parameter (theta): 2.5969 




4.5 Poisson vs. Negative Binomial — Likelihood Ratio Test
The Negative Binomial model has one more parameter than the Poisson model, \(\alpha\). With \(\alpha = 0\) it is the Poisson model (glm.nb() reports \(\theta = 1/\alpha\)), so the two are nested and a likelihood ratio test can compare them:
\[LR = 2\,(\ell_{\text{NB}} - \ell_{\text{Poisson}})\]
Because \(\alpha\) cannot be negative, the null hypothesis \(\alpha = 0\) lies at the edge of its range. If it is true, the statistic is 0 about half of the time and follows \(\chi^2_1\) otherwise, so the p value is half of the \(\chi^2_1\) tail area (Lawless, 1987).
anova(m_pois, m_nb, test="LRT") does not give this test. It subtracts the two residual deviances, which are measured from different saturated models, and it has 0 degrees of freedom because it does not count \(\alpha\).


Code
lr_nb <- as.numeric(2 * (logLik(m_nb) - logLik(m_pois)))
p_nb  <- pchisq(lr_nb, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE) / 2

cat("AIC Poisson        :", round(AIC(m_pois), 2), "\n")


AIC Poisson        : 3899.8 


Code
cat("AIC Negative Binom :", round(AIC(m_nb),   2), "\n")


AIC Negative Binom : 3834.56 


Code
cat("Log-likelihood Pois:", round(logLik(m_pois), 2), "\n")


Log-likelihood Pois: -1941.9 


Code
cat("Log-likelihood NB  :", round(logLik(m_nb),   2), "\n")


Log-likelihood NB  : -1908.28 


Code
cat("Likelihood ratio   :", round(lr_nb, 2), "\n")


Likelihood ratio   : 67.24 


Code
cat("p value            :", format.pval(p_nb, digits=3, eps=0.001), "\n")


p value            : <0.001 


The test rejects the Poisson model (LR = 67.24, p < .001) and the AIC of the Negative Binomial model is 65.24 lower, so the counts are overdispersed, as the ratio in section 4.3 suggested. The coefficients of the two models are nearly the same; it is the standard errors that change. They are about 19% larger in the Negative Binomial model, because the Poisson model assumes less variance than the data have.

text:
6. Model Comparison and Selection

6.1 Information Criteria
AIC penalises model complexity as \(-2\ell + 2k\); BIC uses \(-2\ell + k\ln n\) and imposes a heavier penalty for larger samples, favouring more parsimonious models. Here \(\ell\) is the log-likelihood and \(k\) the number of estimated parameters: the coefficients, plus the residual variance of a Gaussian model or \(\theta\) of a Negative Binomial model.


Code
models <- list(
  "Gaussian — main effects"    = m_gauss_main,
  "Gaussian — + smoker×bmi"    = m_gauss_full,
  "Logistic — admission"       = m_admit_main,
  "Poisson — children"         = m_pois,
  "Neg. Binom — children"      = m_nb,
  "Logistic — Titanic main"    = m_titanic_main,
  "Logistic — Titanic + int."  = m_titanic_int
)

aic_df <- data.frame(
  Model    = names(models),
  k        = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  LogLik   = sapply(models, function(m) round(as.numeric(logLik(m)), 2)),
  AIC      = sapply(models, function(m) round(AIC(m), 2)),
  BIC      = sapply(models, function(m) round(BIC(m), 2)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
